entries.title: 起初,神——你的身份从祂而来
entries.title_en: In the Beginning, God — Your Identity Comes From Him
entries.verse: 创世记一章廿六至廿七节，创世记二章七节
entries.content:
我们一生都在追问两个问题:「我是谁?我的价值从何而来?」而我们寻找答案的方向,几乎总是「向内、向下」——从自己的成就、外貌、才干、别人的评价里,去拼凑一个身份。可圣经的第一句话,却把我们的目光,从「人」猛然转向了「神」:「起初,神创造天地。」(创1:1)故事不是从「人」开始的,是从「神」开始的。在你存在以先,神已经在那里;在你做任何事以先,神已经先动了工。这意味着:你的身份,不是你从无到有挣出来的,而是先于你、从祂而来的。

创世记一章更把这身份的根基,钉得死死的:「神就照着自己的形象造人……」(创1:27)你被造,是照着神的形象——这是宇宙间赋予人价值最高、也最稳固的一句话。它意味着:你的尊贵,不建立在你「做到了什么」上,而刻在你「被造的那一刻」;不是你表现好了才配得,而是神造你时就已经给定了。世界的逻辑是「你要先成为某人,才有价值」;圣经的逻辑却完全相反:在你还一无所有、一无所成、甚至还未睁眼看世界之先,神已经按祂自己的形象,尊贵地造了你。这价值,是天生的,不是挣来的;是被赐的,不是被赚的。

而二章七节又加上一笔极深的真理:「耶和华神……将生气吹在他鼻孔里,他就成了有灵的活人。」(创2:7)人不只是被造,更是被神亲自「吹了一口气」才活的。这道出了人的本相:我们时时刻刻倚靠神而活,我们里面那颗心,本是为着与神相交而造的。所以奥古斯丁说,人心若不安息在神里面,就永不得安息——因为人离了神,就像鱼离了水,无论用多少成就、享乐、认可去填,那个「神形状的空」永远填不满。我们许多的焦虑、疲惫、患得患失,归根到底,都源于向错误的地方讨身份:向一份会失去的工作、一段会变的关系、一个会老去的外貌,去讨那唯有神才给得起的价值。

然而,人堕落之后,神的形象在我们里面被罪玷污、扭曲了;我们凭自己,再也活不出那受造的荣美。但福音的好消息是:神差来了祂的儿子——那位「是神本体的真像」(来1:3)的基督,来修复、更新我们里面破损的形象。凡在基督里的,神都预先定下叫他们「效法他儿子的模样」(罗8:29),把那失落的荣美,一点一点地恢复过来。所以你今天的身份,有了双重的确据:你是神起初按祂形象所造、又亲手赐下气息的人;更是神在基督里重新买赎、正在更新的儿女。今天,你若还在靠表现证明自己、向世界讨身份、为成败而患得患失,愿创世记这开卷第一课释放你:你的价值,从起初就已由神给定,又在基督里被重新印证——它不靠你今天的表现加一分、也不因你今天的失败减一分。

默想:我今天在靠什么来证明自己的价值——成就、外貌、才干、还是别人的认可?我许多的焦虑与患得患失,是否正源于向这些会失去的东西讨身份?若我的价值是神「从起初就给定、又在基督里印证」的,而非我所挣的,这会怎样改变我面对成败、面对别人眼光的态度?

应用:今天当你又想靠某样表现去赢得认可、或因某个失败而觉得自己「不够好」时,停下来,刻意向神(也向自己)宣告一次:我是神按祂形象所造、又在基督里所爱、所赎的人;我的价值不靠今天的表现加减。并在一件你惯常「靠它证明自己」的事上,操练放手,单单安息在这被赐的身份里。

祷告:创造我、又亲自吹气使我存活的主啊,谢谢你在我一无所有、一无所成之先,就按你的形象尊贵地造了我;更谢谢你差来基督,修复我里面被罪玷污的形象,叫我在祂里面重新被更新。我承认,我常向会失去的东西讨身份,为成败患得患失,活得又累又不安。求你叫我今天不再向世界讨我的价值,单单在你里面安息,以认识你、与你同行,为我最深、也夺不走的喜乐。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
We spend our whole lives asking two questions: Who am I? Where does my worth come from? And almost always, we search for the answer by looking “inward and downward” — piecing together an identity from our achievements, our looks, our abilities, other people’s opinions of us. But the very first sentence of Scripture wrenches our gaze away from “man” and turns it sharply toward “God”: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The story does not begin with “man” — it begins with “God.” Before you existed, God was already there; before you did anything at all, God had already been at work. This means your identity was never something you scraped together out of nothing — it precedes you, and comes from him.

Genesis 1 nails this foundation of identity down even more firmly: “So God created man in his own image...” (Genesis 1:27). You were made in the image of God — the single highest, most unshakeable statement of worth in the universe. It means your dignity is not built on what you have “accomplished,” but is stamped into “the moment you were made”; it is not that you become worthy once you perform well, but that God had already given it the moment he made you. The world’s logic says, “You must first become someone, in order to have worth.” Scripture’s logic runs the exact opposite way: while you had nothing, had accomplished nothing, before you had even opened your eyes on the world, God had already, in his own image, made you with dignity. This worth is inborn, not earned; it is given, not achieved.

And 2:7 adds a still deeper truth: “the LORD God... breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature” (Genesis 2:7). Man was not merely made — he became alive because God himself personally “breathed” into him. This tells us who we really are: we live moment by moment dependent on God, and the heart within us was made for fellowship with him. This is why Augustine said the human heart is restless until it rests in God — for apart from God, we are like a fish out of water; no amount of achievement, pleasure, or approval can ever fill that “God-shaped void.” So much of our anxiety, our exhaustion, our constant grasping and fearing loss, ultimately comes from seeking identity in the wrong place — from a job that can be lost, a relationship that can change, a face that will age — trying to extract from them the worth only God can give.

Yet after the fall, God’s image in us was stained and twisted by sin; on our own, we can no longer live out that created beauty. But the good news of the gospel is this: God sent his Son — Christ, who “is the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3) — to repair and renew the broken image within us. All who are in Christ, God has predestined to be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29), restoring, bit by bit, that lost beauty. So your identity today rests on a double assurance: you are the one God made in the beginning in his own image and breathed life into with his own hand; you are also the child God is redeeming and renewing in Christ. If today you are still trying to prove yourself through performance, still begging the world for an identity, still living at the mercy of every success and failure — may this opening lesson of Genesis set you free: your worth was fixed by God from the very beginning, and reaffirmed in Christ — it is not increased by today’s performance, nor diminished by today’s failure.

Meditation: What am I relying on today to prove my worth — achievement, appearance, ability, or others’ approval? Does much of my anxiety and constant worry over gain and loss come from seeking identity in these things that can be lost? If my worth was fixed by God from the beginning, and reaffirmed in Christ, rather than something I earned, how would this change the way I face success and failure, the way I face others’ opinions?

Application: Today, when you again feel the pull to win approval through some performance, or to feel “not good enough” because of some failure, stop, and deliberately declare — to God, and to yourself: I am one God made in his own image, one Christ loves and has redeemed; my worth does not rise or fall with today’s performance. And in one area where you habitually “prove yourself” through something, practice letting go, resting simply in this given identity.

Prayer: Lord who created me and breathed into me to give me life, thank you that before I had anything, before I had accomplished anything, you made me with dignity in your own image; thank you even more for sending Christ to repair the image within me stained by sin, renewing me anew in him. I confess that I often seek identity from things that can be lost, living anxious and unsettled over success and failure. Grant that today I would no longer beg the world for my worth, but rest simply in you, finding in knowing you and walking with you my deepest, unshakeable joy. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 罪的工价乃是死
entries.title_en: The Wages of Sin Is Death
entries.verse: 罗马书六章廿三节
entries.content:
神把人安置在伊甸园中,那里没有匮乏,只有一条界线:「分别善恶树上的果子,你不可吃,因为你吃的日子必定死!」(创2:17)这界线本身就是恩典——神清楚地划出了生命与死亡的分野,并预先警告了后果。撒但却使出牠惯用的诡计,不是叫夏娃恨恶神,而是叫她怀疑神:「神岂是真说……?」牠把夏娃的注意力,从满园可吃的树,拉向那唯一不可吃的一棵;从神的丰盛供应,拉向神的「限制」。夏娃看那棵树「悦人的眼目」,便信了那更悦耳的谎言:神在留一手,神不是真心待你好。这正是罪的起源:不是先有行动,而是先有一颗不信神、怀疑神良善的心。

后果立刻临到,而且远超乎他们所料。羞耻进了门,他们缝无花果树的叶子遮身;推诿也进了门,亚当怪夏娃、又怪神「你所赐给我、与我同居的女人」;而创世记五章那反复出现的短语「就死了」,像丧钟一样,一次又一次地敲响,记录着从亚当到挪亚的每一代人,无一幸免。保罗把这血淋淋的历史,浓缩成一句冷峻的宣告:「因为罪的工价乃是死。」(罗6:23)「工价」二字选得极精准——这不是运气不好、不是随机的惩罚,而是理所应当赚得的报酬,是罪按其本相所结出的果子。死,不只是心跳停止;它首先是与生命源头的隔绝——正如枝子一旦离了树,纵然还挂在枝头几日,终必枯干。人以为跨过神的界线能得着自主与丰富,得着的,却是与神隔绝的死亡。

我们很容易把这段历史当作古老的故事,却忘了自己天天在重演夏娃的诡计。我们也常常只盯着那「唯一不可以」的一样,却对神所赐的一切丰盛视而不见;我们也常常先怀疑神的良善,才敢跨出悖逆的一步——仿佛神若真爱我,怎会不许我要这个、做那个。而当罪成了,我们也和亚当一样,惯于推诿:是环境逼的,是别人的错,甚至暗中怪神把我造成这样。圣经从不许我们把罪轻描淡写成「小小的失误」;它是背叛,后果是死,而且没有人能自己修补这断裂。

然而,就在审判宣告的同一章,恩典的曙光已经闪现:「耶和华神为亚当和他妻子用皮子做衣服给他们穿。」(创3:21)那遮盖羞耻的皮子,必先有牲畜流血、舍命——这是全本圣经第一次,用死亡遮盖了赤露。它预表着那将要来的、真正的遮盖:基督流出的血。这正是罗马书六章廿三节下半句要宣告的好消息:「惟有神的恩赐,在我们的主基督耶稣里,乃是永生。」请留意「工价」与「恩赐」的对比——工价是你该得的,恩赐是你不配得、却白白领受的。罪的工价是死,你我人人都该受;神的恩赐却是永生,藉着基督已经预备好了。这两条路,今天仍摆在每一个人面前,而神已经在基督里,为凡肯来的人,预备了那件用血换来的遮盖。

默想:我是否把某些罪当作「无伤大雅」的小事,忘了圣经说罪的工价是死?我今天在哪一件事上,像夏娃一样只盯着「神不许我要的」,而对神所赐的丰盛视而不见——是不是也在心里悄悄怀疑,神不许,是因为祂在留一手?

应用:今天诚实指认一个你一直轻看、甚至为自己找借口的罪;不要再推诿给环境或别人,照实认它是背叛,又靠着基督向它说不,转而支取神那用血换来的、白白的恩赐。

祷告:圣洁又满有恩典的主,你划下界线本是恩典,我却常像夏娃一样怀疑你的良善,越过界线又推诿己过。我承认罪的工价是死,我无法自己修补这断裂。谢谢你早在伊甸园就预备了流血的遮盖,又在基督里把永生白白赐给我。求你叫我不再轻看罪,天天支取你在基督里所赐的生命。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God placed man in the garden of Eden, a place with no lack, only one boundary: “of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17). That boundary was itself grace — God clearly marked the line between life and death, and warned of the consequence in advance. Satan, however, used his signature trick — not making Eve hate God, but making her doubt God: “Did God actually say...?” He pulled Eve’s attention away from every tree in the garden she could eat from, toward the one she could not; away from God’s abundant provision, toward God’s “restriction.” Eve saw that the tree was “a delight to the eyes,” and so believed the more pleasant-sounding lie: that God was holding out on her, that God did not truly wish her well. This is precisely the origin of sin: not an action first, but first a heart that does not trust God, that doubts his goodness.

The consequences came at once, and far exceeded what they expected. Shame entered, and they sewed fig leaves to cover themselves; blame-shifting entered too, as Adam blamed Eve, and even blamed God — “the woman whom you gave to be with me.” And the phrase that recurs throughout Genesis 5, “and he died,” tolls again and again like a funeral bell, recording how every generation from Adam to Noah, without exception, met the same end. Paul condensed this bloody history into one stark declaration: “For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). The word “wages” is chosen with precision — this is not bad luck, not a random punishment, but the payment rightly earned, the fruit sin bears according to its own nature. Death is not merely the heart stopping; it is, first of all, separation from the source of life — just as a branch, once cut off from the tree, may hang there a few days looking green, but will inevitably wither. Man thought that crossing God’s boundary would bring autonomy and abundance; what he got instead was death — separation from God.

It’s easy to treat this passage as ancient history and forget that we replay Eve’s very trick every day. We too often fixate on the one thing we “can’t have,” blind to the abundance God has already given us; we too often doubt God’s goodness first, before we dare take that step of rebellion — as if, if God truly loved me, how could he refuse me this or that? And when sin is done, we, like Adam, are quick to shift the blame: it was circumstances, it was someone else’s fault, or we secretly blame God for making us this way. Scripture never lets us dismiss sin as a “small mistake”; it is rebellion, its consequence is death, and no one can mend that fracture on their own.

Yet in that very same chapter where judgment is pronounced, a glimmer of grace already flashes: “the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21). That skin covering their shame required first that an animal bleed and die — this is the first time in all of Scripture that death is used to cover nakedness. It foreshadows the true covering yet to come: the blood Christ would shed. This is exactly the good news the second half of Romans 6:23 declares: “but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Notice the contrast between “wages” and “gift” — wages are what you deserve; a gift is what you don’t deserve, yet freely receive. The wages of sin is death, which every one of us deserves; but God’s gift is eternal life, already prepared through Christ. These two roads still stand before every person today, and God, in Christ, has already prepared, for all who are willing to come, that covering purchased with blood.

Meditation: Am I treating certain sins as “harmless” small matters, forgetting that Scripture says the wages of sin is death? In what today am I, like Eve, fixated only on “what God won’t let me have,” blind to the abundance God has given — and quietly doubting, in my heart, that God’s refusal means he’s holding out on me?

Application: Today, honestly name one sin you’ve been treating lightly, or even making excuses for; stop shifting the blame to circumstances or others, own it honestly as rebellion, and by relying on Christ, say no to it, turning instead to draw on God’s free gift purchased with blood.

Prayer: Holy and gracious Lord, the boundaries you set were grace itself, yet I so often, like Eve, doubt your goodness, cross the line, and then shift the blame. I confess the wages of sin is death, and I cannot mend this fracture myself. Thank you that as early as Eden you had already prepared a bloody covering, and in Christ have freely given me eternal life. Let me no longer treat sin lightly, and daily draw on the life you have given me in Christ. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 洪水中的方舟:审判里的拯救
entries.title_en: The Ark in the Flood: Salvation Within Judgment
entries.verse: 彼得前书三章十九至二十节
entries.content:
创世记六章描绘了一幅令人窒息的画面:「耶和华见人在地上罪恶很大,终日所思想的尽都是恶」(创6:5)——不是偶尔失手,而是整个心思意念,日日夜夜,都朝着恶而去。神的回应不是冷眼旁观,而是「心中忧伤」(创6:6):圣洁的神,面对祂亲手所造、所深爱的人类彻底的败坏,心如刀割。这提醒我们,罪从来不是无关痛痒的小事——它伤透了神的心;而神的审判,也从来不是任性的发怒,乃是圣洁对罪恶必然、也必须的回应。

但审判之前,神先给了漫长的忍耐。彼得说,那是「神容忍等待的时候」(彼前3:20)——挪亚造方舟历时上百年,神一次次给那悖逆的世代留出悔改的空间;彼得后书更称挪亚为「传义道」的人(彼后2:5),一边造船,一边劝人悔改,只是无人肯听。神迟迟不降罚,不是因为祂看轻罪,而是「不愿有一人沉沦」(彼后3:9)。方舟本身,正是神预备的一条出路:凡进入其中的,不是靠自己游得够远、爬得够高逃过审判,而是单单因为「在」方舟里面,就与审判无关。

今天的世界厌恶「审判」二字,我们的心也常暗暗盼望有一位只谈慈爱、不谈公义的神——仿佛神的爱能大到把罪一笔勾销,无需付上任何代价。但挪亚的洪水提醒我们:这样的神从不存在。更隐蔽的,是另一种自欺——以为「我若活在挪亚的日子,必定配得上船」,把得救想成自己配得的奖赏,而不是白白临到的恩典。两种心态,都是要绕过神在方舟里所定的那唯一进路。

彼得清楚地把方舟指向了基督:「这水所表明的洗礼,现在藉着耶稣基督复活也拯救你们」(彼前3:21)。挪亚一家不是靠自己的义存活,而是单单因为在神所预备的方舟里面;我们也不是靠自己配得救恩,而是单单因为「在基督里」——祂亲自担当了那本该临到我们的审判,又从死里复活,成了我们唯一的避难所。今天,你若还未进入这方舟,神的门此刻仍然敞开;你若已经在基督里,当效法那「传义道」的挪亚,把这唯一的出路,指给还站在门外的人。

默想:我心里是否也曾偷偷盼望一位只谈慈爱、不谈审判的神?我对「靠恩典白白得救」这件事,是全心信靠,还是仍暗暗觉得自己配得上船?

应用:今天为一位仍站在「方舟之外」的亲友迫切祷告,并求神给你一次机会,像挪亚一样,把基督这唯一的避难所指给他。

祷告:主啊,你是圣洁的神,罪叫你的心忧伤,也必召来公义的审判;你又是何等忍耐的神,迟迟不降罚,只愿人人悔改。谢谢你为我预备了基督这方舟,叫我不是靠自己配得,而是单单因为在祂里面,就脱离了那将来的忿怒。求你叫我今天不再自欺、不再自恃,单单安稳藏身在基督里,也忠心把这救恩传给还在门外的人。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Genesis 6 paints a suffocating picture: “The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5) — not an occasional slip, but the entire bent of mind and thought, day and night, turned toward evil. God’s response was not cold indifference, but “grieved him to his heart” (Genesis 6:6): the holy God, facing the utter corruption of the humanity he had made with his own hands and deeply loved, was cut to the heart. This reminds us that sin has never been a trivial matter — it wounds God’s own heart; and God’s judgment has never been an arbitrary outburst of rage, but the necessary, inevitable response of holiness to evil.

But before judgment, God first gave a long patience. Peter says it was “when God’s patience waited” (1 Peter 3:20) — building the ark took Noah over a hundred years, during which God repeatedly gave that rebellious generation room to repent; 2 Peter even calls Noah “a herald of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5), building the boat while urging people to repent, though no one would listen. God’s delay in bringing judgment was not because he made light of sin, but because he was “not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). The ark itself was the way of escape God had prepared: those who entered it were saved not by swimming far enough or climbing high enough on their own to escape judgment, but simply because they were “in” the ark, and so had nothing to do with the judgment.

Today’s world hates the word “judgment,” and our own hearts often secretly hope for a God who speaks only of love, never of justice — as if God’s love could be so great it simply erases sin, requiring no cost at all. But Noah’s flood reminds us: no such God exists. An even more hidden form of self-deception is another kind: thinking, “If I had lived in Noah’s day, I surely would have deserved a place on the ark” — treating salvation as a reward one deserves, rather than grace that comes freely. Both mindsets try to bypass the one entrance God set within the ark.

Peter makes clear that the ark points to Christ: “Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you... through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:21). Noah’s family did not survive because of their own righteousness, but simply because they were in the ark God had prepared; we too are not saved because we deserve it, but simply because we are “in Christ” — he himself bore the judgment that should have fallen on us, and rose from the dead, becoming our only refuge. If you have not yet entered this ark, God’s door is still open right now; if you are already in Christ, imitate Noah, that “herald of righteousness,” and point out this one way of escape to those still standing outside the door.

Meditation: Have I too, secretly, sometimes hoped for a God who speaks only of love, never of judgment? When it comes to being saved freely by grace, do I trust with my whole heart, or do I still secretly feel I deserve a place on the ark?

Application: Today, pray earnestly for a friend or family member still standing “outside the ark,” and ask God for an opportunity, like Noah, to point them to Christ, the one true refuge.

Prayer: Lord, you are the holy God, whom sin grieves and whose justice must surely bring judgment; you are also the God of great patience, delaying judgment, wishing only that all would repent. Thank you for preparing Christ as my ark, so that I am saved not because I deserve it, but simply because I am in him, delivered from the wrath to come. Let me no longer deceive or rely on myself today, but rest securely hidden in Christ, and faithfully pass on this salvation to those still outside the door. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 巴别塔:为要传扬自己的名
entries.title_en: The Tower of Babel: To Make a Name for Ourselves
entries.verse: 以弗所书四章一至三节
entries.content:
洪水审判之后,人类再一次快速地走上悖逆的老路——创世记十至十一章记载了列国的谱系,和示拿平原上那场著名的建塔运动。人聚集说:「来吧!我们要建造一座城和一座塔,塔顶通天,为要传扬我们的名,免得我们分散在全地上」(创11:4)。这话背后有极深的恐惧,也有极深的骄傲:害怕分散、害怕失去掌控,于是想靠自己的双手,筑起一座通天的纪念碑,证明「我们」了不起,不需要神。

神的回应发人深省:「他们成为一样的人民,都是一样的言语,如今既做起这事来,以后他们所要做的事就没有不成就的了」(创11:6)。这不是神嫉妒人的成就,而是神深知:若容让骄傲无限扩张、不受拦阻,人只会用同一股力量,把自己带向更深的悖逆与毁灭。于是神变乱他们的口音,「使众人分散在全地上」(创11:9)——这审判,骨子里仍是怜悯:祂宁可拦阻人,也不愿看着人在悖逆中一路狂奔到底。

巴别塔是每个人心里那股冲动的缩影:靠自己的表现、成就、声望,建立一个够高、够稳的「自我」,好证明我值得、我安全、我不需要倚靠谁。我们建的塔,也许是事业的高度、朋友圈里的形象、银行户头的数字——都想通天,都想为自己立名。这与保罗的劝勉恰恰相反:「凡事谦虚、温柔、忍耐,用爱心互相宽容」(弗4:2)。真正持久的合一与安稳,从来不是靠自我扩张挣来的,恰恰是巴别塔想避开、却又必然带来的骄傲与分散的反面。

值得留意的是,神后来并没有让「分散的列国」永远失丧——五旬节那日,圣灵降临,使从各国而来、说着不同语言的人,都「按着圣灵所赐的口才说起别国的话来」(徒2:4)。巴别叫人因骄傲而言语变乱、彼此隔绝;五旬节却叫人因基督而言语得通、心灵合一——不是靠人再一次同心合意地为自己立名,而是靠圣灵,叫万族因基督的名,重新联合成一个身体。今天,你在为谁立名、求谁的安稳?愿你放下自己的塔,进入那唯一叫分散之人重新合一的名——耶稣基督的名。

默想:我正在建造的「巴别塔」是什么——哪一样成就、形象或存款数字,是我靠它来立自己的名、求自己安稳?

应用:今天在一件事上,刻意不为「传扬自己的名」,而是把荣耀归给神,并以谦卑与人联络,操练弗4:2-3所说的合一。

祷告:主啊,赦免我像巴别塔的人一样,总想靠自己的成就为自己立名、求自己的安稳。感谢你在基督里、藉着圣灵,叫说不同语言、来自不同地方的人重新合一。求你拆毁我心中骄傲的塔,叫我不再为自己扬名,而是谦卑荣耀你,在基督的名下与人真实联络。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
After the judgment of the flood, humanity once again quickly walked the old road of rebellion — Genesis 10–11 records the genealogies of the nations, and the famous tower-building movement on the plain of Shinar. The people gathered and said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth” (Genesis 11:4). Behind these words lies both deep fear and deep pride: afraid of being scattered, afraid of losing control, they sought to build, with their own hands, a monument reaching to heaven, to prove that “we” are great, that we need no God.

God’s response is deeply instructive: “And this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them” (Genesis 11:6). This is not God being jealous of human achievement, but God knowing full well: if pride is allowed to expand without limit, unchecked, humanity would only use that same power to drive itself into deeper rebellion and destruction. So God confused their language, and “dispersed them over the face of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9) — this judgment, at its core, was still mercy: God would rather stop people than watch them run headlong to the very end of their rebellion.

The Tower of Babel is a miniature of the impulse in every human heart: to build, through our own performance, achievement, and reputation, a “self” tall enough and stable enough to prove that we are worthy, that we are safe, that we need no one. The towers we build may be the height of our careers, our image among friends, the numbers in our bank accounts — all wanting to reach heaven, all wanting to make a name for ourselves. This runs directly opposite to Paul’s exhortation: “with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2). True, lasting unity and security have never been won through self-expansion — they are precisely the opposite of the pride and scattering Babel tried to avoid, yet inevitably brought about.

It’s worth noting that God did not, in the end, leave the “scattered nations” lost forever — on the day of Pentecost, the Spirit descended, and people who had come from every nation, speaking different languages, all began “to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4). Babel caused people, through pride, to have their speech confused and become estranged from one another; Pentecost caused people, through Christ, to be able to communicate and become united in spirit — not by people once again uniting to make a name for themselves, but by the Spirit, uniting all nations, through Christ’s name, back into one body. Today, whose name are you building, whose security are you seeking? May you lay down your own tower, and enter into the one name that alone reunites the scattered — the name of Jesus Christ.

Meditation: What “Tower of Babel” am I building — which achievement, image, or bank balance am I using to make a name for myself, to seek my own security?

Application: Today, in one matter, deliberately choose not to “make a name for yourself,” but give the glory to God, and practice the unity spoken of in Ephesians 4:2–3 by relating to others in humility.

Prayer: Lord, forgive me for being like the people of Babel, always wanting to make a name for myself and secure my own safety through my own achievements. Thank you that in Christ, through the Spirit, you have reunited people who speak different languages and come from different places. Tear down the proud tower in my heart; let me no longer seek fame for myself, but humbly glorify you, genuinely connecting with others under the name of Christ. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 亚伯兰蒙召:凭信心离开
entries.title_en: Abram's Calling: Leaving by Faith
entries.verse: 创世记十二章一节
entries.content:
创世记的镜头,从「列国的谱系」转向了「一个人」——亚伯兰。神的呼召极其干脆:「你要离开本地、本族、父家,往我所要指示你的地去」(创12:1)。神没有先给地图,没有先说明目的地,只说「往我所要指示你的地去」。这呼召的核心,不是一个计划,而是一个位格——神要亚伯兰凭的,不是清楚的蓝图,而是对神本身的信任。

「亚伯兰就照着耶和华的吩咐去了」(创12:4)——这句话轻描淡写,分量却极重。他放下了熟悉的一切:家乡、亲族、安全感,踏进一片陌生之地,只因神说了话。希伯来书后来这样总结他:「因着信,蒙召的时候就遵命出去……出去的时候,还不知往哪里去」(来11:8)。信心从来不是坐在原地,等一切都看清楚了才动身,而是在只看得见神、看不清前路时,仍然迈步跟随。真正跟随神,往往要先松开手里紧抓的安稳。

我们常想要神的应许——祂应许赐福亚伯兰、使他成为大国、叫地上的万族因他得福(创12:2-3)——却不想付跟随的代价:离开、放下、走进未知。我们心里那股「先给我看清楚全程,我才肯动」的念头,其实是不信的另一个名字:我们不是不信神能带领,而是不信祂靠得住,配得我们把手中的安稳交出去。今天,神也许没有叫你搬到远方,却在某件事上呼召你「离开」——离开一个舒适区、一份倚赖、一个不肯放手的计划。

亚伯兰的信心之所以宝贵,不在于他有多完美(他后来两次谎称撒莱是妹子,信心也有起伏),而在于他所信靠的那位是信实的。保罗后来指出,神应许亚伯拉罕的「那一个子孙」,原来「就是基督」(加3:16)——亚伯兰这一步离开,最终开出的道路,通向了那位真正的「后裔」耶稣基督,叫万族因祂真正得福。今天,我们蒙召跟随基督,走的正是同一条信心之路:不是先看清全程才起步,而是因认识、信靠那呼召我们的主,就照着去了。

默想:神在哪一件事上呼召我「离开」熟悉、走进未知?我是紧抓着安稳不放,还是愿意像亚伯兰一样,凭信心迈步跟随?

应用:找出一样你一直紧抓、拦阻你完全跟随神的「本地本族父家」,今天在祷告中松开手,向神的呼召迈出具体的一步。

祷告:主啊,你呼召亚伯兰离开一切、走进未知,他就照着去了;你又藉着他,带来了那位真正叫万族得福的后裔——基督。求你给我这样的信心:不是等看清全程才动,而是在只看见你的时候仍然跟随。帮助我松开紧抓的安稳,顺服你今天对我的呼召。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Genesis’s camera shifts from “the genealogy of nations” to “one man” — Abram. God’s call is remarkably direct: “Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12:1). God did not first give a map, did not first name the destination, only said, “to the land that I will show you.” The heart of this call is not a plan, but a person — what Abram was asked to rely on was not a clear blueprint, but trust in God himself.

“So Abram went, as the LORD had told him” (Genesis 12:4) — this sentence sounds understated, yet carries enormous weight. He laid down everything familiar: home, kin, security, and stepped into unfamiliar territory, simply because God had spoken. Hebrews later summarizes him this way: “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). Faith has never been sitting still, waiting until everything is clear before setting out — it is taking a step forward while seeing only God, not the road ahead. Truly following God often requires first letting go of the security you’re clutching in your hands.

We often want God’s promises — he promised to bless Abram, to make him a great nation, that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:2–3) — yet we don’t want to pay the cost of following: leaving, letting go, walking into the unknown. That voice in our hearts saying, “Let me see the whole path first, and then I’ll move,” is actually another name for unbelief: it’s not that we don’t believe God can lead, but that we don’t believe he’s trustworthy enough to deserve handing over the security in our hands. Today, God may not be calling you to move far away, but he may be calling you to “leave” something — a comfort zone, a dependency, a plan you refuse to let go of.

Abram’s faith is precious not because he was so perfect (he later lied twice, claiming Sarai was his sister; his faith had its ups and downs too), but because the one he trusted was faithful. Paul later points out that the “offspring” God promised to Abraham was, in fact, “Christ” (Galatians 3:16) — this step Abram took in leaving ultimately opened a road leading to that true “offspring,” Jesus Christ, so that all nations would truly be blessed through him. Today, we are called to follow Christ, walking that very same road of faith: not stepping out only after seeing the whole path clearly, but going, simply because we know and trust the Lord who calls us.

Meditation: In what area is God calling me to “leave” the familiar and step into the unknown? Am I clinging tightly to security, or willing, like Abram, to step forward in faith?

Application: Identify the one “country, kindred, father’s house” you’ve been clutching, the thing that’s keeping you from fully following God, and today, in prayer, let go of it and take a concrete step toward God’s call.

Prayer: Lord, you called Abram to leave everything and step into the unknown, and he went; you also, through him, brought forth the true offspring who blesses all nations — Christ. Give me this kind of faith: not waiting to see the whole path before moving, but still following even when I can only see you. Help me let go of the security I’m clutching, and obey your call to me today. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 亚伯兰信神,就算为义
entries.title_en: Abram Believed God, and It Was Counted to Him as Righteousness
entries.verse: 创世记十五章六节，十七章一节
entries.content:
神应许亚伯兰的后裔要多如天上的星,但年岁流逝,他仍无子,应许仿佛遥遥无期,人的血气也渐渐消磨。神再次把他领到帐棚外,指着满天星宿说:「你的后裔将要如此」(创15:5)。这不是空泛的鼓励,而是神主动地、一次又一次地,把祂的应许重新摆在亚伯兰眼前——因为神知道,信心最容易在漫长的等候中枯干。

「亚伯兰信耶和华,耶和华就以此为他的义」(创15:6)。这一节经文,后来被保罗两次直接引用(罗4:3;加3:6),成为「因信称义」这一福音真理最早的旧约根基。保罗引用这节经文时说:「亚伯拉罕信神,这就算为他的义」(罗4:3)。请留意:亚伯兰被算为义,不是因为他做成了什么伟大的事,也不是因为他先攒够了功德,而单单是因为他「信」——信靠那位说话算话的神。称义,从亚伯兰的时代起,就一直是本乎信、凭恩典,而非靠行为、靠血气挣得的。

这也解释了神在十七章向他显现时,为何吩咐:「你当在我面前作完全人」(创17:1)——真正的敬虔,是从对神的信靠里长出来的果子,不是靠自己的努力堆砌起来、想拿去换取神接纳的筹码。然而亚伯兰的信心并非毫无起伏:因等得不耐烦,他听了撒莱的话,与使女夏甲同房,想靠自己的方法「帮神成就应许」,结果带来了长远的纷争(创十六章)。这提醒我们:与神同行是一回事;跑在神前面、靠血气去成全神的应许,又是另一回事——我们许多的挣扎与焦躁,往往不是不信神会成就,而是不信神的时候。

亚伯兰所信的这位神,最终差来了那使「因信称义」全然成就的基督。保罗说,这称义的应许「不是单为他写的,也是为我们将来得算为义之人写的,就是我们这信神使我们的主耶稣从死里复活的人」(罗4:23-24);雅各也说,亚伯拉罕因这信「又得称为神的朋友」(雅2:23)。今天,我们蒙接纳,与亚伯兰同一个根基:不是靠我们做得多好,而是单单因信靠那位为我们死而复活的基督,就被神算为义。你今天是活在这称义的确据里,还是仍不自觉地想用表现,去换取神的接纳?

默想:我在神面前被接纳,是靠「信靠祂」,还是仍暗暗靠「自己做得够好」?我有没有像亚伯兰一样,因等不及而靠血气「帮神成就」?

应用:在一件你一直想靠自己的方法强求的事上,今天选择停下抢跑,凭信心把它交托给神,等候祂的时候。

祷告:主啊,谢谢你,亚伯兰因信你就被算为义;我的称义也照样本乎信、凭你的恩典,不靠我的行为。赦免我常因等不及而靠血气抢跑,或暗暗想用表现换取你的接纳。求你坚固我的信心,叫我凭信等候你的应许,与你同行,不跑在你前面。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God promised Abram that his offspring would be as numerous as the stars in the sky, but the years passed, and he still had no son; the promise seemed ever more distant, and his flesh grew weary. God once again led him outside his tent, and pointing to the sky full of stars, said, “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). This was no vague encouragement, but God actively, again and again, setting his promise back before Abram’s eyes — because God knew that faith is most easily worn thin during a long wait.

“And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). This verse would later be quoted directly by Paul, twice (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6), becoming the earliest Old Testament foundation for the gospel truth of “justification by faith.” When Paul quotes this verse he says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3). Notice: Abram was counted righteous not because he accomplished some great deed, nor because he had first stored up enough merit, but simply because he “believed” — trusted the God who keeps his word. Justification, from Abram’s time onward, has always been by faith, by grace, never earned by works or by human effort.

This also explains why, when God appeared to him again in chapter 17, he commanded, “walk before me, and be blameless” (Genesis 17:1) — true godliness is a fruit that grows out of trust in God, not something built up through our own effort, a chip to be cashed in for God’s acceptance. Yet Abram’s faith was not without its ups and downs: growing impatient with the wait, he listened to Sarai and slept with the servant Hagar, trying, by his own method, to “help God fulfill the promise,” which brought long-lasting strife (chapter 16). This reminds us: walking with God is one thing; running ahead of God, trying to fulfill his promise by our own strength, is another — much of our struggle and restlessness is often not disbelief that God will fulfill his word, but disbelief in God’s timing.

The God Abram believed in ultimately sent the Christ who would fully accomplish “justification by faith.” Paul says this promise of justification “was not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord” (Romans 4:23–24); James also says that through this faith Abraham “was called a friend of God” (James 2:23). Today, we are accepted on the very same foundation as Abram: not by how well we perform, but simply by trusting in the Christ who died and rose for us, and so being counted righteous by God. Are you today living in the assurance of this justification, or still unconsciously trying to trade performance for God’s acceptance?

Meditation: Am I accepted before God by “trusting him,” or am I still secretly relying on “doing well enough”? Have I, like Abram, tried to “help God fulfill his promise” through my own effort because I couldn’t wait?

Application: In one matter where you’ve been trying to force things through your own methods, today choose to stop running ahead, and by faith entrust it to God, waiting for his timing.

Prayer: Lord, thank you that Abram was counted righteous because he believed you; my justification is likewise by faith, by your grace, not by my works. Forgive me for often running ahead through my own effort because I can’t wait, or secretly trying to trade performance for your acceptance. Strengthen my faith, that I may wait for your promises in faith, walk with you, and not run ahead of you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 安息与更新
entries.title_en: Rest and Renewal
entries.content:
安息与更新

「你们得救在乎归回安息;你们得力在乎平静安稳。」(以赛亚书 30:15)

倪柝声提醒我们:真正的安息,不是停止做工,而是停止倚靠自己。神在造物的第七日歇了工,也邀请我们进入祂的安息——把重担卸给那位已为我们成就一切的主。

今天,让身体歇下,更让里面那颗紧绷、想掌控一切的心歇下。安静在主面前,不必挣扎、不必表现,单单让祂的爱重新更新你。

"In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and trust shall be your strength." (Isaiah 30:15) True rest is ceasing to rely on yourself.
entries.content_en:
Rest and Renewal

“In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and trust shall be your strength.” (Isaiah 30:15)

Watchman Nee reminds us: true rest is not ceasing from work, but ceasing to rely on yourself. God rested from his work on the seventh day of creation, and invites us to enter his rest as well — laying down our burdens before the Lord who has already accomplished everything for us.

Today, let your body rest, and even more, let that tense, controlling heart within you rest. Be still before the Lord; there is no need to strive, no need to perform — simply let his love renew you afresh.

"In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and trust shall be your strength." (Isaiah 30:15) True rest is ceasing to rely on yourself.

entries.title: 审判所多玛的神,也是垂听代求的神
entries.title_en: The God Who Judged Sodom Is Also the God Who Hears Intercession
entries.verse: 希伯来书十二章五至六节
entries.content:
所多玛、蛾摩拉罪恶滔天,神定意施行审判。这段经文毫不含糊地宣告:神是圣洁公义的,祂绝不纵容罪恶,罪的泛滥终必招来公义的报应。今天的世界厌恶「审判」二字,常把神简化成一位只谈接纳、从不动怒的神;但创世记十九章提醒我们,神对罪的忿怒是真实的,是祂圣洁本性必然的流露,不是情绪化的失控。

然而同样真实的,是神竟愿意让人参与在祂的心意里。审判之前,神先把祂要做的事告诉了亚伯拉罕(创18:17);亚伯拉罕便近前恳切代求:「无论善恶,你都要剿灭吗?」(创18:23)又说:「将义人与恶人同杀,将义人与恶人一样看待,这断不是你所行的。审判全地的主岂不行公义吗?」(创18:25)他一路从五十个义人求到十个,神也一次次应允:「为这十个的缘故,我也不毁灭那城」(创18:32)。公义与怜悯,在神身上并行不悖——祂必按公义审判罪,也乐意因代求施怜悯;后来平原诸城倾覆之时,「他记念亚伯拉罕……就打发罗得从倾覆之中出来」(创19:29),正是这怜悯的具体成就。

希伯来书提醒我们,神待儿女也有管教:「主所爱的,他必管教」(来12:6)。神对不悔改之罪的审判,与神对儿女的管教,性质并不相同——前者是公义对罪应得的报应,后者是父家造就儿女的爱;但两者都表明,神绝不肯对罪视若无睹,总是严肃看待,也总是先给恩慈与代求留出空间。我们心里若只想要一位纵容一切、从不审判也不管教的神,其实是在拒绝真爱;真爱必包含对罪的严肃。

亚伯拉罕的代求,只能求到十个人的地步就再没有下文——他毕竟是有限的人。但希伯来书告诉我们,有一位远比亚伯拉罕更完全的中保:「凡靠着他进到神面前的人,他都能拯救到底;因为他是长远活着,替他们祈求」(来7:25)。基督的代求,不会像亚伯拉罕那样半路停下,祂长远活着,一直为属祂的人祈求——所以「那些在基督耶稣里的,就不定罪了」(罗8:1)。今天,我们既当敬畏这位不以罪为无罪的神,也当效法亚伯拉罕,为身处「所多玛」中的人恳切代求,因为审判的神,也是垂听祷告、差来那位长远代求之基督的神。

默想:我是否只想要「慈爱纵容」的神,却回避那位「审判罪」的神?我有没有像亚伯拉罕一样,为身边活在罪中、面临审判的人恳切代求?

应用:今天为一个你所在乎、却活在明显悖逆中的人,像亚伯拉罕一样,恳切地为他向神代求,并感谢基督正在天上长远为你我祈求。

祷告:主啊,你是圣洁公义、不以罪为无罪的神,也是垂听代求、极愿施怜悯的神。感谢你差来基督,作那位长远活着、为我们祈求的中保,使我们在祂里面不再定罪。求你叫我既敬畏你的审判,又存怜悯的心,为身边活在罪中的人恳切代求,像亚伯拉罕一样站在你面前。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Sodom and Gomorrah’s sin had reached its full measure, and God resolved to bring judgment. This passage declares, without hedging, that God is holy and just, that he never tolerates sin, and that sin left unchecked will inevitably bring just retribution. Today’s world despises the word “judgment,” often reducing God to one who speaks only of acceptance, never of anger; but Genesis 19 reminds us that God’s wrath against sin is real, the necessary overflow of his holy nature, not an emotional loss of control.

Yet equally real is that God was willing to let a human being participate in his purposes. Before judgment, God first told Abraham what he was about to do (Genesis 18:17); Abraham drew near and interceded earnestly: “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?” (Genesis 18:23), and said, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). He worked his way down from fifty righteous people to ten, and each time God agreed: “For the sake of ten I will not destroy it” (Genesis 18:32). Justice and mercy coexist in God without contradiction — he must judge sin according to justice, yet delights to show mercy in response to intercession; later, when the cities of the plain were overthrown, “God remembered Abraham... and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow” (Genesis 19:29), a concrete fulfillment of that very mercy.

Hebrews reminds us that God also disciplines his children: “The Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). God’s judgment on unrepented sin, and God’s discipline of his children, differ in nature — the former is justice’s due recompense for sin, the latter is the love of a father’s household shaping his children; but both show that God will never turn a blind eye to sin — he always takes it seriously, and always makes room first for grace and intercession. If our hearts want only a God who tolerates everything, never judging, never disciplining, we are actually rejecting true love; true love must include a seriousness about sin.

Abraham’s intercession could only reach down to ten, and went no further — he was, after all, a finite man. But Hebrews tells us there is a far more perfect mediator than Abraham: “he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Christ’s intercession will never stop halfway as Abraham’s did — he lives forever, continually interceding for those who belong to him — so “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Today, we should both fear this God who does not treat sin as nothing, and imitate Abraham, interceding earnestly for those living in “Sodom” around us — because the God who judges is also the God who hears prayer and has sent that Christ who forever intercedes.

Meditation: Do I want only a God of “tolerant love,” while avoiding the God who “judges sin”? Have I, like Abraham, interceded earnestly for those around me living in sin and facing judgment?

Application: Today, earnestly intercede before God, like Abraham, for someone you care about who is living in obvious rebellion, and give thanks that Christ is right now, forever, interceding for you and me in heaven.

Prayer: Lord, you are the holy and just God who does not treat sin as nothing, and also the God who hears intercession and delights to show mercy. Thank you for sending Christ as that mediator who lives forever, interceding for us, so that we are no longer condemned in him. Let me both fear your judgment and hold a heart of mercy, interceding earnestly for those around me living in sin, standing before you as Abraham did. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 献上你的以撒
entries.title_en: Offer Up Your Isaac
entries.verse: 创世记廿二章十四节
entries.content:
神对亚伯拉罕发出一个几乎不近人情的呼召:「你带着你的儿子,就是你独生的儿子,你所爱的以撒……把他献为燔祭」(创22:2)。以撒是神应许多年才赐下的独生子,是亚伯拉罕一生的盼望所系,是神亲口应许「从以撒生的才要称为你的后裔」(来11:18)的那一位。神所要的,偏偏是他最珍爱、最舍不得的那一个——这呼召撕开了亚伯拉罕心里最深处那道防线。

「亚伯拉罕清早起来」就去了(创22:3)。这份顺服令人震撼——不是因为他不爱以撒,而是因为他更信神。希伯来书说,他「以为神还能叫人从死里复活;他也仿佛从死中得回他的儿子来」(来11:19)。他没有把以撒看作自己抓在手里的东西,而是早已把他连同应许一起,交托给那位赐下应许、也能成就应许的神。在举刀的一刻,神拦住他,预备了一只公羊代替以撒;亚伯拉罕就给那地方起名「耶和华以勒」——神必预备(创22:14)。

神今天未必叫我们献上儿女,却常常触碰我们心中的「以撒」——那个我们最珍爱、最不肯交出、甚至已悄悄取代神地位的人或事。我们常以为,越紧抓,就越安全;但这试验恰恰揭穿了这个谎言:凡我们紧抓不肯交出的,往往正悄悄辖制着我们。这不是神要毁掉我们所爱的,而是要问:在你心里,神,是不是真的居首位?

更奇妙的是,亚伯拉罕当年没有走完的那一步——把独生爱子真正献上——神自己后来亲自走完了。保罗说:「神既不爱惜自己的儿子,为我们众人舍了,岂不也把万物和他一同白白地赐给我们吗?」(罗8:32)亚伯拉罕的以撒被公羊代替,神却没有为祂的爱子预备代替——耶稣基督亲自成了那真正的、一次献上就成全了的祭。你的「以撒」是什么?你肯不肯把它放上祭坛,像亚伯拉罕一样,深信「耶和华必预备」——正如祂早已在各各他,为你预备了那真正的羔羊?

默想:此刻我心中的「以撒」是谁、是什么——那个我最珍爱、最不肯交出、甚至已排在神前面的?若神当年为祂的爱子都没有预备代替,这如何加深我对「耶和华必预备」的信心?

应用:今天在祷告中,具体地把你的「以撒」献给神,向祂承认:你在我心中居首位,这一样也归你作主;并默想神为你舍了祂儿子这一事实,操练放手。

祷告:主啊,你试验亚伯拉罕,要他献上最爱的以撒,他就顺服了;你自己却没有为你的爱子预备代替,亲自把耶稣赐给我们众人。求你光照我心中那个不肯交出的「以撒」,给我信心把它放上祭坛,深信你必预备,也深信得着你,远胜过我所紧抓的一切。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God issued Abraham an almost inhuman call: “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love... offer him as a burnt offering” (Genesis 22:2). Isaac was the only son God had given after long years of promise, the hope of Abraham’s whole life, the very one God had personally promised, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named” (Hebrews 11:18). What God asked for was precisely the one Abraham cherished most, could least bear to part with — this call tore open the deepest defense in Abraham’s heart.

“Abraham rose early in the morning” and went (Genesis 22:3). This obedience is stunning — not because he didn’t love Isaac, but because he trusted God even more. Hebrews says he “considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back” (Hebrews 11:19). He did not treat Isaac as something he clutched in his own hands, but had already handed him over, along with the promise itself, to the God who gave the promise and was able to fulfill it. At the moment he raised the knife, God stopped him, and provided a ram in Isaac’s place; Abraham named that place “The LORD Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14).

God may not ask us to offer up our children today, but he often touches the “Isaac” in our hearts — that person or thing we cherish most, are least willing to give up, that may have already quietly taken God’s place. We often think that the tighter we hold on, the safer we are; but this test exposes exactly that lie: whatever we clutch and refuse to hand over is often exactly what is quietly enslaving us. This is not God wanting to destroy what we love, but asking: in your heart, is God truly first?

More wonderfully still, the step Abraham did not have to complete that day — actually offering up his only beloved son — God himself later walked to completion. Paul says: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). Abraham’s Isaac was replaced by a ram, but God prepared no substitute for his own beloved Son — Jesus Christ himself became that true sacrifice, offered once and completely accomplished. What is your “Isaac”? Are you willing to place it on the altar, like Abraham, deeply believing that “the LORD will provide” — just as he already provided, at Calvary, the true Lamb for you?

Meditation: Who or what is the “Isaac” in my heart right now — the thing I cherish most, am least willing to give up, that may have already displaced God? If God did not spare even his own beloved Son from substitution, how does this deepen my confidence that “the LORD will provide”?

Application: Today in prayer, concretely offer your “Isaac” to God, acknowledging to him: you have first place in my heart, this too belongs to you; and meditate on the fact that God gave up his Son for you, practicing letting go.

Prayer: Lord, you tested Abraham, asking him to offer up his beloved Isaac, and he obeyed; yet you yourself provided no substitute for your own beloved Son, giving Jesus up for us all. Shine your light on the “Isaac” in my heart that I refuse to hand over, and give me faith to place it on the altar, deeply believing that you will provide, and that having you far outweighs anything I might cling to. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 不要惧怕,因为我与你同在
entries.title_en: Fear Not, For I Am With You
entries.verse: 创世记廿六章廿四节
entries.content:
以撒承接了父亲亚伯拉罕的应许,一生大体平顺,却也遇饥荒、争水井、受人排挤——非利士人一次次填塞他挖的井,把他从一处赶到另一处。他没有兵力抗衡,只能一再退让、再挖新井,活得像个不断被挤压的边缘人。就在他孤单、前路不明的这个夜晚,神向他显现,说:「我是你父亲亚伯拉罕的神,不要惧怕,因为我与你同在,要赐福给你」(创26:24)。神稳固他的,不是环境的改善,而是一个应许:我与你同在。

「不要惧怕,因为我与你同在」——这是圣经反复出现的安慰,也是抵挡恐惧最根本的武器。以撒的处境没有立刻变好,他并没有从此不再被欺压,但神的同在改变了一切:有神同在,饥荒中有供应,争竞中有护庇,漂泊中有方向。我们的平安,从来不建立在「问题都解决了」上,而建立在「那位掌管一切、又爱我的神与我同在」上。真正的平安,不是环境的产物,而是关系的产物。

值得注意的是,以撒听见应许后,第一件事不是松一口气、继续挖井,而是就在那里筑了一座坛,求告耶和华的名(创26:25)。真信神同在的人,第一反应是敬拜,不只是松一口气。我们今天面对恐惧时,常常只顾着「解决问题」,却忘了敬拜那位应许同在的神,仿佛神的同在只是达成目的的手段,而不是目的本身。

这应许在旧约反复出现(如对雅各、约书亚),最终在新约有了最具体、最贴身的成就——神的儿子道成肉身,「人要称他的名为以马内利……神与我们同在」(太1:23)。以撒所信靠的「与他同在」的神,如今在基督里,亲自住进了我们中间;希伯来书更把这应许接续到每一个信徒身上:「我总不撇下你,也不丢弃你」(来13:5)。今天,当恐惧袭来、前路不明时,神对你说的仍是同一句话:不要惧怕,我与你同在。你的回应,是继续被恐惧驱使,还是像以撒一样,筑一座坛、敬拜那位在基督里与你同在的神?

默想:我的平安,是押在「问题解决」上,还是押在「神与我同在」上?此刻什么恐惧,需要用「不要惧怕,我与你同在」来对付?

应用:今天把一件让你恐惧的事带到神面前,以「你与我同在」向自己宣告,并像以撒一样以敬拜回应,而非被恐惧驱使。

祷告:主啊,你曾对以撒说「不要惧怕,因为我与你同在」,又在基督里成了以马内利,亲自住进我们中间。求你叫我的平安不建立在环境改善上,而扎根于你的同在。当恐惧袭来时,叫我以敬拜回应你,信靠那位总不撇下我、与我同在的神。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Isaac inherited his father Abraham’s promise, and his life was largely smooth, yet he too faced famine, disputes over wells, and rejection by others — the Philistines repeatedly stopped up the wells he dug, driving him from one place to another. He had no army to resist, only retreating again and again, digging new wells, living like a constantly squeezed outsider. On this very night, when he was alone, with no clear way forward, God appeared to him and said: “I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you” (Genesis 26:24). What steadied him was not an improvement in his circumstances, but a promise: I am with you.

“Fear not, for I am with you” — this is a comfort that recurs again and again throughout Scripture, and the most fundamental weapon against fear. Isaac’s situation did not immediately improve; he was not spared from oppression from that point on, but God’s presence changed everything: with God present, there was provision in famine, protection amid strife, direction in wandering. Our peace has never rested on “all problems being solved,” but on “the God who governs all things and loves me being with me.” True peace is not the product of circumstance — it is the product of relationship.

It’s worth noting that the first thing Isaac did upon hearing this promise was not to breathe a sigh of relief and go on digging wells, but to build an altar right there and call upon the name of the LORD (Genesis 26:25). Someone who truly believes God is present responds first with worship, not merely relief. When we face fear today, we’re often so focused on “solving the problem” that we forget to worship the God who promised his presence — as if God’s presence were merely a means to an end, not the end itself.

This promise recurs throughout the Old Testament (as with Jacob, Joshua), finding its most concrete, most intimate fulfillment in the New Testament — the Son of God became flesh, and “they shall call his name Immanuel... God with us” (Matthew 1:23). The God “with him” whom Isaac trusted has now, in Christ, personally moved in among us; Hebrews extends this promise to every believer: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Today, when fear strikes and the way ahead is unclear, God still says to you the same words: Fear not, I am with you. How will you respond — continue being driven by fear, or, like Isaac, build an altar and worship the God who is with you in Christ?

Meditation: Is my peace staked on “the problem being solved,” or staked on “God being with me”? What fear right now needs to be met with “Fear not, I am with you”?

Application: Today, bring something that frightens you before God, declare over yourself “you are with me,” and respond, like Isaac, with worship rather than being driven by fear.

Prayer: Lord, you once said to Isaac, “Fear not, for I am with you,” and in Christ you became Immanuel, personally moving in among us. Let my peace not be built on improving circumstances, but rooted in your presence. When fear strikes, let me respond to you with worship, trusting the God who will never leave me, who is with me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 抓住神的雅各
entries.title_en: Jacob Who Grasped for God
entries.verse: 创世记廿八章十五至十六节
entries.content:
雅各这个名字,意思是「抓夺者」。他一出生就抓着哥哥的脚跟,长大后用一碗红豆汤骗取长子的名分,又假冒以扫、欺骗年迈眼瞎的父亲,骗得了本该属于哥哥的祝福——这是一连串精心策划的谎言,不是一时冲动的失手。为了逃避以扫的追杀之怒,他仓皇孤身离家,前途茫茫,身后是被他伤透的家,身前是完全未知的旷野。就是这样一个诡诈斑斑的人,神却在旷野的伯特利向他显现。

雅各梦见一个梯子立在地上,梯子的头顶着天,神的使者在梯子上,上去下来;耶和华站在梯子以上,重申赐福的应许:「我也与你同在……总不离弃你」(创28:15)。请注意:此刻的雅各毫无可夸——他正因自己的诡诈而仓皇逃命,活该受审判,而非蒙福。神向他显现、赐福,完全出于恩典,与雅各当不当得毫无关系。这正是福音的核心:神的爱临到我们,不是因我们够好,而是在我们还作罪人、还在逃亡时。

雅各醒来,惊讶地说:「耶和华真在这里,我竟不知道!」(创28:16)恩典常常临到我们「不知道」的时候——在我们最不配、最狼狈、甚至正为自己的罪逃窜的处境里,神已经在那里,并未撇下。今天你或许正因自己的失败与诡诈而愧疚、想躲开神,但伯特利的神提醒你:祂临到的,恰恰是这样的雅各,不是那些以为自己配得的人。

那座连接天地的梯子,并非只是雅各一次的异梦。多年以后,耶稣对拿但业说:「你们将要看见天开了,神的使者上去下来在人子身上」(约1:51)——祂亲自宣告,自己就是那真正的梯子:唯一连接圣洁的神与堕落的人、天与地之间那道再无缺口的通道。雅各靠一场梦瞥见了这梯子;我们却因认识基督,天天活在这已经打开、永不再合上的道路里。今天,你若正因失败而觉得自己离神很远,当记得:那道梯子已经立好,而立梯子的一位,正亲自寻找像雅各这样的逃亡者。

默想:我是否以为神的赐福要等我「够好」才临到?伯特利的雅各——一个正在逃亡的诡诈者却蒙神显现——如何改变我对恩典的理解?

应用:今天当你因自己的失败而想躲避神时,反倒来到祂面前,承认「你真在这里」,支取那不靠你表现的恩典。

祷告:主啊,你向逃亡中的雅各显现、赐福,全然是恩典,不是因他配得;你又在基督里,亲自成了连接天地的梯子。谢谢你的爱也这样临到我——在我还诡诈、还失败、还逃避的时候。求你叫我不再以为要够好才蒙你悦纳,而是安息在你不靠我表现的信实里。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The name Jacob means “grasper” or “supplanter.” From birth he grasped his brother’s heel; grown, he traded a bowl of red stew for the birthright, then impersonated Esau to deceive his aging, blind father, stealing the blessing that should have belonged to his brother — a carefully planned string of lies, not a momentary lapse. To escape Esau’s murderous fury, he fled alone in a panic, leaving behind a family he had deeply wounded, heading into a completely unknown wilderness. It was to a man so thoroughly marked by deceit that God appeared, at Bethel in the wilderness.

Jacob dreamed of a ladder set on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending on it; the LORD stood above it, reaffirming the promise of blessing: “I am with you... I will not leave you” (Genesis 28:15). Notice: at this moment Jacob had nothing to boast of — he was fleeing in a panic precisely because of his own deceit, deserving judgment, not blessing. God appeared to him and blessed him purely out of grace, having nothing to do with whether Jacob deserved it. This is exactly the heart of the gospel: God’s love comes to us not because we are good enough, but while we are still sinners, still fleeing.

Jacob woke and said in astonishment, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it” (Genesis 28:16). Grace often reaches us in the moments we “don’t know” — in the very place where we are least deserving, most disheveled, even actively fleeing from our own sin, God is already there, and has not abandoned us. Today you may feel ashamed of your own failures and deceit, wanting to hide from God, but the God of Bethel reminds you: he comes precisely to a Jacob like this, not to those who think themselves worthy.

That ladder connecting heaven and earth was not merely a single dream Jacob once had. Years later, Jesus said to Nathanael, “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51) — he personally declared that he himself is the true ladder: the one, unbroken passage connecting the holy God and fallen humanity, heaven and earth. Jacob glimpsed this ladder through one dream; we, because we know Christ, live every day on this road that has already been opened, and will never again be closed. Today, if you feel far from God because of your failures, remember: that ladder is already set up, and the one who set it up is himself personally seeking out fugitives like Jacob.

Meditation: Do I think God’s blessing has to wait until I’m “good enough” before it comes? How does Jacob at Bethel — a fugitive, a deceiver, who yet had God appear to him — change my understanding of grace?

Application: Today, when you want to hide from God because of your own failures, come before him instead, acknowledging “you really are here,” and draw on grace that doesn’t depend on your performance.

Prayer: Lord, you appeared to and blessed the fleeing Jacob purely out of grace, not because he deserved it; and in Christ you personally became the ladder connecting heaven and earth. Thank you that your love reaches me the same way — while I am still deceitful, still failing, still fleeing. Let me no longer think I must be good enough to be accepted by you, but rest in your faithfulness that doesn’t depend on my performance. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 种什么,收什么
entries.title_en: Whatever You Sow, That You Will Also Reap
entries.verse: 箴言十七章一节
entries.content:
那个惯用诡诈的雅各,逃到舅舅拉班那里,却遇上了一个比他更精于算计的人。雅各爱拉结,甘心为她做工七年,谁知新婚之夜竟被拉班掉包,新妇成了利亚;为娶得拉结,他又多做了七年苦工。此后在牲畜、工价上,舅甥二人斗智斗力,尔虞我诈,彼此提防。当年欺骗父亲、哄骗哥哥的雅各,如今终于尝到了被欺骗的滋味——他种的,开始收了。

圣经的原则在此清楚显明:「不要自欺,神是轻慢不得的。人种的是什么,收的也是什么」(加6:7)。雅各用诡诈对待别人,如今也在诡诈中被人对待、饱受家庭纷争之苦——妻妾相争、儿女不和,这些都成了他后半生沉重的重担。神并没有立刻毁掉雅各,却藉着这些经历,一点一点对付他里面那个「抓夺、算计」的旧性。管教,是神爱中的雕琢,不是祂弃绝的记号。

这对我们是严肃的提醒:我们今天所撒的种,将来必要收成。我们如何待人——是诚实还是诡诈、是恩慈还是苛刻——都不会白费,迟早在自己身上、在关系里显出果效。箴言的智慧同样指向这一点:「设筵满屋,大家相争,不如有块干饼,大家相安」(箴17:1)——雅各家中不缺筵席,却满了相争;真正的丰盛,不在于外面的富足,而在于关系里的诚实与平安。

然而这原则也有一个惊人的例外——不是被废掉,而是被基督在十字架上承担了。「我们都如羊走迷,各人偏行己路,耶和华使我们众人的罪孽都归在他身上」(赛53:6)。我们本该照着自己所撒的诡诈、悖逆,收取那早该临到的审判;基督却在十字架上,收取了我们所种的一切恶果,好叫凡信靠祂的人,能「顺着圣灵撒种……从圣灵收永生」(加6:8)。今天,你是继续撒诡诈算计的种、等着自食其果,还是因基督已经替你收了那本该临到的收成,转而撒下诚实与恩慈的种?

默想:我近来在待人上,撒的是诚实、恩慈的种,还是诡诈、算计、苛刻的种?我是否正在「收」自己从前所种的?

应用:今天在一段关系里,刻意撒下与从前不同的种——用诚实代替算计、用恩慈代替苛刻,把结果交给神。

祷告:主啊,你藉着雅各的遭遇提醒我:种什么,收什么。感谢你在十字架上,亲自收取了我早该自食的恶果。求你光照我待人中那些诡诈、算计的地方,叫我甘心撒下诚实与恩慈的种,也谢谢你的管教不是要毁我,而是要炼净我、重塑我。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Jacob, so used to deceit, fled to his uncle Laban’s house, only to run into someone even more calculating than himself. Jacob loved Rachel, and willingly worked seven years for her, only to be tricked on his wedding night — the bride switched, and it was Leah instead; to marry Rachel, he worked another seven hard years. After that, over livestock and wages, uncle and nephew matched wits and schemed against each other, each wary of the other. The Jacob who once deceived his father and tricked his brother now finally tasted what it was like to be deceived himself — what he had sown was beginning to be reaped.

Scripture’s principle is made plain here: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Jacob treated others with deceit, and now was treated with deceit in turn, suffering deeply from family strife — rivalry between wives, discord among children — all becoming heavy burdens in the second half of his life. God did not immediately destroy Jacob, but through these experiences, bit by bit dealt with that old nature within him of “grasping and scheming.” Discipline is the carving work of God’s love, not a mark of his rejection.

This is a solemn reminder to us: the seeds we sow today will surely be harvested. How we treat others — honestly or deceitfully, with kindness or harshness — is never wasted; sooner or later it will bear fruit in ourselves, in our relationships. The wisdom of Proverbs points to the same thing: “Better is a dry morsel with quiet than a house full of feasting with strife” (Proverbs 17:1) — Jacob’s household lacked no feast, yet was full of strife; true abundance is not found in outward wealth, but in honesty and peace within relationships.

Yet this principle has one astonishing exception — not abolished, but borne by Christ on the cross. “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). We ourselves should have reaped the judgment long overdue for the deceit and rebellion we sowed; but Christ, on the cross, reaped every evil fruit we had sown, so that all who trust in him could instead “sow to the Spirit... reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Galatians 6:8). Today, will you keep sowing seeds of deceit and calculation, waiting to reap the consequences yourself, or, because Christ has already reaped for you the harvest that should have been yours, turn instead to sow seeds of honesty and kindness?

Meditation: In how I’ve treated people lately, have I been sowing seeds of honesty and kindness, or seeds of deceit, calculation, and harshness? Am I currently “reaping” what I sowed before?

Application: Today, in one relationship, deliberately sow a different kind of seed than before — replace calculation with honesty, replace harshness with kindness, and leave the outcome to God.

Prayer: Lord, through Jacob’s experience you remind me: whatever I sow, I will reap. Thank you that on the cross you personally reaped the evil fruit I should have reaped myself. Shine your light on the places where I deal deceitfully and calculatingly with others; let me willingly sow seeds of honesty and kindness, and thank you that your discipline is not meant to destroy me, but to refine and reshape me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 雅各变以色列:在破碎中被更新
entries.title_en: Jacob Becomes Israel: Renewed Through Brokenness
entries.verse: 哥林多后书五章二十节
entries.content:
雅各要回乡,却怕即将重逢的以扫。在雅博渡口,他打发一切过了河,只剩自己一人。当夜,有一人与他摔跤,直到黎明。那人见胜不过他,就摸了他的大腿窝,雅各的大腿窝就扭了。原来与他摔跤的,是神自己。雅各一生靠自己的力量抓夺、争斗,神却要在这一夜,摸着他,叫他「瘸」了。

倪柝声常讲「对付」与「破碎」:神真正要得着的,不是雅各外面的作为,而是要折服他里面那个刚强、自恃、凡事靠自己的天然生命。当雅各的大腿窝被摸、走路一瘸一拐时,那个「抓夺者」终于不再靠自己的腿站立,只能紧紧抓住神,说:「你不给我祝福,我就不容你去」(创32:26)。神在破碎他之处,正是要祝福他。

于是神给他改名:不再叫雅各(抓夺者),要叫以色列(与神较力得胜)。真正的得胜,不是靠自己的强,而是在被神折服、瘸腿倚靠祂之后。这也是我们属灵生命的功课:神常在我们最刚强、最自恃的地方摸我们一下,叫我们「瘸」了、不能再靠自己,好叫我们学会全然倚靠祂。破碎,是神更新我们的方式。

次日,雅各要面对那个他亏欠了一生的哥哥以扫。他战战兢兢,却在见面时俯伏于地;以扫的反应远超他所求所想:「以扫跑来迎接他,将他抱住,又搂着他的颈项,与他亲嘴,两个人就哭了」(创33:4)。那被摸瘸了大腿窝、不再靠自己站立的雅各,如今也不再靠诡诈掌控局面,只能诚实地面对、恳求和好——而和好,竟白白临到他。这地上的和好,让我们想起一场更大、更深的和好——不是雅各与以扫的和好预表了它,而是同一位神,同一种「先降服、才和好」的次序:「神在基督里,叫世人与自己和好……我们替基督求你们与神和好」(林后5:19-20)。我们与神为敌,本无资格求和,基督却主动成就了这和好,又差遣我们去传这和好的信息。雅各先在雅博渡口被破碎、降服,才在与以扫相见时经历真实的和好——这次序值得留意:先被神对付,才能真正与人和好。今天,你是否也需要先在神面前被摸一下、放下自恃,才能走向那个你亏欠、或亏欠你的人,求和好、也传这和好?

默想:神有没有在我某处「大腿窝」上摸了一下,叫我不能再靠自己?我是抗拒这破碎,还是像雅各一样,反倒紧紧抓住神求祝福?

应用:今天在一处你惯常靠自己刚强、掌控的地方,主动松手、承认自己的软弱,转而紧紧倚靠神;并在一段亏欠的关系里,主动求和好。

祷告:主啊,你摸雅各的大腿窝,叫那抓夺者瘸了,却也在那里祝福他、更新他,又领他走向与以扫的和好。求你也对付我里面那个刚强自恃、凡事靠自己的生命。叫我甘心被你破碎,学会瘸腿倚靠你,也甘心传扬你在基督里所成就的和好。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Jacob was heading home, but feared the reunion with Esau that awaited him. At the ford of the Jabbok, he sent everyone else across the river, leaving himself alone. That night, a man wrestled with him until daybreak. When the man saw that he could not prevail against Jacob, he touched his hip socket, and Jacob’s hip was wrenched. It turns out the one wrestling with him was God himself. All his life Jacob had relied on his own strength to grasp and strive, but this very night, God touched him, and made him “limp.”

Watchman Nee often spoke of “dealing” and “breaking”: what God truly wanted to obtain was not Jacob’s outward actions, but to subdue the strong, self-reliant, always-relying-on-himself natural life within him. When Jacob’s hip socket was touched and he began to walk with a limp, the “grasper” finally could no longer stand on his own legs, and could only cling tightly to God, saying, “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26). Precisely where God broke him was where he intended to bless him.

So God gave him a new name: no longer Jacob (the grasper), but Israel (he who strives with God and prevails). True victory is not won through one’s own strength, but comes after being subdued by God, walking with a limp, relying on him. This is also a lesson for our spiritual lives: God often touches us precisely at the place where we are strongest, most self-reliant, making us “limp,” no longer able to rely on ourselves, so that we learn to depend on him completely. Brokenness is God’s way of renewing us.

The next day, Jacob had to face the brother he had wronged his whole life, Esau. He approached trembling, but bowed to the ground when they met; Esau’s response far exceeded anything he could have asked or imagined: “Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept” (Genesis 33:4). Jacob, whose hip had been touched and made lame, no longer standing on his own, no longer controlling the situation through deceit, could only face things honestly, plead for reconciliation — and reconciliation came to him, freely. This earthly reconciliation reminds us of a far greater, far deeper reconciliation — not that Jacob and Esau’s reconciliation foreshadowed it, but that it is the same God, the same order of “first submission, then reconciliation”: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself... we implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:19–20). We were enemies of God, with no grounds to seek peace, yet Christ proactively accomplished this reconciliation, and sends us to proclaim this message of reconciliation. Jacob was first broken and submitted at the Jabbok, only then experiencing genuine reconciliation when meeting Esau — this order is worth noting: only after being dealt with by God can one truly be reconciled with others. Today, do you too need to first be touched by God, laying down your self-reliance, before you can move toward the person you’ve wronged, or who has wronged you, to seek reconciliation, and to proclaim this reconciliation as well?

Meditation: Has God touched some “hip socket” of mine, making me unable to rely on myself any longer? Do I resist this brokenness, or, like Jacob, instead cling tightly to God, seeking his blessing?

Application: Today, in an area where you habitually rely on your own strength and control, proactively let go, acknowledge your own weakness, and turn instead to depend on God; and in a relationship where you owe someone, proactively seek reconciliation.

Prayer: Lord, you touched Jacob’s hip socket, making that grasper limp, yet also blessed and renewed him there, and led him toward reconciliation with Esau. Deal also with that strong, self-reliant, always-relying-on-myself life within me. Let me be willing to be broken by you, learn to depend on you though limping, and willingly proclaim the reconciliation you have accomplished in Christ. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 记念神的创造
entries.title_en: Remembering God's Creation
entries.content:
记念神的创造

「诸天述说神的荣耀;穹苍传扬他的手段。」(诗篇 19:1)

安息日不只是停下工作,更是抬起头来,重新看见那位创造万有的神。祂造这一切,不是要我们只顾使用,而是要我们透过受造之物惊叹、敬拜那位赐下这一切的主。

今天,走到户外,看一看天空、树木、阳光,让每一样受造之物都成为把你的心引向创造主、以祂为乐的邀请。

"The heavens declare the glory of God." (Psalm 19:1) Let creation lift your eyes to the Creator, and turn wonder into worship.
entries.content_en:
Remembering God’s Creation

“The heavens declare the glory of God; the sky above proclaims his handiwork.” (Psalm 19:1)

The Sabbath is not only about stopping work — it is about lifting up your eyes, and seeing afresh the God who created all things. He made all this not merely for us to use, but so that, through what he made, we would marvel at and worship the Lord who gave it all.

Today, step outside, look at the sky, the trees, the sunlight, and let every created thing become an invitation drawing your heart toward the Creator, delighting in him.

"The heavens declare the glory of God." (Psalm 19:1) Let creation lift your eyes to the Creator, and turn wonder into worship.

entries.verse: 诗篇卅八篇四节
entries.content:
创世记这几章记载了一连串令人不安的事:底拿被示剑玷污受辱、西缅和利未血腥报复、流便的乱伦、以扫后裔的兴起。这不是一幅英雄画卷,而是一份诚实的记录——底拿是暴力之下无辜的受害者,西缅、利未的血腥报复与流便的乱伦,则是这蒙拣选之家自己犯下的罪。圣经从不为尊者讳,也不掩盖恶行加给无辜者的伤害,它既照实写下人的败坏,也不忽略受害者的哀伤。

诗人的哀叹道出了这光景:「我的罪孽高过我的头,如同重担叫我担当不起」(诗38:4)。人靠自己无力自救,罪的重担压得人抬不起头。创世记正是要我们看清这一点:人若只看自己,只有绝望;救恩的盼望,从来不在人的良善,而在神的怜悯。

而在这一切失败之中,神并没有撇弃雅各一家。祂吩咐雅各再上伯特利,重新向神筑坛(创35:1)。神的怜悯,不因人的软弱而收回;祂仍信守应许,继续藉着这满是缺陷的家,推进祂的救赎计划。这给每一个看清自己软弱的人极大的安慰:我们的指望不在自己站得多稳,而在那位满有怜悯、信实不改变的神。

这正是全本圣经不断诉说的故事:人的败坏一次次显明,神的怜悯却一次次没有断绝。这怜悯,最终在十字架上得着了最具体的形状——「他被挂在木头上,亲身担当了我们的罪,使我们既然在罪上死,就得以在义上活」(彼前2:24)。诗人扛不起的罪孽重担,基督亲自背了;创世记这几章暴露的暴力、情欲、诡诈,不是要我们绝望地看着自己,而是要把我们逼到十字架前——因为唯有在那里,重担才真正卸下。今天,你若正被某个罪的重担压得抬不起头,不要遮掩,也不要靠自己硬撑,而是把它带到那位已经亲身担当了它的主面前。

默想:我是否想靠自己的良善站在神面前,却发现罪孽高过我的头?我能否把指望从「自己够好」转向「神的怜悯」?

应用:今天诚实地向神承认一处你无力靠自己胜过的软弱,不再遮掩,而是投靠祂的怜悯,把重担卸给那亲身担当了它的主。

祷告:主啊,创世记照实写下人的软弱,也照实显出你的怜悯。我承认我的罪孽高过我的头,靠自己担当不起。谢谢你在基督里亲身担当了这重担,使我在罪上死,在义上活。求你叫我不靠自己的良善,单单投靠你不改变的信实与怜悯。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
These chapters of Genesis record a string of disturbing events: Dinah defiled and violated by Shechem, Simeon and Levi’s bloody vengeance, Reuben’s incest, the rise of Esau’s descendants. This is not a heroic tale, but an honest record — Dinah was an innocent victim of violence, while Simeon and Levi’s bloody vengeance and Reuben’s incest were sins this chosen family committed itself. Scripture never spares the dignified from disgrace, nor does it hide the harm evil inflicts on the innocent; it records human corruption faithfully, and does not overlook the victim’s grief.

The psalmist’s lament captures this condition: “my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me” (Psalm 38:4). Man has no power to save himself; the weight of sin presses him down until he cannot lift his head. Genesis wants us to see this clearly: if a person looks only at themselves, there is only despair; the hope of salvation has never been in human goodness, but in God’s mercy.

Yet in the midst of all this failure, God did not abandon Jacob’s household. He commanded Jacob to go up to Bethel again, and build an altar to God there once more (Genesis 35:1). God’s mercy is not withdrawn because of human weakness; he still keeps his promise, and continues to advance his plan of redemption through this deeply flawed family. This gives enormous comfort to anyone who has seen their own weakness clearly: our hope does not rest on how firmly we stand, but on the merciful, unchangingly faithful God.

This is exactly the story told again and again throughout the whole Bible: human corruption is exposed time and again, yet God’s mercy is never once cut off. This mercy finally took its most concrete shape on the cross — “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness” (1 Peter 2:24). The burden of iniquity the psalmist could not carry, Christ himself carried; the violence, lust, and deceit exposed in these chapters of Genesis are not meant to leave us staring in despair at ourselves, but to drive us to the foot of the cross — for only there is the burden truly laid down. Today, if you are being crushed, unable to lift your head, under the weight of some sin, don’t cover it up, and don’t grit your teeth and try to bear it alone — bring it before the Lord who has already personally carried it.

Meditation: Am I trying to stand before God on my own goodness, only to find my iniquities go over my head? Can I shift my hope from “being good enough myself” to “God’s mercy”?

Application: Today, honestly confess to God one weakness you cannot overcome on your own, no longer covering it up, but turning instead to his mercy, laying the burden down before the Lord who has personally carried it.

Prayer: Lord, Genesis records human weakness honestly, and just as honestly reveals your mercy. I confess my iniquities go over my head, too heavy for me to bear on my own. Thank you that in Christ you personally bore this burden, so that I might die to sin and live to righteousness. Let me not rely on my own goodness, but turn simply to your unchanging faithfulness and mercy. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 神的拣选,出于祂的怜悯
entries.title_en: God's Election Comes From His Mercy
entries.verse: 罗马书九章十一、十五节
entries.content:
创世记三十七至三十八章,埋下了一条日后通向君王、通向弥赛亚的线。约瑟被哥哥们卖到埃及,犹大则在一段极不光彩的事件中,与他玛生下法勒斯——而弥赛亚的家谱,竟经过这条满是污点的血脉(太1:3)。神拣选人、成就救恩,常常不循人所以为的「合理」路线,反倒偏偏拣选那看起来最不配的一支。

保罗正是引用雅各与以扫的例子,阐明神主权的拣选:「双子还没有生下来,善恶还没有做出来……只因召人的主……神就对利百加说:将来大的要服事小的」,又说:「我要怜悯谁,就怜悯谁」(罗9:11-15)。神的拣选,不基于人的善行、资格或表现,而全然出于祂主权的怜悯。保罗紧接着更进一步:「这不在乎那定意的,也不在乎那奔跑的,只在乎发怜悯的神」(罗9:16)——不管你多么努力「奔跑」,拣选的根源从来不在人这一边。这既叫我们无从自夸,也叫我们满心感恩。

这真理谦卑我们,也安慰我们。谦卑——因为我们蒙恩得救,没有一样是我们赚来的,全是神主动的怜悯;安慰——因为既然神的拣选不靠我们的表现,我们的得救就不会因我们的软弱而动摇。今天,当你想靠自己的好行为在神面前记功,或因自己的失败而怀疑神是否还要你时,记得:一切都本于祂的怜悯,不本于你的奔跑。

犹大与他玛这段污点历史尤其显明这真理:神拣选进入弥赛亚家谱的,不是那个看起来最体面的支派,而是那个犯了乱伦之罪、却终于承认「她比我更有义」(创38:26)的犹大。神的怜悯,专门临到那些配不上、却肯承认自己配不上的人。今天,你是站在「我配得神的拣选」的位置上,还是像犹大一样,坦然承认自己一无可夸,单单仰赖那发怜悯的神?

默想:我是否暗暗以为,神拣选我、悦纳我,是因为我比别人好一点?「一切本于神的怜悯」如何拆毁我的自夸,也稳固我的安全感?

应用:今天为你的得救,专门向神献上感谢——不是因你配,而是因祂主权的怜悯白白临到你,正如临到满有污点的犹大一支。

祷告:主啊,你的拣选与救恩,全然出于你主权的怜悯,不基于我的善行或资格。求你除去我一切的自夸,叫我在你面前彻底谦卑;也叫我因你的拣选不靠我的表现,而在软弱中仍有稳固的确据。愿一切荣耀归你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Genesis 37–38 lays down a thread that would one day lead to a king, to the Messiah. Joseph was sold by his brothers into Egypt, while Judah, in a deeply shameful episode, fathered Perez with Tamar — and the Messiah’s genealogy runs precisely through this blood-stained line (Matthew 1:3). God’s election of people, his accomplishing of salvation, often does not follow what humans consider the “reasonable” route, but instead chooses the very branch that looks least deserving.

Paul precisely uses the example of Jacob and Esau to explain God’s sovereign election: “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad... she was told, The older will serve the younger,” and, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” (Romans 9:11–15). God’s election is not based on human good works, qualifications, or performance, but entirely on his sovereign mercy. Paul goes further still: “it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (Romans 9:16) — no matter how hard you “run,” the source of election was never on the human side. This leaves us with no ground to boast, and yet fills us with gratitude.

This truth both humbles us and comforts us. It humbles us — because our being saved by grace is none of it earned by us; it is entirely God’s proactive mercy. It comforts us — because since God’s election does not depend on our performance, our salvation will not be shaken by our weakness. Today, when you’re tempted to keep score of your own good deeds before God, or doubt whether God still wants you because of your failures, remember: everything rests on his mercy, not on your running.

This tainted history of Judah and Tamar makes this truth especially clear: the one God chose to enter the Messiah’s genealogy was not the tribe that looked the most respectable, but Judah, the one who committed the sin of incest, yet finally admitted, “She is more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26). God’s mercy specifically reaches those who don’t deserve it, yet are willing to admit they don’t deserve it. Today, are you standing in the position of “I deserve God’s election,” or, like Judah, openly acknowledging you have nothing to boast of, relying simply on the God who shows mercy?

Meditation: Do I secretly think God chose me, accepted me, because I’m a little better than others? How does “everything rests on God’s mercy” tear down my self-boasting, and also secure my sense of safety?

Application: Today, give thanks to God specifically for your salvation — not because you deserve it, but because his sovereign mercy freely reached you, just as it reached the deeply tainted line of Judah.

Prayer: Lord, your election and salvation rest entirely on your sovereign mercy, not on my good works or qualifications. Take away all my boasting, and humble me completely before you; and because your election doesn’t depend on my performance, let me have firm assurance even in weakness. May all glory be yours. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 无人看见的地方,神与他同在
entries.title_en: Where No One Sees, God Is With Him
entries.verse: 创世记四十一章卅八节
entries.content:
约瑟被卖为奴,又因拒绝主母的引诱而被诬陷下监。表面看,一个正直的人一路吃亏、越走越低——先失去自由,又失去名誉,最后被关进监牢,似乎连神当年赐下的应许也一并埋葬了。然而经文反复出现一句话:「耶和华与约瑟同在」——在波提乏家如此,在监狱里也如此。约瑟的高升,不是从顺境来的,而是从一连串的冤屈与低谷中,由神一步步带出来的。

值得留意的是约瑟在「无人看见」时的选择。主母天天引诱他,他却说:「我怎能作这大恶,得罪神呢?」(创39:9)在没有人会知道、没有人会追究的处境里,他仍以「不得罪神」为最高界线。真正的品格,不是在众目睽睽下的表演,而是在暗处、在无人监督时的坚守。约瑟敬畏的,不是会不会被人发现,而是那位始终看见的神——这敬畏,正是他在漫长低谷中没有变质、没有苦毒的秘诀。

我们常常把「行为正直」与「被人看见」暗暗挂钩:若这件事没人会知道,我们的道德标准也悄悄松动。约瑟却提醒我们,真正的顺服不是靠外在的监督维系的,乃是出于对神的敬畏——祂看得见我们做的一切,即使全世界都看不见。今天,你在无人监督之处的选择,才最真实地显出你信的是一位怎样的神。

到了四十一章,连法老都看出:「像这样的人,有神的灵在他里头,我们岂能找得着呢?」(创41:38)神在暗中的同在与陶造,终必在明处显出果效——约瑟从监牢一步登上埃及宰相之位,成了赐粮给万民、也赐粮给自己家人的人。这正预表了那一位更伟大的受苦者与拯救者:耶稣同样被自己的弟兄出卖、被诬陷、被弃于死地,却在受苦的深处从未被神撇下,最终从死里复活、被高举,成了赐生命的粮给普世万民的主。今天你或许正走在一段无人看见、似乎白白吃亏的低谷里;但请记得,那位与约瑟同在、也曾亲历更深羞辱的神子,也与你同在,你在暗处的忠心,祂都看见,也都不会白费。

默想:在无人看见、无人追究的地方,我是否仍以「不得罪神」为界?我能否相信,神在我低谷、吃亏时仍与我同在?

应用:今天在一件「没人会知道」的事上,刻意选择正直,像约瑟一样以敬畏那位看得见的神为界。

祷告:主啊,你与约瑟同在,连在监狱、在暗处都不离开他;你的儿子也曾亲历被出卖、被弃绝的羞辱。求你叫我在无人看见时,仍以不得罪你为界,在低谷吃亏时,仍相信你与我同在。求你陶造我的品格,叫我暗处的忠心,终在你所定的时候显出果效。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Joseph was sold as a slave, then falsely accused and imprisoned for refusing his master’s wife’s seduction. On the surface, an upright man kept losing out, sinking lower and lower — first his freedom, then his reputation, and finally thrown into prison, as if even the promise God had once given him were being buried along with him. Yet the text repeats one phrase again and again: “the LORD was with Joseph” — true in Potiphar’s house, true in prison too. Joseph’s rise did not come from favorable circumstances, but was brought about, step by step, by God, out of a series of injustices and low points.

It’s worth noting Joseph’s choice in the moments “no one saw.” His master’s wife tempted him day after day, yet he said, “How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9). In a situation where no one would know, no one would investigate, he still held “not sinning against God” as his highest boundary. True character is not a performance under public scrutiny, but faithfulness in the dark, when no one is watching. What Joseph feared was not whether he’d be discovered, but the God who always sees — this fear is precisely the secret of how he never soured, never grew bitter, through his long stretch in the depths.

We often quietly link “upright behavior” to “being seen”: if no one will ever know about something, our moral standards quietly loosen. Joseph reminds us that true obedience is not sustained by external oversight, but flows from the fear of God — he sees everything we do, even when the whole world doesn’t. Today, your choices in places no one supervises are what most truly reveal what kind of God you actually believe in.

By chapter 41, even Pharaoh could see it: “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?” (Genesis 41:38). God’s hidden presence and shaping work will eventually bear visible fruit in the open — Joseph rose from prison straight to the position of Egypt’s prime minister, becoming the one who gave grain to the nations, and to his own family. This foreshadows a far greater sufferer and Savior: Jesus was likewise betrayed by his own brothers, falsely accused, given over to death, yet in the depths of his suffering was never abandoned by God, and was finally raised from the dead and exalted, becoming the Lord who gives the bread of life to all the world. Today you may be walking through a low point that no one sees, that seems like a pointless loss; but remember, the God who was with Joseph, and the Son who personally experienced an even deeper humiliation, is with you too — your faithfulness in the dark, he sees, and it will not be wasted.

Meditation: In places no one sees, no one holds me accountable, do I still hold “not sinning against God” as my boundary? Can I believe that God is with me even in my low points, even when I’m losing out?

Application: Today, in one matter “no one will know about,” deliberately choose integrity, like Joseph, bounded by the fear of the God who sees.

Prayer: Lord, you were with Joseph, never leaving him even in prison, even in the dark; your Son also personally experienced the shame of being betrayed and rejected. Let me, when no one sees, still hold to not sinning against you, and when losing out in a low point, still believe you are with me. Shape my character, and let my faithfulness in the dark bear fruit at the time you have appointed. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 神的手,在暗中动工
entries.title_en: God's Hand, at Work Unseen
entries.verse: 创世记四十三章九节
entries.content:
饥荒逼着约瑟的哥哥们下埃及买粮,他们不认得眼前这位埃及宰相,正是当年被他们卖掉的弟弟。约瑟没有立刻相认,而是藉着一连串的试验——扣留西缅、索要便雅悯——来察看哥哥们的心是否已经改变。这不是报复,而是要看见真实的悔改。

转折点出现在犹大身上。当年正是犹大提议把约瑟卖掉换钱(创37:26-27),如今面对同样要不要「舍出一个兄弟」的抉择,他却对父亲说:「我为他作保;你可以从我手中追讨,我若不带他回来交在你面前,我情愿永远担罪」(创43:9)。那个曾经出卖兄弟、事不关己的犹大,如今甘愿把自己押上,为便雅悯的性命作保、承担一切后果。这不是一句轻率的承诺,而是把自己的自由、名誉,甚至永远的罪责,都押在这一个「保」字上。

果然,哥哥们变了。当年他们冷酷地把约瑟卖掉、又眼看父亲伤心而无动于衷;如今面对便雅悯可能受害,犹大甘愿自己代替他作奴仆,以免年迈的父亲再受丧子之痛(创44:33-34)。当年推卸责任的人,如今甘愿担当。神在这些年间,藉着环境与良心,悄悄地在他们心里动了工——真悔改从来不是嘴上的懊悔,而是行动上从「推卸」到「担当」的具体转变。

犹大甘愿「作保」的这一幕,遥遥指向了那一位真正、完全的保人。希伯来书说,「耶稣就作了更美之约的中保」(来7:22)——中保,就是保人,是那位愿意承担我们的罪责、以自己作抵押的那一位。犹大的担保还有限度,只押上今生的自由;基督却押上了自己的生命,亲身担当了我们本该永远承担的罪责,把我们从那真正的「为奴之地」赎出来。今天,神也许正藉着你生命中的某些「饥荒」与试验,在对付、更新你——但更要紧的是,记得那位已经完全为你「作保」、替你担罪的主。

默想:神是否正藉着我生命中的某些难处,在悄悄对付、改变我?在我身上,有没有从「推卸」到「担当」、从冷酷到舍己的真实转变?

应用:今天在一件你惯常推卸的事上,像转变后的犹大一样,主动挺身担当责任;并默想基督已经完全为你作保的事实。

祷告:主啊,你在漫长的岁月里、在人看不见的地方动工,改变了约瑟哥哥们的心。感谢你在基督里,亲自为我作了更美之约的中保,担当了我永远的罪责。求你也在我身上耐心动工,藉着环境与试验,把我从推卸变为担当、从冷酷变为舍己。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Famine forced Joseph’s brothers down to Egypt to buy grain; they did not recognize that the Egyptian prime minister before them was precisely the brother they had once sold. Joseph did not reveal himself right away, but through a series of tests — detaining Simeon, demanding Benjamin — examined whether his brothers’ hearts had truly changed. This was not revenge, but a search for genuine repentance.

The turning point comes with Judah. It was Judah who once proposed selling Joseph for money (Genesis 37:26–27); now, facing the same choice of whether to “give up a brother,” he instead says to his father: “I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever” (Genesis 43:9). The Judah who once betrayed a brother and felt nothing is now willing to stake himself — pledging his own safety for Benjamin’s life, bearing all the consequences. This is no reckless promise, but staking his own freedom, his reputation, even eternal guilt, on this one word: pledge.

And indeed, the brothers had changed. Back then they coldly sold Joseph, and watched their father grieve unmoved; now, facing the possibility of harm to Benjamin, Judah is willing to become a slave in his place, so their aging father would not suffer the loss of another son (Genesis 44:33–34). Those who once shirked responsibility are now willing to bear it. Over these years, God, through circumstance and conscience, had quietly been at work in their hearts — true repentance is never mere verbal regret, but a concrete shift, in action, from “shirking” to “bearing.”

This scene of Judah’s willingness to “pledge himself” points far ahead to the one true, complete Guarantor. Hebrews says, “Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22) — a guarantor is one who pledges, one willing to bear our guilt, staking himself as collateral. Judah’s pledge had its limits, staking only his freedom in this life; but Christ staked his very life, personally bearing the guilt we should have borne forever, redeeming us out of that true “house of slavery.” Today, God may be dealing with, renewing you, through some “famine” or trial in your life — but more importantly, remember the Lord who has already completely “pledged himself” for you, bearing your guilt.

Meditation: Is God quietly dealing with, changing me, through some hardship in my life right now? Is there, in me, a genuine shift from “shirking” to “bearing,” from coldness to self-giving?

Application: Today, in one matter you habitually shirk, like the transformed Judah, proactively step forward and bear responsibility; and meditate on the fact that Christ has already completely pledged himself for you.

Prayer: Lord, over long years, in places no one could see, you worked to change the hearts of Joseph’s brothers. Thank you that in Christ, you personally became the guarantor of a better covenant, bearing my eternal guilt. Work patiently in me too, through circumstances and trials, turning me from shirking to bearing, from coldness to self-giving. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
