entries.title: 你们的意思是恶,神的意思是好
entries.title_en: You Meant Evil, But God Meant It for Good
entries.verse: 创世记四十五章五节，四十七章九节
entries.content:
约瑟终于向哥哥们表明身份。哥哥们惊惶失措,以为大祸临头。约瑟却说了一句震撼人心的话:「不要因为把我卖到这里自忧自恨。这是神差我在你们以先来,为要保全生命……从前你们的意思是要害我,但神的意思原是好的」(创45:5,50:20)。同一件事——被卖为奴,约瑟看见了两层:人的恶意,与神更高的美意。

这是圣经对「神的护理」最有力的宣告之一。约瑟没有否认哥哥们的行为是恶——「你们的意思是要害我」;但他也看见,在人一切的恶背后,神有一个更高、更善的旨意在成就——「神的意思原是好的,要保全许多人的性命」。神没有认可罪,却能使万事——包括别人加给我们的伤害——互相效力,成就祂的美意。

正因约瑟看见了神的手,他才能真正地饶恕。饶恕最深的根基,不是「假装没事」或「对方不算错」,而是相信:神掌管一切,连别人的恶意,祂都能翻转为祝福;所以我不必自己报复,也不必被苦毒吞噬。今天,若有人加给你伤害,你能否也这样仰望——人的意思或许是恶,但神的意思,在祂儿女身上,总是好的?

这句话的回响,贯穿了整本圣经,直到十字架。使徒彼得对钉死耶稣的群众说:「他既按着神的定旨先见被交与人,你们就藉着无法之人的手,把他钉在十字架上,杀了」(徒2:23)——人的恶意是真实的罪,神的美意也是真实的成就,两者并存,而非互相抵消。约瑟被卖,预告了那更大的「被卖」:耶稣被自己的门徒出卖、被自己的百姓弃绝,人的意思是要害死祂,神的意思却是要藉这十字架,拯救普天下的罪人。今天,若有人加给你伤害,你所信的,不只是「约瑟式的护理」,更是那位曾亲历被出卖、被杀害,却使人间最大的恶转成人类最大救恩的主。

晚年在法老面前,雅各回顾一生,说的却不是得意的成就,而是「我寄居在世的年日是一百三十岁,我平生的年日又少又苦,不及我列祖在世寄居的年日」(创47:9)。这不是一句抱怨的按语,而是一位历尽诡诈、丧子之痛、饥荒漂泊的老人,最诚实的自白。约瑟看见了「神的意思原是好的」,雅各却只看见「又少又苦」——但正是这又少又苦的一生,被神从头到尾护理、成就,最终使全家在埃及团聚、存活。神的美意,不需要我们此刻就能看懂或说出口,才是真实的。

默想:有谁曾恶意伤害我,我至今难以饶恕?我能否相信,神能使这伤害「互相效力」,成就祂在我身上的美意?

应用:把一个伤害过你的人带到神面前,学约瑟的眼光,把「报复的权柄」交给神,并求祂给你饶恕的心。

祷告:主啊,约瑟在人的恶意背后,看见了你更高的美意,因而能饶恕;十字架更显明,你能使人间最大的恶,成就最大的救恩。求你也给我这样的眼光——相信你掌管一切,连别人加给我的伤害,你都能翻转为祝福。叫我不再被苦毒捆绑,能像约瑟一样,把审判交给你,以饶恕回应。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Joseph finally revealed his identity to his brothers. They were terrified, thinking disaster was upon them. But Joseph said something stunning: “do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life... As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 45:5; 50:20). The very same event — being sold as a slave — Joseph saw on two levels: human malice, and God’s higher good purpose.

This is one of Scripture’s most powerful declarations of God’s providence. Joseph did not deny that his brothers’ actions were evil — “you meant evil against me” — but he also saw that behind all human evil, God had a higher, better purpose being accomplished — “God meant it for good, to preserve many people alive.” God did not approve of the sin, yet he can make all things — including the harm others do to us — work together to accomplish his good purpose.

It was precisely because Joseph saw the hand of God that he was able to truly forgive. The deepest foundation of forgiveness is not “pretending nothing happened” or “the other person wasn’t really wrong,” but believing: God governs all things, and even others’ malice, he can turn into blessing; so I don’t need to take revenge myself, nor be swallowed by bitterness. Today, if someone has harmed you, can you look up in this same way — the other person’s intent may have been evil, but God’s intent, for his children, is always good?

The echo of this statement runs through the whole Bible, all the way to the cross. The apostle Peter said to the crowd who crucified Jesus: “this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23) — human malice was a real sin, and God’s good purpose was a real accomplishment, the two coexisting, not canceling each other out. Joseph’s being sold foretold an even greater “selling”: Jesus was betrayed by his own disciples, rejected by his own people, and while men meant to kill him, God meant, through this very cross, to save sinners across the whole world. Today, if someone has harmed you, what you believe is not merely “Joseph-style providence,” but the very Lord who personally experienced being betrayed and killed, yet turned humanity’s greatest evil into humanity’s greatest salvation.

In his old age, before Pharaoh, Jacob looked back on his life, and what he said was not proud achievement, but, “The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers” (Genesis 47:9). This is not a complaining aside, but the most honest confession of an old man who had endured deceit, the loss of a son, famine, and displacement. Joseph saw that “God meant it for good”; Jacob saw only “few and evil” — yet it was precisely this few and evil life that God governed and brought to fulfillment from beginning to end, finally reuniting and preserving the whole family in Egypt. God’s good purpose does not need us to be able to see or say it right now, in order to be real.

Meditation: Who has harmed me with malice, whom I still find hard to forgive to this day? Can I believe that God can make this harm “work together” to accomplish his good purpose in me?

Application: Bring someone who has hurt you before God, adopt Joseph’s perspective, hand over the “right of retribution” to God, and ask him for a heart of forgiveness.

Prayer: Lord, behind human malice Joseph saw your higher good purpose, and so was able to forgive; the cross shows even more clearly that you can turn humanity’s greatest evil into humanity’s greatest salvation. Give me this same vision — believing that you govern all things, and that even the harm others do to me, you can turn into blessing. Let me no longer be bound by bitterness, but, like Joseph, hand judgment over to you, and respond with forgiveness. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 神必与你们同在,领你们回去
entries.title_en: God Will Be With You, and Bring You Back
entries.verse: 创世记四十八章廿一节
entries.content:
创世记以一连串的死亡结束——雅各死了,约瑟也死了。然而在死亡的阴影中,响起的却是盼望的声音。雅各临终为儿孙祝福,对约瑟说:「我要死了,但神必与你们同在,领你们回到你们列祖之地」(创48:21)。他们身在埃及,眼睛却望向神所应许的家乡。

约瑟甚至嘱咐,将来神领他们出埃及时,要把他的骸骨一同带上去(创50:25)。这是何等的信心——他相信神的应许必不落空,即使自己看不到那一天,甚至已经死了。他一生经历了太多——被卖、被诬、被高举——最终把一切都锚定在一个确据上:神信实,祂所应许的必定成就。死亡不是终点,神的应许才是。

希伯来书这样描述雅各、约瑟这一类活在应许中、却看不见应许成就的人:「这些人都是存着信心死的,并没有得着所应许的,却从远处望见,且欢喜迎接,又承认自己在世上是客旅,是寄居的」(来11:13)。我们很容易只用「眼前能不能看见」来衡量信心是否有意义,但约瑟提醒我们:真信心恰恰是在看不见应许成就时,仍然凭信心而活、而安排身后事。你今天所等候的,是不是一件你可能一生都看不到成就、却仍愿意凭信心为它预备的事?

约瑟嘱咐带走他骸骨的信心,最终在一位真正胜过死亡的主身上得着了成就。「基督已经从死里复活,成为睡了之人初熟的果子」(林前15:20)——约瑟的骸骨终有一天要归回应许之地,而属基督的人,连身体也要复活,归回那「更美的家乡」(来11:16)。今天,无论你身处何等的「埃及」——不如意的处境、看不到尽头的等待,甚至死亡本身——都可以像约瑟一样,把盼望锚定在神的信实上:祂必与你同在,也必领你回那更美的家乡。

默想:我的盼望,是锚定在眼前的处境,还是锚定在「神必成就祂应许」的信实上?约瑟至死不渝的确据,如何坚固我此刻的等待?

应用:今天在一件看不到尽头的等待中,像约瑟一样宣告神的信实,把盼望重新锚定在「神必与我同在、领我回家」的应许上。

祷告:主啊,约瑟至死仍紧握你的应许,深信你必看顾、必领你的子民回到应许之地;基督的复活,更把这盼望坚立在永不动摇的根基上。求你也叫我把盼望锚定在你的信实上,而非眼前的处境。无论我身处何等的「埃及」,叫我确信你必与我同在,也必领我回到那更美的家乡。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Genesis ends with a string of deaths — Jacob died, and Joseph died too. Yet in the shadow of death, a voice of hope still sounds. Jacob, blessing his sons and grandsons on his deathbed, said to Joseph: “Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers” (Genesis 48:21). They were in Egypt, yet their eyes looked toward the homeland God had promised.

Joseph even instructed that when God one day led them out of Egypt, they should carry his bones along with them (Genesis 50:25). What faith this was — he believed God’s promise would surely not fail, even if he himself would not see that day, even though he would already be dead. He had experienced so much in his life — being sold, falsely accused, exalted — and in the end, anchored it all on one assurance: God is faithful, and what he has promised will surely be accomplished. Death is not the end; God’s promise is.

Hebrews describes people like Jacob and Joseph, who lived within the promise yet never saw it fulfilled, this way: “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). We easily measure whether faith has meaning only by “can I see it now,” but Joseph reminds us: true faith is precisely living by faith, and arranging for what happens after death, even while unable to see the promise fulfilled. Is there something you’re waiting for today that you may never see fulfilled in your lifetime, yet are still willing to prepare for by faith?

The faith Joseph showed in instructing that his bones be carried away finally found its fulfillment in a Lord who truly conquered death. “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20) — Joseph’s bones would one day return to the promised land, and those who belong to Christ, even their bodies, will be raised, returning to that “better country” (Hebrews 11:16). Today, whatever “Egypt” you find yourself in — unfavorable circumstances, a wait with no end in sight, even death itself — you can, like Joseph, anchor your hope in God’s faithfulness: he will surely be with you, and will surely bring you back to that better homeland.

Meditation: Is my hope anchored in my present circumstances, or anchored in the faithfulness of “God will surely fulfill his promise”? How does Joseph’s unwavering assurance, held even to death, strengthen my waiting right now?

Application: Today, in some wait with no end in sight, declare God’s faithfulness like Joseph, re-anchoring your hope in the promise that “God will surely be with me, and will surely bring me home.”

Prayer: Lord, Joseph held fast to your promise even to death, deeply believing you would watch over your people and surely bring them back to the promised land; Christ’s resurrection has established this hope on an even more unshakeable foundation. Let me too anchor my hope in your faithfulness, not in my present circumstances. Whatever “Egypt” I find myself in, let me be assured you will surely be with me, and will surely bring me back to that better homeland. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 在主里得自由
entries.title_en: Freedom in the Lord
entries.content:
在主里得自由

「所以天父的儿子若叫你们自由,你们就真自由了。」(约翰福音 8:36)

倪柝声提醒我们:真正的自由,不是随心所欲,而是脱离那非靠自己不可、非表现不可的重担。在基督里,你的被接纳早已成定局,不必再挣扎证明。

今天,把那颗紧绷、想靠自己达标的心放下来。你是神所爱、已蒙救赎的儿女——安息在这自由里,单单享受作神儿女的坦然。

"If the Son sets you free, you are free indeed." (John 8:36) Freedom is resting in a love you no longer have to earn.
entries.content_en:
Freedom in the Lord

"So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed." (John 8:36)

Watchman Nee reminds us: true freedom is not doing whatever you please, but being freed from the burden of always having to rely on yourself, always having to perform. In Christ, your acceptance is already settled — there’s no more need to strive to prove it.

Today, lay down that tense heart that keeps trying to earn its own way. You are God’s beloved, already-redeemed child — rest in this freedom, and simply enjoy the openness of being God’s child.

"If the Son sets you free, you are free indeed." (John 8:36) Freedom is resting in a love you no longer have to earn.

entries.title: 神听见,神记念
entries.title_en: God Heard, God Remembered
entries.verse: 出埃及记二章廿三至廿五节
entries.content:
约瑟那一代过去了,新王不认识约瑟,以色列人在埃及沦为奴隶,受尽苦役。他们在重担下哀号。经文这样记着:「神听见他们的哀声,就记念他与亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各所立的约。神看顾以色列人,也知道他们的苦情」(出2:24-25)。四个动词——听见、记念、看顾、知道——道出了神的心。

以色列人受苦已久,似乎神沉默、遥远;但圣经告诉我们,神从未忘记。祂「听见」他们的哀声,祂「记念」祂的约,祂「看顾」、祂「知道」他们的苦情。神的「记念」不是想起一件遗忘的事,而是要为所记念的采取行动——祂即将兴起摩西,施行拯救。神的时候未到时,不等于神不在;祂的沉默,不是祂的漠然。

这对每一个在漫长苦难中、觉得神好像没听见的人是深深的安慰。你的哀声,神听见;你的苦情,神知道;祂与你所立的约,祂记念。祂或许还未出手,但祂从未睡着。今天,若你正在「埃及」的重担下哀号,请相信:那位听见、记念、看顾、知道的神,必按祂的时候施行拯救。

神「听见、记念、看顾、知道」的这四个动词,最终在新约中,有了最具体的成就方式——不是遥远地垂听,而是亲自成为奴仆的样式,进到我们的苦境里。「儿女既同有血肉之体,他也照样亲自成了血肉之体,特要藉着死败坏那掌死权的,就是魔鬼,并要释放那些一生因怕死而为奴仆的人」(来2:14-15)。以色列人在埃及为奴,盼望神差一位拯救者;我们本是罪与死的奴仆,神却亲自差来祂的儿子,道成肉身,藉着自己的死,胜过那真正辖制我们的权势。今天,若你正在「埃及」的重担下哀号,请相信:那位听见、记念、看顾、知道的神,不仅要施行拯救,更早已在基督里,亲自成了释放你的那一位。

默想:我是否曾因苦难久久不得解脱,而以为神没听见、不记念?「神听见、记念、看顾、知道」这四个动词,如何安慰此刻的我?

应用:今天把你长久的苦情向神倾诉,并以「你听见、你知道」向自己宣告,信靠祂必按时施行拯救。

祷告:主啊,当以色列人在埃及哀号,你听见、你记念、你看顾、你知道;你更亲自成了血肉之体,藉着死败坏那掌死权的。求你叫我在漫长的苦难中,也确信你从未忘记我。你或许还未出手,但你从不睡着。求你按你的时候,施行你的拯救。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Joseph’s generation passed, a new king who did not know Joseph arose, and the Israelites were reduced to slavery in Egypt, worn down by hard labor. They groaned under the burden. The text records: “God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. God saw the people of Israel — and God knew” (Exodus 2:24–25). Four verbs — heard, remembered, saw, knew — reveal God’s heart.

The Israelites had suffered for a long time; it seemed God was silent, distant. But Scripture tells us God never forgot. He “heard” their groaning, he “remembered” his covenant, he “saw,” he “knew” their affliction. God’s “remembering” is not recalling something forgotten, but taking action for what is remembered — he was about to raise up Moses, to bring about deliverance. God’s timing not yet having come does not mean God is absent; his silence is not indifference.

This is deep comfort for anyone in long suffering who feels as if God has stopped listening. Your groaning, God hears; your affliction, God knows; the covenant he made with you, he remembers. He may not yet have acted, but he has never fallen asleep. Today, if you are groaning under the burden of your own “Egypt,” believe this: the God who hears, remembers, sees, and knows will surely bring deliverance in his own time.

These four verbs — “heard, remembered, saw, knew” — ultimately found their most concrete fulfillment in the New Testament — not a distant listening, but personally taking on the form of a slave, entering into our affliction. “Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). The Israelites, enslaved in Egypt, hoped God would send a deliverer; we were slaves of sin and death, yet God personally sent his Son, the Word made flesh, and through his own death, conquered the power that truly enslaved us. Today, if you are groaning under the burden of your own “Egypt,” believe this: the God who hears, remembers, sees, and knows will not only bring deliverance — he has already, in Christ, personally become the one who sets you free.

Meditation: Have I, because of prolonged suffering with no relief, thought that God didn’t hear, didn’t remember? How do these four verbs — “God heard, remembered, saw, knew” — comfort me right now?

Application: Today, pour out your long-held affliction to God, and declare to yourself, “you hear, you know,” trusting that he will surely bring deliverance in his own time.

Prayer: Lord, when the Israelites groaned in Egypt, you heard, you remembered, you saw, you knew; you even personally took on flesh and blood, destroying through death the one who holds the power of death. Let me, in long suffering, also be assured that you have never forgotten me. You may not yet have acted, but you never sleep. Bring about your deliverance in your own time. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你是谁差我去?——祂说:我必与你同在
entries.title_en: Who Am I That I Should Go? — He Said: I Will Be With You
entries.verse: 出埃及记四章十至十一节
entries.content:
神在燃烧却不烧毁的荆棘中向摩西显现,差他去带领以色列人出埃及。但曾经意气风发、如今在旷野牧羊四十年的摩西,已经全然没了自信。他一再推辞:「我是什么人,竟能去见法老?」又说:「我素日不是能言的人……我是拙口笨舌的」(出3:11,4:10)。他盯着的,全是自己的不能。

神的回答意味深长。祂没有说「你行的,你有本事」,反而说:「我必与你同在」(出3:12)。神也没有否认摩西的口才不好,却反问:「谁造人的口呢?……岂不是我耶和华吗?」(出4:11)神呼召的根据,从来不是我们的能力,而是祂的同在与供应。祂使用人,不是因人够格,而是因祂够大。摩西的问题是「我是谁」,神把焦点转向「我是谁」——「我是自有永有的」。

我们推辞神的呼召,常常也是盯着自己的不能:我不够好、不会说、没恩赐、没资格。但这恰恰把焦点放错了地方。若一切靠我,当然不能;但神从不叫我们靠自己。祂说「我必与你同在」——这就够了。今天神在某件事上呼召你,你是继续数算自己的不能,还是仰望那位说「我与你同在」的神?

保罗后来也经历过同样的软弱与呼召张力,神给他的回答与摩西所听见的如出一辙:「我的恩典够你用的,因为我的能力是在人的软弱上显得完全」(林后12:9)。神呼召摩西,不是要他变得口才便给,而是要藉着他的拙口笨舌,更清楚地显出这拯救本是神的作为,不是人的本事。希伯来书更进一步说,「摩西为仆人,在神的全家诚然尽忠……但基督为儿子,治理神的家」(来3:5-6)——摩西是那伟大拯救故事里忠心的仆人,却不是故事的终点;那真正配得着「我是自有永有的」这名号的,是耶稣基督自己,祂亲自完成了摩西所预表、却无法完成的拯救。今天神在某件事上呼召你,你是继续数算自己的不能,还是仰望那位说「我必与你同在」、又亲自成就了整个救赎的主?

默想:我在哪件神的呼召上,一直盯着「我不能」而推辞?若真信「神必与我同在」,我的推辞还站得住吗?

应用:今天在一件你因「自觉不够」而回避的呼召或责任上,不再看自己的不能,而是仰望神的同在,踏出一步。

祷告:主啊,摩西盯着自己的不能推辞,你却说「我必与你同在」;基督更亲自完成了摩西所不能完成的救赎。求你叫我不再以自己的软弱、拙口为借口,而是仰望你的同在与供应。你使用人不因人够格,而因你够大;求你也这样使用我。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God appeared to Moses in a burning bush that was not consumed, and sent him to lead the Israelites out of Egypt. But Moses, once spirited and confident, had by now spent forty years as a shepherd in the wilderness, and had entirely lost his self-assurance. He kept making excuses: “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?” and, “I am not eloquent... I am slow of speech and of tongue” (Exodus 3:11; 4:10). All he could see was his own inability.

God’s answer is deeply meaningful. He did not say, “You can do it, you’re capable,” but instead said, “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12). Nor did God deny that Moses was a poor speaker, but instead asked, “Who has made man’s mouth?... Is it not I, the LORD?” (Exodus 4:11). The ground of God’s calling has never been our ability, but his presence and provision. He uses people not because they are qualified, but because he is great. Moses’s question was “Who am I,” and God turned the focus to “Who am I” — “I AM WHO I AM.”

We often make excuses when God calls us too, staring at our own inability: I’m not good enough, I can’t speak well, I have no gifts, I’m not qualified. But this is exactly focusing on the wrong place. If everything depended on us, of course we couldn’t; but God never calls us to rely on ourselves. He says, “I will be with you” — that is enough. Today, if God is calling you to something, will you keep counting up your inabilities, or look to the God who says, “I am with you”?

Paul later experienced the same tension between weakness and calling, and God’s answer to him echoed exactly what Moses heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). God did not call Moses in order to make him eloquent, but precisely through his slow tongue, to make it clearer still that this deliverance was God’s work, not human ability. Hebrews goes further: “Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant... but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:5–6) — Moses was a faithful servant in that great story of deliverance, but not the end of the story; the one truly worthy of the name “I AM WHO I AM” is Jesus Christ himself, who personally accomplished the deliverance Moses foreshadowed but could never complete. Today, if God is calling you to something, will you keep counting up your inabilities, or look to the Lord who says, “I will be with you,” and who has personally accomplished the whole work of redemption?

Meditation: In what calling of God am I always staring at “I can’t” and making excuses? If I truly believe “God will be with me,” does my excuse still hold up?

Application: Today, in one calling or responsibility you’ve avoided because you feel “not enough,” stop looking at your own inability, and instead look to God’s presence, and take a step forward.

Prayer: Lord, Moses stared at his own inability and made excuses, but you said, “I will be with you”; Christ personally accomplished the redemption Moses could not complete. Let me no longer use my own weakness, my slow tongue, as an excuse, but look to your presence and provision. You use people not because they are qualified, but because you are great; use me this same way too. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 叫世人知道:祂是耶和华
entries.title_en: That the World May Know: He Is the LORD
entries.verse: 出埃及记九章十五至十六节
entries.content:
神藉摩西一次次向法老要求释放以色列人,法老却一次次硬着心。于是神降下大灾。神明说祂如此行的目的:「其实,我叫你存立,是特要向你显我的大能,并要使我的名传遍天下」(出9:16)。十灾不是随意的天灾,而是神有目的的作为——祂要向法老、向埃及、向全地显明:唯有耶和华是神。

值得注意的是,每一灾都直接冲击埃及所拜的一个偶像:尼罗河变血、蛙灾、日头变黑……一样一样地击碎埃及人所倚靠的假神,显明它们的虚空,也显明耶和华独一的主权。这提醒我们:神看重祂的名、祂的荣耀被人认识,超过我们所能想象。「叫世人知道我是耶和华」这句话在出埃及记反复出现(出7:5,7:17,14:4),几乎是整卷书的主旋律。

法老的心刚硬,是一个严肃的警戒:人一次次抗拒神清楚的作为,良心就会越来越硬,直到无可挽回。但经文同时也说耶和华使法老的心刚硬——人的悖逆与神的主权,并行不悖。保罗后来直接引用这节经文说:「我将你兴起来,特要在你身上彰显我的权能,并要使我的名传遍天下」(罗9:17),又总结:「神要怜悯谁就怜悯谁,要叫谁刚硬就叫谁刚硬」(罗9:18)。这真理令人敬畏,却也叫我们无可自夸——我们今天还能悔改、还能软化,本身就是神的怜悯,而非我们比法老更好。

神向法老所显的大能与烈怒,与神向凡投靠祂之人所显的怜悯,是同一位神两面的作为——祂自称:「耶和华,耶和华,是有怜悯有恩典的神,不轻易发怒……万不以有罪的为无罪」(出34:6-7)。十字架正是这两者最终交汇之处:神的公义没有被搁置,罪的刑罚全然临到了基督;神的怜悯也没有被牺牲,凡投靠基督的都得存活,正如逾越节那日门框上有血的家。今天,我们既要敬畏这位显明大能、必被尊为圣的神,也当省察:我生命中有没有像法老一样,一再抗拒神清楚的提醒、任凭己心刚硬的地方?

默想:我是否也有一再抗拒神清楚提醒、任凭己心刚硬的地方?神「要使我的名传遍天下」的心意,如何校正我看待神行事的目的?

应用:今天在一处你一直硬着心、不肯顺服的地方,趁着还有今日,软化你的心,向神降服。

祷告:主啊,你降十灾,是要叫世人知道你是耶和华,是要击碎一切虚假的偶像。求你叫我敬畏你的大能与荣耀,也谢谢你在基督里,让公义与怜悯同时成就。求你除去我心中像法老一样刚硬、一再抗拒你的地方,叫我趁着还有今日,向你降服。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God, through Moses, repeatedly demanded that Pharaoh release the Israelites, but Pharaoh hardened his heart again and again. So God sent great plagues. God plainly stated his purpose in doing so: “for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exodus 9:16). The ten plagues were not random natural disasters, but God’s purposeful action — he intended to show Pharaoh, Egypt, and the whole earth: the LORD alone is God.

It’s worth noting that each plague directly struck one of the idols Egypt worshiped: the Nile turned to blood, the plague of frogs, the darkening of the sun... one by one, shattering the false gods the Egyptians relied on, exposing their emptiness, and displaying the LORD’s sole sovereignty. This reminds us: God cares about his name, about his glory being known, far more than we can imagine. The phrase “that the world may know that I am the LORD” recurs throughout Exodus (Exodus 7:5; 7:17; 14:4), almost the main theme of the whole book.

Pharaoh’s hardened heart is a solemn warning: when a person resists God’s clear works again and again, their conscience grows harder and harder, until it becomes irreversible. But the text also says the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart — human rebellion and God’s sovereignty stand side by side, not contradicting one another. Paul later quotes this verse directly, saying, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Romans 9:17), and concludes: “So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Romans 9:18). This truth is awe-inspiring, yet also leaves us no ground to boast — that we can still repent, still soften, today is itself God’s mercy, not because we are better than Pharaoh.

The great power and fierce wrath God displayed toward Pharaoh, and the mercy God displays toward all who take refuge in him, are two sides of the same God’s action — he calls himself: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger... who will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:6–7). The cross is precisely where these two finally converge: God’s justice was not set aside — the full punishment for sin fell on Christ; God’s mercy was not sacrificed either — all who take refuge in Christ live, just as on that Passover day, the households with blood on the doorframe were spared. Today, we should both fear this God who displays great power and must be honored as holy, and examine ourselves: is there, in my life, a place like Pharaoh’s, where I keep resisting God’s clear reminders, letting my heart go hard?

Meditation: Do I too have a place where I keep resisting God’s clear reminders, letting my heart go hard? How does God’s intent, “that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth,” correct how I view the purpose of God’s actions?

Application: Today, in a place where you’ve been hard-hearted, refusing to submit, soften your heart while it is still today, and yield to God.

Prayer: Lord, you sent the ten plagues to make the world know you are the LORD, to shatter every false idol. Let me fear your power and glory, and thank you that in Christ, justice and mercy were both accomplished at once. Remove the places in my heart that are hard like Pharaoh’s, that keep resisting you, and let me yield to you while it is still today. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 逾越节的羔羊
entries.title_en: The Passover Lamb
entries.verse: 出埃及记十二章十三节
entries.content:
第十灾——击杀长子——临到之前,神设立了逾越节。每家要宰一只没有残疾的羔羊,把血涂在门框上。神说:「我一见这血,就越过你们去」(出12:13)。当灭命的使者经过,凡门上有血的,长子就得存活;没有血的,长子就被击杀。生与死之间的分别,不在于人的好坏,而在于门上有没有羔羊的血。

这是全本圣经救恩的缩影。以色列人得救,不是因为他们比埃及人更好——他们同样是罪人,同样理当受审判;他们得救,唯独因为羔羊的血遮盖了他们。审判照样临到,但羔羊代替他们受了死。保罗后来明说:「我们逾越节的羔羊基督已经被杀献祭了」(林前5:7)。逾越节的每一只羔羊,都指向那位真羔羊——为我们流血、使审判越过我们的耶稣基督。

施洗约翰第一次见到耶稣时,脱口而出的正是这个身份:「看哪,神的羔羊,除去世人罪孽的」(约1:29)。这不是一句巧合的比喻,而是整本圣经血祭传统的高峰。约翰福音甚至记下,耶稣被钉十字架时骨头一根也没有折断——「这些事成了,为要应验经上的话说:他的骨头一根也不可折断」(约19:36),这原是逾越节羔羊的条例(出12:46)。耶稣钉死的那一刻,连细节都在宣告:祂就是真正的逾越节羔羊。

这提醒我们:我们蒙拯救脱离神公义的审判,不靠自己的行为,唯靠基督的血。躲避审判的路,不是把自己变得够好,而是藏身在羔羊的血下。今天,你是否已藉着信,让基督的血遮盖了你?你的确据,不在于你有多好,而在于门上那血——已经为你流了。

默想:我得救的把握,是建立在「我够好」上,还是建立在「羔羊的血遮盖了我」上?我是否已藏身在基督的血下?

应用:今天默想基督作为逾越节羔羊为你所流的血,以此为你得救的确据,并为这救恩献上感谢。

祷告:主啊,逾越节的羔羊预表了基督——那位为我流血、使审判越过我的真羔羊,连钉死时骨头都不折断的细节,都在应验你古时的话。谢谢你,我得救不靠自己的好,唯靠你的血遮盖。求你叫我安息在这确据里,一生因你舍命的爱而感恩敬拜。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Before the tenth plague — the killing of the firstborn — struck, God instituted the Passover. Each household was to slaughter a lamb without blemish, and put the blood on the doorframes. God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). When the destroying angel passed through, wherever there was blood on the door, the firstborn was spared; wherever there was none, the firstborn was struck down. The distinction between life and death did not depend on whether people were good or bad, but on whether there was the blood of a lamb on the door.

This is the whole Bible’s salvation story in miniature. The Israelites were saved not because they were better than the Egyptians — they were equally sinners, equally deserving judgment; they were saved solely because the blood of the lamb covered them. Judgment still came, but the lamb died in their place. Paul later states plainly: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Every Passover lamb pointed to the true Lamb — Jesus Christ, who shed his blood for us, so that judgment would pass over us.

When John the Baptist first saw Jesus, this very identity burst from his lips: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). This is no coincidental metaphor, but the summit of the whole Bible’s tradition of blood sacrifice. John’s Gospel even records that when Jesus was crucified, not one of his bones was broken — “For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: Not one of his bones will be broken” (John 19:36), which was originally the regulation for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46). At the very moment of Jesus’s death, even the details were declaring: he is the true Passover Lamb.

This reminds us: we are saved from God’s just judgment not by our own works, but solely by Christ’s blood. The way to escape judgment is not to make ourselves good enough, but to hide ourselves under the lamb’s blood. Today, have you, through faith, let Christ’s blood cover you? Your assurance rests not on how good you are, but on that blood on the door — already shed for you.

Meditation: Is my assurance of salvation built on “I am good enough,” or built on “the lamb’s blood has covered me”? Have I already hidden myself under Christ’s blood?

Application: Today, meditate on the blood Christ shed for you as the Passover Lamb, let it be the assurance of your salvation, and give thanks for this salvation.

Prayer: Lord, the Passover lamb foreshadowed Christ — the true Lamb who shed his blood for me, so that judgment would pass over me; even the detail that his bones were not broken at his death fulfilled your ancient word. Thank you that I am saved not by my own goodness, but solely by your covering blood. Let me rest in this assurance, worshiping you all my life in gratitude for your self-giving love. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 云柱火柱:祂亲自引领
entries.title_en: The Pillar of Cloud and Fire: He Personally Leads
entries.verse: 出埃及记十三章廿一节
entries.content:
以色列人出了埃及,前有旷野、后有追兵,前路茫茫。但神没有撇下他们独自摸索:「日间,耶和华在云柱中领他们的路;夜间,在火柱中光照他们,使他们日夜都可以行走」(出13:21)。这云柱火柱,是神同在与引领的记号——祂亲自走在前头,带领祂的子民。

倪柝声常提醒我们:属灵的道路,不是靠自己筹划、靠自己看清全程,而是紧紧跟随神的引领,一步一步地走。云柱停,他们就停;云柱行,他们就行(民9:17-23)。他们不能自作主张地抢先,也不能落后不动,只能学习一件功课:注视神的引领,与祂的脚步同行。真正的带领,不在乎我们看清多远,而在乎我们是否亦步亦趋地跟随。

我们常想要一张「整条路的地图」,神却往往只给「下一步的亮光」。这正是要我们时刻依靠祂、注视祂,而非一次拿够了就自己走。我们里面那股急着「看清全程才肯动」的冲动,其实是不信的另一种表现——仿佛神的带领若不能让我一眼望穿终点,就不够可靠。但云柱火柱从不曾一次照亮全程,只照亮当下一步,神却从未有一天失约。

云柱火柱最终指向了那一位说「我是世界的光,跟从我的,就不在黑暗里走,必要得着生命的光」的主(约8:12)。以色列人蒙引领,靠的是外在看得见的记号;我们蒙引领,却有那真光亲自内住,又赐下祂的话:「你的话是我脚前的灯,是我路上的光」(诗119:105)。今天,神未必用云柱火柱,却藉着祂的话语、圣灵的引导、环境的开关,一步步引领愿意跟随的人。你今天是急着自己筹划全程,还是安心跟随那走在前头、又亲自成了世界之光的主?

默想:我是想要一张「全程的地图」,还是愿意一步一步跟随神「下一步的亮光」?我此刻是抢在神前面,还是亦步亦趋地注视祂的引领?

应用:今天在一个前路不明的决定上,不急着自己筹划全程,而是安静寻求神「下一步」的引导,跟随祂而行。

祷告:主啊,你曾用云柱火柱日夜引领你的子民,又在基督里亲自成了世界的光。求你也这样引领我——藉着你的话、你的灵、你的安排。叫我不抢在你前面,也不落后不动,而是时刻注视你的引领,与你的脚步同行,一步一步跟随那走在前头的你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The Israelites had left Egypt, with the wilderness ahead and pursuers behind, the way forward uncertain. But God did not leave them to find their own way: “the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night” (Exodus 13:21). This pillar of cloud and fire was a mark of God’s presence and leading — he himself walked ahead, leading his people.

Watchman Nee often reminds us: the spiritual road is not something we plan out ourselves, not something we chart from beginning to end ourselves, but is walked step by step, closely following God’s leading. When the cloud stopped, they stopped; when the cloud moved, they moved (Numbers 9:17–23). They could not rush ahead on their own initiative, nor could they lag behind and stay put — they could only learn one lesson: fix their eyes on God’s leading, and walk in step with him. True guidance does not depend on how far ahead we can see, but on whether we follow closely, step by step.

We often want “a map of the whole road,” but God often gives only “light for the next step.” This is precisely meant to make us depend on him and fix our eyes on him at all times, rather than grabbing enough at once and then walking off on our own. That urge within us to “see the whole way clearly before I’ll move” is actually another form of unbelief — as if God’s guidance weren’t reliable unless it let us see all the way to the destination in one glance. But the pillar of cloud and fire never once illuminated the whole road at once, only the next step — yet God never once broke his promise, not for a single day.

The pillar of cloud and fire ultimately points to the Lord who said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). The Israelites were guided by an outward, visible sign; we are guided by that true Light himself dwelling within us, and by his word given to us: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). Today, God may not use a pillar of cloud and fire, but through his word, the Spirit’s guidance, and the opening and closing of circumstances, he leads, step by step, all who are willing to follow. Are you today rushing to plan out the whole road yourself, or content to follow closely the Lord who walks ahead, who has personally become the light of the world?

Meditation: Do I want “a map of the whole road,” or am I willing to follow God’s “light for the next step,” one step at a time? Am I right now rushing ahead of God, or following closely, step by step, watching his leading?

Application: Today, in a decision where the way forward is unclear, don’t rush to plan out the whole road yourself; instead, quietly seek God’s guidance for the “next step,” and follow him.

Prayer: Lord, you once led your people day and night with a pillar of cloud and fire, and in Christ you personally became the light of the world. Lead me too — through your word, your Spirit, your arrangements. Let me not rush ahead of you, nor lag behind and stay put, but always fix my eyes on your leading, walking in step with you, following you, who walks ahead, one step at a time. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 属灵的加油站
entries.title_en: Spiritual Refuelling
entries.content:
属灵的加油站

「得力在乎平静安稳。」(以赛亚书 30:15)

就像刚出埃及的以色列人需要在神面前重新得力,我们的灵人也需要补给。得力不是靠咬牙硬撑,而是回到神面前,以祂为乐、重新支取祂的力量。

今天,不要急着奔跑或盘算,先安静在神的同在里。让那位领你出「埃及」的神,重新更新你、坚固你,再上路。

"In quietness and confidence shall be your strength." (Isaiah 30:15) Recharge your spirit in God's presence today.
entries.content_en:
Spiritual Refuelling

"In quietness and trust shall be your strength." (Isaiah 30:15)

Just as the Israelites, freshly out of Egypt, needed to be renewed with strength before God, our spirits too need replenishing. Strength doesn’t come from gritting your teeth and pushing through — it comes from returning before God, delighting in him, and drawing on his strength afresh.

Today, don’t rush to run or scheme — first be still in God’s presence. Let the God who led you out of your "Egypt" renew you, strengthen you, and then send you on your way.

"In quietness and confidence shall be your strength." (Isaiah 30:15) Recharge your spirit in God’s presence today.

entries.title: 够用的吗哪——祂天天喂养你,好叫你倚靠祂
entries.title_en: Enough Manna — He Feeds You Daily, So That You Would Depend On Him
entries.verse: 出埃及记十六章十七至十八节
entries.content:
以色列人出了埃及,却在旷野里没有食物,便向摩西、亚伦发怨言,甚至说宁可死在埃及的肉锅旁。神的回应出人意料:祂不责罚,反而应许说:「我要将粮食从天降给你们」,每天早晨赐下吗哪(出16:4)。这粮食有个规矩——只可拾取当天所需,多拾的必生虫变臭;唯独安息日前一天可拾两份。

「各人按着自己的饭量收取」,多收的没有余,少收的没有缺(出16:18)。神不多给,也不少给,祂所赐的是「够用的」。祂为什么不一次降下够吃四十年的粮,让人省心?因为神要的不只是喂饱他们的肚腹,更是天天更新他们对祂的倚靠。吗哪每早晨新鲜降下,是要他们每早晨重新仰望那位供应的神。

原句「人活着,不是单靠食物,乃是靠耶和华口里所出的一切话」(申8:3)最早是摩西对以色列人说的;主耶稣后来在旷野受试探时,原样引用了这句话(太4:4)。吗哪最深的功课,不是「神会喂饱我」,而是「神自己比祂所赐的更甘甜」。祂让我们尝到饥饿,好叫我们尝到祂的供应;祂使供应只够一天,好叫我们的心不黏着在粮食上,而是黏着在祂身上。

这功课最终在耶稣自己身上得着了最完全的成就。祂对众人说:「我就是生命的粮。你们的祖宗在旷野吃过吗哪,还是死了……我是从天上降下来生命的粮;人若吃这粮,就必永远活着」(约6:48-51)。旷野的吗哪终究会生虫变臭,吃过的人终究会死;唯有这从天上降下来的真粮,吃了就永远活着。你今天是否也在为「明天够不够」而焦虑?神给你的,或许正好够今天用——不多,不少。这不是祂的吝啬,而是祂的智慧:祂要你每一天都回到祂面前支取,好叫你在倚靠中,发现祂比一切供应都更令你满足,而祂自己,才是那真正叫你永远活着的粮。

默想:我是渴望「一次拥有足够」以求安心,还是愿意「天天倚靠神」?这背后,是我信靠供应本身,还是信靠那位供应的主,那位从天上降下来的生命之粮?

应用:今天在一件让你为「明天」忧虑的事上,只求神赐下「今天够用」的恩典,并在祷告中把明天单单交给祂。

祷告:天上的父,你曾天天以吗哪喂养你的百姓,叫他们学习倚靠你;又在基督里,亲自成了从天降下的生命之粮。求你也教我不为明天忧虑,天天到你面前支取够用的恩典。更求你叫我看见:你所赐的一切供应,都不如你自己甘甜。愿我以你为我心中的粮,以你为乐。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The Israelites had left Egypt, but found no food in the wilderness, and grumbled against Moses and Aaron, even saying they would rather have died back in Egypt by the meat pots. God’s response was unexpected: he did not punish them, but instead promised, “I am about to rain bread from heaven for you,” giving manna every morning (Exodus 16:4). This bread came with a rule — only that day’s portion could be gathered; whatever was gathered in excess would breed worms and stink — except on the day before the Sabbath, when a double portion could be gathered.

“Each of them gathered as much as he could eat” — whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack (Exodus 16:18). God gave neither too much nor too little — what he gave was “enough.” Why didn’t he simply send down forty years’ worth of grain at once, sparing everyone the trouble? Because what God wanted was not merely to fill their stomachs, but to renew, day by day, their dependence on him. The manna fell fresh every morning, so that every morning they would look up anew to the God who provides.

The original saying, “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3), was first spoken by Moses to the Israelites; the Lord Jesus, later tempted in the wilderness, quoted this very verse verbatim (Matthew 4:4). The deepest lesson of the manna is not “God will feed me,” but “God himself is sweeter than what he gives.” He let them taste hunger, so that they would taste his provision; he made the provision sufficient for only one day, so that their hearts would not stick to the food, but stick to him.

This lesson finally found its most complete fulfillment in Jesus himself. He said to the crowd: “I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died... I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:48–51). The manna in the wilderness would eventually breed worms and stink, and those who ate it would eventually die; only this true bread come down from heaven, once eaten, gives life forever. Are you today also anxious about whether “tomorrow will be enough”? What God gives you may be precisely enough for today — no more, no less. This is not his stinginess, but his wisdom: he wants you to return before him every single day to draw on it, so that in this dependence, you would discover he is more satisfying than any provision — and that he himself is the true bread that makes you live forever.

Meditation: Do I long to “have enough all at once” so I can feel secure, or am I willing to “depend on God daily”? Underneath this, am I trusting the provision itself, or trusting the Lord who provides, the bread of life come down from heaven?

Application: Today, in something that’s making you anxious about “tomorrow,” ask God only for the grace that’s “enough for today,” and in prayer, hand tomorrow entirely over to him.

Prayer: Father in heaven, you once fed your people with manna every day, teaching them to depend on you; and in Christ, you personally became the bread of life come down from heaven. Teach me too not to worry about tomorrow, but to come before you every day to draw on grace that is enough. And let me see: everything you provide is not as sweet as you yourself. May I make you the bread of my heart, and delight in you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 西奈山的雷声——律法显明神的圣洁
entries.title_en: Thunder at Sinai — The Law Reveals God's Holiness
entries.verse: 出埃及记二十章三至四、七至八、十二至十七节
entries.content:
神在西奈山降临,山上有雷轰、闪电、密云、角声,全山大大震动,百姓战兢(出19:16-18)。这不是一位随和的神,而是一位圣洁、可畏、如烈火般的神。祂就在这样的威严中颁布十诫,而开宗明义的第一句是:「除了我以外,你不可有别的神。」

然而次序很要紧:神先宣告祂是谁——「我是耶和华你的神,曾将你从埃及地为奴之家领出来」(出20:2)——然后才颁布诫命。恩典在前,律法在后。神不是说「你若守诫命,我就救你」,而是「我已经救了你,如今你要如此而行」。十诫从来不是得救的阶梯,而是蒙救赎之民的生活样式。前四诫关乎人与神,后六诫关乎人与人;爱神与爱人,律法一以贯之。

但律法还有一个更深的作用:它像一面镜子,照出我们的污秽。有谁能说自己从未拜过偶像(哪怕是心中的偶像)、从未妄称主名、从未动过贪心?保罗说:「律法本是叫人知罪」(罗3:20)。十诫的雷声,是要震碎我们的自义,叫我们看见自己无法达到神的标准,像一位训蒙的师傅,「引我们到基督那里,使我们因信称义」(加3:24)。

主耶稣说,祂来不是要废掉律法,乃是要成全(太5:17)。祂替我们守全了我们守不全的律法,又替我们担当了我们干犯律法的刑罚。所以基督徒守诫命,不再是为了换取神的接纳,而是因为已蒙接纳,出于爱回应那位先爱我们的神。律法叫我们知罪,恩典叫我们知恩,基督叫我们既知罪又蒙恩。

默想:我是把神的诫命当作「换取祂喜悦的条件」,还是「回应祂救恩的爱」?这两种心态,会带出何等不同的顺服?

应用:今天默想十诫,求圣灵光照出一条你最容易忽略的诫命(尤其像「不可贪恋」这类内心的罪),向神认罪,并支取基督的恩典。

祷告:圣洁的神,你在西奈山以威严颁布律法,叫我看见你的圣洁,也看见我的亏欠。我承认我无法靠自己守全你的诫命。感谢你差主耶稣替我成全了律法、担当了刑罚,又叫律法作我的师傅,引我到基督那里。求你叫我不再靠行为换取你的接纳,而是因已蒙接纳,出于爱来遵行你的话。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God descended on Mount Sinai amid thunder, lightning, thick cloud, and trumpet blast; the whole mountain shook violently, and the people trembled (Exodus 19:16–18). This is not a mild-mannered God, but a holy, awesome God, like a consuming fire. It was in this very majesty that he gave the Ten Commandments, opening with: “You shall have no other gods before me.”

Yet the order matters greatly: God first declares who he is — “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2) — and only then gives the commandments. Grace comes first, law follows. God does not say, “If you keep the commandments, I will save you,” but, “I have already saved you; now live this way.” The Ten Commandments were never a ladder to salvation, but the shape of life for an already-redeemed people. The first four commandments concern people and God, the last six concern people and one another; loving God and loving people run through the law as one thread.

But the law has an even deeper function: it is like a mirror, exposing our filth. Who can say they have never worshiped an idol (even an idol in the heart), never taken the Lord’s name in vain, never coveted? Paul says, “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). The thunder of the Ten Commandments is meant to shatter our self-righteousness, to make us see we cannot reach God’s standard, acting like a guardian, “to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24).

The Lord Jesus said he did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17). He kept, in our place, the law we could not keep whole, and bore, in our place, the penalty for our transgressing it. So a Christian’s keeping of the commandments is no longer to trade for God’s acceptance, but, having already been accepted, a response of love to the God who first loved us. The law makes us know sin; grace makes us know favor; Christ makes us know both sin and favor together.

Meditation: Do I treat God’s commandments as “conditions to trade for his pleasure,” or as “a response of love to his salvation”? What different kind of obedience would each of these mindsets produce?

Application: Today, meditate on the Ten Commandments, ask the Spirit to shine light on one commandment you most easily overlook (especially an inward sin like “do not covet”), confess it to God, and draw on Christ’s grace.

Prayer: Holy God, you gave the law at Sinai with majesty, so that I would see your holiness, and also see my own lack. I confess I cannot keep your commandments fully on my own. Thank you for sending the Lord Jesus to fulfill the law in my place, to bear its penalty for me, and to let the law be my guardian, leading me to Christ. Let me no longer trade works for your acceptance, but, already accepted, keep your word out of love. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 不可欺压寄居的——因为你也曾是寄居的
entries.title_en: Do Not Oppress the Sojourner — For You Too Were Once a Sojourner
entries.verse: 出埃及记廿二章廿一节；廿三章八节
entries.content:
颁布十诫之后,神接着赐下许多具体的律例,规范以色列人日常的生活。其中反复出现一个主题:如何对待社会中最无助的人——寄居的、孤儿、寡妇、穷人。神说:「不可亏负寄居的,也不可欺压他,因为你们在埃及地也作过寄居的」(出22:21)。又说:「不可受贿赂;因为贿赂能叫明眼人变瞎了」(出23:8)。

请留意神给的理由:「因为你们在埃及地也作过寄居的。」神没有说「因为这是规矩」,而是唤起他们的记忆——你们曾经也是无依无靠、任人欺压的外人,是我把你们领了出来。换句话说,你如何对待弱者,取决于你是否记得自己曾经的光景,以及神如何白白地怜悯了你。唯有被恩待的人,才懂得恩待人。

这正是福音的逻辑。我们在灵里也曾是在以色列国民以外、与神隔绝、在应许之外的人(弗2:12);是基督用祂的血,把我们这些远离的人领近了。约翰说得直接:「我们爱,因为神先爱我们」(约壹4:19)——不是我们先有爱、才蒙神爱,而是神先白白爱了不配的我们,我们的爱才有了源头与力量。一个真正明白自己蒙了何等大恩的人,不可能对身边的弱者冷漠。若我们轻看穷人、偏待有钱有势的、在不公面前沉默,恰恰暴露出我们还没真正尝到福音的滋味。

神对公义的看重,不是外加在信仰上的一个社会议题,而是从祂的心肠里流淌出来的。祂是「为孤儿寡妇伸冤、又怜爱寄居的」的神(申10:18)。跟随这样一位神,就不能对不义视而不见。今天在你的生活圈里,谁是那「寄居的」——被忽略、被占便宜、发不出声音的人?福音若真进了你的心,必会驱使你向他们伸出手。

默想:我是否常在不知不觉中偏待「有用的人」、轻看「无助的人」?这暴露出我对神恩典的哪些遗忘?

应用:今天留意一个身边容易被忽略或亏负的人(同事、邻舍、陌生人),用一个具体的行动善待他,不求回报。

祷告:怜悯的主,你吩咐你的百姓善待寄居的,因为他们也曾是寄居的。我承认,我常常忘记自己也曾是与你隔绝的外人,是你先爱了我、用基督的血把我领近。求你叫我因记得所蒙的恩,而向身边的弱者存怜悯的心;叫我恨恶不义,像你恨恶不义一样。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
After giving the Ten Commandments, God went on to give many concrete ordinances, governing the Israelites’ daily life. Among them, one theme recurs again and again: how to treat the most helpless in society — the sojourner, the orphan, the widow, the poor. God says, “You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (Exodus 22:21). And, “you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted” (Exodus 23:8).

Notice the reason God gives: “for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.” God did not say, “because it’s the rule,” but instead stirs up their memory — you too were once helpless, foreign, at others’ mercy, and I brought you out. In other words, how you treat the weak depends on whether you remember your own former condition, and how freely God showed you mercy. Only someone who has been treated with grace truly knows how to treat others with grace.

This is exactly the logic of the gospel. We too were once, in the spirit, outside the commonwealth of Israel, alienated from God, strangers to the promise (Ephesians 2:12); it was Christ who, by his blood, brought us near, though we were far off. John says it plainly: “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19) — it’s not that we loved first and so were loved by God, but that God first freely loved undeserving us, and only then did our love have a source and a strength. Someone who truly understands how great a grace they’ve received cannot be indifferent to the weak around them. If we look down on the poor, favor the rich and powerful, or stay silent in the face of injustice, this exposes exactly that we haven’t truly tasted the gospel yet.

God’s regard for justice is not a social issue tacked onto faith, but flows out from his own heart. He is the God who “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner” (Deuteronomy 10:18). Following such a God, one cannot turn a blind eye to injustice. Today, in your own circle, who is the “sojourner” — the overlooked, the taken advantage of, the voiceless? If the gospel has truly entered your heart, it will surely drive you to reach out to them.

Meditation: Do I unconsciously favor “useful people” and look down on “the helpless”? What does this expose about what I’ve forgotten of God’s grace?

Application: Today, notice someone near you who is easily overlooked or wronged (a coworker, a neighbor, a stranger), and treat them well through one concrete action, expecting nothing in return.

Prayer: Merciful Lord, you commanded your people to treat the sojourner well, because they too were once sojourners. I confess I often forget that I too was once a stranger cut off from you, and that you loved me first, bringing me near by Christ’s blood. Let me, because I remember the grace I’ve received, hold a merciful heart toward the weak around me; let me hate injustice, as you hate injustice. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 照山上的样式——属天的蓝图
entries.title_en: According to the Pattern on the Mountain — The Heavenly Blueprint
entries.verse: 出埃及记廿五章四十节
entries.content:
神在山上把建造会幕的样式一一指示摩西,从约柜、陈设饼的桌子、灯台,到帐幕的每一个细节,末了郑重叮嘱:「要谨慎做这些物件,都要照着在山上指示你的样式」(出25:40)。会幕的一钉一环,都不是出于摩西的创意,而是照着神所显明的属天蓝图。人不可加,也不可减。

这里藏着一个极深的属灵原则:凡属神的事,都有神自己的样式,断不能凭人的聪明去构想。会幕是天上真帐幕的影儿(来8:5),它所预表的,乃是基督并祂的救恩——约柜里的法版指向那完全遵行神旨意的主,施恩座指向祂舍命所成就的救赎,幔子指向祂为我们裂开的身体。摩西若擅自改动一分,所立的就不再是神的见证,而成了人手的宗教。希伯来书更进一步说,天上的本物,当用「更美的祭物」去洁净,因为基督「并不是进了人手所造的圣所……乃是进了天堂,如今为我们显在神面前」(来9:24)——地上会幕不过是那更美真圣所的影像,基督才是真正、直接进到神面前的那一位。

我们今日事奉神,最大的危险不是不热心,而是凭着「自己以为好」的方式去做神的工。神所要的,从来不是我们为祂设计什么,而是我们照祂所启示的去顺服。属灵的建造若掺进了人的意思,外面或许华美,里面却失了神的同在。真正的事奉,是先上到山上,看清神的样式,再下山照着去行。

亲爱的,你我这个人,也是神要按祂的样式来建造的殿。祂有祂为你所定的蓝图,不容你我自作主张地拆改。你是否肯放下自己的构想,天天上到神面前,支取祂的心意,让祂照着祂的样式,把基督一点一点建造在你里面?外面的工作可以由人评判,里面的样式唯有神知道。

默想:我在事奉与生活中,有多少是「照神的样式」,又有多少是「照我以为好的」?我肯不肯上到山上,先看清祂的心意?

应用:今天在一件你正凭己意推动的事上,停下来,安静到神面前寻求祂的样式;宁可慢一点,也要照祂的意思而行。

祷告:主啊,你吩咐摩西凡事都要照山上的样式而行,不容一点人的加添。我承认我常凭自己以为好的去做你的工,掺进了许多己意。求你叫我肯上到山上,看清你的蓝图;更求你照你的样式,把基督建造在我里面,使我成为你所要的居所。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
On the mountain, God showed Moses the pattern for the tabernacle piece by piece — from the ark, the table for the bread of the Presence, the lampstand, down to every detail of the tent — and at the end solemnly charged him: “And see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain” (Exodus 25:40). Not one peg or ring of the tabernacle was Moses’s own invention; all was according to the heavenly blueprint God had shown him. Nothing was to be added, nothing taken away.

Hidden here is a very deep spiritual principle: everything that belongs to God has God’s own pattern, and can never be conceived by human cleverness. The tabernacle is a shadow of the true tent in heaven (Hebrews 8:5), and what it foreshadows is Christ and his salvation — the tablets of the law inside the ark point to the Lord who fully carried out God’s will, the mercy seat points to the redemption he accomplished through his death, the curtain points to his body torn for us. If Moses had altered even a fraction on his own, what was set up would no longer be God’s testimony, but a religion of human hands. Hebrews goes further, saying the heavenly realities themselves need to be cleansed with “better sacrifices,” because Christ “has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24) — the earthly tabernacle was only an image of that better, true sanctuary; Christ is the one who truly, directly entered God’s presence.

Our greatest danger in serving God today is not a lack of zeal, but doing God’s work according to what “seems good to ourselves.” What God wants was never for us to design something for him, but for us to obey what he has revealed. If spiritual building work is mixed with human ideas, it may look magnificent outwardly, yet lose God’s presence within. True service is first going up the mountain to see God’s pattern clearly, and only then coming down to act accordingly.

Beloved, you and I are also a temple God intends to build according to his pattern. He has a blueprint set for you, and does not allow you or me to alter it by our own will. Are you willing to lay down your own designs, go up before God day by day, draw on his intent, and let him build Christ into you, bit by bit, according to his own pattern? The outward work can be judged by others, but the inward pattern only God knows.

Meditation: In my service and life, how much is “according to God’s pattern,” and how much is “according to what I think is good”? Am I willing to go up the mountain first, to see his intent clearly?

Application: Today, in something you’ve been pushing forward by your own will, stop, be still before God, and seek his pattern; better to go slower, yet act according to his intent.

Prayer: Lord, you commanded Moses to do everything according to the pattern shown on the mountain, allowing no human addition. I confess I often do your work according to what I think is good, mixing in much of my own will. Let me be willing to go up the mountain and see your blueprint clearly; and, according to your pattern, build Christ into me, so that I become the dwelling place you intend. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 洗净才可近前——事奉神,不可随便
entries.title_en: Cleansed Before Drawing Near — Serving God Is No Casual Matter
entries.verse: 出埃及记三十章十九至二十节
entries.content:
神吩咐要造一个铜盆,放在会幕和祭坛之间,盛满了水。亚伦和他的儿子们每逢进会幕事奉、或到坛前献祭,「必用水洗濯,免得死亡」(出30:20)。请注意那句话——「免得死亡」。近前事奉圣洁的神,从来不是一件可以随随便便的事;不洁而擅入,是要付上性命的。

我们这一代信徒,很容易把亲近神看得太轻。我们迟到、分心,带着满心的污秽和世俗就冲到神面前,唱几首诗歌,讲几句祷告,仿佛神欠我们什么。可是圣经里的这位神,是又真又活、圣洁可畏的神。祭司若不先在铜盆前洗净,就不得近前。这幅图画在质问我们:我到底把与神的相会,当成了什么?

感谢神,今天我们不再靠铜盆的水,乃是靠基督——祂用自己的血洗净我们的良心,又「用水藉着道」把我们洗净(弗5:26)。希伯来书说得更加坦然:「我们既因耶稣的血得以坦然进入至圣所……身体用清水洗净了,就当存着诚心和充足的信心来到神面前」(来10:19-22)。铜盆的水年年重洗,基督的血却一次洗净,永远有效——但这绝不意味着我们可以随便;恰恰相反,正因祂付了这么大的代价洗净我们,我们更当存敬畏的心,天天让祂洁净我们的手和心,才近前事奉。廉价的亲近,是对那宝血的轻慢。

你上一次带着敬畏、预备好自己来到神面前,是什么时候?若诚实说,我们大多数的「灵修」和「事奉」,都太随便、太仓促、太不当一回事了。神配得我们全心的、洁净的、预备好的敬拜。今天,别再匆匆冲进冲出;先停下来,让神洗净你,然后带着敬畏与渴慕,近前来。祂是圣洁的,也要祂的子民圣洁。

默想:我亲近神、事奉神的态度,是敬畏而预备的,还是随便又仓促的?这反映出我心里如何看待祂?

应用:今天在灵修或聚会之前,特意留几分钟安静下来,认罪、求神洁净你的心,预备好了再近前——不再匆匆忙忙。

祷告:圣洁的主,祭司若不先洗净就不得近前事奉你,免得死亡。我承认我太多次带着污秽和随便的心冲到你面前,轻看了亲近你这件事的宝贵。感谢你用基督的宝血一次洗净了我,又给我开了一条又新又活的路。求你叫我天天存敬畏的心,让你洁净我的手与心,以圣洁、预备、全心的敬拜来到你面前。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God commanded that a bronze basin be made, placed between the tent of meeting and the altar, filled with water. Whenever Aaron and his sons entered the tent to serve, or came near the altar to offer sacrifice, “they shall wash with water, so that they may not die” (Exodus 30:20). Notice that phrase — “so that they may not die.” Drawing near to serve the holy God was never something to be taken casually; entering unclean was a matter of life and death.

Our generation of believers finds it all too easy to take drawing near to God too lightly. We show up late, distracted, rushing into God’s presence full of filth and worldliness, sing a few songs, say a few prayers, as if God owed us something. But the God of Scripture is the true and living God, holy and awesome. If the priest did not first wash at the bronze basin, he could not draw near. This picture questions us: what exactly have I made of meeting with God?

Thank God, today we no longer rely on the water of the bronze basin, but on Christ — he cleanses our conscience with his own blood, and “cleansing her by the washing of water with the word” (Ephesians 5:26). Hebrews puts it even more plainly: “since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus... having our bodies washed with pure water, let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:19–22). The water of the bronze basin had to be washed in year after year, but Christ’s blood cleanses once, forever effective — yet this in no way means we can be careless; on the contrary, precisely because he paid such a great price to cleanse us, we should hold him in even greater reverence, letting him cleanse our hands and hearts daily before we draw near to serve. Cheap intimacy is contempt for that precious blood.

When was the last time you came before God with reverence, having prepared yourself? If we’re honest, most of our “devotions” and “service” are far too casual, too rushed, taken far too lightly. God deserves our wholehearted, cleansed, prepared worship. Today, stop rushing in and out; first pause, let God cleanse you, then draw near with reverence and longing. He is holy, and requires his people to be holy too.

Meditation: Is my attitude in drawing near to and serving God reverent and prepared, or careless and rushed? What does this reflect about how I truly regard him in my heart?

Application: Today, before your devotions or gathering, deliberately spend a few minutes being still, confessing sin, asking God to cleanse your heart, and preparing yourself before drawing near — no longer rushing.

Prayer: Holy Lord, the priests could not draw near to serve you without first being washed, lest they die. I confess I have too often rushed into your presence full of filth and carelessness, taking lightly the preciousness of drawing near to you. Thank you for cleansing me once, forever, with Christ’s precious blood, and opening for me a new and living way. Let me hold a reverent heart day by day, letting you cleanse my hands and heart, coming before you in holy, prepared, wholehearted worship. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 金牛犊,与那有恩典的神
entries.title_en: The Golden Calf, and the God of Grace
entries.verse: 出埃及记卅四章六至七节
entries.content:
摩西还在山上与神相会,山下的百姓就等不及了。他们对亚伦说:「起来!为我们做神像,可以在我们前面引路。」于是他们把金环铸成一只牛犊,向它下拜献祭,说这就是领他们出埃及的神(出32:1-4)。刚刚才在雷声中听过「除我以外你不可有别神」的百姓,转眼就造了偶像。人心真是一座不停歇的偶像工厂。

我们或许笑他们愚昧,但我们的心与他们何异?偶像未必是金牛犊,它可以是事业、婚姻、儿女、名声、安全感——任何一样我们对自己说「有了它,我才活得下去」的东西。当神「显得太慢」、太遥远,我们就转向那些看得见、抓得住、能立刻给我们掌控感的替代品。金牛犊的本质,是想要一位听我使唤的神。

然而这段经文最震撼的,不是人的悖逆,而是神的恩典。百姓犯了如此大罪,本该被灭绝;摩西却为他们代求,神竟然应允。更叫人惊讶的是,神主动向摩西宣告祂的名:「耶和华,耶和华,是有怜悯有恩典的神,不轻易发怒,并有丰盛的慈爱和诚实……赦免罪孽、过犯和罪恶」(出34:6-7)。正是在人背叛到极点的地方,神却启示了祂恩典的深度。

这恩典最终指向十字架。神「万不以有罪的为无罪」,罪必被追讨——可是在基督身上,公义与慈爱相遇了:祂追讨了罪,却是追讨在那替我们受死的圣子身上,「神设立耶稣作挽回祭,是凭着耶稣的血,藉着人的信,要显明神的义」(罗3:25)。所以我们不必像那些百姓一样,靠自造的偶像来换取安全感;我们有一位真正「有怜悯有恩典」的神,祂已在十字架上证明了祂的爱。放下你的金牛犊吧——它给不了你真正要的,唯有祂能。

默想:在我心里,有哪一样东西是我的「金牛犊」——我以为「有了它才活得下去」的替代品?

应用:今天诚实指认一个你正在倚靠、用来换取安全感或掌控感的偶像,把它带到神面前,宣告唯有祂是你的神,求祂的恩典释放你。

祷告:有怜悯有恩典的主,我承认我的心像一座偶像的工厂,常常在你显得太慢时,转向那些看得见、抓得住的替代品。感谢你,竟在人背叛到极点之处启示你恩典的深度,又在十字架上让公义与慈爱相遇,亲自成了那挽回祭。求你拆毁我心中的金牛犊,叫我以你——那位真正有恩典的神——为我唯一的倚靠和满足。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Moses was still meeting with God on the mountain, and the people below couldn’t wait. They said to Aaron: “Up, make us gods who shall go before us.” So they cast their gold rings into a calf, bowed down and sacrificed to it, saying this was the god who brought them out of Egypt (Exodus 32:1–4). The very people who had just heard, amid thunder, “You shall have no other gods before me,” turned right around and made an idol. The human heart really is a never-resting idol factory.

We may laugh at their foolishness, but how different are our hearts from theirs? The idol need not be a golden calf — it can be career, marriage, children, reputation, a sense of security — anything we tell ourselves, “with this, I can go on living.” When God “seems too slow,” too distant, we turn to substitutes we can see, grasp, that give us instant control. The essence of the golden calf is wanting a god who obeys our commands.

Yet the most shocking thing in this passage is not human rebellion, but God’s grace. The people had committed so great a sin they deserved to be destroyed; but Moses interceded for them, and God actually agreed. Even more astonishing, God proactively declared his name to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness... forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin” (Exodus 34:6–7). It was precisely at the point of humanity’s utmost betrayal that God revealed the depth of his grace.

This grace ultimately points to the cross. God “will by no means clear the guilty” — sin must be dealt with — yet in Christ, justice and mercy meet: he dealt with sin, but dealt with it upon the holy Son who died in our place — “God put forward [Jesus] as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith... it was to show God’s righteousness” (Romans 3:25). So we don’t need to be like those people, relying on self-made idols to secure ourselves; we have a God who is truly “merciful and gracious,” who has already proven his love on the cross. Lay down your golden calf — it cannot give you what you truly need; only he can.

Meditation: In my heart, what is my “golden calf” — the substitute I think “I can’t live without”?

Application: Today, honestly name an idol you’re currently relying on for security or control, bring it before God, declare that he alone is your God, and ask for his grace to set you free.

Prayer: Merciful and gracious Lord, I confess my heart is like an idol factory, often turning to visible, graspable substitutes when you seem too slow. Thank you that precisely at the point of humanity’s utmost betrayal, you revealed the depth of your grace, and on the cross let justice and mercy meet, personally becoming that propitiation. Tear down the golden calf in my heart, and let you — the truly gracious God — be my only reliance and satisfaction. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 在祂的同在里安息
entries.title_en: Resting in His Presence
entries.content:
在祂的同在里安息

「我必亲自和你同去，使你得安息。」(出埃及记 33:14)

这一周,我们随着以色列人走过旷野——天降的吗哪、西奈的雷声、金牛犊的失败,又看见那位「有怜悯有恩典」的神。走到这里,你或许也累了。

神给摩西的应许,今天也给你:不是先给你力量再上路,而是「我必亲自和你同去」。真正的安息,不在于路好走,而在于有祂同行。今天,停下来,安息在祂的同在里。

"My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." (Exodus 33:14)
entries.content_en:
Resting in His Presence

"My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." (Exodus 33:14)

This week, we walked with the Israelites through the wilderness — manna falling from heaven, thunder at Sinai, the failure of the golden calf — and saw the God who is "merciful and gracious." By now, you too may be weary.

The promise God gave Moses is given to you today as well: not strength first, then the road, but "My presence will go with you." True rest is not found in an easy road, but in his walking with you. Today, stop, and rest in his presence.

"My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." (Exodus 33:14)

entries.title: 甘心乐意的奉献——心被恩感的人,拦都拦不住
entries.title_en: Willing, Joyful Giving — A Heart Moved by Grace Cannot Be Held Back
entries.scripture: 出卅五至四十章（参廿五至三十章）
entries.verse: 出埃及记卅五章廿一节，卅六章七节
entries.content:
会幕的样式已经启示,如今要动工建造。神没有派人挨家收税,乃是说:「凡乐意献的可以拿耶和华的礼物来」(出35:5)。结果如何?「凡心里受感和甘心乐意的」都把金银、宝石、细麻、山羊毛拿来(出35:21)。他们献得如此踊跃,以致工匠不得不来对摩西说:百姓所拿来的已经「有余」了,摩西只好下令止住(出36:6-7)。这是圣经里少有的一幕:不是催人多奉献,而是拦人别再送。

是什么叫一群刚出为奴之地、家底并不丰厚的人如此慷慨?不是律法的强逼,而是「心里受感」。他们亲眼见过红海分开、吗哪降下、西奈的荣耀,一颗被神的作为所折服的心,自然要把最好的献上。真正的奉献从来不是从空钱包里挤出来的义务,而是从满溢的心里流出来的喜乐。神所喜爱的,不是勉强舍出的人,乃是「捐得乐意的人是神所喜爱的」(林后9:7)。

这也暴露出我们奉献时的光景。我们常常斤斤计较、给得勉强,是因为神在我们心中还不够大、不够甜。当一个人真的看见神是何等美善、自己所蒙的是何等大恩,奉献就不再是被割肉的疼,而是得着更大喜乐的途径。会幕之所以建得成,不是因为百姓被逼,而是因为百姓被神的荣耀充满了心。

那使以色列人「拦都拦不住」地献上金银的荣耀,最终在十字架上,以一种更深的方式向我们显明。保罗说:「你们知道我们主耶稣基督的恩典:他本来富足,却为你们成了贫穷,叫你们因他的贫穷,可以成为富足」(林后8:9)。以色列人是把有余的献给神,基督却是把自己所有的一切——祂的荣耀、祂的丰富——全然倾倒,为要使贫穷的我们成为富足。你有没有发现,你最舍不得给的地方,往往就是神在你心里还没坐上宝座的地方?所以要祈求的,不是先改变你的账本,而是先俘获你的心;当你想起基督那更深的「甘心贫穷」,你的手自然会松开。今天不妨问自己:若有一件事叫我像那些百姓一样「拦都拦不住」地献上,那会是什么?那,就是我心被恩感的记号。

默想:我的奉献(时间、钱财、才干),是出于「不得不」的义务,还是「拦不住」的喜乐?这反映出神在我心中有多大?

应用:今天凭着感恩,在一处你一向给得勉强的地方(奉献、服事、款待),甘心乐意地多献上一点,不为交差,只为回应神。

祷告:满有荣耀的神,昔日你的百姓因心里受感,把礼物献得有余,连工都得止住;基督更是甘心成了贫穷,叫我们因他的贫穷成为富足。我承认我常常给得勉强、算得精细,因为你在我心中还不够大。求你俘获我的心,叫我先看见你的美善与大恩,好叫奉献成为我的喜乐,而非重担。愿我以甘心乐意的手,回应你白白的恩典。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The pattern for the tabernacle had already been revealed; now the work of building it began. God did not send collectors door to door, but said, “Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD’s contribution” (Exodus 35:5). What happened? “Everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him” brought gold, silver, precious stones, fine linen, goat hair (Exodus 35:21). They gave so eagerly that the craftsmen had to come tell Moses: what the people had brought was “more than enough” — Moses had to order them to stop (Exodus 36:6–7). This is a rare scene in Scripture: not urging people to give more, but stopping them from sending more.

What made a people freshly out of slavery, with no great wealth, so generous? Not the compulsion of law, but “their hearts stirred.” They had seen with their own eyes the Red Sea part, the manna fall, the glory at Sinai — a heart overwhelmed by God’s works naturally offers its very best. True giving has never been a duty squeezed out of an empty wallet, but a joy overflowing from a full heart. What God delights in is not someone who gives reluctantly, but this: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

This also exposes our own condition when we give. We often calculate and give reluctantly because God is not yet big enough, not yet sweet enough, in our hearts. When someone truly sees how good God is, how great the grace they’ve received, giving is no longer a painful cutting-away, but a path to greater joy. The tabernacle was not built because the people were forced, but because their hearts were filled with God’s glory.

That glory which made the Israelites “unable to be stopped” from offering gold and silver was finally shown to us, in an even deeper way, on the cross. Paul says: “you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Israelites gave from their surplus to God, but Christ poured out everything he had — his glory, his riches — completely, so that we, the poor, might become rich. Have you noticed that the place you’re most reluctant to give is often exactly the place where God has not yet taken the throne of your heart? So what to pray for is not first changing your ledger, but first capturing your heart; when you remember Christ’s deeper “willing poverty,” your hands will naturally open. Today, ask yourself: if there were one thing that would move me, like those people, to give “unstoppably,” what would it be? That is the sign that my heart has been moved by grace.

Meditation: Is my giving (of time, money, ability) out of “obligation I can’t avoid,” or “joy that can’t be stopped”? What does this reflect about how big God is in my heart?

Application: Today, out of gratitude, in one area where you’ve always given reluctantly (giving, service, hospitality), give a little more willingly and joyfully — not to check a box, but simply in response to God.

Prayer: Glorious God, in ancient days your people’s hearts were so stirred that they gave more than enough, and even the work had to be stopped; Christ was even more willing to become poor, so that we, through his poverty, might become rich. I confess I often give reluctantly, calculating carefully, because you are not yet big enough in my heart. Capture my heart, let me see your goodness and great grace first, so that giving becomes my joy, not my burden. May I respond to your free grace with willing, joyful hands. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 馨香的燔祭——每一样祭都指向基督
entries.title_en: The Pleasing Aroma of the Burnt Offering — Every Sacrifice Points to Christ
entries.verse: 利未记一章十节
entries.content:
利未记一开头,神就细细吩咐各样的祭:燔祭、素祭、平安祭。在今天的人看来,这些宰杀牲畜、洒血献脂的规条,既陌生又难懂。但请记住一件事:这一切「原是后事的影儿;那形体却是基督」(西2:17)。每一样祭,都从不同的角度,预表那位要来的救主。

燔祭是把全牲烧在坛上,一无保留,作馨香的火祭献给耶和华——它预表基督将自己完全献上,毫无保留地顺服父神,「当作馨香的供物和祭物,献与神」(弗5:2)。素祭是细面调油、没有酵,历代解经者多从其纯净无酵中,看见主耶稣那全然无瑕的完美人性的影儿。平安祭则是献祭的人与神、与人一同分享,预表藉着基督,我们与神和好,得以在祂里面同得安息与相交。

要紧的是那句「没有残疾的」(利1:10)。凡献给神的,必须是无瑕疵的;稍有残疾,神就不悦纳。这标准何等之高,高到没有一个罪人、没有一只牲畜能真正满足。它是在遥指那位独一「无瑕疵、无玷污的羔羊」(彼前1:19)——唯有基督,才是那真正无残疾、蒙神全然悦纳的祭物。希伯来书告诉我们,基督到世上来的时候就说:「祭物和礼物是你不愿意的,你曾给我预备了身体……我来了,为要照你的旨意行」(来10:5-7)——祂来,不是要献上牛羊,而是献上祂自己的身体,一次成全了这一切影儿所指向的实体。

亲爱的,我们读这些古老的祭礼,不是为了考据,而是为了在其中一次又一次地遇见基督。当你看见燔祭,就看见主的全然摆上;看见那无残疾的要求,就看见唯有主能满足;然后你会明白:祂已经一次献上,把一切都成全了。我们如今所能献的,不再是牛羊,乃是「将身体献上,当作活祭」(罗12:1),来回应祂那馨香的舍己。

默想:我读旧约的祭礼时,是把它当作陌生的古制,还是在其中寻见基督?我又是否把自己当作活祭,回应祂的舍己?

应用:今天默想「燔祭全然摆上」的画面,求主光照:我的生命里,有哪一样是我一直留着、不肯完全交给祂的?把它放上坛。

祷告:主啊,古时的祭都是影儿,你才是那无瑕无疵、蒙神悦纳的真祭。感谢你如燔祭一般,将自己毫无保留地献上,成了馨香;你来,原是为要照父的旨意行。我承认我常常留着自己,不肯全然摆上。求你叫我在这些古老的祭礼中一再遇见你,又叫我以身体为活祭,回应你舍己的大爱。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
At the opening of Leviticus, God gives detailed instructions for each kind of offering: the burnt offering, the grain offering, the peace offering. To people today, these regulations of slaughtering animals, sprinkling blood, and burning fat seem both strange and hard to understand. But remember one thing: all of this is “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17). Each offering, from a different angle, foreshadows the Savior who was to come.

The burnt offering was the whole animal burned on the altar, held back in nothing, offered as a pleasing fire offering to the LORD — it foreshadows Christ offering himself completely, obeying the Father without reserve, “a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). The grain offering was fine flour mixed with oil, without leaven; many interpreters through the ages have seen in its purity, its being unleavened, a shadow of the Lord Jesus’s utterly spotless, perfect humanity. The peace offering was shared between the one offering it, God, and other people, foreshadowing that through Christ, we are reconciled to God, and are able to enjoy rest and fellowship together in him.

What matters is that phrase, “without blemish” (Leviticus 1:10). Whatever was offered to God had to be spotless; the slightest blemish, and God would not accept it. How high a standard this is — so high that no sinner, no animal, could ever truly satisfy it. It points far ahead to that one “lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19) — only Christ is the truly unblemished offering, fully accepted by God. Hebrews tells us that when Christ came into the world, he said: “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me... Behold, I have come to do your will” (Hebrews 10:5–7) — he came not to offer bulls and goats, but to offer his own body, once for all fulfilling the reality to which all these shadows pointed.

Beloved, we read these ancient sacrificial rites not for the sake of study, but to meet Christ in them, again and again. When you see the burnt offering, you see the Lord’s total self-giving; when you see the requirement of “without blemish,” you see that only the Lord can satisfy it; and then you will understand: he has already offered himself once, and fulfilled it all. What we can offer now is no longer bulls and goats, but “to present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1), responding to his fragrant self-giving.

Meditation: When I read the Old Testament sacrifices, do I treat them as a strange ancient custom, or do I find Christ in them? Do I offer myself as a living sacrifice, in response to his self-giving?

Application: Today, meditate on the picture of “the burnt offering, held back in nothing”; ask the Lord to shine light: what is there in my life that I’ve been holding onto, unwilling to fully hand over to him? Place it on the altar.

Prayer: Lord, the ancient sacrifices were all shadows; you are the true sacrifice, without blemish, fully accepted by God. Thank you for offering yourself, like the burnt offering, without reserve, becoming a pleasing aroma; you came to do the Father’s will. I confess I often hold myself back, unwilling to give fully. Let me meet you again and again in these ancient sacrifices, and offer my body as a living sacrifice, in response to your great, self-giving love. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 虽然不知道,还是有罪——赎罪祭里的严肃与恩典
entries.title_en: Even Unknowingly, Still Guilty — Severity and Grace in the Sin Offering
entries.verse: 利未记五章十七节
entries.content:
利未记四至七章讲的是赎罪祭与赎愆祭。其中有一句话叫人不寒而栗:「若有人犯罪……他虽然不知道,还是有了罪,就要担当他的罪孽」(利5:17)。在神面前,罪不因「我不是故意的」「我不知道」就自动一笔勾销。神的标准是客观的:违背了就是违背了,无知并不免罪。

这与今天流行的观念正相反。人常说「我又没害着谁」「我良心过得去」,仿佛罪的轻重取决于我们的感觉和动机。但圣经告诉我们,罪的本质是干犯了圣洁之神的诫命,它的严重不由我们评估,而由神的圣洁来衡量。连无心之失都需要献祭遮盖,更何况我们那些明知故犯的罪?律法在这里毫不含糊地拆穿了人的自义。

然而,赎罪祭的存在本身,就是天大的恩典。神大可以一犯罪就击杀,祂却设立了献祭的路,让有罪的人可以藉着一个替代者的血得赦免——因为若不流血,罪就不得赦免(参利17:11;来9:22)。这幅严肃的图画在预备人心:罪必须付上血的代价,而人自己付不起。它叫我们不敢轻看罪,也叫我们渴望一位真正能除罪的救主。

那位救主已经来了。牛羊的血只能遮盖罪,不能除去罪,年年都要重献;唯有基督的血,一次献上,就把罪彻底除去。希伯来书说:「我们凭这旨意,靠耶稣基督,只一次献上他的身体,就得以成圣」(来10:10),又说这一次的献上,永远成全了那些得以成圣的人(来10:11-14)。所以基督徒面对罪,既不轻慢——因为罪曾把神的儿子钉上十字架;也不绝望——因为祂的血已经把我们洗净,一次,永远。求神叫我们对罪有神那样的严肃,也对赦免有神那样的确信。

默想:我是否常以「不是故意的」「没那么严重」来轻看自己的罪?若照神的圣洁来衡量,我会如何看待它?

应用:今天求圣灵光照一件你一向不当回事的「小罪」,不再为它辩解,而是认真认罪,并支取基督宝血的赦免。

祷告:圣洁公义的神,你说人虽然不知道,犯了罪还是有罪,叫我看见我无法用无知或动机为自己开脱。我承认我常轻看自己的罪。感谢你设立赎罪的路,更感谢主耶稣只一次献上自己的身体,就永远成全了我的成圣。求你叫我既严肃地看待罪,又确信地支取你的赦免。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Leviticus 4–7 speaks of the sin offering and the guilt offering. Among them is a chilling statement: “if anyone sins... though he does not know it, he is guilty and shall bear his iniquity” (Leviticus 5:17). Before God, sin is not automatically wiped away just because “I didn’t mean to” or “I didn’t know.” God’s standard is objective: a violation is a violation; ignorance does not clear the guilt.

This runs directly opposite to today’s popular thinking. People often say, “I didn’t hurt anyone,” “my conscience is clear,” as if the severity of sin depended on our own feelings and motives. But Scripture tells us the essence of sin is violating the commandment of a holy God; its severity is not measured by our own assessment, but by God’s holiness. Even an unintentional slip required a sacrifice to cover it — how much more the sins we knowingly commit? The law here unflinchingly exposes human self-righteousness.

Yet the very existence of the sin offering is itself immense grace. God could well have struck down anyone who sinned on the spot, yet he established a way of sacrifice, so that the guilty could be forgiven through a substitute’s blood — for without the shedding of blood, there is no forgiveness of sins (cf. Leviticus 17:11; Hebrews 9:22). This solemn picture prepares the heart: sin must be paid for with blood, and no one can pay that price himself. It makes us unwilling to take sin lightly, and makes us long for a Savior who can truly remove sin.

That Savior has already come. The blood of bulls and goats could only cover sin, not remove it, and had to be offered again year after year; only Christ’s blood, offered once, thoroughly removes sin. Hebrews says: “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10), and that this one offering perfects forever those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:11–14). So a Christian, facing sin, neither takes it lightly — for sin once nailed God’s Son to the cross — nor despairs — for his blood has washed us clean, once, forever. May God let us take sin as seriously as he does, and hold the same confidence in forgiveness as he gives.

Meditation: Do I often excuse my own sin with “I didn’t mean to” or “it’s not that serious”? Measured by God’s holiness, how would I see it?

Application: Today, ask the Spirit to shine light on one “small sin” you’ve always dismissed; stop making excuses for it, take it seriously, confess it, and draw on the forgiveness of Christ’s blood.

Prayer: Holy and righteous God, you say that even unknowingly, a person who sins is still guilty, showing me I cannot excuse myself with ignorance or intention. I confess I often take my own sin lightly. Thank you for establishing a way of atonement, and even more, thank you that the Lord Jesus, offering his own body once, forever perfected my sanctification. Let me take sin seriously, and confidently draw on your forgiveness. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 只一次献上就成全了——从没完没了的献祭,到一次到永远
entries.title_en: Offered Once, and It Was Finished — From Endless Sacrifice to Once for All
entries.verse: 希伯来书七章廿七节
entries.content:
利未记八至十章记载祭司的就职:亚伦和他的儿子受膏、献祭、开始供职。以色列的献祭制度就此运转起来——但那是一套没完没了的制度。祭司每天都要献祭,而且「必须先为自己的罪,后为百姓的罪献祭」(来7:27),因为他们自己也是罪人。血流了又流,祭献了又献,却没有一次能真正解决问题。

这其实是一切宗教的写照。宗教的逻辑是:我要不断地做、不断地献、不断地努力,好换取神的悦纳;可是无论献多少,心里总不踏实,因为你永远不确定「够了没有」。那位每天重复献祭的祭司,正是每一个想靠自己表现来换取接纳之人的缩影——永远在做,永远不安。

就在这神圣职分开始的同一章,亚伦的两个儿子拿答、亚比户「各拿自己的香炉,盛上火,加上香,在耶和华面前献上凡火,是耶和华没有吩咐他们的」,结果「就有火从耶和华面前出来,把他们烧灭」(利10:1-2)。这幅严厉的画面提醒我们:近前事奉这位神,从不是照自己的意思随便行事,即便是受膏的祭司也不例外。希伯来书后来这样劝勉信徒:「我们既得了不能震动的国,就当感恩,照神所喜悦的,用虔诚、敬畏的心事奉神;因为我们的神乃是烈火」(来12:28-29)——基督成全了献祭,却从未叫祂的圣洁变得可以轻慢。

然而希伯来书说,主耶稣「不像那些大祭司……因为他只一次将自己献上,就把这事成全了」(来7:27)。祂是无罪的祭司,不需要先为自己赎罪;祂所献的是祂自己,一次献上,直到永远。祂在十字架上说「成了」(约19:30)——不是「我尽力了」,而是「全办妥了」。那没完没了的循环,在祂这里画上了句号。

这就是福音与宗教的天壤之别。宗教说「因为我做,所以神接纳我」;福音说「因为基督已经成全,所以神接纳我」。若你今天仍在灵里疲于奔命,总觉得要多做点什么才配得神的爱,请听主那句「成了」。你不必再为自己的罪献祭了——那一次,已经够了,够到永远。你如今的顺服,不是为赚取接纳,而是活在那已成就的接纳里、又存虔诚敬畏之心的感恩。

默想:我与神的关系,是建立在「我做了多少」上,还是建立在「基督已成全」上?哪一个让我心里真正踏实?

应用:今天指认一处你仍在「靠表现换取神(或人)接纳」的疲惫,把它带到十字架前,以主那句「成了」来安息,不再证明自己。

祷告:主耶稣,那些祭司每天献祭,永不得完;你却只一次将自己献上,就把一切都成全了。我承认我常像那疲惫的祭司,想靠不停地做来换取接纳,心里总不踏实。感谢你在十字架上说「成了」。求你叫我安息在你已成的救恩里,以虔诚敬畏、感恩而非交易的心来跟随你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Leviticus 8–10 records the ordination of the priests: Aaron and his sons were anointed, offered sacrifices, and began their service. Israel’s sacrificial system was now running — but it was an endless system. The priests had to offer sacrifices every day, and “he had to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people” (Hebrews 7:27), because they themselves were sinners too. Blood flowed again and again, sacrifices were offered again and again, yet not one of them ever truly solved the problem.

This is really a portrait of all religion. Religion’s logic is: I must keep doing, keep offering, keep striving, to earn God’s favor; yet no matter how much you offer, your heart is never at ease, because you can never be sure whether it’s “enough.” The priest who daily repeated his sacrifice is precisely a miniature of everyone who tries to earn acceptance through their own performance — forever working, forever restless.

In this very same chapter, at the start of this sacred office, Aaron’s two sons Nadab and Abihu “each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them,” and “fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them” (Leviticus 10:1–2). This severe scene reminds us: drawing near to serve this God is never something to be done however one pleases, not even for anointed priests. Hebrews later exhorts believers this way: “let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29) — Christ fulfilled the sacrifice, but never made his holiness something to be trifled with.

Yet Hebrews says the Lord Jesus “is not like those high priests... because he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27). He is the sinless priest, needing no atonement for himself first; what he offered was himself, offered once, forever. On the cross he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30) — not “I did my best,” but “it is entirely done.” That endless cycle came to a full stop in him.

This is the world of difference between the gospel and religion. Religion says, “Because I do, God accepts me.” The gospel says, “Because Christ has already finished it, God accepts me.” If you’re today still running yourself ragged in spirit, always feeling you must do more to deserve God’s love, hear the Lord’s word, “It is finished.” You no longer need to offer sacrifices for your own sin — that one offering was already enough, enough forever. Your obedience now is not to earn acceptance, but to live within the acceptance already accomplished, with a grateful heart of reverence and awe.

Meditation: Is my relationship with God built on “how much I’ve done,” or built on “Christ has already finished it”? Which one truly settles my heart?

Application: Today, name one area where you’re still exhausted trying to “earn acceptance from God (or others) through performance,” bring it to the foot of the cross, and rest in the Lord’s word, “It is finished,” no longer trying to prove yourself.

Prayer: Lord Jesus, those priests offered sacrifices every day, never finished; but you offered yourself once, and finished it all. I confess I’m often like that weary priest, trying to earn acceptance through endless doing, my heart never settled. Thank you for saying “It is finished” on the cross. Let me rest in the salvation you have already accomplished, following you with a reverent, grateful heart, not a transactional one. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
