entries.title: 你们要圣洁——分别为圣,不是可有可无
entries.title_en: You Shall Be Holy — Being Set Apart Is Not Optional
entries.verse: 马太福音十五章十一节
entries.content:
利未记十一至十四章,细细分辨洁净与不洁净:可吃的、不可吃的,身体的洁净、衣物房屋的处理。贯穿其间的,是神反复申明的一句话:「你们要圣洁,因为我是圣洁的」(利11:45)。神把祂的百姓从万民中分别出来,要他们连日常饮食起居,都活出与外邦人不一样的分别为圣。

今天很多信徒把「圣洁」当作一个过时、扫兴的词,仿佛那是律法主义者才在意的东西。我们更爱谈恩典、谈自由,却把圣洁悄悄挪到一边。可是神的心意从未改变:「那召你们的既是圣洁,你们在一切所行的事上也要圣洁」(彼前1:15)。蒙恩,从来不是叫我们照旧活在污秽里,而是叫我们分别归神。

主耶稣把这分别推向更深处。祂说:「入口的不能污秽人,出口的乃能污秽人」(太15:11)。真正的不洁,不在于吃了什么、碰了什么,而在于人心里所发出来的——恶念、苟合、凶杀、贪婪。外面的洁净规条,原是要指向内心的洁净。神要的不只是干净的手,更是干净的心;保罗也提醒我们身体本身仍然重要:「你们的身子就是圣灵的殿……你们是重价买来的,所以要在你们的身子上荣耀神」(林前6:19-20)——圣洁从心里发出,却也活在身体的每一个选择里。

这就叫我们无法躲在「反正靠恩典」的借口后面,继续纵容心里的污秽。分别为圣是要付代价的:它意味着在这个什么都可以的时代,甘愿为神的缘故活得不一样——在娱乐上、言语上、金钱上、两性上,划出别人不划的界线。你今天生活中,有哪一处是你一直用「恩典」来遮掩、其实是不肯分别为圣的?神的呼召很清楚:你们要圣洁,因为我是圣洁的。

默想:我是不是把「圣洁」当成扫兴的旧观念,而更爱谈不必付代价的「恩典」?神所要的洁净,是外面的,还是里面的?

应用:今天求神指出一处你一直纵容、却用「靠恩典」来遮掩的不洁(眼目、言语、隐秘的习惯),为神的缘故,向它划一条清楚的界线。

祷告:圣洁的主,你一再吩咐:「你们要圣洁,因为我是圣洁的。」我承认我常爱谈恩典、却不肯付分别为圣的代价,任由心里的污秽存留。主耶稣说,污秽人的是从心里出来的——求你不只洁净我的手,更洁净我的心与身体的每一个选择。叫我甘愿为你的缘故,在这弯曲的世代活得不一样。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Leviticus 11–14 carefully distinguishes clean from unclean: what may be eaten, what may not, the cleansing of the body, the handling of clothing and houses. Running through it all is one phrase God repeatedly states: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11:45). God set his people apart from all nations, wanting even their daily eating and living to look different, set apart, from the Gentiles.

Today, many believers treat “holiness” as an outdated, killjoy word, as if it were something only legalists cared about. We prefer to talk about grace, about freedom, and quietly set holiness aside. But God’s intent has never changed: “as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15). Being saved by grace has never meant we go on living in the same filth as before, but that we are set apart, belonging to God.

The Lord Jesus pushed this separation even deeper. He said: “it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth” (Matthew 15:11). True uncleanness is not about what you eat or touch, but what comes out from within — evil thoughts, sexual immorality, murder, greed. The outward rules of cleanliness were meant, all along, to point to the cleanness of the heart. God wants not just clean hands, but a clean heart; Paul also reminds us the body itself still matters: “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit... you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20) — holiness flows from the heart, yet is also lived out in every choice of the body.

This means we cannot hide behind the excuse “it’s all grace anyway” and keep indulging the filth in our hearts. Being set apart costs something: it means, in an age where anything goes, being willing to live differently for God’s sake — drawing lines in entertainment, in speech, in money, in sexuality, that others don’t draw. Today in your life, is there some area you’ve been covering with “grace,” when really you’re just unwilling to be set apart? God’s calling is clear: you shall be holy, for I am holy.

Meditation: Do I treat “holiness” as an outdated, killjoy idea, preferring instead to talk about a “grace” that costs nothing? Is the cleanliness God wants outward, or inward?

Application: Today, ask God to point out one uncleanness you’ve been indulging, covering it with “it’s all grace” (in what you look at, what you say, a hidden habit), and for God’s sake, draw a clear line against it.

Prayer: Holy Lord, you say again and again: “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” I confess I often love to talk about grace, yet refuse to pay the cost of being set apart, letting the filth in my heart remain. The Lord Jesus said what defiles a person comes from within — cleanse not only my hands, but my heart and every choice of my body. Let me be willing, for your sake, to live differently in this crooked generation. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 归到羊头上,带到无人之地——赎罪日与替罪的羔羊
entries.title_en: Placed on the Goat's Head, Carried to a Solitary Place — The Day of Atonement and the Scapegoat
entries.verse: 利未记十六章二十至廿二节
entries.content:
利未记十六章是整卷书的高峰:赎罪日。一年一度,大祭司要为全民赎罪。仪式的核心是两只公山羊:一只被宰杀,血带进至圣所,洒在施恩座上,平息神对罪的忿怒;另一只活着,由大祭司两手按在它头上,「承认以色列人诸般的罪孽过犯……把这罪都归在羊的头上」,然后送到旷野无人之地(利16:21-22)。一只说明罪的赎价,一只说明罪的挪去——两只羊,合起来讲明一件事:罪如何被彻底处理。

请注意那「按手」的动作。大祭司按手在羊头上认罪,象征把百姓的罪转移到那无辜牲畜的身上。牲畜没有犯罪,却要担当罪、被带离营外。这就是圣经反复宣讲的「替代」:有罪的当死,无辜的却替他受;审判临到替身,罪人因此得释放。整个赎罪日,都在为一件将来的大事作预表。

那件大事,就是各各他。施洗约翰指着耶稣说:「看哪,神的羔羊,除去世人罪孽的!」(约1:29)基督既是那被宰的羊——祂作了挽回祭,用自己的血平息了神对罪的忿怒(罗3:25);又是那被逐的羊,担当我们的罪,把罪带离了我们,不再追讨(利16:22)。希伯来书说,那用血赎罪的祭牲,身子要被烧在营外;「所以,耶稣要用自己的血叫百姓成圣,也就在城门外受苦」(来13:11-12)——祂被弃在营外羞辱之地,成就了这除罪之工。赎罪日一年一次、年年重复,证明它不能真正除罪;而基督一次献上,就永远成就了这一切。

这意味着什么?意味着信靠基督的人,罪已经被「带到无人之地」,再也追不回来了。神说:「我要赦免他们的罪孽,不再记念他们的罪恶」(耶31:34)。撒但、或你的良心,或许还想把旧账翻出来;但那只羊早已消失在旷野,神叫我们的过犯离我们,如同东离西那样远(诗103:12)。今天,你可以带着一个被彻底洁净的良心,坦然无惧地来到神面前。

默想:我是否真的相信,我的罪已被基督「带到无人之地」、神不再记念?还是我仍活在被旧罪控告的阴影里?

应用:今天把一件仍在控告、缠累你的旧罪,藉着基督——那被宰又被逐的羔羊——郑重地交出去,宣告它已被带到无人之地,不再定你的罪。

祷告:圣洁又满有恩典的神,赎罪日的两只羊,一只流血,一只被逐,都在预表主耶稣。感谢你,祂既用自己的血平息了你的忿怒,又把我的罪担到营外无人之地。我承认我常仍活在旧罪的控告里。求你叫我确信:我的罪已被除去,你不再记念。叫我以被洁净的良心,坦然来到你面前。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Leviticus 16 is the whole book’s climax: the Day of Atonement. Once a year, the high priest would make atonement for the whole nation. At the core of the ritual are two male goats: one is slaughtered, its blood carried into the Most Holy Place and sprinkled on the mercy seat, to appease God’s wrath against sin; the other is kept alive, and the high priest lays both hands on its head, “confessing over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel... putting them on the head of the goat,” and it is sent away into the wilderness, to a solitary land (Leviticus 16:21–22). One goat shows the price of sin paid; the other shows sin carried away — the two goats together declare one thing: how sin is fully dealt with.

Notice the action of “laying on of hands.” The high priest laid his hands on the goat’s head to confess sin, symbolizing the transfer of the people’s sin onto that innocent animal. The animal committed no sin, yet had to bear it, and be carried outside the camp. This is exactly the “substitution” Scripture proclaims again and again: the guilty deserved death, but the innocent bore it in their place; judgment fell on the substitute, and the sinner was thereby released. The entire Day of Atonement was a foreshadowing of a future great event.

That great event is Calvary. John the Baptist, pointing to Jesus, said: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Christ is both the goat that was slain — he became the propitiation, appeasing God’s wrath against sin with his own blood (Romans 3:25) — and the goat that was sent away, bearing our sin, carrying it away from us, no longer to be counted against us (Leviticus 16:22). Hebrews says that the bodies of the animals whose blood was brought in to make atonement for sin were burned outside the camp; “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:11–12) — he was cast out to a place of shame outside the camp, and there accomplished this work of removing sin. The Day of Atonement, repeated year after year, proved that it could not truly remove sin; but Christ, offered once, accomplished all of it forever.

What does this mean? It means that for those who trust in Christ, their sin has already been “carried to a solitary place,” never to be retrieved again. God says: “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). Satan, or your own conscience, may still try to dig up the old ledger; but that goat has long since vanished into the wilderness, and God has removed our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12). Today, you can come before God with a conscience fully cleansed, openly and without fear.

Meditation: Do I truly believe my sin has been “carried to a solitary place” by Christ, no longer remembered by God? Or am I still living in the shadow of accusation over old sins?

Application: Today, take an old sin that is still accusing and burdening you, and, through Christ — the Lamb both slain and sent away — solemnly hand it over, declaring it has been carried to a solitary place, and no longer condemns you.

Prayer: Holy and gracious God, the two goats of the Day of Atonement — one bled, one was sent away — both foreshadowed the Lord Jesus. Thank you that he both appeased your wrath with his own blood, and carried my sin outside the camp to a solitary place. I confess I still often live under the accusation of old sin. Let me be assured: my sin has been removed, and you remember it no more. Let me come before you with a cleansed conscience, openly and without fear. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 安息在已成的洁净里
entries.title_en: Resting in an Already-Accomplished Cleansing
entries.content:
安息在已成的洁净里

「因为他一次献祭，便叫那得以成圣的人永远完全。」(希伯来书 10:14)

这一周,我们走过利未记的祭坛与血——燔祭、赎罪祭、赎罪日的两只羊。所有的献祭都指向同一件事:罪必须被处理,而我们自己处理不了。

好消息是:该献的祭,基督已经一次献上;该流的血,祂已经流尽。你不必再为洗净自己而奔忙。今天,安息在祂已成就的洁净里——不是因为你做得够好,而是因为祂已成全。

"For by one sacrifice he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy." (Hebrews 10:14)
entries.content_en:
Resting in an Already-Accomplished Cleansing

"For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified." (Hebrews 10:14)

This week, we walked through Leviticus’s altars and blood — the burnt offering, the sin offering, the two goats of the Day of Atonement. All the sacrifices pointed to the same thing: sin must be dealt with, and we cannot deal with it ourselves.

The good news is: the sacrifice that needed to be offered, Christ has already offered once; the blood that needed to be shed, he has already shed completely. You no longer need to rush about trying to cleanse yourself. Today, rest in the cleansing he has already accomplished — not because you’ve done well enough, but because he has already finished it.

"For by one sacrifice he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy." (Hebrews 10:14)

entries.title: 不可效法列国——分别为圣的生活
entries.title_en: Do Not Imitate the Nations — A Life Set Apart
entries.verse: 利未记十八章三至五节，十九章廿六至廿八节
entries.content:
利未记十八至二十章,神密集地颁布关乎生活的诫命,尤其是性、家庭、公义与敬拜的界限。开篇神就定下总纲:「你们从前住的埃及地,那里人的行为,你们不可效法;我要领你们到的迦南地,那里人的行为也不可效法」(利18:3)。神的百姓,是被夹在两种文化之间的——身后是埃及,身前是迦南,而神说:两样都不可学。

神为什么如此在意这些看似琐碎的界限?因为祂在每一段诫命之后,反复盖上同一个印:「我是耶和华。」这些规条不是随意的禁忌,乃是从神的性情里流出来的。祂是圣洁的,所以祂的百姓也当圣洁:「你们要圣洁,因为我耶和华你们的神是圣洁的」(利19:2)。道德的标准不是社会约定,不随时代与民意浮动,而扎根在神那不变的本性里。

今天的世代最恨恶「界限」二字。人以「爱」「自由」「真我」之名,把神所划的线一条条抹去,尤其在性与婚姻上,把神所称为可憎的,当作时尚来追。可是神的话没有过期:效法列国的结果,不是自由,而是那地要「吐出它的居民」(利18:25)。离了造物主所定的界限,人得着的从不是解放,而是败坏。保罗在新约里说的其实是同一件事:「不要效法这个世界,只要心意更新而变化,叫你们察验何为神的善良、纯全、可喜悦的旨意」(罗12:2)——「不要效法」这四个字,跨越两约,始终是神百姓的标记。

然而基督徒的圣洁,不是靠咬牙自律去挣得神的接纳,而是因已蒙接纳、已被分别为圣,而甘心活出与神性情相称的生命。神先说「我是把你们从埃及地领出来的耶和华」,然后才说「所以你们要圣洁」。次序永远是:先救赎,后顺服。今天你我活在一个「埃及」与「迦南」之间的世界,神的呼召依然清晰:不要效法,要分别为圣,因为你是属祂的。

默想:在性、金钱、言语或敬拜上,我最容易「效法」的,是身后的「埃及」还是身前的「迦南」?我把神的界限当作捆绑,还是当作祂圣洁性情的流露?

应用:今天指认一处你正随从潮流、越过神所划界限的领域,重新立定心志,为神的缘故守住那条线。

祷告:圣洁的耶和华,你一再说「我是耶和华」,叫我知道你的诫命不是随意的禁忌,而是你圣洁本性的流露。我承认我常以自由为名,效法这世代,越过你所划的界限。感谢你先救赎了我,才呼召我圣洁。求你叫我因属你,而心意更新而变化,甘心分别为圣,在这弯曲的世代守住你的界限。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Leviticus 18–20, God densely gives commandments concerning life, especially the boundaries of sex, family, justice, and worship. At the very opening, God sets down the general principle: “You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you” (Leviticus 18:3). God’s people were caught between two cultures — Egypt behind them, Canaan ahead — and God says: imitate neither.

Why does God care so much about these seemingly trivial boundaries? Because after each set of commandments, he stamps the same seal again and again: “I am the LORD.” These rules are not arbitrary taboos, but flow out of God’s own character. He is holy, so his people must also be holy: “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (Leviticus 19:2). The standard of morality is not a social convention, does not shift with the times or public opinion, but is rooted in God’s unchanging nature.

Today’s generation hates the very word “boundary.” In the name of “love,” “freedom,” and “being true to yourself,” people erase, one by one, the lines God has drawn, especially in sex and marriage, chasing after what God calls detestable as if it were fashion. But God’s word has not expired: the result of imitating the nations is not freedom, but the land “vomiting out its inhabitants” (Leviticus 18:25). Apart from the boundaries the Creator has set, what people gain is never liberation, but corruption. Paul, in the New Testament, says essentially the same thing: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect” (Romans 12:2) — those four words, “do not be conformed,” span both covenants, and remain, always, the mark of God’s people.

Yet a Christian’s holiness is not earned by gritting one’s teeth in self-discipline to win God’s acceptance, but is a willing outflow of life fitting one’s character to God’s, precisely because one has already been accepted, already set apart. God first says, “I am the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” and only then says, “so you shall be holy.” The order is always: redemption first, obedience after. Today, you and I live in a world caught between “Egypt” and “Canaan,” and God’s call remains just as clear: do not imitate, be set apart, because you belong to him.

Meditation: In sex, money, speech, or worship, which am I most tempted to “imitate” — the “Egypt” behind me, or the “Canaan” ahead? Do I treat God’s boundaries as a restraint, or as the outflow of his holy character?

Application: Today, name an area where you’ve been following the current and crossing a boundary God has drawn, and recommit yourself to holding that line for God’s sake.

Prayer: Holy LORD, you say again and again, “I am the LORD,” letting me know your commandments are not arbitrary taboos, but the outflow of your holy nature. I confess I often, in the name of freedom, imitate this generation, crossing the boundaries you have drawn. Thank you for redeeming me first, before calling me to holiness. Let me, because I belong to you, be transformed by the renewal of my mind, willingly set apart, holding fast to your boundaries in this crooked generation. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 神所定的节期——在祂面前欢乐
entries.title_en: God's Appointed Feasts — Rejoicing Before Him
entries.verse: 利未记廿三章四十一至四十三节
entries.content:
利未记二十三章,神为祂的百姓定下一年的节期:逾越节、初熟节、五旬节、住棚节……这些日子的核心,是「圣会」——放下日常的劳碌,聚集到神面前。特别是住棚节,神吩咐他们要住在棚里七日,「好叫你们世世代代知道,我领以色列人出埃及地的时候曾使他们住在棚里」(利23:43)。节期,是神为祂百姓设立的、有规律的欢乐与记念。

请注意:神竟然「命令」祂的百姓欢乐。论到住棚节,祂说要「在耶和华你们的神面前欢乐七日」(利23:40)。喜乐在圣经里不是可有可无的情绪,而是神对祂儿女的旨意。我们常以为敬虔就是苦着脸、绷着弦,但神设立节期,恰恰是要祂的百姓定期停下来,数算祂的恩典,在祂面前放声欢乐。以神为乐,是敬拜的核心,也是我们受造的目的。

而这一切节期,都在指向基督。保罗说:「我们逾越节的羔羊基督已经被杀献祭了」(林前5:7)。逾越节预表祂为我们受死,初熟节预表祂从死里复活、成为初熟的果子,五旬节预表圣灵的浇灌;至于住棚节,则遥指那日——「神的帐幕在人间,他要与人同住」(启21:3)。保罗后来直接把这些节期称为「后事的影儿」:「不拘在饮食上,或节期、月朔、安息日都不可让人论断你们;这些原是后事的影儿,那形体却是基督」(西2:16-17)。以色列的节期表,其实是一幅救恩的日历。

你有没有为自己的灵魂,安排「节期」?在忙乱不休的生活里,我们太容易让日子一天天滑过,从不停下来记念、庆祝、以神为乐。神知道我们需要这样的节奏,所以祂命定节期。今天,不妨刻意停下,像住棚节的百姓一样,回想神如何一路领你出「埃及」,然后在祂面前,真真实实地欢乐一次。祂配得你的喜乐。

默想:我的敬虔,是绷着脸的义务,还是以神为乐的欢庆?我有没有在生活里,为记念神、以祂为乐留出「节期」?

应用:今天特意停下来,数算过去一年神在你身上的恩典,并为其中一件,向祂发出实实在在的感恩与喜乐。

祷告:满有恩慈的神,你竟命令你的百姓欢乐,又藉着节期叫他们记念你的拯救。我承认我常把敬虔活成了苦差,忘了以你为乐才是我受造的目的。感谢你,一切节期都不过是影儿,而你——那为我被杀的逾越节羔羊——才是形体本身。求你叫我在忙碌中停下来,记念你的恩,在你面前真实地欢乐。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Leviticus 23, God set an annual calendar of feasts for his people: Passover, Firstfruits, Pentecost, the Feast of Booths... At the core of these days is the “holy convocation” — laying aside daily labor and gathering before God. Especially the Feast of Booths: God commanded them to live in booths for seven days, “that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:43). The feasts were rhythmic joy and remembrance, established by God for his people.

Notice: God actually “commands” his people to rejoice. Concerning the Feast of Booths he says they are to “rejoice before the LORD your God seven days” (Leviticus 23:40). Joy in Scripture is not an optional emotion, but God’s will for his children. We often think godliness means a solemn, tense face, but God established the feasts precisely so that his people would regularly stop, count his grace, and rejoice out loud before him. Delighting in God is the core of worship, and the very purpose for which we were made.

And all these feasts point to Christ. Paul says: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Passover foreshadows his death for us, Firstfruits foreshadows his resurrection from the dead as the firstfruits, Pentecost foreshadows the outpouring of the Spirit; as for the Feast of Booths, it points far ahead to that day — “the dwelling place of God is with man; he will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). Paul later directly calls these feasts “a shadow of the things to come”: “Let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). Israel’s calendar of feasts is, in fact, a calendar of salvation.

Have you arranged “feasts” for your own soul? In our restless, hurried lives, it’s all too easy to let the days slip by, never stopping to remember, celebrate, delight in God. God knows we need this rhythm, so he appointed the feasts. Today, why not deliberately stop, and, like the people at the Feast of Booths, remember how God has led you all the way out of your own “Egypt,” and then genuinely rejoice before him. He is worthy of your joy.

Meditation: Is my godliness a grim-faced duty, or a celebration of delighting in God? Have I set aside “feast times” in my life to remember God and delight in him?

Application: Today, deliberately stop and count God’s grace to you over the past year, and offer him genuine thanks and joy for one of them.

Prayer: God of abundant grace, you actually command your people to rejoice, and through the feasts, cause them to remember your salvation. I confess I often turn godliness into a chore, forgetting that delighting in you is the very purpose for which I was made. Thank you that all the feasts were only shadows, and you — the Passover lamb slain for me — are the substance itself. Let me stop in the midst of my busyness, remember your grace, and truly rejoice before you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 禧年——释放与归回
entries.title_en: The Year of Jubilee — Release and Return
entries.verse: 利未记廿五章十七节
entries.content:
利未记二十五章,神设立了安息年与禧年。每逢第五十年,号角吹响,全地要「宣告自由」:卖掉的地业归还原主,卖身为奴的得释放,债务一笔勾销,各人归回本家(利25:10)。这是神写进以色列社会根基里的一条奇特律法——每隔一段时间,一切都要重新归零,重新开始。

禧年的背后,是一个颠覆性的宣告:地和人,都不是终极地属于债主或地主的,乃是属于神的。神说:「地不可永卖,因为地是我的;你们在我面前是客旅,是寄居的」(利25:23)。人不能永远地霸占别人的产业与自由,因为在神面前,谁都不是绝对的拥有者。正是在这样的根基上,神吩咐:「你们彼此不可亏负,只要敬畏你们的神」(利25:17)。如何待人,取决于是否敬畏那位真正的主人。

而禧年最终指向的,是基督。主耶稣在拿撒勒会堂展开以赛亚书,读到「叫那受压制的得自由,报告神悦纳人的禧年」,然后说:「今天这经应验在你们耳中了」(路4:18-21)。祂来,是要成就那真正的、永远的禧年——不只是免去地上的债,更是免去我们对神所欠的、还不清的罪债,释放我们这些被罪掳去、卖给死亡的人,叫我们归回天父的家。保罗后来这样宣告这自由的确据:「基督释放了我们,叫我们得以自由;所以要站立得稳,不要再被奴仆的轭挟制」(加5:1)。

你今天是否背着还不清的债——不只是钱财,更是那压得你喘不过气的罪咎、羞耻、无法弥补的过去?禧年的号角,在基督里已经吹响了。祂说,你的债,一笔勾销;你这卖了自己的,如今得赎、得自由、得归家。真认识这恩典的人,也必成为向别人「宣告自由」的人——不再牢牢抓住别人的亏欠,而是像神赦免我们那样去赦免、去释放。

默想:我心里是否压着一笔「还不清的债」——罪咎、羞耻、或别人欠我的?基督的禧年,如何改变我背负与释放的方式?

应用:今天在基督的禧年里,向神支取一项你一直无法放下的罪咎的赦免;同时,主动「宣告自由」——饶恕一个你一直抓着不放的人。

祷告:救赎的主,你设立禧年,叫被掳的得释放、负债的得自由、流离的得归家;你更在基督里成就了那真正的禧年。我承认我常背着还不清的罪债,也常牢牢抓住别人的亏欠。感谢你一笔勾销了我的债,释放我归回天父的家,使我能站立得稳,不再被奴仆的轭挟制。求你叫我因蒙了释放,也去释放别人。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Leviticus 25, God established the sabbatical year and the Year of Jubilee. Every fiftieth year, the trumpet would sound, and throughout the land “liberty” was to be proclaimed: land that had been sold was returned to its original owner, those sold into slavery were released, debts were wiped clean, and everyone returned to their own family (Leviticus 25:10). This is a remarkable law God wrote into the very foundation of Israelite society — every so often, everything was to be reset to zero, to begin again.

Behind the Year of Jubilee is a subversive declaration: neither land nor people ultimately belong to a creditor or landowner — they belong to God. God says: “The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). No one can permanently seize another’s inheritance or freedom, because before God, no one is an absolute owner. It is on precisely this foundation that God commands: “You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 25:17). How you treat people depends on whether you fear the true Owner.

And the Year of Jubilee ultimately points to Christ. The Lord Jesus, in the synagogue at Nazareth, unrolled the scroll of Isaiah, reading “to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor,” and then said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:18–21). He came to accomplish the true, eternal Jubilee — not merely canceling earthly debts, but canceling the sin-debt we owed God and could never repay, releasing us who were captives of sin, sold to death, so that we could return to the Father’s house. Paul later declares this assurance of freedom: “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1).

Are you today carrying a debt you can’t repay — not just money, but the guilt, shame, or unretrievable past pressing down on you until you can’t breathe? The trumpet of Jubilee has already sounded in Christ. He says your debt is entirely canceled; you, who sold yourself, are now redeemed, freed, and brought home. Anyone who truly understands this grace will also become someone who “proclaims liberty” to others — no longer clutching tightly to what others owe them, but forgiving and releasing, just as God forgave us.

Meditation: Is there an “unpayable debt” weighing on my heart — guilt, shame, or something someone owes me? How does Christ’s Jubilee change how I carry it, and how I release it?

Application: Today, in Christ’s Jubilee, draw from God the forgiveness of a guilt you’ve never been able to let go of; at the same time, proactively “proclaim liberty” — forgive someone you’ve been holding onto.

Prayer: Redeeming Lord, you established the Year of Jubilee, so that captives would be freed, debtors released, wanderers brought home; and you have accomplished, in Christ, the true Jubilee. I confess I often carry an unpayable sin-debt, and often hold tightly to what others owe me. Thank you for canceling my debt entirely, freeing me to return to the Father’s house, so I can stand firm, no longer under a yoke of slavery. Let me, because I have been released, go and release others too. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 祂专爱你,拣选你——不是因你,乃是因祂的爱
entries.title_en: He Set His Love on You, Chose You — Not Because of You, But Because of His Love
entries.verse: 申命记七章七至八节
entries.content:
民数记一至四章,神吩咐摩西数点以色列的人数,按支派、按宗族一一登记,编排营地与行军的次序。乍看是一堆冰冷的数字与名册,但请把它放在神话语的亮光下来读:神认识祂百姓中的每一个人,一个都不漏。他们在祂眼中,不是一团模糊的人群,而是一个一个被记名、被数点、被安置的人。

更深的一层,是神为什么拣选这群人。摩西后来把答案说得明明白白:「耶和华专爱你们,拣选你们,并非因你们的人数多于别民,原来你们的人数在万民中是最少的。只因耶和华爱你们……」(申7:7-8)神的拣选,从来不是因为以色列够大、够强、够可爱,恰恰相反——他们是最少的。神爱他们,唯一的理由,是「因为祂爱他们」。祂的爱,不建立在被爱者的条件上,而扎根在祂自己自由的心意里。

这是圣经里最叫人得安慰、也最叫人谦卑的真理之一。保罗说,神「从创立世界以前,在基督里拣选了我们」(弗1:4)。若神爱我是因为我够好、够有用,那么当我软弱、失败、无用的时候,这爱就摇摇欲坠。但神的爱既然从起初就不是因为我,我的起伏就动摇不了它。主耶稣对门徒说得更直白:「不是你们拣选了我,是我拣选了你们」(约15:16)——连门徒与祂的关系,起点也不是人主动的选择,而是祂主动的拣选。祂爱你,不是因为你可爱,而是祂的爱,使你成为祂所宝贝的。

你今天是否在用自己的表现,来衡量神还爱不爱你?求神把这段话刻在你心里:祂专爱你、拣选你,不是因为你在万民中出众,而是因为祂定意要爱你。这样的爱,不会因你今天的失败而减少,也不会因你明天的努力而增多。你所能做的,就是安息在这不改变的爱里,并因这爱而火热地回应祂。

默想:我是否常凭自己的表现来判断神爱我多少?若神的爱「并非因我」,而是「因祂自己」,这如何改变我面对失败时的心?

应用:今天当你软弱、失败、觉得自己没用时,不去挣扎「证明」什么,而是安息在「祂专爱我、拣选我」这不变的事实里,并向祂献上感恩。

祷告:满有慈爱的神,你拣选你的百姓,并非因他们强大可爱,乃因你定意爱他们;你更亲口对我说,是你拣选了我,不是我拣选了你。我承认我常凭表现来揣测你的爱,患得患失。感谢你在创立世界以前,就在基督里拣选了我;你的爱不因我而起,也不因我而灭。求你叫我安息在这不变的爱中,又因这爱火热地回应你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Numbers 1–4, God commands Moses to number the people of Israel, registering them tribe by tribe, clan by clan, arranging the order of the camp and the march. At first glance, this looks like a pile of cold numbers and rosters, but read it in the light of God’s word: God knows every single person among his people, not one missed. In his eyes they are not a blurry mass, but individuals, each named, each counted, each placed.

The deeper question is why God chose this particular people. Moses later states the answer plainly: “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples. It is because the LORD loves you...” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). God’s election was never because Israel was big enough, strong enough, lovable enough — quite the opposite, they were the fewest. The only reason God loved them was “because he loved them.” His love is not built on the condition of the one loved, but is rooted in his own free will.

This is one of the most comforting, and most humbling, truths in Scripture. Paul says God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). If God loved me because I’m good enough, useful enough, then this love would totter whenever I’m weak, failing, useless. But since God’s love was never because of me from the very start, my ups and downs cannot shake it. The Lord Jesus said to his disciples even more plainly: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16) — even the starting point of the disciples’ relationship with him was not their own initiative in choosing, but his proactive choosing. He loves you not because you are lovable, but his love is what makes you his treasured one.

Are you today measuring whether God still loves you by your own performance? Let God engrave this passage on your heart: he set his love on you, chose you, not because you stood out among the nations, but because he determined to love you. Such love will not decrease because of today’s failure, nor increase because of tomorrow’s effort. All you can do is rest in this unchanging love, and, because of this love, respond to him fervently.

Meditation: Do I often judge how much God loves me by my own performance? If God’s love is “not because of me” but “because of himself,” how would this change my heart when I face failure?

Application: Today, when you feel weak, failing, or useless, don’t struggle to “prove” anything — instead rest in the unchanging fact that “he set his love on me, he chose me,” and offer him thanks.

Prayer: God of abundant love, you chose your people not because they were strong or lovable, but because you determined to love them; you have spoken to me directly too — that you chose me, not I you. I confess I often gauge your love by my own performance, riding an emotional roller coaster. Thank you that before the foundation of the world you chose me in Christ; your love does not rise because of me, nor fall because of me. Let me rest in this unchanging love, and respond to you fervently because of it. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 愿耶和华向你仰脸——祭司的祝福
entries.title_en: The LORD Lift Up His Countenance Upon You — The Priestly Blessing
entries.verse: 民数记六章廿四至廿六节
entries.content:
民数记六章,神把一段祝福的话交给亚伦和他的子孙,叫他们如此为以色列人祝福:「愿耶和华赐福给你,保护你。愿耶和华使他的脸光照你,赐恩给你。愿耶和华向你仰脸,赐你平安」(民6:24-26)。这是圣经里最古老、最著名的祝福。它的核心,不是赐下什么物件,而是神的「脸」——祂亲自向你转过脸来。

请细想「使他的脸光照你」「向你仰脸」是何等的图画。在人间,一个人若向你转过脸、以笑脸相待,意味着悦纳、亲近、恩宠;若掉过脸去,便是拒绝与疏远。这祝福的至深处,是神应许要以祂喜悦的面容对着你。真正的福,从来不只是神手里的赏赐,而是神脸上的悦纳——是得着神自己。得着许多恩赐却见不着神的脸,那不是真正的祝福。

这向我们仰脸的神,今天在何处向我们显明祂的脸?保罗说,那吩咐光从黑暗里照出来的神,「已经照在我们心里,叫我们得知神荣耀的光显在耶稣基督的面上」(林后4:6)。古时亚伦口中所祝的「愿主的脸光照你」,如今在基督的面上得着了最丰满的彰显。主耶稣自己也对腓力说:「人看见了我,就是看见了父」(约14:9)。我们若要看见神向我们仰起的、满有恩慈的脸,只需要定睛看主耶稣。

亲爱的,你今天是抬头仰望祂的脸,还是只盯着祂手中的恩赐?许多时候,我们向神求这求那,却忽略了那最深的祝福——祂自己向我们仰脸,赐我们平安。愿你今天不忙着向神要东西,而是安静下来,让祂的脸光照你,在祂悦纳的目光里,得着那世界给不了、也夺不去的平安。

默想:我所渴望的「祝福」,是神手里的恩赐,还是神脸上的悦纳?我是仰望祂的脸,还是只盯着祂的手?

应用:今天安静片刻,不向神求任何东西,只默想「主的脸在基督里向我仰起、光照我」,在祂的悦纳里安息,领受祂所赐的平安。

祷告:满有恩慈的神,你藉着祭司的祝福,应许向你的百姓仰脸、赐下平安;你更在主耶稣的面上,向我显明你荣耀恩慈的脸——看见祂,就是看见你。我承认我常只顾着向你要恩赐,却忽略了你自己才是至深的福。求你的脸光照我,叫我在你悦纳的目光里,得着那世界夺不去的平安。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Numbers 6, God gave Aaron and his sons a blessing to speak, that they would bless the people of Israel this way: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26). This is the oldest, most famous blessing in Scripture. Its core is not the giving of some object, but God’s “face” — his turning his own face toward you.

Consider carefully what a picture “make his face to shine upon you,” “lift up his countenance upon you” is. Among people, when someone turns their face toward you, greets you with a smiling face, it means acceptance, closeness, favor; if they turn their face away, it means rejection and estrangement. The deepest core of this blessing is God’s promise to turn toward you with a face of delight. True blessing has never been merely the reward in God’s hand, but the acceptance on God’s face — it is obtaining God himself. To receive many gifts yet never see God’s face is not true blessing.

Where does this God who lifts up his face toward us show us his face today? Paul says the God who commanded light to shine out of darkness “has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The blessing Aaron once spoke, “may the Lord’s face shine upon you,” has now found its fullest display in the face of Christ. The Lord Jesus himself said to Philip: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). If we want to see the face God has lifted up toward us, full of grace, we need only fix our eyes on the Lord Jesus.

Beloved, are you today lifting your eyes to look at his face, or only staring at what’s in his hand? So often, we ask God for this and that, yet overlook the deepest blessing — his own face lifted toward us, giving us peace. May you today not be busy asking God for things, but instead be still, and let his face shine upon you, obtaining, in his gaze of acceptance, a peace the world cannot give, and cannot take away.

Meditation: Is the “blessing” I long for the gift in God’s hand, or the acceptance on God’s face? Am I looking at his face, or only staring at his hand?

Application: Today, be still for a while, ask God for nothing, simply meditate on “the Lord’s face lifted toward me in Christ, shining on me,” rest in his acceptance, and receive the peace he gives.

Prayer: God of abundant grace, through the priestly blessing you promised to lift your face toward your people and give them peace; you have shown me your glorious, gracious face even more fully in the face of the Lord Jesus — to see him is to see you. I confess I often only care about asking you for gifts, overlooking that you yourself are the deepest blessing. Let your face shine upon me, that in your gaze of acceptance I would receive the peace the world cannot take away. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 耶和华的膀臂岂是缩短了吗?
entries.title_en: Is the LORD's Arm Shortened?
entries.verse: 民数记十一章廿三节
entries.content:
以色列人一路有云柱火柱引导:云彩停,他们就安营;云彩起,他们就起行(民9:17)。神的同在与带领,具体到这个地步。可是百姓却一路发怨言:嫌没有肉吃,厌恶天降的吗哪,哭着怀念埃及的鱼、黄瓜、韭菜。神就要赐下多得叫他们吃到厌腻的鹌鹑;摩西却难以置信:这六十万步行的男人,哪来这么多肉?

神的回答掷地有声:「耶和华的膀臂岂是缩短了吗?现在要看我的话向你应验不应验」(民11:23)。这句话,是对一切「神恐怕做不到」之疑虑的当头棒喝。那位分开红海、天降吗哪、使磐石出水的神,难道供应不了肉食?问题从来不在神的能力有没有短缺,而在我们的信心敢不敢相信祂的能力。

我们何尝不是那发怨言的百姓?口里说信神全能,心里却为明天的难处焦虑不已,仿佛神的膀臂真的缩短了、够不着我们的处境。保罗警戒我们,不要重蹈旷野一代的覆辙:「你们也不要发怨言,像他们有发怨言的」(林前10:10)。怨言的根,是不信——是暗暗断定神不够好、不够大、顾不到我。它虽藏在抱怨的话语里,却是直指着神的心。

保罗后来给以弗所教会的祝福,正是这句诘问的回声:「神能照着运行在我们心里的大力充充足足地成就一切,超过我们所求所想的」(弗3:20)。今天你正盯着的那座「山」,那件看起来连神也搬不动的难处,请听祂问你:「我的膀臂岂是缩短了吗?」祂邀请你,不是先看环境有多大,而是先看祂有多大。真正的信心,不是没有难处,而是在难处面前,仍敢说「神能」。停止怨言,举目仰望那位膀臂从未缩短的神,然后,静看祂的话如何应验。

默想:我的怨言与焦虑背后,是否藏着一个念头——「神这一次恐怕不够、顾不到我」?我是盯着难处的大,还是神的大?

应用:今天把一件你一直为之焦虑、觉得「连神也难办」的事,郑重地交托给神,不再抱怨,而是宣告「耶和华的膀臂并未缩短」,静候祂的作为。

祷告:全能的神,你的膀臂分开红海、天降吗哪,从未缩短;你更能照着运行在我们心里的大力,成就超过我们所求所想的。我却常像旷野的百姓,口称你全能,心里却为难处焦虑、暗发怨言,仿佛你顾不到我。求你赦免我的不信。叫我在那看似无解的难处面前,不盯着环境的大,而仰望你的大,敢于相信你能。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The Israelites were guided the whole way by the pillar of cloud and fire: when the cloud stopped, they camped; when the cloud lifted, they set out (Numbers 9:17). God’s presence and leading were this concrete. Yet the people grumbled the whole way — complaining there was no meat to eat, despising the manna from heaven, weeping with longing for Egypt’s fish, cucumbers, and leeks. God was about to give them so much quail they would eat until they were sick of it; yet Moses found it hard to believe: where would enough meat come from for six hundred thousand men on foot?

God’s answer rings out like a bell: “Is the LORD’s hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not” (Numbers 11:23). This sentence is a direct blow to every doubt of “surely God can’t do this.” The God who parted the Red Sea, rained down manna, brought water from the rock — could he really fail to provide meat? The question was never whether God’s power was lacking, but whether our faith dared to believe in his power.

Aren’t we too, so often, that grumbling people? With our mouths we say we believe God is almighty, yet in our hearts we’re anxious about tomorrow’s troubles, as if God’s arm really had shortened, unable to reach our situation. Paul warns us not to repeat the wilderness generation’s mistake: “nor grumble, as some of them did” (1 Corinthians 10:10). The root of grumbling is unbelief — a quiet conclusion that God isn’t good enough, big enough, doesn’t care enough about me. Though hidden inside complaining words, it points straight at God’s heart.

Paul’s later blessing to the Ephesian church is exactly the echo of this challenge: “Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us” (Ephesians 3:20). That “mountain” you’re staring at today, that difficulty that seems like even God can’t move — hear him ask you: “Is my arm shortened?” He invites you not to first look at how big the circumstances are, but first to look at how big he is. True faith is not the absence of difficulty, but still daring to say, “God can,” in the face of difficulty. Stop grumbling, lift your eyes to the God whose arm has never shortened, and then quietly watch how his word comes true.

Meditation: Behind my grumbling and anxiety, is there a hidden thought — “God probably isn’t enough this time, can’t handle me”? Am I staring at how big the difficulty is, or how big God is?

Application: Today, take something you’ve been anxious about, something that feels “even God would have trouble with,” and solemnly hand it over to God — no longer grumbling, but declaring “the LORD’s arm has not shortened,” and quietly watch what he does.

Prayer: Almighty God, your arm parted the Red Sea, rained down manna, and has never shortened; you are even able to do far more abundantly than we ask or think, according to the power at work within us. Yet I’m often like the wilderness people — calling you almighty with my mouth, yet anxious and quietly grumbling in my heart, as if you couldn’t handle my situation. Forgive my unbelief. Let me, in the face of seemingly unsolvable difficulty, not stare at how big the circumstances are, but look to how big you are, and dare to believe you can. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 到我这里来得安息
entries.title_en: Come to Me and Find Rest
entries.content:
到我这里来得安息

「凡劳苦担重担的人可以到我这里来，我就使你们得安息。」(马太福音 11:28)

这一周,我们走过利未记的诫命与节期,又随着以色列人在旷野起行——云彩起就走,云彩停就歇。他们的安息,系于神的同在。

你或许也走得疲惫,背着自己扛不动的重担。主耶稣今天向你发出邀请:不是叫你先卸下重担才配来,而是「到我这里来」,让祂使你得安息。真正的安息,不在于难处除去,而在于来到祂面前。

"Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28)
entries.content_en:
Come to Me and Find Rest

"Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28)

This week, we walked through Leviticus’s commandments and feasts, and journeyed with the Israelites through the wilderness — setting out when the cloud lifted, resting when the cloud stopped. Their rest depended on God’s presence.

You too may be weary from the road, carrying a burden you cannot bear. The Lord Jesus invites you today: not asking you to first lay down your burden before you’re fit to come, but "come to me," and let him give you rest. True rest is not found in the removal of difficulty, but in coming before him.

"Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28)

entries.title: 他们是我们的食物——信心如何看见巨人
entries.title_en: They Are Bread for Us — How Faith Sees Giants
entries.verse: 民数记十四章八至九节
entries.content:
摩西打发十二个探子窥探迦南地。四十天后他们回来,都承认那地果然流奶与蜜;可是十个探子接着说:那地的居民高大强壮,城邑坚固宽大,我们在他们面前「就如蚱蜢一样」(民13:33)。同样一片土地,同样一批巨人,惟有迦勒和约书亚看见的完全不同。

迦勒和约书亚说:「耶和华若喜悦我们,就必将我们领进那地……不要怕那地的居民;因为他们是我们的食物……有耶和华与我们同在,不要怕他们!」(民14:8-9)何等惊人的信心!别人眼中吞不下的巨人,在他们眼中不过是「食物」——是神要为他们摆上、必被吞灭的对象。差别不在巨人的大小,而在他们把谁放在巨人旁边一同衡量:十个探子把巨人和自己比,当然绝望;迦勒把巨人和神比,于是无惧。

这就是信心与不信的分水岭。不信,是盯着难处、把神晾在一边,于是越看越怕;信心,是把难处放在神面前重新丈量,于是越看越有把握。保罗后来这样总结这种信心的逻辑:「神若帮助我们,谁能敌挡我们呢?」(罗8:31)以色列人因为不信,在旷野漂流四十年,倒毙旷野,与应许之地擦肩而过——不是因为巨人太大,而是因为他们的神在心里太小。不信,是要付极大代价的。

今天你的迦南地里,站着什么样的巨人?一个看不到尽头的难处、一段熬不出去的关系、一个你以为神也无能为力的困境?问题不是巨人在不在,而是你把它跟谁比。若你把它单独看,它必吞了你;若你把它放在那位与你同在的神面前,它不过是祂要为你挪去的「食物」。求神给你迦勒那样的眼光:不是无视巨人,而是更清楚地看见神。

默想:面对我生命中的「巨人」,我是像十个探子把它跟自己比,还是像迦勒把它跟神比?这决定了我是恐惧还是刚强。

应用:今天把一件让你恐惧、觉得跨不过去的难处,刻意放在「有耶和华与我同在」这句话的旁边重新衡量,并凭信心向前迈一步。

祷告:与我同在的神,当年十个探子盯着巨人而绝望,迦勒却因看见你而无惧。我承认我常把难处跟自己比,越看越怕,把你晾在一边。求你赦免我的不信,给我迦勒那样的眼光,叫我把每一个「巨人」都放在你面前衡量,深信若你帮助我们,谁能敌挡我们呢。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Moses sent twelve spies to scout the land of Canaan. Forty days later they returned, all agreeing the land truly flowed with milk and honey; but ten of the spies went on to say: the inhabitants of the land were tall and strong, their cities fortified and very large, and before them we were “like grasshoppers” (Numbers 13:33). The very same land, the very same giants — only Caleb and Joshua saw something entirely different.

Caleb and Joshua said: “If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land... Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us... the LORD is with us; do not fear them” (Numbers 14:8–9). What astonishing faith! Giants others couldn’t swallow, in their eyes were nothing but “bread” — something God would serve up for them, sure to be consumed. The difference was not in the size of the giants, but in what they measured the giants against: the ten spies compared the giants to themselves, and of course despaired; Caleb compared the giants to God, and so was unafraid.

This is the watershed between faith and unbelief. Unbelief stares at the difficulty and sets God aside, so the more you look, the more afraid you become; faith places the difficulty before God and measures it again, so the more you look, the more assured you become. Paul later summarized this logic of faith this way: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). Because of unbelief, the Israelites wandered forty years in the wilderness and died there, missing the promised land by a hair — not because the giants were too big, but because their God was too small in their hearts. Unbelief costs an enormous price.

What kind of giant stands in your own Canaan today? A difficulty with no end in sight, a relationship that won’t heal, a predicament you think even God can’t handle? The question isn’t whether the giant exists, but who you compare it to. If you look at it alone, it will surely swallow you; if you place it before the God who is with you, it is nothing but “bread” he will remove for you. Ask God to give you Caleb’s eyes — not to ignore the giant, but to see God more clearly.

Meditation: Facing the “giants” in my life, am I, like the ten spies, comparing them to myself, or, like Caleb, comparing them to God? This determines whether I live in fear or in strength.

Application: Today, take a difficulty that frightens you, that feels insurmountable, and deliberately place it beside the phrase “the LORD is with us,” measuring it again, and step forward one step in faith.

Prayer: God who is with me, back then ten spies stared at giants and despaired, but Caleb was unafraid because he saw you. I confess I often compare my difficulties to myself, growing more afraid the more I look, setting you aside. Forgive my unbelief; give me Caleb’s eyes, so that I place every “giant” before you and measure it, deeply believing that if you help us, who can be against us. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我就是你的分——以神自己为产业
entries.title_en: I Am Your Portion — God Himself as Inheritance
entries.verse: 民数记十八章二十节
entries.content:
当以色列各支派分得迦南地为产业时,惟独利未支派没有分到一块地。神对亚伦说:「你在以色列人的境内不可有产业,在他们中间也不可有分。我就是你的分,是你的产业」(民18:20)。别的支派得的是地,利未人得的是神自己。乍看是亏了,细想却是天大的福气——他们所得的,是那位赐地之人本身。

这里藏着一个属灵的分野:人所能得着的,有两种。一种是神手中的赏赐——产业、供应、各样的好处;另一种是神自己。神让利未人失去了前者,为要叫他们单单得着后者。而失去地上一份产业的人,反倒成了最富足的人,因为得着「耶和华是我的分」的人,是万有都归他的人。耶利米在废墟中也发出同样的心声:「耶和华是我的分,因此,我要仰望他」(哀3:24)。

我们里面的天性,总是紧紧抓着「分」——要有看得见、抓得住的保障:存款、房子、地位、人脉。神有时会像对利未人那样,不让我们得着某一份地上的产业,为的是把我们的心从「神的赏赐」引向「神自己」。若你得着了万物却没有神,你一无所有;若你失去了万物却得着神,你便拥有一切。诗人也这样唱:「除你以外,在天上我有谁呢?除你以外,在地上我也没有所爱慕的。我的肉体和我的心肠衰残;但神是我心里的力量,又是我的福分,直到永远」(诗73:25-26)。真正的丰盛,是能说出这样的话。

你今天所倚靠、当作「产业」的,是什么?若有一天神把它挪去,你还剩下什么?利未人给我们看见一条更美的路:让神自己成为你的产业。这样的人,得失之间有一种别人夺不去的安稳——因为他所抓住的,不是会朽坏的地土,而是永不改变的神。今天,你能否向祂坦然说一句:主啊,除你以外,在天上我有谁呢?你是我的分,直到永远。

默想:我心里真正当作「产业」、失去就活不下去的是什么?我能否说「耶和华是我的分」,并以祂自己为最大的满足?

应用:今天默想「主是我的分」,把一样你一直紧抓、当作保障的东西,在祷告中松开手,宣告神自己才是你的产业。

祷告:主啊,你叫利未人失去地上的产业,却把你自己赐给他们作分。我承认我常紧抓那些看得见的保障,把它们当作产业,却忽略了你自己才是至宝。求你把我的心从你的赏赐,引向你自己;叫我能真心说:耶和华是我的分,除你以外,我在天上还有谁?奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
When each tribe of Israel received a share of the land of Canaan as their inheritance, the tribe of Levi alone received no land. God said to Aaron: “You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (Numbers 18:20). The other tribes received land; the Levites received God himself. At first glance it seems like a loss, but on closer thought, it is an immense blessing — what they received was the one who gives the land itself.

Hidden here is a spiritual distinction: there are two kinds of things a person can receive. One is the reward in God’s hand — inheritance, provision, various benefits; the other is God himself. God let the Levites lose the former, in order that they would obtain solely the latter. And the one who lost a share of earthly inheritance became instead the richest — because whoever has “the LORD as my portion” has one to whom all things belong. Jeremiah, amid the ruins, cried out the same conviction: “The LORD is my portion, therefore I will hope in him” (Lamentations 3:24).

Our nature always clings tightly to “a portion” — wanting visible, graspable security: savings, a house, status, connections. God sometimes, as with the Levites, withholds from us a certain earthly inheritance, in order to turn our hearts from “God’s gifts” to “God himself.” If you gain everything but not God, you have nothing; if you lose everything but gain God, you have everything. The psalmist sang the same way: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:25–26). True abundance is being able to say these words.

What is it you rely on today, what you treat as your “inheritance”? If God took it away one day, what would you have left? The Levites show us a better road: let God himself become your inheritance. A person like this has a security in gain and loss that no one can take away — because what they hold onto is not perishable land, but the never-changing God. Today, can you say to him plainly: Lord, whom have I in heaven but you? You are my portion, forever.

Meditation: What do I truly treat in my heart as my “inheritance,” the thing I couldn’t live without losing? Can I say “the LORD is my portion,” and find in him my greatest satisfaction?

Application: Today, meditate on “the Lord is my portion,” and in prayer, let go of one thing you’ve always clutched, treated as your security, declaring that God himself is your inheritance.

Prayer: Lord, you let the Levites lose their earthly inheritance, but gave them yourself as their portion. I confess I often clutch tightly to visible securities, treating them as my inheritance, while overlooking that you yourself are the true treasure. Turn my heart from your gifts to yourself; let me truly be able to say: the LORD is my portion, whom have I in heaven but you? In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 神非人,必不致说谎——祂的话必定成就
entries.title_en: God Is Not Man, That He Should Lie — His Word Will Surely Be Fulfilled
entries.verse: 民数记廿三章十九节
entries.content:
巴勒王重金聘请术士巴兰来咒诅以色列,巴兰三番四次张口,出来的却全是祝福。他自己也不得不承认:「神非人,必不致说谎,也非人子,必不致后悔。他说话岂不照着行呢?他发言岂不要成就呢?」(民23:19)神所应许要祝福的,没有任何咒诅、任何势力能够翻转。祂的话,就是祂的信实。

这正是神与人根本的不同。人会说谎,会反悔,会应许了却做不到,或做得到却变了心;神却不然。祂的性情决定了祂的话:祂既是真实的,就必不说谎;祂既是不改变的,就必不后悔。祂开口应许的,断没有落空的可能。这不是一句空泛的安慰,而是宇宙间最坚实的根基——神的话,比天地更牢靠。保罗后来这样描述这信实的另一面:「我们纵然失信,他仍是可信的,因为他不能背乎自己」(提后2:13)——连我们的软弱失信,都不能叫神变成不信实的神。

就在这卷书稍前,当百姓被火蛇所咬、濒临死亡时,神吩咐摩西造一条火蛇的像挂在杆子上;摩西便用铜造了一条蛇,凡被咬的一望这蛇就活了(民21:8-9)。主耶稣亲自指着这件事说:「摩西在旷野怎样举蛇,人子也必照样被举起来」(约3:14)。那被举起的铜蛇,预表钉在十字架上的基督;神应许「一望就活」,而祂的话,如巴兰所被迫承认的,是必定成就的。你只管仰望,祂必守约。

你今天是否在怀疑神的应许?是否觉得祂给你的话,恐怕要落空了?请把你的信心,从自己浮动的感觉,转回到神不改变的性情上。祂「非人,必不致说谎」。祂在圣经里给你的每一个应许——赦免、同在、看顾、末了的荣耀——都因祂是这样一位神,而稳如泰山。人会叫你失望,神绝不会。祂说了,就必成就。

默想:我信靠神的应许,是凭自己起伏的感觉,还是凭神不改变、不说谎的性情?哪一个更稳妥?

应用:今天找出一处你正在怀疑的神的应许,把它写下来,宣告「神非人,必不致说谎」,选择相信祂必成就,并照此而行。

祷告:信实的神,巴兰想咒诅,你却使他只能祝福,因为你所应许的无人能翻转。你「非人,必不致说谎」,你的话必定成就;我们纵然失信,你仍是可信的。我承认我常凭自己的感觉怀疑你的应许。求你叫我把信心扎根在你不改变的性情上;更感谢你,那被举起的铜蛇预表了被钉的基督——叫我只管仰望,就必得生。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
King Balak hired the sorcerer Balaam at great cost to curse Israel; time and again Balaam opened his mouth, yet only blessing came out. He himself had to admit: “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?” (Numbers 23:19). Nothing God has promised to bless can be overturned by any curse, any power. His word is his faithfulness.

This is exactly the fundamental difference between God and man. Man lies, changes his mind, promises but fails to deliver, or delivers but changes heart; God is not so. His character determines his word: because he is true, he must not lie; because he is unchanging, he must not change his mind. What he opens his mouth to promise can never possibly fall through. This is not a vague comfort, but the most solid foundation in the universe — God’s word is more reliable than heaven and earth. Paul later describes another side of this faithfulness: “if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13) — even our weakness and unfaithfulness cannot make God become an unfaithful God.

Just a bit earlier in this book, when the people, bitten by fiery serpents, were on the verge of death, God commanded Moses to make a bronze image of a fiery serpent and set it on a pole; Moses made a bronze serpent, and whoever was bitten, looked at it, and lived (Numbers 21:8–9). The Lord Jesus himself pointed to this event and said: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). That lifted-up bronze serpent foreshadowed Christ nailed to the cross; God promised “look and live,” and his word, as Balaam was forced to admit, will surely be fulfilled. You need only look, and he will surely keep his word.

Are you today doubting God’s promise? Do you feel that the word he gave you will probably fall through? Turn your faith away from your own fluctuating feelings, back to God’s unchanging character. He “is not man, that he should lie.” Every promise he gives you in Scripture — forgiveness, presence, care, final glory — is as solid as a mountain, precisely because he is this kind of God. People will let you down; God never will. What he has said, he will surely fulfill.

Meditation: Do I trust God’s promises based on my own fluctuating feelings, or based on God’s unchanging, non-lying character? Which is more reliable?

Application: Today, find a promise of God you’re currently doubting, write it down, declare “God is not man, that he should lie,” choose to believe he will fulfill it, and act accordingly.

Prayer: Faithful God, Balaam wanted to curse, yet you made him only able to bless, because no one can overturn what you have promised. You “are not man, that you should lie”; your word will surely be fulfilled; even if we are faithless, you remain faithful. I confess I often doubt your promises based on my own feelings. Let me root my faith in your unchanging character; and thank you, that lifted-up bronze serpent foreshadowed the crucified Christ — let me simply look, and I will surely live. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 新的一代——神的应许不因人的失败而落空
entries.title_en: A New Generation — God's Promise Does Not Fail Because of Human Failure
entries.verse: 民数记廿六章六十五节
entries.content:
民数记二十六章,神再一次数点百姓。这一次数的,是新的一代。上一代——那些在加低斯不信、悖逆、发怨言的成年人,除了迦勒和约书亚,都已倒毙旷野。经文特意点明:「连一个人也没有存留」,惟有耶孚尼的儿子迦勒和嫩的儿子约书亚(民26:65)。神对那一代的审判是真实的,祂的话一句没有落空。

但同样真实的是:神并没有因为一代人的失败,就废弃祂的应许。老一代倒下了,新一代却站起来,数点、编队、预备进入那应许之地。神的计划从不系于某一代人的成败;人会失败,神的旨意却一往无前。祂能在旧的废墟上,兴起全新的开始。这是何等的安慰:我们的失败真实,神的信实却更真实。耶利米后来在耶路撒冷的废墟中,唱出同一个真理:「我们不致消灭,是出于耶和华诸般的慈爱;是因他的怜悯不致断绝。每早晨,这都是新的;你的诚实极其广大」(哀3:22-23)。

这也提醒我们:每一代人,都要为自己回应神。新一代不能靠父辈的经历得救,也不必被父辈的失败捆死。他们站在同一片旷野的边缘,面对同样的应许,神要看的,是他们自己肯不肯信、肯不肯进去。属灵的产业不能世袭;上一代的吗哪喂不饱这一代的灵魂,各人都要亲自认识、亲自跟随这位神。

你今天或许正为过去的失败、或上一代留下的烂摊子而灰心,以为一切都完了。但神在民数记里给我们看见:祂专会在「一代倒下」之处,兴起新的一代。祂的怜悯每早晨都是新的。无论你的昨天多么不堪,神的应许仍然摆在你前头;今天,轮到你回应了——不要重蹈不信的覆辙,起来,进去得地为业。

默想:我是否被过去的失败、或原生家庭的破口捆住,以为神的应许与我无关?神如何在「旧的倒下」处兴起「新的开始」?

应用:今天不再让过去的失败定义你的将来,凭信心在一件事上作出「新一代」的回应——起来跟随神所指示的下一步。

祷告:信实的神,老一代因不信倒毙旷野,你却兴起新的一代,承受你不落空的应许。我承认我常被过去的失败与亏欠捆住,以为再没有指望。感谢你专在旧的废墟上兴起新的开始,你的怜悯每早晨都是新的,你的诚实极其广大。求你叫我不重蹈不信的覆辙,起来回应你,进去得着你所应许的。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Numbers 26, God numbers the people once again. This time, it is a new generation. The previous generation — those adults who, at Kadesh, disbelieved, rebelled, and grumbled — had all, except Caleb and Joshua, died in the wilderness. The text specifically notes: “not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun” (Numbers 26:65). God’s judgment on that generation was real; not one of his words failed.

But equally real is this: God did not abolish his promise because one generation failed. The old generation fell, but a new generation rose up, was numbered, organized, and prepared to enter the promised land. God’s plan was never tied to the success or failure of any one generation; people may fail, but God’s will presses ever forward. He can raise up an entirely new beginning on the ruins of the old. What comfort this is: our failure is real, but God’s faithfulness is more real still. Jeremiah, later amid the ruins of Jerusalem, sang out the same truth: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

This also reminds us: each generation must respond to God for itself. The new generation could not be saved by their fathers’ experience, nor need they be bound to death by their fathers’ failure. They stood at the edge of the same wilderness, facing the same promise, and what God looked at was whether they themselves were willing to believe, willing to go in. Spiritual inheritance cannot be passed down automatically; the previous generation’s manna cannot feed this generation’s soul — each person must personally know, personally follow, this God.

You may today be discouraged over past failures, or a mess left by the previous generation, thinking everything is over. But Numbers shows us: God specializes in raising up a new generation exactly where “one generation has fallen.” His mercies are new every morning. However unbearable your yesterday, God’s promise still stands before you; today, it’s your turn to respond — don’t repeat the mistake of unbelief; rise up, go in, and possess the land.

Meditation: Am I bound by past failures, or by a breach left by my family of origin, thinking God’s promise has nothing to do with me? How does God raise up a “new beginning” exactly where “the old has fallen”?

Application: Today, no longer let past failure define your future; respond by faith, as the “new generation” would, in one matter — rise up and follow the next step God shows you.

Prayer: Faithful God, the old generation died in the wilderness because of unbelief, but you raised up a new generation to inherit your unfailing promise. I confess I am often bound by past failures and debts, thinking there’s no more hope. Thank you for specializing in raising up a new beginning on the ruins of the old; your mercies are new every morning, and great is your faithfulness. Let me not repeat the mistake of unbelief, but rise up and respond to you, going in to receive what you have promised. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 不可食言——在神面前说话算数
entries.title_en: You Shall Not Break Your Word — Being a Person of Your Word Before God
entries.scripture: 民三十至卅三章四十九节
entries.verse: 民数记三十章二节
entries.content:
民数记三十章讲的是许愿。神定下规矩:「人若向耶和华许愿或起誓,要约束自己,就不可食言,必要按口中所出的一切话行」(民30:2)。在神面前开口应许的,就必须兑现;言语一旦出口,就带着约束的重量。神看重人的话,因为祂自己就是一位说话算数的神。

我们活在一个言语廉价的时代。人随口承诺,转身就忘;签了约又毁约,立了誓又反悔;话说得漂亮,却没打算兑现。渐渐地,连我们自己都不把自己的话当真了。可是圣经的标准截然不同:「你向神许愿,偿还不可迟延……你许的愿应当偿还」(传5:4)。在神眼中,食言不是小事,而是对祂圣洁之名的轻慢。

主耶稣把这标准提到更纯净的高度。祂说,不必起誓赌咒,因为「你们的话,是,就说是;不是,就说不是;若再多说就是出于那恶者」(太5:37)。一个真正诚实的人,不需要靠发誓来加重自己的话,因为他平日的每一句「是」都算数。基督徒的可信,不在于把话说得多满,而在于说出的话必定去行——是就是是。这信实的源头,是那位「无谎言的神」自己:祂「在万古之先所应许的永生」(多1:2),从起初就没有一句会落空。

神所看重的诚信,不只在大事上,更在无人知晓的小承诺里。你答应了却一拖再拖的事、你在神面前立过又悄悄放下的志、你随口对人许下又不了了之的诺——在神眼中,都记着。求神叫我们作说话算数的人,言出必行,因为我们所事奉的,是一位「说话岂不照着行」的神。你的可信,是你信仰的一张名片。

默想:我是一个说话算数的人吗?我向神、向人许下的承诺,有多少是认真兑现的,又有多少是随口说说?

应用:今天检视一个你答应了却一直拖延或搁置的承诺(对神、对家人、对同事),采取具体行动去兑现它。

祷告:信实守约的神,你吩咐人许愿就不可食言,因为你自己就是那位无谎言、说话算数的神。我承认我常轻看自己的话,承诺了却不兑现,在你面前立志又悄悄放下。求你赦免我的轻慢,叫我作一个言出必行的人,连无人知晓的小承诺也存诚实,好叫我的可信,能见证那位说了就必成就的神。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Numbers 30 speaks of vows. God set down a rule: “If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth” (Numbers 30:2). Whoever makes a promise before God must fulfill it; once a word leaves the mouth, it carries the weight of obligation. God takes human words seriously, because he himself is a God who keeps his word.

We live in an age of cheap words. People make casual promises and forget them the moment they turn around; they sign contracts and break them, take vows and go back on them; they say beautiful things with no intention of following through. Gradually, we stop taking even our own words seriously. But Scripture’s standard is entirely different: “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it... Pay what you vow” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). In God’s eyes, breaking one’s word is no small matter — it is contempt for his holy name.

The Lord Jesus raised this standard to an even purer height. He said there was no need to swear oaths, because “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’; anything more than this comes from evil” (Matthew 5:37). A truly honest person doesn’t need an oath to add weight to their word, because their everyday “yes” already counts. A Christian’s credibility lies not in how grand their words sound, but in whether the words spoken are surely carried out — yes means yes. The source of this faithfulness is the “God who never lies” himself: he “promised before the ages began” (Titus 1:2) — from the very beginning, not one of his words has ever failed.

The integrity God values is not only in grand matters, but in small promises no one else knows about. The thing you promised but keep putting off, the resolution you made before God and quietly dropped, the casual promise you made to someone and let fade away — God remembers all of it. May God make us people of our word, who follow through on what they say, because the one we serve is a God whose “word will surely come true.” Your credibility is a calling card for your faith.

Meditation: Am I a person of my word? Of the promises I’ve made to God and to others, how many have I earnestly kept, and how many were just idle talk?

Application: Today, examine a promise you made but have kept delaying or shelving (to God, to family, to a coworker), and take concrete action to fulfill it.

Prayer: Faithful, covenant-keeping God, you command that whoever vows must not break their word, because you yourself are the one who never lies, who always keeps his word. I confess I often take my own words lightly, promising without following through, making resolutions before you and quietly dropping them. Forgive my carelessness; let me be someone who follows through on what they say, keeping integrity even in small promises no one else knows about, so that my trustworthiness testifies to the God whose every word surely comes to pass. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 逃城——奔向那位为我们预备的避难所
entries.title_en: The City of Refuge — Running to the Shelter Prepared for Us
entries.scripture: 民卅三章五十节至卅六章
entries.verse: 民数记卅五章卅四节
entries.content:
以色列进迦南前,神吩咐要设立六座「逃城」。若有人误杀了人,报血仇的可以追讨他的命;但那误杀人的,只要逃进逃城,就得庇护,不至被杀,直到站在会众面前受审(民35:11-12)。在一个「以命偿命」的世界里,神为走投无路、被追杀的人,预备了一个可以奔逃、可以存活的地方。

逃城的背后,是神对祂所住之地的看重:「你们不可玷污所住之地,就是我住在其中之地,因为我耶和华住在以色列人中间」(民35:34)。神是圣洁的,祂不容血债玷污祂的居所;但同一位神,也满有怜悯,为犯了不可挽回之错的人,开了一条生路。圣洁与怜悯,在逃城里一同彰显——罪必须被处理,而走投无路的人,也必有可奔的避难所。

希伯来书用「逃往避难所」的说法来描写福音里的盼望,呼应着逃城的图画:神给我们应许,「好叫我们这逃往避难所、持定摆在我们前头指望的人可以大得勉励」(来6:18)。我们每一个人,都是那「误杀了人」、被律法的追讨紧紧逼在身后、走投无路的罪人;而基督,就是神为我们预备的那座逃城。奔进祂里面的,追讨的刀就砍不着;因为祂已替我们受了那一刀。所罗门也曾这样唱:「耶和华的名是坚固台;义人奔入便得安稳」(箴18:10)——在这幅图画里,逃城所指向的,正是这位可奔入、可安稳的主自己。

你今天是否正被追赶——被过去的罪、被良心的控告、被那句「你死定了」的声音穷追不舍?不要站在原地任凭它追上你,也不要指望靠自己的表现挡住它。起来,奔向那座逃城。逃城的门为一切奔来的人敞开,不问你跑得多狼狈、来得多晚。在基督里,你不再是被定罪的逃犯,而是蒙庇护的儿女。奔向祂,就得存活。

默想:我被什么「追赶」——罪咎、控告、恐惧?我是想靠自己挡住它,还是肯奔向基督这座真逃城?

应用:今天把一件一直追赶、控告你的罪或恐惧,藉着祷告「奔进」基督里,支取祂已为你受刑、你不再被定罪的庇护。

祷告:圣洁又满有怜悯的神,你为误杀人的预备逃城,叫走投无路的人有可奔的避难所。感谢你,基督就是我的逃城,是那坚固台;当律法与罪咎在身后追讨,我一奔进祂里面,那刀就砍不着我,因祂已替我受了。求你叫我不再靠自己抵挡控告,而是一次次奔向你,在你里面得庇护、得存活。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Before Israel entered Canaan, God commanded that six “cities of refuge” be established. If someone accidentally killed another, the avenger of blood could pursue his life; but the one who had killed unintentionally, if he fled to a city of refuge, would find shelter, and not be killed, until he stood before the congregation for judgment (Numbers 35:11–12). In a world of “life for life,” God prepared a place to flee to, a place to survive, for those who were desperate, hunted.

Behind the cities of refuge is God’s regard for the land where he dwells: “You shall not pollute the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel” (Numbers 35:34). God is holy, and he does not allow bloodguilt to pollute his dwelling place; yet this same God is also full of mercy, opening a way of life for those who have committed an irreversible wrong. Holiness and mercy are both displayed together in the cities of refuge — sin must be dealt with, and yet the desperate must have a refuge to flee to.

Hebrews uses the language of “fleeing for refuge” to describe the hope in the gospel, echoing the picture of the cities of refuge: God gives us his promise, “so that we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18). Each one of us is that person who “accidentally killed someone,” hard-pressed from behind by the law’s pursuit, with nowhere left to go; and Christ is the city of refuge God has prepared for us. Whoever flees into him, the pursuing sword cannot touch; because he has already taken that blow for us. Solomon sang the same way: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10) — in this picture, what the city of refuge points to is precisely this Lord himself, the one you can run into, the one who makes you safe.

Are you today being pursued — by past sin, by an accusing conscience, by the relentless voice saying “you’re finished”? Don’t stand still and let it catch up to you, and don’t hope to block it with your own performance. Rise up, and run to that city of refuge. Its gates are open to all who come running, no matter how disheveled you look, how late you arrive. In Christ, you are no longer a condemned fugitive, but a sheltered child. Run to him, and you will live.

Meditation: What is “pursuing” me — guilt, accusation, fear? Do I want to block it myself, or am I willing to run to Christ, this true city of refuge?

Application: Today, take a sin or fear that has been pursuing and accusing you, and through prayer, “run into” Christ, drawing on the shelter of the fact that he has already been punished in your place, and you are no longer condemned.

Prayer: Holy and merciful God, you prepared a city of refuge for those who killed unintentionally, so that the desperate would have a place to flee. Thank you, Christ is my city of refuge, my strong tower; when the law and guilt pursue from behind, the moment I run into him, that sword cannot touch me, because he has already taken it for me. Let me no longer resist accusation on my own, but run to you again and again, finding shelter and life in you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你是我们世世代代的居所
entries.title_en: You Have Been Our Dwelling Place in All Generations
entries.content:
你是我们世世代代的居所

「主啊，你世世代代作我们的居所。」(诗篇 90:1)

这一周,我们随以色列人走完了旷野的漂流——不信、审判、新的一代,直到站在应许之地的边缘。四十年风尘仆仆,他们没有一处固定的家,惟有神,是他们一路的居所。

这首诗,正是神人摩西在旷野写下的。房屋会朽坏,世代会更替,惟有神自己,是每一代人可以安歇的家。今天,不论你脚下的路多么飘摇,愿你在祂里面歇下——祂是你世世代代的居所。

"Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout all generations." (Psalm 90:1)
entries.content_en:
You Have Been Our Dwelling Place in All Generations

"Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout all generations." (Psalm 90:1)

This week, we walked with the Israelites through the end of the wilderness wandering — unbelief, judgment, a new generation — all the way to standing at the edge of the promised land. Forty years of travel-worn wandering, with no fixed home anywhere — only God was their dwelling place all along the way.

This psalm was written by Moses, the man of God, in the wilderness. Houses decay, generations pass, but God himself alone is the home every generation can rest in. Today, however unsteady the road beneath your feet, may you rest in him — he is your dwelling place, generation after generation.

"Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout all generations." (Psalm 90:1)

entries.title: 他总不撇下你——回望旷野的怜悯
entries.title_en: He Will Never Leave You — Looking Back on the Wilderness Mercy
entries.verse: 申命记四章三、卅一节
entries.content:
申命记是摩西的临别信息。四十年旷野将尽,新一代站在应许之地门口,摩西一开口,先带他们回望走过的路:何烈山的立约、探子的失败、旷野的漂流。他要他们记住的,不是自己的表现有多糟(那确实很糟),而是神的怜悯有多长阔。

他说:「耶和华你神原是有怜悯的神;他总不撇下你,不灭绝你,也不忘记他起誓与你列祖所立的约」(申4:31)。以色列一路悖逆、拜偶像、发怨言,按他们所该得的,早该被灭绝;然而神没有撇下他们。祂守约,不是因为他们守约,而是因为祂是有怜悯的神,不忘记自己起的誓。神的信实,不建立在我们的忠心上,而扎根在祂自己的性情与誓言里。

这份「总不撇下」的应许,在新约里向我们再次响起,而且被推到了极致。希伯来书说:「主曾说:我总不撇下你,也不丢弃你」(来13:5)。保罗更进一步宣告,这撇不下的爱,连宇宙间最大的力量也拆不散:「无论是死,是生,是天使,是掌权的,是有能的,是现在的事,是将来的事……都不能叫我们与神的爱隔绝;这爱是在我们的主基督耶稣里的」(罗8:38-39)。昔日对旷野以色列人说的话,今天照样对每一个在基督里的人说,而且加了双重的保证。

回望是一种属灵的操练。当我们只盯着眼前的难处或自己的失败,很容易灰心;但当我们像摩西那样,带着百姓回望神一路的怜悯,信心就重新被点燃。今天,不妨也回望你自己的「旷野」:那些你以为撑不过去、神却一路带你走过来的时刻。数算祂的信实,你会发现——祂从未撇下你,将来也不会。

默想:我是常盯着自己的失败而灰心,还是肯回望神一路「总不撇下」的怜悯?这两种目光,带来何等不同的信心?

应用:今天花几分钟,具体回望神在你过去某段「旷野」中的信实,写下来,并为「祂总不撇下我」向祂献上感恩。

祷告:满有怜悯的神,以色列一路悖逆,你却总不撇下他们,只因你守约、有怜悯。我承认我也常跌倒、时冷时热,以为你早该对我失望。感谢你在基督里再次应许:「我总不撇下你,也不丢弃你」,又叫没有一样受造之物能使我与你的爱隔绝。求你叫我常常回望你的信实,在你不改变的怜悯里,重得信心与力量。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Deuteronomy is Moses’s farewell message. Forty years in the wilderness were nearly at an end; the new generation stood at the door of the promised land, and as Moses begins to speak, he first leads them to look back over the road they had traveled: the covenant at Horeb, the spies’ failure, the wilderness wandering. What he wants them to remember is not how bad their own performance had been (which it truly had been), but how vast and long God’s mercy was.

He says: “the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them” (Deuteronomy 4:31). Israel, the whole way, rebelled, worshiped idols, and grumbled; by what they deserved, they should long ago have been destroyed; yet God did not leave them. He kept the covenant not because they kept it, but because he is a merciful God who does not forget the oath he swore. God’s faithfulness is not built on our loyalty, but is rooted in his own character and his own oath.

This promise of “never leaving” echoes again in the New Testament, and is pushed to the utmost extreme. Hebrews says: “the Lord has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Paul goes further, declaring that this love which will not let go cannot be torn apart even by the greatest powers in the universe: “neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers... will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). What was once said to the wilderness generation of Israel is spoken today, in exactly the same way, to everyone in Christ — and with a double assurance added.

Looking back is a spiritual discipline. When we stare only at the difficulty in front of us or our own failure, it’s easy to grow discouraged; but when, like Moses, we lead the people to look back over God’s mercy along the whole road, faith is rekindled. Today, why not also look back over your own “wilderness” — those moments you thought you couldn’t survive, yet God carried you through all the way. Count his faithfulness, and you’ll find — he has never left you, and never will.

Meditation: Do I often stare at my own failures and grow discouraged, or am I willing to look back at God’s mercy of “never leaving” along the way? What different kind of faith do these two ways of looking bring?

Application: Today, spend a few minutes concretely looking back at God’s faithfulness in some past “wilderness” of yours, write it down, and give him thanks for “he never left me.”

Prayer: God of abundant mercy, Israel rebelled the whole way, yet you never left them, only because you keep covenant and are merciful. I confess I too often fall, running hot and cold, thinking you must have given up on me long ago. Thank you for promising again in Christ: “I will never leave you nor forsake you,” and that no created thing can separate me from your love. Let me often look back on your faithfulness, regaining faith and strength in your unchanging mercy. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你要尽心爱耶和华——祂配得你全部的爱
entries.title_en: You Shall Love the LORD With All Your Heart — He Is Worthy of Your Whole Love
entries.verse: 申命记六章四至五节
entries.content:
申命记六章,摩西向以色列宣告那段被称为「示玛」(Shema,意即「你要听」)的话,成了以色列信仰的心跳:「以色列啊,你要听!耶和华我们神是独一的主。你要尽心、尽性、尽力爱耶和华你的神」(申6:4-5)。整本律法千百条诫命,归根到底,是这一件事:全心全人地爱这位独一的神。

请注意,神所要的第一件事,不是我们的行为、事奉或奉献,而是我们的爱——而且是「尽心、尽性、尽力」毫无保留的爱。神不满足于分一杯羹,祂要的是我们心的全部。这不是神自私,而是因为祂配得,也因为唯有全心爱神的人,才能真正得着满足。我们受造,原是为了以神为至宝、为至爱;心若不安放在祂身上,就永远在别处流浪。

主耶稣被问及诫命中哪一条最大时,引用的正是这句话:「你要尽心、尽性、尽意爱主你的神。这是诫命中的第一,且是最大的」(太22:37-38)。可见这诫命从未过时。它也拆穿了一个我们常有的错觉——以为基督徒的核心是「做对的事」;不,核心是「爱对的对象」。行为可以伪装,爱却假不来。神先要的是你的心。保罗后来活出了这诫命的极致:「我也将万事当作有损的,因我以认识我主基督耶稣为至宝」(腓3:8)——这不是苦修式的牺牲,而是一颗真正被神夺去的心,自然而然的选择。

但我们必须诚实:谁能真的「尽心尽性尽力」爱神?没有一个。我们的爱三心二意、忽冷忽热。正因如此,福音才是好消息——那位完全爱父的基督,替我们守全了这条最大的诫命,又用祂的爱把我们的冷心融化。「我们爱,因为神先爱我们」(约壹4:19)。今天,不必假装你的爱已经满分,而是求那位可爱的神,亲自把你的心夺回来,叫你越来越以祂为乐、为爱。

默想:神所要我最先献上的,是我的行为,还是我的心?我对神的爱,是「尽心尽性尽力」,还是留着大半给别的?

应用:今天诚实地向神承认你爱祂的冷淡,并求祂藉着默想祂的美善重新点燃你的爱;选一件事,单单为「爱祂」而做,不为别的。

祷告:配得敬爱的神,你所要的第一件事,是我尽心、尽性、尽力地爱你。我承认我的爱三心二意、忽冷忽热,常把心分给了别的。感谢主耶稣替我守全了这最大的诫命,又以祂的爱融化我的冷心。求你亲自夺回我的心,叫我也能说,认识你为至宝,越来越以你为乐、为爱。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Deuteronomy 6, Moses proclaims to Israel the passage known as the “Shema” (meaning “Hear”), which became the heartbeat of Israel’s faith: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). All the thousands of commandments in the whole law come down, at bottom, to this one thing: loving this one God with the whole heart, the whole person.

Notice, the first thing God wants is not our behavior, our service, or our offerings, but our love — and a love that is “with all your heart, all your soul, all your might,” holding nothing back. God is not satisfied with a share of the cup; he wants the whole of our heart. This is not God being selfish — it’s because he is worthy, and because only someone who loves God wholeheartedly can truly find satisfaction. We were made to treasure and love God above all else; if the heart is not anchored in him, it will wander elsewhere forever.

When the Lord Jesus was asked which commandment was greatest, he quoted exactly this passage: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment” (Matthew 22:37–38). This shows this commandment has never expired. It also exposes a misconception we often have — thinking the core of being a Christian is “doing the right things”; no, the core is “loving the right object.” Behavior can be faked, but love cannot. God wants your heart first. Paul later lived out the extreme of this commandment: “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8) — this is not ascetic self-sacrifice, but the natural choice of a heart truly captured by God.

But we must be honest: who can truly love God “with all their heart, soul, and might”? Not one of us. Our love is half-hearted, running hot and cold. And this is exactly why the gospel is good news — Christ, who perfectly loved the Father, fulfilled this greatest commandment in our place, and melts our cold hearts with his love. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Today, you don’t need to pretend your love is already perfect — instead, ask the lovely God himself to capture your heart back, so that you increasingly delight in him, and love him more.

Meditation: Is the first thing God wants from me my behavior, or my heart? Is my love for God “with all my heart, soul, and might,” or do I keep most of it for something else?

Application: Today, honestly confess to God your coldness in loving him, and ask him to rekindle your love by meditating on his goodness; choose one thing to do purely “out of love for him,” for no other reason.

Prayer: God worthy of love and adoration, the first thing you want is for me to love you with all my heart, soul, and might. I confess my love is half-hearted, running hot and cold, often divided among other things. Thank you that the Lord Jesus fulfilled this greatest commandment in my place, and melts my cold heart with his love. Capture my heart back for yourself, so I too can say that knowing you is my treasure, delighting in you and loving you more and more. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你要谨慎,免得忘记——丰足时最大的危险
entries.title_en: Take Care, Lest You Forget — The Greatest Danger in Abundance
entries.verse: 申命记八章三节，十章十二至十三节
entries.content:
摩西预先看见一个危险:等以色列进了那流奶与蜜之地,盖了美好的房屋,牛羊加多,金银增添,一切都丰足了,他们的心会怎样?摩西警告:「你要谨慎,免得忘记耶和华你的神」(申8:11)。人在患难中容易呼求神,却在丰足中容易忘记神。饥饿时人人想起吗哪,饱足后却渐渐以为「这货财是我力量、我能力得来的」(申8:17)。

这话扎心,因为它说的就是我们。旷野的四十年,神「苦炼你,任你饥饿,将你和你列祖所不认识的吗哪赐给你吃,使你知道,人活着不是单靠食物,乃是靠耶和华口里所出的一切话」(申8:3)。神让他们经历缺乏,不是要害他们,而是要教他们一件唯有在缺乏中才学得会的功课:真正维系生命的,不是食物,而是神。可惜人一饱足,就忘了这功课,把供应当成了理所当然,把神挤到了角落。

今天我们大多不缺吃穿,反倒活在一种「温水煮青蛙」的属灵危机里。不是逼迫叫我们离弃神,而是舒适叫我们不再需要神;不是苦难叫我们冷淡,而是丰足叫我们忘记。我们的日程排满了,心里塞满了,神的位置却越来越小——我们没有公开否认祂,只是不知不觉地,不再真的倚靠祂、渴慕祂了。保罗后来给提摩太的嘱咐,正是这功课的新约版本:「你要嘱咐那些今世富足的人,不要自高,也不要倚靠无定的钱财;只要倚靠那厚赐百物给我们享受的神」(提前6:17)。

所以摩西的话对我们格外要紧:「你要谨慎。」丰足本身不是罪,忘记神才是。求神给我们警醒的心:在享受祂的恩赐时,不忘恩赐的源头;在一切顺利时,仍天天需要祂、寻求祂。数算恩典而归荣耀与神,是丰足时唯一的解药。今天,你的「丰足」——无论是物质、才干还是顺境——有没有正悄悄把神从你心里挤出去?趁着还听得见这句警告,回到祂面前。

默想:在我丰足、顺利的领域里,神的位置是变大了还是变小了?我是把供应当作理所当然,还是常记得那位供应的主?

应用:今天在一件你一向视为理所当然的丰足(健康、收入、才干)上,刻意停下来向神感恩,并承认你仍然需要祂。

祷告:赐恩的神,你警告你的百姓,免得他们丰足时忘记你。我承认我常在患难中呼求你,却在顺境中把你挤到角落,把你的恩赐当作理所当然,倚靠那无定的钱财过于倚靠你。求你叫我谨慎警醒,在享受恩赐时不忘恩赐的源头,在一切顺利时仍天天渴慕你、倚靠你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Moses foresaw a danger: once Israel entered that land flowing with milk and honey, built fine houses, multiplied their flocks and herds, increased their silver and gold, and had everything in abundance, what would their hearts become? Moses warns: “take care, lest you forget the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 8:11). People easily cry out to God in hardship, yet easily forget God in abundance. When hungry, everyone remembers the manna; once full, they gradually think “my power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17).

This word cuts deep, because it describes us. During the forty years in the wilderness, God “humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3). God let them experience lack not to harm them, but to teach them a lesson learnable only in lack: what truly sustains life is not food, but God. Unfortunately, once people are full, they forget this lesson, take provision for granted, and push God into a corner.

Today most of us lack neither food nor clothing; instead we live in a kind of “boiling frog” spiritual crisis. It is not persecution that makes us leave God, but comfort that makes us no longer need him; it is not hardship that makes us cold, but abundance that makes us forget. Our schedules are packed, our hearts crammed full, yet God’s place grows smaller and smaller — we haven’t openly denied him, we’ve simply, unconsciously, stopped truly depending on him, stopped longing for him. Paul’s later instruction to Timothy is exactly the New Testament version of this lesson: “As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17).

So Moses’s word is especially urgent for us: “Take care.” Abundance itself is not sin; forgetting God is. Ask God to give us a watchful heart: not forgetting the source of the gift while enjoying his gifts; still needing him, still seeking him daily, even when everything goes smoothly. Counting our blessings and giving glory to God is the only cure for abundance. Today, is your “abundance” — whether material, talent, or favorable circumstance — quietly crowding God out of your heart? While you can still hear this warning, return to him.

Meditation: In the areas of my life where I have abundance and things go smoothly, has God’s place grown bigger or smaller? Do I take provision for granted, or do I remember the Lord who provides?

Application: Today, in one abundance you’ve always taken for granted (health, income, ability), deliberately stop to thank God, and acknowledge you still need him.

Prayer: God of grace, you warned your people not to forget you when they became prosperous. I confess I often cry out to you in hardship, yet push you into a corner in favorable times, taking your gifts for granted, relying on uncertain riches more than on you. Let me be watchful and careful, not forgetting the source of the gift while enjoying it, still longing for you and depending on you daily even when everything goes smoothly. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
