entries.title: 不可加添,也不可删减——照神的话敬拜
entries.title_en: Neither Add Nor Take Away — Worship According to God's Word
entries.verse: 申命记十二章卅二节
entries.content:
进入迦南后,以色列将被四围拜偶像的民族包围,那些民族有一套又一套自创的敬拜:高处的祭坛、树下的偶像、五花八门的仪式。摩西反复叮嘱:不要问「这些国民怎样事奉他们的神,我也要照样行」;相反,神怎样吩咐,就怎样敬拜。总纲是这一句:「凡我所吩咐的,你们都要谨守遵行,不可加添,也不可删减」(申12:32)。

这条原则至关重要:敬拜神,要照神自己所定的方式,而不是照我们觉得好的方式。人的天性总想在神的话上「加添」——添些自己觉得更热闹、更感人、更有效的东西;或者「删减」——把神吩咐了却不合我们口味的部分悄悄拿掉。可是神说,两样都不可。祂的话是完备的,既不缺,也不需要我们去补。真正的敬拜,是顺服,不是创意。

为什么神如此看重这一点?因为敬拜的核心问题是:到底谁说了算?一旦我们开始按自己的喜好增删神的话,我们敬拜的就不再是神,而是一个照我们形象改造过的神。金牛犊事件的可怕正在于此——他们不是要拜别的神,而是要照自己的方式拜耶和华。神却不接受。祂要人照祂所启示的真理来亲近祂。启示录末了,神对祂的话再次发出同样严厉的警告:「若有人在这预言上加添什么,神必将写在这书上的灾祸加在他身上;这书上的预言,若有人删去什么,神必从这书上所写的生命树和圣城删去他的分」(启22:18-19)——从摩西到约翰,神对祂话语的完整性,始终守得这样严。

今天这警告依然响亮。我们很容易凭感觉、凭潮流、凭「有没有效果」来决定信仰与敬拜的内容,把神的话当作可增可减的建议。但神的话不是自助餐,由我们挑喜欢的取、不喜欢的留。求神叫我们存敬畏的心,回到圣经,照祂所吩咐的信、所吩咐的行——不加添,也不删减,因为祂的话已经全备。

默想:在我的信仰里,有没有我凭喜好「加添」或悄悄「删减」的神的话?我是照神所定的方式亲近祂,还是照自己觉得好的方式?

应用:今天求圣灵指出一处你一直回避或淡化的圣经教导,不再删减,而是谦卑地领受它、遵行它。

祷告:圣洁的神,你吩咐你的百姓照你的话敬拜,不可加添,也不可删减,从摩西到启示录都是如此严肃。我承认我常凭喜好增删你的话,把不合口味的悄悄放下,把自以为好的添上去。求你赦免我,叫我存敬畏的心回到你全备的话语,照你所启示的来信、来行、来敬拜你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Once in Canaan, Israel would be surrounded by idol-worshiping nations on every side, nations with all kinds of self-invented forms of worship: altars on high places, idols under trees, all sorts of rituals. Moses repeatedly instructs: don’t ask “how do these nations serve their gods, that I also may do likewise”; instead, worship however God has commanded. The general principle is this: “Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32).

This principle is crucial: worshiping God must be according to the way God himself has set, not according to what we think is good. Human nature always wants to “add” to God’s word — adding things we think are more exciting, more moving, more effective; or “take away” — quietly removing parts God commanded that don’t suit our taste. But God says neither is allowed. His word is complete, neither lacking anything nor needing us to supplement it. True worship is obedience, not creativity.

Why does God care so much about this? Because the core question of worship is: who ultimately decides? Once we start adding to or subtracting from God’s word according to our own preference, what we worship is no longer God, but a god remade in our own image. This is exactly the horror of the golden calf incident — they weren’t trying to worship a different god, but to worship the LORD in their own way. God did not accept it. He wants people to draw near to him according to the truth he has revealed. At the end of Revelation, God issues this same severe warning about his word once more: “if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city” (Revelation 22:18–19) — from Moses to John, God has always guarded the integrity of his word this strictly.

This warning still rings out loudly today. We too easily let feelings, trends, or “whether it works” decide the content of our faith and worship, treating God’s word as a suggestion that can be added to or subtracted from. But God’s word is not a buffet, where we pick what we like and leave what we don’t. Ask God to give us a reverent heart, to return to Scripture, to believe and act as he has commanded — neither adding nor taking away, because his word is already complete.

Meditation: In my faith, is there anything I’ve “added” out of preference, or quietly “removed,” from God’s word? Do I draw near to him in the way he has set, or in the way I think is good?

Application: Today, ask the Spirit to point out one biblical teaching you’ve been avoiding or downplaying; no longer subtract from it, but humbly receive it and obey it.

Prayer: Holy God, you commanded your people to worship according to your word, neither adding nor taking away, from Moses all the way to Revelation, always this solemn. I confess I often add to or subtract from your word according to my preference, quietly setting aside what doesn’t suit my taste, adding what I think is good. Forgive me; let me return, with a reverent heart, to your complete word, believing, acting, and worshiping you according to what you have revealed. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 作完全人——并那位要来的先知
entries.title_en: Be Blameless — And the Prophet Yet to Come
entries.verse: 申命记十八章十三至十四节
entries.content:
申命记十八章,摩西一面禁止百姓效法外邦人去观兆、占卜、交鬼——那些想绕过神、偷窥未来、操控命运的手段;一面吩咐他们:「你要在耶和华你的神面前作完全人」(申18:13)。「完全」在这里,不是指毫无瑕疵的道德满分,而是指一颗对神完全、专一、不掺杂的心——不脚踏两条船,不一面拜神一面又暗中倚靠别的。

外邦人观兆占卜的根,是不信——是不肯把自己的前途交在神手里,想靠自己抓住掌控权。「作完全人」的反面,正是这种掺杂与不安:表面信神,暗地里却给自己留后路,靠人脉、靠算计、靠种种「以防万一」的倚靠。神所要的,是一颗肯把全部的未知与不安,都单单交托给祂的心。完全,就是无保留地信靠。

然而摩西接着说了一句极重要的话:「耶和华你的神要从你们弟兄中间给你兴起一位先知,像我,你们要听从他」(申18:15)。这位「像摩西的先知」,历世历代无人完全应验,直到彼得在圣殿门口指着复活的基督,直接引用这句话说:「摩西曾说:主神要从你们弟兄中间给你们兴起一位先知像我,凡他向你们所说的,你们都要听从」(徒3:22)。摩西传神的话,基督却是神的话;摩西是仆人,基督是儿子。真正的「完全人」,不是我们靠努力做成的,而是这位完全信靠父、完全遵行父旨意的基督——祂替我们作了那完全人,又把祂的完全分给我们。

所以「作完全人」不是一道叫我们绝望的高标准,而是一个恩典的邀请:这位应许中要来、又亲自完全信靠父神的基督,愿意一点一点对付我们心里的掺杂,领我们归于专一。你今天心里有没有「留后路」的暗角——那些你没真正交托、还牢牢抓在自己手里的未来?求这位又真又活的主,把你的心夺得更专一,叫你能坦然无惧地,只倚靠祂。

默想:我在神面前是「完全人」吗——还是表面信神,暗地里却给自己留了许多「以防万一」的后路?我的心哪里还有掺杂?

应用:今天指认一处你没有真正交托、还牢牢抓在自己手里的未来或倚靠,在祷告中把它交给神,操练对祂专一的信靠。

祷告:主啊,你吩咐你的百姓作完全人,把前途单单交托给你,不去倚靠别的。我承认我的心常有掺杂,表面信你,暗地里却留着许多后路。感谢你差那位「像摩西的先知」——完全信靠父的基督,替我作成了完全,又把祂的完全分给我。求你对付我心中的掺杂,叫我归于专一,坦然只倚靠你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Deuteronomy 18, Moses, on the one hand, forbids the people from imitating the Gentiles in seeking omens, practicing divination, or consulting mediums — those means by which people try to bypass God, peek at the future, and control their own destiny; on the other hand, he commands them: “You shall be blameless before the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 18:13). “Blameless” here does not mean flawless moral perfection, but a heart wholly, singly devoted to God, without mixture — not straddling two boats, not worshiping God on the surface while secretly relying on something else.

The root of the Gentiles’ seeking omens and divination is unbelief — an unwillingness to place their future in God’s hands, wanting instead to seize control for themselves. The opposite of “being blameless” is precisely this kind of mixture and unease: outwardly believing in God, yet secretly leaving oneself a back door — relying on connections, on calculation, on all kinds of “just in case” fallbacks. What God wants is a heart willing to entrust every uncertainty and anxiety solely to him. Being blameless means trusting without reservation.

Yet Moses goes on to say something extremely important: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen” (Deuteronomy 18:15). This “prophet like Moses” was not fully fulfilled by anyone throughout all the generations, until Peter, at the temple gate, pointing to the risen Christ, directly quoted this verse: “Moses said, The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you” (Acts 3:22). Moses delivered God’s word, but Christ is God’s Word; Moses was a servant, Christ is the Son. The true “blameless one” is not something we achieve through effort, but this Christ, who fully trusted the Father, fully carried out the Father’s will — he became the blameless one in our place, and shares his blamelessness with us.

So “being blameless” is not a hopelessly high standard, but an invitation of grace: this Christ, promised to come, who himself fully trusted God the Father, is willing, bit by bit, to deal with the mixture in our hearts, leading us into singleness of devotion. Do you today have a hidden corner where you’ve “left yourself a back door” — a future you haven’t truly entrusted, still gripping tightly in your own hands? Ask this true and living Lord to capture your heart more fully, so that you can rely, openly and without fear, on him alone.

Meditation: Am I “blameless” before God — or do I outwardly believe in him while secretly keeping many “just in case” back doors? Where is there still mixture in my heart?

Application: Today, name one future or reliance you haven’t truly entrusted, still gripping tightly in your own hands, and in prayer, hand it over to God, practicing singular trust in him.

Prayer: Lord, you commanded your people to be blameless, entrusting their future solely to you, relying on nothing else. I confess my heart is often mixed, believing in you on the surface while secretly keeping many back doors. Thank you for sending that “prophet like Moses” — Christ, who fully trusted the Father, becoming blameless in my place, and sharing his blamelessness with me. Deal with the mixture in my heart, bring me to singleness of devotion, and let me rely on you alone, openly and without fear. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 不可憎恶——被恩待的人如何看待他人
entries.title_en: You Shall Not Abhor — How the Graced Regard Others
entries.verse: 申命记廿三章七至八节
entries.content:
申命记二十一至二十五章,是一大串关乎日常生活的律例:婚姻、财产、诉讼、借贷、待人。其间穿插着一条出人意料的诫命:「不可憎恶以东人,因为他是你的弟兄。不可憎恶埃及人,因为你在他的地上作过寄居的」(申23:7)。以东人是雅各的哥哥以扫的后裔,历史上多次与以色列为敌;埃及则是曾奴役他们四百年之地。按人之常情,这两族最该被恨。神却说:不可憎恶。

神给的理由,再一次是记忆:以东是「你的弟兄」,埃及是「你曾寄居之地」。神不许祂的百姓把仇恨代代相传,而是要他们记得两件事——彼此同源的血脉,以及自己曾经寄人篱下的卑微。一个记得自己也曾是「寄居的」、也曾软弱无助、也曾蒙人接纳的人,就没有资格居高临下地憎恶别人。恨的根,往往是遗忘;而恩慈的根,是记得自己所蒙的恩。

这直指福音的核心。我们对别人是宽是苛,总是暴露出我们有没有真正尝到神的恩典。若我记得自己在神面前也曾是仇敌、是外人、是一无可取却蒙收纳的罪人,我就无法对得罪我的人怀恨到底。保罗说,要「彼此饶恕,正如神在基督里饶恕了你们一样」(弗4:32)。主耶稣的命令更进一步,不只是不憎恶,而是主动去爱:「要爱你们的仇敌,为那逼迫你们的祷告」(太5:44)。不肯放下对别人的憎恶,常常是因为我们忘了自己被赦免得何等彻底。

你心里有没有一个「以东人」——一个你觉得最有理由去恨、去记恨、去老死不相往来的人?神今天对你说的,和对以色列说的一样:不可憎恶。这不是要你假装伤害没发生,而是求神用「我自己也曾蒙赦免」的记忆,融化你心里的恨,叫你能一步步走向饶恕,甚至为他祷告。被恩待的人,才恨不下去。

默想:我心里有没有一个我觉得「最有理由去恨」的人?我对他的态度,暴露出我有没有真正记得自己所蒙的赦免?

应用:今天为一个你一直心怀怨恨的人祷告,求神融化你的恨;若合宜,主动跨出一步,向他表达善意或饶恕。

祷告:满有恩慈的神,你吩咐你的百姓不可憎恶以东人、埃及人,因为他们要记得自己的血脉与卑微。我承认我心里常存着对某些人的憎恶,记恨不放。求你叫我记起:我在你面前也曾是仇敌、是外人,却蒙你彻底赦免、收纳。愿这记忆融化我心里的恨,叫我不但不憎恶,更能为得罪我的人祷告、饶恕他。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Deuteronomy 21–25 is a long series of ordinances concerning daily life: marriage, property, lawsuits, lending, treatment of others. Woven among them is an unexpected commandment: “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother. You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in his land” (Deuteronomy 23:7). The Edomites were descendants of Jacob’s brother Esau, and had historically been Israel’s enemies many times; Egypt was the land that had enslaved them for four hundred years. By human nature, these two nations should be the most hated. Yet God says: do not abhor them.

The reason God gives is, once again, memory: Edom is “your brother,” Egypt is “the land where you sojourned.” God does not allow his people to pass hatred down from generation to generation, but wants them to remember two things — their shared bloodline, and their own former lowly state as sojourners under someone else’s roof. Someone who remembers they too were once a “sojourner,” once weak and helpless, once received by others, has no standing to look down and abhor others. The root of hatred is often forgetting; the root of kindness is remembering the grace one has received.

This points straight to the heart of the gospel. Whether we are gracious or harsh toward others always exposes whether we have truly tasted God’s grace. If I remember that I too was once an enemy, an outsider, an utterly undeserving sinner before God, yet was received, I cannot hold onto hatred against those who wrong me. Paul says, “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). The Lord Jesus’s command goes further still, not merely not abhorring, but proactively loving: “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Refusing to let go of abhorrence toward others is often because we’ve forgotten how completely we ourselves have been forgiven.

Do you have an “Edomite” in your heart — someone you feel you have every reason to hate, to hold a grudge against, to never speak to again? What God says to you today is the same as what he said to Israel: do not abhor. This doesn’t mean pretending the hurt never happened, but asking God to use the memory “I too was once forgiven” to melt the hatred in your heart, so that you can move, step by step, toward forgiveness, even praying for them. Someone treated with grace cannot go on hating.

Meditation: Is there someone in my heart I feel I have “every reason to hate”? Does my attitude toward them expose whether I have truly remembered the forgiveness I received?

Application: Today, pray for someone you’ve held a grudge against, asking God to melt your hatred; if appropriate, proactively take a step to show them kindness or forgiveness.

Prayer: God of abundant grace, you commanded your people not to abhor the Edomites or Egyptians, because they were to remember their shared bloodline and their own lowliness. I confess I often harbor abhorrence toward certain people, holding onto grudges. Let me remember: I too was once your enemy, an outsider, yet you completely forgave and received me. May this memory melt the hatred in my heart, so that I not only stop abhorring, but can pray for and forgive those who wrong me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 永久的膀臂在你以下
entries.title_en: The Everlasting Arms Are Beneath You
entries.content:
永久的膀臂在你以下

「永生的 神是你的居所；他永久的膀臂在你以下。」(申命记 33:27)

这一周,我们随摩西回顾了律法与恩典——爱神、不忘记神、照神的话而活。整卷申命记,是一位将死的老仆人,把百姓的手,再一次放回神的手里。

你或许也走得疲惫、脚步发软。但请记得:托住你的,从不是你自己的力量,而是神「永久的膀臂」。它在你以下,你便跌不出祂的手。今天,歇在这双膀臂里。

"The eternal God is your refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms." (Deuteronomy 33:27)
entries.content_en:
The Everlasting Arms Are Beneath You

"The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms." (Deuteronomy 33:27)

This week, we followed Moses in reviewing the law and grace — loving God, not forgetting God, living by God’s word. The whole book of Deuteronomy is a dying old servant placing the people’s hand, once more, back into God’s hand.

You too may be weary from walking, your steps growing weak. But remember: what holds you up was never your own strength, but God’s "everlasting arms." They are beneath you, so you cannot fall out of his hand. Today, rest in these arms.

"The eternal God is your refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms." (Deuteronomy 33:27)

entries.title: 隐秘的事属神——与未知同行的信心
entries.title_en: The Secret Things Belong to the LORD — Faith That Walks With the Unknown
entries.verse: 申命记廿九章廿九节
entries.content:
摩西把神的律法都摆在百姓面前,末了说了一句意味深长的话:「隐秘的事是属耶和华我们神的;惟有明显的事是永远属我们和我们子孙的,好叫我们遵行这律法上的一切话」(申29:29)。神把世界分成了两半:一半是「隐秘的」——那些祂没有向我们解释的、我们怎么想也想不通的事;另一半是「明显的」——祂已经清楚启示、要我们去遵行的旨意。

我们的麻烦,常常是把这两半弄反了。对于「隐秘的事」,我们非要弄个明白:为什么是我?为什么是现在?这苦难到底有什么意义?我们盯着神没有解释的部分,焦虑、质问、钻牛角尖,仿佛非得看懂全局才肯往前走。而对于「明显的事」——神清清楚楚吩咐的爱人、饶恕、诚实、圣洁——我们反倒拖延、打折、置之不理。

这节经文温柔又坚定地把我们摆正:隐秘的事,交给神;明显的事,去遵行。保罗后来引用申命记三十章的话——「这话却离你甚近,就在你口中,在你心里,使你可以遵行」(申30:14)——直接应用在福音上:「这道离你不远,正在你口里,在你心里——就是我们所传信主的道」(罗10:8)。神已经启示、要我们相信顺服的,从来不是遥不可及的奥秘,而是近在口边、近在心里的道。信心不是把一切都想通了才安心,而是在没想通的时候,依然信靠那位全知全善的神,并专心去做那已经清楚知道的事。

你今天是否卡在一件「隐秘的事」上,因为想不通而寸步难行?神邀请你,把那想不通的,放在祂手里——祂知道,就够了;然后,转过身去,做好那件你明明知道该做的事。与未知同行的平安,不在于拿到答案,而在于信靠那位掌管答案的神。祂隐藏的,出于智慧;祂显明的,足够你走今天的路。

默想:我是否总盯着神没有解释的「隐秘的事」而焦虑,却拖延着神已经清楚吩咐的「明显的事」?

应用:今天把一件你一直想不通、放不下的事,交托在神手里;同时,选一件神已清楚吩咐、你却一直拖延的事去遵行。

祷告:全知全善的神,隐秘的事属你,明显的事属我们,好叫我们遵行;你的道也从不遥远,近在我们口边心里。我承认我常盯着你没有解释的部分焦虑质问,却对你清楚吩咐的旨意拖延打折。求你叫我肯把想不通的交在你手里,信你的智慧;又叫我专心去行那已经明明知道的,在与未知同行中,得着信靠你的平安。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Moses laid all of God’s law before the people, and at the end said something deeply meaningful: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). God has divided the world into two halves: one half is “the secret things” — those things he has not explained to us, that we can never quite figure out no matter how we think about them; the other half is “the revealed things” — the will he has already clearly disclosed, that he wants us to carry out.

Our trouble is often getting these two halves backwards. Regarding “the secret things,” we insist on figuring them out: why me? Why now? What possible meaning could this suffering have? We stare at the part God hasn’t explained, growing anxious, questioning, obsessing, as if we won’t move forward until we’ve understood the whole picture. Yet regarding “the revealed things” — what God has clearly commanded, to love, forgive, be honest, be holy — we instead delay, discount, or ignore them.

This verse gently yet firmly sets us straight: hand the secret things to God; go and do the revealed things. Paul later quotes the words of Deuteronomy 30 — “the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it” (Deuteronomy 30:14) — and applies it directly to the gospel: “the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim) (Romans 10:8). What God has already revealed, wanting us to believe and obey, was never some far-off mystery, but a word close at hand, close to the heart. Faith is not becoming at ease only once everything is figured out — it is, when things aren’t figured out, still trusting the all-knowing, all-good God, and wholeheartedly doing what is already clearly known.

Are you today stuck on some “secret thing,” unable to move because you can’t figure it out? God invites you to place what you can’t figure out in his hands — he knows, and that is enough; then turn around and do the thing you clearly know you should do. The peace of walking with the unknown is not found in getting the answer, but in trusting the God who holds the answer. What he has hidden comes from wisdom; what he has revealed is enough for you to walk today’s road.

Meditation: Do I always stare anxiously at the “secret things” God hasn’t explained, while delaying the “revealed things” God has clearly commanded?

Application: Today, hand over to God one thing you’ve been unable to figure out, unable to let go of; at the same time, choose one thing God has clearly commanded that you’ve been delaying, and go do it.

Prayer: All-knowing, all-good God, the secret things belong to you, the revealed things belong to us, that we may do them; your word is never far off, but near, in our mouth and heart. I confess I often stare anxiously and questioningly at what you haven’t explained, while delaying and discounting what you have clearly commanded. Let me be willing to place what I can’t figure out in your hands, trusting your wisdom; and let me wholeheartedly do what I already clearly know, finding, in walking with the unknown, the peace of trusting you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 再没有先知像摩西——直到那位更大的来到
entries.title_en: No Prophet Like Moses Again — Until the Greater One Came
entries.verse: 申命记卅四章十节
entries.content:
申命记以摩西之死作结。他登上尼波山,远远眺望那应许之地,却不得进去;神亲自埋葬了他,没有人知道他的坟墓在哪里。圣经给他写下极高的悼词:「以后以色列中再没有兴起先知像摩西的。他是耶和华面对面所认识的」(申34:10)。摩西是律法的颁布者、以色列的领袖、神的忠仆,旧约里无人能及。

然而「再没有先知像摩西」这句话,本身就带着一个悬念:那么,神早先应许的「一位先知像我」(申18:15),又在哪里呢?整本旧约,就带着这份未了的期待往前走。摩西再伟大,也只是仆人;他能把百姓领到应许之地的边缘,自己却进不去;他能传神的话,却不能除去人的罪。他指向的,是一位比他更大的。

那位更大的,就是耶稣基督。约翰说:「律法本是藉着摩西传的;恩典和真理都是由耶稣基督来的」(约1:17)。希伯来书说得更清楚:「摩西为仆人……但基督为儿子,治理神的家」(来3:5-6)。摩西把律法交给我们,叫我们知道自己达不到;基督却把恩典与真理带给我们,亲自成全了律法,又领我们进入那真正的安息之地。摩西所不能的,基督都成了。

这提醒我们:不要停在任何伟大的仆人身上——无论是圣经中的英雄,还是今天我们所敬重的属灵前辈。他们再好,也只是指路的仆人,不是那位救主。一切最好的仆人,都在指向那位更好的儿子。今天,让你的目光越过一切「摩西」,定睛在基督身上;唯有祂,能领你进入摩西领不进的地方。

默想:我是否把某个属灵伟人(或自己敬重的领袖)当成了终点,而忘了他们都只是指向基督的仆人?

应用:今天有意识地把你对某位属灵榜样的仰慕,转向那位他所指向的基督——为一处「摩西所不能、基督却成全」的恩典感恩。

祷告:满有恩典的神,摩西何等伟大,却仍只是仆人,进不了应许之地,除不去人的罪。感谢你差来那位更大的——你的儿子耶稣基督,祂带来恩典与真理,成全了律法,领我进入摩西领不进的安息。求你叫我不停在任何仆人身上,而是越过一切「摩西」,单单定睛于基督。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Deuteronomy ends with Moses’s death. He climbed Mount Nebo and looked out from a distance over the promised land, yet was not allowed to enter; God himself buried him, and no one knows where his grave is. Scripture writes him an extremely high eulogy: “there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (Deuteronomy 34:10). Moses was the giver of the law, the leader of Israel, God’s faithful servant — no one in the Old Testament could compare to him.

Yet the phrase “there has not arisen a prophet like Moses again” itself carries a suspense: so where, then, is that “prophet like me” God had promised earlier (Deuteronomy 18:15)? The whole Old Testament moves forward carrying this unresolved expectation. However great Moses was, he was still only a servant; he could lead the people to the edge of the promised land, yet could not enter himself; he could deliver God’s word, but could not remove people’s sin. He points to someone greater than himself.

That greater one is Jesus Christ. John says: “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Hebrews says it even more clearly: “Moses was faithful... as a servant... but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:5–6). Moses handed us the law, so that we would know we cannot reach it; Christ brought us grace and truth, personally fulfilling the law, and leading us into that true rest. What Moses could not do, Christ has done.

This reminds us: don’t stop at any great servant — whether a hero in Scripture, or a spiritual mentor we respect today. However good they are, they are only servants pointing the way, not the Savior. Every best servant points to that better Son. Today, let your gaze pass beyond every “Moses,” and fix on Christ; only he can lead you into the place Moses could not lead you into.

Meditation: Have I treated some spiritual giant (or a leader I admire) as the destination, forgetting they are all just servants pointing to Christ?

Application: Today, deliberately turn your admiration for some spiritual example toward the Christ they point to — give thanks for one grace “Moses could not accomplish, but Christ has fulfilled.”

Prayer: God of abundant grace, however great Moses was, he was still only a servant, unable to enter the promised land, unable to remove people’s sin. Thank you for sending the greater one — your Son Jesus Christ, who brought grace and truth, fulfilled the law, and led me into the rest Moses could not lead me into. Let me not stop at any servant, but pass beyond every “Moses,” fixing my eyes solely on Christ. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你当刚强壮胆——因为我必与你同在
entries.title_en: Be Strong and Courageous — For I Will Be With You
entries.verse: 约书亚记一章九节
entries.content:
摩西死了,重担落在约书亚肩上:要带领这一大群人渡过约旦河,攻取那住着巨人和坚城的迦南地。这是何等叫人胆怯的任务。神却一再对他说同一句话:「你当刚强壮胆!不要惧怕,也不要惊惶;因为你无论往哪里去,耶和华你的神必与你同在」(书1:9)。短短几节里,「刚强壮胆」出现了三次。

值得注意的是:神吩咐约书亚刚强,却不是叫他靠自己壮胆。神给出的理由,从来不是「因为你很能干」「因为敌人不堪一击」,而是「因为耶和华你的神必与你同在」。真正的勇气,不是一种性格,而是一种信心——不是自我感觉良好,而是深信那位全能的神与我同去。勇气的源头在神,不在我;我越小看自己、越仰望祂,反而越刚强。

神也给了约书亚勇气的另一个根基:祂的话。祂吩咐约书亚昼夜思想遵行律法书(书1:8)——因为面对未知,叫人站立得稳的,是抓住神已经说过的话。恐惧最爱在「不确定」里生长,而神的应许是黑暗里的锚。希伯来书后来把这份应许接续到每一个信徒身上,并给出了一个大胆的结论:「主曾说:我总不撇下你,也不丢弃你。所以我们可以放胆说:主是帮助我的,我必不惧怕;人能把我怎么样呢?」(来13:5-6)当约书亚把心思定在「神与我同在」「神已应许赐这地」上,巨人和坚城就不再是拦阻,而是神要成就应许的舞台。

你今天面前是否也有一条「约旦河」——一个叫你胆怯、想退缩的任务、决定或未来?神对约书亚说的话,今天也对你说:刚强壮胆,不要惧怕,因为我必与你同在。这份勇气不必你凭空挤出来,它是从「神与我同在」这个事实里长出来的。抓住祂的应许,举步向前;那位吩咐你刚强的神,必亲自与你同去。

默想:我所缺的勇气,是想靠自己挤出来,还是从「神与我同在」的应许里支取?我的胆怯背后,是不是忘了谁与我同去?

应用:今天面对一件让你胆怯、想退缩的事,把神「我必与你同在」的应许抓在手里,凭信心跨出你一直不敢跨的那一步。

祷告:全能的神,你三次吩咐约书亚刚强壮胆,理由不是他能干,而是你必与他同在。我承认我面对难处常胆怯退缩,想靠自己挤出勇气,却忘了你与我同去。求你叫我把勇气的根扎在你的同在与应许上,抓住你的话,举步向前,好叫我也能放胆说:主是帮助我的,我必不惧怕。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Moses had died, and the weight fell on Joshua’s shoulders: to lead this great crowd across the Jordan and take the land of Canaan, full of giants and fortified cities. What a terrifying task. Yet God said the same thing to him again and again: “Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). In just a few verses, “be strong and courageous” appears three times.

It’s worth noting: God commanded Joshua to be strong, but not to draw that strength from himself. The reason God gives is never “because you are so capable,” “because the enemy is weak,” but “because the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.” True courage is not a personality trait — it is a form of faith — not feeling good about yourself, but deeply believing the almighty God goes with me. The source of courage is God, not me; the more I think little of myself and look to him, the stronger I actually become.

God also gave Joshua another foundation for courage: his word. He commanded Joshua to meditate on the Book of the Law day and night, and to do it (Joshua 1:8) — because facing the unknown, what makes a person stand firm is holding onto what God has already said. Fear loves to grow in “uncertainty,” and God’s promise is an anchor in the darkness. Hebrews later extends this promise to every believer, and draws a bold conclusion: “He has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you. So we can confidently say, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?” (Hebrews 13:5–6). When Joshua fixed his mind on “God is with me,” “God has promised this land,” the giants and fortified cities were no longer obstacles, but the very stage on which God would fulfill his promise.

Do you today have your own “Jordan River” — a task, decision, or future that makes you afraid, makes you want to retreat? What God said to Joshua, he says to you today too: be strong and courageous, do not be afraid, for I will be with you. This courage doesn’t need to be squeezed out of nothing by you — it grows out of the fact that “God is with me.” Hold onto his promise, and step forward; the God who commands you to be strong will personally go with you.

Meditation: Is the courage I lack something I want to squeeze out of myself, or something I draw from the promise “God is with me”? Behind my fearfulness, have I forgotten who goes with me?

Application: Today, facing something that makes you afraid, makes you want to retreat, hold onto God’s promise “I will be with you,” and by faith take the step you’ve never dared to take.

Prayer: Almighty God, you told Joshua three times to be strong and courageous, not because he was capable, but because you would be with him. I confess I often grow afraid and retreat when facing difficulty, wanting to squeeze out courage myself, forgetting you go with me. Let me root my courage in your presence and your promise, hold onto your word, and step forward, so that I too can confidently say: the Lord is my helper, I will not be afraid. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 营中的隐藏之罪——亚干的教训
entries.title_en: Hidden Sin in the Camp — The Lesson of Achan
entries.verse: 约书亚记七章十三节
entries.content:
耶利哥城奇迹般地陷落,以色列士气高涨。接下来那座小小的艾城,照理不在话下;谁知却大败而归,三十六人阵亡。约书亚俯伏在神面前哀求,神的回答却指向一个隐藏的根源:「以色列啊,你们中间有当灭的物,你们若不除掉,在仇敌面前必站立不住!」(书7:13)原来,有一个叫亚干的人,私自把当灭之物——一件美衣、银子、金子——藏在自己帐棚的地里。全营的失败,竟系于一个人隐藏的罪。

这件事揭开一个严肃的属灵真相:隐藏的罪,拦阻神的同在。亚干以为神看不见,以为藏得够深就没事,以为那不过是「一点点」私欲,与别人无干。可是罪从不是私事。它像营中的一处溃烂,悄悄夺去了神百姓的能力。希伯来书后来这样警戒教会:「又要谨慎,恐怕有人失了神的恩;恐怕有毒根生出来扰乱你们,因此叫众人沾染污秽」(来12:15)——一个人心里没有对付的毒根,足以扰乱、玷污一整个群体,亚干正是这话最早的例证。

神对付这罪的方式是:把它揪出来,摆在光中。祂叫约书亚一支派一支派、一家一家地把亚干查出来。这过程叫人战兢,却是恩典——因为唯有被显明的罪,才能被除去;藏着的罪,只会继续作祟。神今天也这样光照我们:祂把手指按在那件我们一直遮掩、以为无伤大雅的事上,不是要羞辱我们,而是要我们把它带到光中,好叫祂的同在与能力得以恢复。

亲爱的,你帐棚的地里,埋着什么?那件你一直不肯拿出来、告诉自己「就这一点点、没关系」的隐藏之罪?求圣灵鉴察你,把你里面的亚干指给你看。不要护着它、藏着它——那要叫你屡战屡败;把它挖出来,带到神面前,认它、弃它。当隐藏的罪被对付,神的同在与能力,就必重新回到你身上。

默想:我心里的「帐棚」下,有没有埋着一件我一直遮掩、以为「一点点没关系」的隐藏之罪?它是否正暗暗夺去我属灵的能力,甚至连累身边的人?

应用:今天求圣灵鉴察你,指出一处你一直遮掩的隐藏之罪,把它带到光中向神认明,并采取具体行动弃绝它。

祷告:鉴察人心的神,亚干把当灭之物藏在帐棚地里,全营就在仇敌面前站立不住。我承认我里面也常藏着一些以为「无伤大雅」的隐藏之罪,恐怕毒根滋生,连累身边的人。求你的光照进我心,把我里面的亚干指给我看;赐我勇气把它挖出来、认明、弃绝,好叫你的同在重新回到我身上。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Jericho fell miraculously, and Israel’s morale soared. The small city of Ai that followed should, by all reason, have been no problem; yet, unexpectedly, Israel was badly defeated, thirty-six men killed. Joshua fell down before God in anguish, and God’s answer pointed to a hidden root cause: “O Israel, there is an accursed thing among you; you cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the accursed thing from among you!” (Joshua 7:13). It turned out a man named Achan had secretly hidden devoted things — a beautiful cloak, silver, gold — under his own tent. The defeat of the whole camp hinged on one man’s hidden sin.

This event uncovers a solemn spiritual truth: hidden sin obstructs God’s presence. Achan thought God couldn’t see, thought if it was hidden deep enough it would be fine, thought it was just “a little bit” of personal desire, none of anyone else’s business. But sin is never a private matter. It’s like a festering sore in the camp, quietly stealing God’s people’s power. Hebrews later warns the church this way: “See to it... that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:15) — an undealt-with root of bitterness in one person’s heart is enough to trouble and defile an entire community, and Achan is the earliest example of this word.

God’s way of dealing with this sin was: to root it out, and put it in the light. He had Joshua search it out, tribe by tribe, family by family, until Achan was found. This process was terrifying, yet it was grace — because only sin that is exposed can be removed; sin that stays hidden will only continue to do harm. God shines his light on us the same way today: he puts his finger on the thing we’ve been covering up, thinking harmless, not to shame us, but so that we would bring it into the light, that his presence and power might be restored.

Beloved, what is buried under your own tent floor? That hidden sin you’ve never been willing to bring out, telling yourself, “it’s just this little bit, it’s fine”? Ask the Spirit to search you, and show you the Achan within you. Don’t guard it, don’t hide it — that will make you fail battle after battle; dig it out, bring it before God, confess it, forsake it. When hidden sin is dealt with, God’s presence and power will return to you.

Meditation: Under my own “tent,” is there a hidden sin I’ve been covering up, thinking “it’s just a little, no big deal”? Is it quietly stealing my spiritual power, even affecting those around me?

Application: Today, ask the Spirit to search you, point out a hidden sin you’ve been covering up, bring it into the light before God and confess it, and take concrete action to forsake it.

Prayer: God who searches the heart, Achan hid the devoted things under his tent floor, and the whole camp could not stand before the enemy. I confess I too often hide things I think are “harmless,” fearing a root of bitterness may grow and affect those around me. Let your light shine into my heart, and show me the Achan within; give me courage to dig it out, confess it, and forsake it, so that your presence would return to me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 日头停住——那位为你争战的神
entries.title_en: The Sun Stood Still — The God Who Fights For You
entries.verse: 约书亚记十章十三节
entries.content:
约书亚记九至十二章,记载以色列迅速攻取迦南。其中最惊人的一幕,是基遍一役:约书亚为了追击敌军,竟向神祈求日头停住,神就应允——「日头在天当中停住,不急速下落,约有一日之久」(书10:13)。经文还加了一句解释:在这日以前以后,「耶和华听人的祷告,没有像这日的」。那一天,连日月星辰都听凭神差遣,为祂百姓的争战效力。

但这段经文真正的重点,不是天文奇观,而是那句点睛的话:这一切「是因耶和华为以色列争战」(书10:14)。以色列攻城略地,看似是他们在打仗,骨子里却是神在为他们争战。他们要做的,是听命、起来、向前;胜利,却是神成就的。约书亚记一次次告诉我们:得地为业不是靠人的刀剑,而是靠那位为祂百姓争战、连日头都听祂调度的神。

这纠正我们一个常有的错觉:以为属灵的争战全靠自己咬牙硬拼。的确,我们要顺服、要行动、要付上努力;但决定胜负的,从不是我们的实力,而是神的大能。保罗说,我们「并不是与属血气的争战」(弗6:12),而那位为我们争战的,是曾在十字架上「仗着十字架夸胜」、掳掠了一切执政掌权者的基督(西2:15)。真正的得胜,是站在那位已经得胜的主一边。

你今天面对的那场「仗」——那个顽固的罪、那段难熬的处境、那个看似攻不下的难关——你是想独自硬扛,还是仰望那位为你争战的神?祂能叫日头停住,岂不能为你成就所需的一切?你的本分是顺服祂、起来向前;胜败,交给那位从不打败仗的神。举目看祂,然后照祂的话起行。

默想:面对属灵的争战,我是想靠自己的实力硬拼,还是仰望那位「为以色列争战」的神?我把胜负押在谁身上?

应用:今天把一场你一直独自硬扛的「争战」交给神,宣告「耶和华为我争战」,照祂的话去顺服、行动,把结果交在祂手里。

祷告:大能的神,基遍一役,你叫日头停住,为你的百姓争战——胜利从来是你成就的。我承认我常以为属灵的争战全靠自己咬牙硬拼,忘了你才是那位为我争战的神。感谢你,基督已在十字架上胜过一切仇敌。求你叫我顺服你、起来向前,把胜负交给那位从不打败仗的主。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Joshua 9–12 records how Israel quickly conquered Canaan. Among the most astonishing scenes is the battle of Gibeon: Joshua, pursuing the enemy, actually asked God for the sun to stand still, and God granted it — “the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies... the sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day” (Joshua 10:13). The text adds an explanation: before or since, “there has been no day like it, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man.” That day, even the sun, moon, and stars submitted to God’s command, working for his people’s battle.

But the true point of this passage is not the astronomical wonder, but this pivotal statement: all this happened “because the LORD fought for Israel” (Joshua 10:14). Israel taking cities and territory looked like their own fighting, but at its core it was God fighting for them. What they had to do was obey, rise up, move forward; the victory, however, was God’s accomplishment. Joshua tells us again and again: possessing the land as an inheritance depends not on human swords, but on the God who fights for his people, who commands even the sun.

This corrects a misconception we often have: thinking spiritual warfare depends entirely on gritting our teeth and fighting it out ourselves. Indeed, we must obey, act, and put in effort; but what decides victory or defeat was never our own strength, but God’s power. Paul says we “do not wrestle against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12), and the one who fights for us is Christ, who on the cross “triumphed over them by the cross,” disarming every ruler and authority (Colossians 2:15). True victory is standing on the side of the Lord who has already won.

That “battle” you face today — a stubborn sin, a hard-to-endure situation, a difficulty that seems impossible to break through — do you want to fight it alone, or look to the God who fights for you? He can make the sun stand still — can he not accomplish everything you need? Your duty is to obey him and move forward; victory or defeat, hand over to the God who never loses. Lift your eyes to him, and then act according to his word.

Meditation: Facing spiritual battle, do I want to grit my teeth and fight it out on my own strength, or look to the God who “fights for Israel”? Whose hands have I placed victory or defeat in?

Application: Today, hand over a “battle” you’ve been fighting alone to God, declare “the LORD fights for me,” obey and act according to his word, and place the outcome in his hands.

Prayer: Mighty God, at the battle of Gibeon you made the sun stand still, fighting for your people — victory has always been your accomplishment. I confess I often think spiritual battle depends entirely on my own gritted-teeth effort, forgetting you are the God who fights for me. Thank you, Christ has already triumphed over every enemy on the cross. Let me obey you and move forward, handing victory and defeat to the Lord who never loses. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 将这山地给我——八十五岁仍然火热的信心
entries.title_en: Give Me This Hill Country — Faith Still Burning at Eighty-Five
entries.verse: 约书亚记十四章十一节
entries.content:
分地的时候,八十五岁的迦勒站出来,向约书亚提出一个请求。四十五年前,他作探子进迦南,别人都因巨人而丧胆,唯独他和约书亚说「我们能得胜」;为此他在旷野多漂流了四十年。如今他老了,却毫无退休养老之意,反而说:「我还是强壮,像摩西打发我去的那天一样;无论是争战,是出入,我的力量那时如何,现在还是如何」(书14:11)。然后他指着那座还住着巨人的山地说:将这山地给我!

迦勒身上有一种叫人肃然起敬的东西:几十年过去,他的信心非但没有随年岁冷却,反而依旧火热。别人挑平原、挑容易的,他偏偏求那座最难啃、还盘踞着巨人的山。因为他心里有一句话,圣经反复为他盖章:他「专心跟从耶和华以色列的神」(书14:14)。专心——不是三分钟热度,不是年轻时冲一冲、年老了就歇一歇,而是一生之久、始终如一地跟从神。

这正是对我们许多人的拷问。我们太容易在信仰上「退休」:年轻时热心追求,渐渐地被生活磨平了棱角,把冒险交给别人,自己挑最安稳的路走,美其名曰「成熟」。可是迦勒到八十五岁,还在求山地、还想打仗、还要为神攻下新的疆土。保罗晚年下在监里,说的却是同一种心志:「我不是以为自己已经得着了;我只有一件事,就是忘记背后,努力面前的,向着标竿直跑」(腓3:13-14)。他给我们看见:跟随神不是一段青春的激情,而是一生的赛程;真正的成熟,不是热情熄灭,而是信心越老越坚。

你如今在信仰的哪个阶段?是越走越退缩、越挑越安稳,还是像迦勒、像保罗一样,还敢指着那座难山说「将这山地给我」?求神叫我们不做属灵的退休者,而是一生专心跟从祂,至死忠心。也许神今天正把一座「山地」摆在你面前——一件需要信心、需要争战才能得着的事。别绕开它;凭着那从未冷却的信心,求神把它给你。

默想:我的信心是随年岁越走越退缩、越挑越安稳,还是像迦勒一样越老越火热、还敢求难山?我是「专心」跟从神,还是三分钟热度?

应用:今天找出一座你一直绕开的「山地」——一件需要信心与争战的事,像迦勒一样求神把它交给你,并踏出第一步去攻取。

祷告:信实的神,迦勒八十五岁仍然刚强,因他一生专心跟从你,还敢求那住着巨人的山地。我承认我常在信仰上想「退休」,被生活磨平了热心,专挑安稳的路走。求你叫我不做属灵的退休者,而像迦勒、像保罗一样,忘记背后,努力面前,一生专心跟从你,越老越火热,还敢为你攻取新的疆土。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
When the land was being divided, eighty-five-year-old Caleb stepped forward and made a request of Joshua. Forty-five years earlier, he had gone into Canaan as a spy; everyone else lost heart because of the giants, but he and Joshua alone said, “we are able to overcome it.” For this he had wandered an extra forty years in the wilderness. Now he was old, yet had no thought of retirement — instead he said: “I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming” (Joshua 14:11). Then, pointing to the hill country still occupied by giants, he said: give me this hill country!

There is something in Caleb that commands deep respect: decades had passed, and his faith, far from cooling with age, still burned. Others picked the plains, the easy places; he alone asked for the hardest, most stubborn mountain, still infested with giants. Because there was one thing in his heart, which Scripture repeatedly stamps with approval: he “wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel” (Joshua 14:14). Wholly — not three minutes of enthusiasm, not a burst in youth and rest in old age, but following God consistently, for a whole lifetime.

This is precisely an interrogation of many of us. We too easily “retire” from our faith: eager in pursuit when young, gradually worn smooth by life, leaving adventure to others, choosing the safest road for ourselves, dignifying it with the name “maturity.” But Caleb, at eighty-five, was still asking for hill country, still wanting to fight, still wanting to conquer new territory for God. Paul, in his old age, imprisoned, expressed the very same resolve: “Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on... forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal” (Philippians 3:12–14). They show us: following God is not a season of youthful passion, but a lifelong race; true maturity is not passion dying out, but faith growing firmer with age.

Where are you now in your walk of faith? Are you retreating further and further, picking safer and safer options, or, like Caleb and Paul, still daring to point at that difficult mountain and say, “give me this hill country”? Ask God to make us not spiritual retirees, but people who follow him wholeheartedly for life, faithful unto death. Perhaps God is today placing a “hill country” before you — something that requires faith, that requires a fight, to obtain. Don’t go around it; with that never-cooling faith, ask God to give it to you.

Meditation: Does my faith retreat further and pick safer options as I age, or, like Caleb, burn hotter with age, still daring to ask for difficult mountains? Am I “wholly” following God, or just three minutes of enthusiasm?

Application: Today, find a “hill country” you’ve been going around — something that requires faith and a fight — and, like Caleb, ask God to give it to you, and take the first step to take it.

Prayer: Faithful God, Caleb at eighty-five was still strong, because he had wholly followed you for a lifetime, and still dared to ask for the mountain infested with giants. I confess I often want to “retire” in my faith, my zeal worn smooth by life, always picking the safe road. Let me not be a spiritual retiree, but, like Caleb and Paul, forget what lies behind, strain forward to what lies ahead, follow you wholly for a lifetime, burn hotter with age, and still dare to conquer new territory for you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 另有一安息为神子民存留
entries.title_en: There Remains a Rest for the People of God
entries.content:
另有一安息为神子民存留

「这样看来，必另有一安息日的安息为 神的子民存留。」(希伯来书 4:9)

这一周,我们随约书亚渡过约旦河,攻城、得地、分业。以色列终于从旷野的漂流,进入了神所应许的安息之地。

然而希伯来书说,那地上的安息还不是终点;真正的安息,是在基督里——停下自己的劳苦,安歇在祂已成就的救恩中。今天,不必再靠自己去挣、去争、去证明;进入祂,就进入了安息。

"There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God." (Hebrews 4:9)
entries.content_en:
There Remains a Rest for the People of God

"So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God." (Hebrews 4:9)

This week, we crossed the Jordan with Joshua, took cities, possessed the land, and divided the inheritance. Israel finally moved from wandering in the wilderness into the land of rest God had promised.

Yet Hebrews says that earthly rest is not the final destination; true rest is in Christ — laying down our own labor, resting in the salvation he has already accomplished. Today, you no longer need to strive, struggle, and prove yourself; entering him is entering rest.

"There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God." (Hebrews 4:9)

entries.title: 一句也没有落空——神应许的可靠
entries.title_en: Not One Word Failed — The Reliability of God's Promise
entries.verse: 约书亚记廿一章四十五节
entries.content:
约书亚记的末尾,以色列已经分地完毕,各支派安居在神所赐的产业上。作者在此写下一句掷地有声的总结:「耶和华应许赐福给以色列家的话一句也没有落空,都应验了」(书21:45)。从亚伯拉罕蒙召算起,这块应许之地等了几百年;其间有为奴、有旷野、有巨人、有坚城——可是到头来,神所应许的,一句都没有落空。

「一句也没有落空」——请让这句话在心里多停留一会儿。神的应许不是一堆美好的愿望,不是「大概会、也许能」;而是「必定成就」。祂说过的每一句话,都像已经盖了印、存了档,时候一到,分毫不差地兑现。以色列的历史,就是神信实的一份见证清单:祂说要赐地,就赐了;说要同在,就同在了;说要得胜,就得胜了。

我们的难处,常常不是神不信实,而是我们太健忘、太性急。应许还没兑现的时候,我们就慌了、疑了,以为神忘了、神变卦了。但神的时间表不等于我们的时间表;祂从不迟延,也从不落空——「主所应许的尚未成就,有人以为他是耽延,其实不是耽延,乃是宽容你们,不愿有一人沉沦」(彼后3:9)。保罗说,神的应许「在基督都是是的」(林后1:20)——在基督里,神对你说过的每一句话,都有了最坚实的担保。

你今天是否正抓着神的一个应许,却迟迟不见兑现,几乎要灰心了?约书亚记提醒你:数算神过去的信实,好叫你相信祂将来的应许。祂昔日待以色列一句不落空,今日待你也必如此。祂的应许不会过期,也不会打折,祂的「迟延」里藏着的是宽容,不是遗忘。安心等候,并照祂的话去行——那位说话算数的神,必成就祂向你所应许的一切。

默想:当神的应许迟迟未兑现时,我是慌乱疑惑,还是数算祂过去的信实而安心等候?

应用:今天写下一个你正在等候的神的应许,再数算三件神过去为你成就的事,以此坚固你今天的信心。

祷告:信实的神,你向以色列所应许的,一句也没有落空,都应验了。我承认我常健忘又性急,应许未成就时就疑惑你、以为你忘了。感谢你,你的应许在基督里都是是的,你的迟延里藏着的是宽容。求你叫我数算你过去的信实,安心等候你将来的成就,深信你说过的每一句话都必兑现。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
At the end of the book of Joshua, Israel has finished dividing the land, and each tribe is settling into the inheritance God gave them. The author here writes a resounding summary: “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (Joshua 21:45). Counting from Abraham’s calling, this promised land had been waited for across several hundred years; in between were slavery, wilderness, giants, fortified cities — yet in the end, not one word God had promised failed.

“Not one word failed” — let this phrase linger in your heart a moment longer. God’s promises are not a pile of nice wishes, not “probably will, maybe can”; but “will surely come to pass.” Every word he has spoken is like something already sealed and filed away, to be fulfilled precisely, to the letter, when the time comes. Israel’s history is a record of testimony to God’s faithfulness: he said he would give the land, and he gave it; he said he would be present, and he was present; he said they would be victorious, and they were victorious.

Our trouble is often not that God is unfaithful, but that we are too forgetful, too impatient. When a promise hasn’t yet been fulfilled, we panic and doubt, thinking God has forgotten, or changed his mind. But God’s timetable is not our timetable; he never delays, and never fails — “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). Paul says God’s promises “in [Christ] are Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20) — in Christ, every word God has spoken to you has the most solid guarantee.

Are you today holding onto one of God’s promises, yet seeing it long unfulfilled, nearly discouraged? Joshua reminds you: count God’s faithfulness in the past, so that you can believe his promises for the future. As he dealt with Israel, not one word failing, so he will deal with you today. His promises will not expire, will not be discounted; his “delay” hides patience within it, not forgetting. Wait in peace, and act according to his word — the God who keeps his word will surely accomplish everything he has promised you.

Meditation: When God’s promise is long delayed in coming, am I panicking and doubting, or counting his past faithfulness and waiting in peace?

Application: Today, write down a promise of God you’re currently waiting for, then count three things God has accomplished for you in the past, to strengthen your faith today.

Prayer: Faithful God, not one word of what you promised Israel failed; all came to pass. I confess I’m often forgetful and impatient, doubting you and thinking you’ve forgotten when a promise hasn’t yet been fulfilled. Thank you, your promises in Christ are all Yes, and your delay hides patience within it. Let me count your past faithfulness, wait in peace for what you will accomplish, and deeply believe that every word you’ve spoken will surely be fulfilled. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 至于我和我家——今日就要选择
entries.title_en: As for Me and My House — Choose Today
entries.verse: 约书亚记廿四章十五节
entries.content:
约书亚年纪老迈,召聚全以色列作临别的嘱咐。他把话说得斩钉截铁:「若是你们以事奉耶和华为不好,今日就可以选择所要事奉的……至于我和我家,我们必定事奉耶和华」(书24:15)。约书亚不容百姓含糊、骑墙、脚踏两条船。他把选择摆在他们面前:要么事奉耶和华,要么事奉别的神——今天就定。

「今日就可以选择」——信仰不是一个可以无限期拖延的问题。我们很多人活在一种属灵的「待定」状态里:没有公开拒绝神,也没有全心归向祂;一只脚在教会,一只脚在世界;想跟随主,又舍不得放下别的。约书亚说,这样不行。事奉神是要「选择」的,是要做决定、要表态、要划清界限的。骑墙,本身就是一种拒绝。主耶稣后来对老底嘉教会说得更不留情面:「你也不冷也不热……你既如温水,也不冷也不热,所以我必从我口中把你吐出去」(启3:15-16)。神宁可你冷,也不要你温吞。

更叫人敬佩的,是约书亚那句「至于我和我家」。他不等别人先决定,不看大多数人往哪边倒;他为自己、也为全家立定心志。真正的信仰领袖,是先在自己家里把神的位置立起来的人。他没有把信仰留给孩子长大后「自己决定」,而是带头宣告:在我这个家,耶和华是主。这是何等的魄力与担当。

今天,同样的选择摆在你面前——不是一次就永远了事,而是每一天、每件事上,你都在选择事奉谁。你的时间、金钱、精力、心思,诚实地说,正在事奉哪一位「神」?约书亚的挑战今天依然响亮:别再骑墙,今日就选择。你,和你的家,要事奉谁?愿你也能坚定地说:至于我和我家,我们必定事奉耶和华。

默想:我是否活在属灵的「待定」状态——没拒绝神,也没全心归向祂,活得不冷不热?我的时间与金钱,诚实说正在事奉哪一位「神」?

应用:今天在一件你一直骑墙、含糊的事上做出明确的选择,宣告事奉耶和华;若你有家庭,带头在家中立定这个心志。

祷告:主啊,约书亚不容百姓骑墙,斩钉截铁地说「至于我和我家,我们必定事奉耶和华」;你更宁可我冷,也不要我不冷不热。我承认我常活在属灵的待定里,一只脚在你这里,一只脚在世界。求你赐我约书亚的魄力,今日就做出选择,全心事奉你;也求你叫我在自己家中带头,把你的位置立起来。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Joshua, now old, gathered all Israel for a farewell charge. He spoke without ambiguity: “if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve... But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). Joshua would not allow the people to be vague, to straddle the fence, to have one foot in each camp. He set the choice before them: either serve the LORD, or serve other gods — decide today.

“Choose this day” — faith is not an issue that can be indefinitely postponed. So many of us live in a kind of spiritual “limbo”: not openly rejecting God, but not wholeheartedly turning to him either; one foot in church, one foot in the world; wanting to follow the Lord, yet unwilling to let go of other things. Joshua says this will not do. Serving God requires a “choice” — a decision, a declared position, a clear line drawn. Straddling the fence is itself a form of refusal. The Lord Jesus later put it even more bluntly to the Laodicean church: “you are neither cold nor hot... So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3:15–16). God would rather you be cold than lukewarm.

Even more admirable is Joshua’s phrase, “as for me and my house.” He didn’t wait for others to decide first, didn’t watch which way the majority leaned; he set his resolve for himself, and for his whole family. A true spiritual leader is someone who first establishes God’s place in their own home. He didn’t leave faith for the children to “decide for themselves” when they grew up, but led out, declaring: in this house, the LORD is Lord. What resolve and responsibility this shows.

Today, the same choice stands before you — not something settled once for all time, but something you choose every day, in every matter: whom will you serve. Your time, your money, your energy, your thoughts — honestly speaking, which “god” are they currently serving? Joshua’s challenge still rings out today: stop straddling the fence, choose today. You, and your household, whom will you serve? May you too be able to say firmly: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

Meditation: Am I living in spiritual “limbo” — not rejecting God, yet not wholeheartedly turning to him, living neither cold nor hot? Honestly, which “god” are my time and money currently serving?

Application: Today, make a clear choice in one matter you’ve been fence-sitting or vague about, declaring you will serve the LORD; if you have a family, lead out in your household to establish this resolve.

Prayer: Lord, Joshua would not allow the people to straddle the fence, declaring firmly, “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD”; you would rather I be cold than lukewarm. I confess I often live in spiritual limbo, one foot with you, one foot in the world. Give me Joshua’s resolve, to make a choice today, serving you wholeheartedly; and let me lead out in my own household, establishing your place there. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 没有赶出——半心顺服的代价
entries.title_en: Did Not Drive Them Out — The Cost of Half-Hearted Obedience
entries.verse: 申命记十二章二节
entries.content:
约书亚死后,以色列进入士师时代。士师记一开头,反复出现一句沉重的话:某支派「没有赶出」那地的居民,任凭他们住在自己中间。神明明吩咐要把拜偶像的迦南人尽都赶出,以色列却因贪图安逸、惧怕强敌、或觉得「差不多就行了」,一次次打了折扣。表面上是宽容,实际上是不彻底的顺服。

这半心的顺服,埋下了极大的祸根。神早已警告:留下的迦南人,必成为他们「肋下的荆棘」,他们的神必成为以色列的网罗。果然,那些没有赶出去的偶像,渐渐把以色列的心勾了去;士师记于是陷入一个可悲的循环:犯罪、受压、哀求、蒙拯救,然后再次犯罪。这一切的起点,就是当初那句「没有赶出」。

这正是对我们的警戒。我们对待自己生命中的罪,常常也是「没有赶出」——不是公然放纵,而是留一点、纵容一点、给它留个角落,告诉自己「这点小毛病无伤大雅」。可是罪从不会安分地待在角落里;你给它留多大地方,它就长多大,最终反过来辖制你。保罗的劝勉正针对这种留有余地的心态:「总要披戴主耶稣基督,不要为肉体安排,去放纵私欲」(罗13:14)——不给肉体留地步,才是彻底的顺服。

神所要的,是彻底的顺服。主耶稣说:「若是你的右眼叫你跌倒,就剜出来丢掉」(太5:29)。祂用最决绝的比喻,是要我们对罪毫不姑息。你今天生命中,有没有一个你一直「没有赶出」、总给它留着地方的罪或妥协?趁它还没长大、还没成为你「肋下的荆棘」,求神给你决心,把它彻底赶出去。半心的顺服,迟早要你付上全心的代价。

默想:我生命中有没有一个我一直「没有赶出」、总给它留个角落的罪或妥协?我对付罪,是彻底的,还是「差不多就行」?

应用:今天指认一个你一直姑息、纵容的「小」罪,不再给它留地方,采取决绝的行动把它赶出去。

祷告:圣洁的神,以色列因「没有赶出」迦南人,后来那些偶像就成了他们肋下的荆棘、脚前的网罗。我承认我对付自己的罪也常常半心半意,总给它留个角落,以为无伤大雅。求你赐我彻底顺服的决心,像主所教导的那样毫不姑息,不再为肉体安排、放纵私欲,把每一个妥协赶出去,免得它日后反过来辖制我。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
After Joshua’s death, Israel entered the age of the judges. At the very start of Judges, a heavy phrase recurs again and again: some tribe “did not drive out” the inhabitants of that land, letting them dwell among them. God had clearly commanded that the idol-worshiping Canaanites be entirely driven out, yet Israel, out of a love of ease, fear of strong enemies, or a feeling that “close enough is good enough,” discounted it again and again. On the surface it was tolerance; in reality it was incomplete obedience.

This half-hearted obedience planted an enormous root of disaster. God had already warned: the Canaanites left behind would become “thorns in your sides,” and their gods would become a snare to Israel. Sure enough, those idols they had failed to drive out gradually stole Israel’s heart away; Judges then falls into a tragic cycle: sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, and then sin again. The starting point of all this was that early phrase, “did not drive out.”

This is exactly a warning to us. How we deal with sin in our own lives is often also “did not drive out” — not openly indulging it, but leaving a little of it, tolerating a little, giving it a corner, telling ourselves “this small flaw is harmless.” But sin never stays quietly in its corner; however much room you give it, it will grow to fill it, and eventually turn around and enslave you. Paul’s exhortation is aimed precisely at this mindset of leaving room: “put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires” (Romans 13:14) — leaving no room for the flesh is what makes obedience complete.

What God wants is complete obedience. The Lord Jesus said: “If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away” (Matthew 5:29). He uses the most decisive metaphor because he wants us to show no leniency toward sin whatsoever. Is there a sin or compromise in your life today that you’ve always “not driven out,” always leaving it a place? Before it grows and becomes your own “thorn in the side,” ask God for the resolve to drive it out completely. Half-hearted obedience will, sooner or later, cost you the price of wholehearted surrender.

Meditation: Is there a sin or compromise in my life that I’ve always “not driven out,” always leaving it a corner? Do I deal with sin completely, or with a “close enough” attitude?

Application: Today, name a “small” sin you’ve been tolerating and indulging, and, giving it no more room, take decisive action to drive it out.

Prayer: Holy God, because Israel “did not drive out” the Canaanites, those idols later became thorns in their sides, a snare at their feet. I confess I too often deal with my own sin half-heartedly, always leaving it a corner, thinking it harmless. Give me the resolve for complete obedience, showing no leniency as the Lord taught, making no provision for the flesh, driving out every compromise, lest it later turn around and enslave me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 大能的勇士啊——神在软弱中的能力
entries.title_en: O Mighty Man of Valor — God's Power in Weakness
entries.verse: 以赛亚书四十章廿九至卅一节
entries.content:
米甸人年年来抢掠,以色列躲进山洞,苦不堪言。就在这时,神的使者向一个躲在酒醡里打麦子的人显现,称呼他:「大能的勇士啊,耶和华与你同在!」(士6:12)基甸听了大概哭笑不得——他哪里像大能的勇士?他自认是玛拿西支派中最贫穷的,家里他又是最小的。可是神看他,不是照他现在的样子,而是照祂要藉着他成就的。

神拣选基甸的方式,更是耐人寻味。基甸招聚了三万二千人,神却嫌太多,一路减到只剩三百人。为什么?神说:「跟随你的人过多,我不能将米甸人交在他们手中,免得以色列人向我夸大,说:『是我们自己的手救了我们』」(士7:2)。神偏要用最少的、最弱的,好叫得胜之后,没有人能把功劳归给自己。神的能力,专在人的软弱上显得完全;人越无可夸,神的荣耀越彰显。

这给一切自觉软弱、无用、不配的人极大的安慰。你是否常盯着自己的不能、自己的渺小,觉得神不可能用你?基甸的故事告诉你:神向来不是用那些自以为强的人,而是用那些肯承认自己软弱、单单倚靠祂的人。先知也说:「疲乏的,他赐能力;软弱的,他加力量……那等候耶和华的必重新得力」(赛40:29-31)。力量的秘诀,不在于你多强,而在于你肯不肯等候、支取祂的力量。

今天,你或许正像躲在酒醡里的基甸,又累又怕,自觉一无是处。请听神怎样称呼你——不是照你的软弱,而是照祂的同在与呼召。不要靠自己咬牙硬撑,那只会更快跌倒;要来到祂面前,安静等候,让那位赐能力给疲乏之人的神,重新加你力量。你的软弱,恰是神显能力的地方;你的等候,正是神加力量的时候。

默想:我是否总盯着自己的软弱与渺小,以为神不能用我?神为何偏要用最弱的基甸、最少的三百人?

应用:今天不再靠自己硬撑,把一件让你疲乏、自觉无力的事带到神面前,安静等候祂,支取祂所赐的力量。

祷告:赐能力的神,你称躲在酒醡里的基甸为「大能的勇士」,又减到三百人才得胜,免得人夸自己。我承认我常盯着自己的软弱,又常靠自己硬撑到跌倒。求你叫我肯承认软弱、单单倚靠你;叫我像等候你的人那样重新得力,如鹰展翅上腾。愿我的软弱,成为你显能力的地方。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The Midianites came year after year to plunder, and Israel hid in mountain caves, in bitter distress. It was at this time that the angel of the LORD appeared to a man threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it, calling him: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor!” (Judges 6:12). Gideon must have found this almost laughable — how was he a mighty man of valor? He considered himself the poorest in the tribe of Manasseh, and the least in his father’s house. But God saw him not as he currently was, but as what he intended to accomplish through him.

The way God chose Gideon is even more intriguing. Gideon gathered thirty-two thousand men, but God thought that was too many, and reduced it all the way down to three hundred. Why? God said: “The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, My own hand has saved me” (Judges 7:2). God deliberately used the fewest, the weakest, so that after the victory, no one could claim the credit for themselves. God’s power is made perfect precisely in human weakness; the less a person has to boast of, the more God’s glory is displayed.

This gives enormous comfort to everyone who feels weak, useless, unworthy. Do you often stare at your own inability, your own smallness, feeling God could never use you? Gideon’s story tells you: God has never used those who think themselves strong, but those who are willing to admit their weakness, relying solely on him. The prophet also says: “He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength... but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:29–31). The secret of strength is not how strong you are, but whether you are willing to wait and draw on his strength.

Today, you may be like Gideon hiding in the winepress, tired and afraid, feeling utterly useless. Listen to how God addresses you — not according to your weakness, but according to his presence and calling. Don’t grit your teeth and try to push through on your own — that will only make you fall faster; come before him, wait quietly, and let the God who gives strength to the weary renew your strength. Your weakness is precisely where God’s power is displayed; your waiting is precisely when God adds strength.

Meditation: Do I always stare at my own weakness and smallness, thinking God cannot use me? Why did God deliberately use the weakest Gideon, the fewest three hundred?

Application: Today, stop gritting your teeth on your own; bring something that exhausts you, that makes you feel powerless, before God, wait quietly on him, and draw on the strength he gives.

Prayer: God who gives strength, you called Gideon, hiding in the winepress, a “mighty man of valor,” and reduced him to three hundred before giving victory, lest anyone boast in themselves. I confess I often stare at my own weakness, and often grit my teeth on my own until I fall. Let me be willing to admit weakness, relying solely on you; let me, like those who wait on you, renew my strength, mounting up with wings like eagles. May my weakness become the place where you display your power. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 旧事已过——从循环的旧我到基督里的新造
entries.title_en: The Old Has Passed Away — From the Cyclical Old Self to New Creation in Christ
entries.verse: 哥林多后书五章十七节
entries.content:
士师记像一个转不出去的怪圈:以色列犯罪、受欺压、哀求、神兴起士师拯救,可士师一死,他们又故态复萌,而且一次比一次堕落。这一段(士9-12),亚比米勒的血腥、耶弗他的鲁莽,都透着一股挥之不去的败坏气息。你几乎能听见那句叹息:他们怎么总也学不乖?——其实,这正是没有被更新的「旧人」的写照:同样的坑,一次次掉进去;同样的罪,一次次重犯。

这怪圈,靠人自己是转不出来的。以色列换了一个又一个士师,却换不掉那颗悖逆的心;正如我们下了一个又一个决心,却改不掉那些根深蒂固的老毛病。问题不在于缺少榜样、缺少规条、缺少努力,而在于那颗心本身需要被重造。旧的修修补补,成不了新的;唯有从里面被更新,循环才可能被打破。

这正是福音带来的惊人应许:「若有人在基督里,他就是新造的人,旧事已过,都变成新的了」(林后5:17)。在基督里,神做的不是给旧我贴几张膏药,而是把我们重新造过——赐下一颗新心、一个新生命。保罗解释这更新的根基说:「我们的旧人和他同钉十字架,使罪身灭绝,叫我们不再作罪的奴仆」(罗6:6)——这不是我们努力变好的结果,而是神在我们里面动的新工。士师救不了以色列脱离那循环,但基督能把我们从「旧我」的死循环里,彻底救出来。

你是否也困在某个转不出去的怪圈里——同一个罪、同一种失败、同一段破裂,屡战屡败,几乎认定自己「就这样了,改不了了」?福音对你说:在基督里,你是新造的人,旧事已过。这不是叫你更努力地修补旧我,而是邀请你支取那已经赐给你的新生命,靠着祂里面更新的大能,一步步活出那个新造的自己。改变的盼望,不在你的决心里,在基督更新你的大能里。

默想:我是否困在某个转不出去的怪圈,认定自己「改不了了」?我改变的盼望,是放在自己的决心上,还是基督更新我的大能上?

应用:今天把一个你屡战屡败、几乎放弃的「旧我」老毛病带到神面前,不再靠决心修补,而是宣告「我在基督里是新造的人」,求祂的更新之力。

祷告:更新我的神,士师换了一个又一个,以色列却总在同样的罪里打转,正如我常在同样的失败里屡战屡败。感谢你,在基督里我是新造的人,旧事已过,都变成新的了,我的旧人已经与他同钉十字架。求你叫我不再靠自己的决心修补旧我,而是支取你所赐的新生命,靠你更新的大能,活出那个新造的自己。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Judges reads like a vicious cycle with no way out: Israel sins, is oppressed, cries out, God raises up a judge to deliver them, but as soon as the judge dies, they revert to their old ways, and each time worse than before. This section (Judges 9–12) — Abimelech’s bloodshed, Jephthah’s rashness — carries a lingering scent of corruption. You can almost hear the sigh: why do they never learn? — This is, in fact, exactly a portrait of the unrenewed “old self”: falling into the same pit, again and again; committing the same sin, again and again.

This vicious cycle cannot be escaped by human effort alone. Israel changed judge after judge, yet could never change that rebellious heart; just as we make resolution after resolution, yet cannot fix those deeply rooted old flaws. The problem isn’t a lack of examples, rules, or effort, but that the heart itself needs to be remade. Patching up the old cannot make it new; only being renewed from within can possibly break the cycle.

This is exactly the astonishing promise the gospel brings: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). In Christ, what God does is not slap a few patches on the old self, but remake us entirely — giving a new heart, a new life. Paul explains the foundation of this renewal: “our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin” (Romans 6:6) — this is not the result of our own effort to become better, but a new work God does within us. The judges could not save Israel from that cycle, but Christ can rescue us completely from the death-cycle of the “old self.”

Are you too trapped in some vicious cycle you can’t escape — the same sin, the same kind of failure, the same broken relationship, failing again and again, nearly convinced that “this is just how I am, I can’t change”? The gospel says to you: in Christ, you are a new creation, the old has passed away. This doesn’t call you to try harder at patching up the old self, but invites you to draw on the new life already given to you, and, by the power that renews you within him, step by step live out that new creation. The hope of change is not in your resolve, but in Christ’s power to renew you.

Meditation: Am I trapped in some vicious cycle I can’t escape, convinced “I can’t change”? Is my hope for change placed in my own resolve, or in Christ’s power to renew me?

Application: Today, bring an “old self” flaw you’ve failed against again and again, nearly given up on, before God; instead of trying to patch it up with resolve, declare “I am a new creation in Christ,” and ask for his renewing power.

Prayer: God who renews me, judge after judge came, yet Israel kept spinning in the same sin, just as I often fail again and again in the same failure. Thank you that in Christ I am a new creation, the old has passed away, all has become new, my old self has been crucified with him. Let me no longer try to patch up my old self by my own resolve, but draw on the new life you have given, and, by your renewing power, live out that new creation. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 奇妙的名——大能的士师与那真正的拯救者
entries.title_en: Wonderful Is His Name — The Mighty Judge and the True Deliverer
entries.verse: 士师记十三章十八节
entries.content:
参孙的故事,叫人扼腕。他生来就被分别为拿细耳人,天生神力,是神兴起来拯救以色列脱离非利士人的士师。可是这个力大无穷的人,却管不住自己:任性、放纵情欲、一次次玩弄他与神所立的分别为圣之约,直到头发被剃、双眼被剜、沦为敌人磨坊里的奴隶。外面的力气无人能敌,里面的私欲却把他毁了。

参孙的悲剧,是一则严峻的警告:恩赐再大,若没有圣洁与自制护着,迟早要成为绊倒自己的东西。神给了他别人没有的力量,他却从未真正治死自己的情欲,以为凭恩赐可以一路任性下去。多少有恩赐的人,不是败在能力不足,而是败在没有对付的私欲上。神所看重的,从来不只是我们能做什么,更是我们是什么样的人。恩赐叫人有用,品格才叫人站立得住。

然而在参孙出生之前,有一个耐人寻味的细节。他父亲玛挪亚问那显现的使者叫什么名字,使者回答:「你何必问我的名,我名是奇妙的」(士13:18)。这「奇妙」二字,后来在以赛亚书里再次响起——那要来的婴孩,「他名称为奇妙策士、全能的神」(赛9:6)。参孙这残缺的拯救者所指向的,是那位真正、完全的拯救者:基督。

参孙至死才拯救了以色列一时,自己却葬身瓦砾;基督却藉着自己的死,一次而永远地拯救了祂的百姓,并且复活得胜。一切旧约的士师、英雄,都带着裂痕,都在喊着:我们不够,你需要一位更好的拯救者!今天,不要把盼望放在任何有恩赐却有缺陷的人身上(包括你自己),而要仰望那位名为「奇妙」的主。也求祂帮助你,不重蹈参孙的覆辙——让品格配得上恩赐,叫圣洁护住你的力量。

默想:我是否更看重自己「能做什么」(恩赐),而忽略了「是什么样的人」(品格)?我生命中有没有没被对付、迟早会绊倒我的私欲?

应用:今天诚实面对一个你一直纵容、以为「靠恩赐无妨」的私欲,求神帮助你治死它,让你的品格配得上祂给你的恩赐。

祷告:圣洁的神,参孙力大无穷,却因管不住自己的私欲而毁了自己。求你警戒我:不叫恩赐成为我骄傲放纵的本钱,而叫圣洁与自制护住你所给的一切。感谢你差来那位名为「奇妙」的真拯救者——祂藉着死与复活,永远地救了我。求你叫我不重蹈参孙的覆辙,叫我的品格配得上你的恩赐。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Samson’s story is a lament. He was set apart as a Nazirite from birth, born with supernatural strength, a judge God raised up to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Yet this man of boundless strength could not control himself: willful, indulging his lusts, toying again and again with the vow of consecration he had made with God, until his hair was shaved, his eyes gouged out, and he was reduced to a slave grinding grain in his enemies’ mill. Outwardly no one could match his strength; inwardly his own lusts destroyed him.

Samson’s tragedy is a severe warning: however great the gift, if not guarded by holiness and self-control, it will sooner or later become the very thing that trips you up. God gave him strength no one else had, yet he never truly put his lusts to death, thinking he could go on being willful on the strength of his gift alone. So many gifted people fail not from lack of ability, but from undealt-with lust. What God values has never been only what we can do, but who we are as people. Gifts make a person useful; character is what makes a person stand firm.

Yet there is an intriguing detail before Samson’s birth. His father Manoah asked the angel who appeared to him what his name was, and the angel answered: “Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?” (Judges 13:18). This word “wonderful” echoes again later in Isaiah — the child who was to come, “his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6). This flawed deliverer, Samson, points to the true, complete Deliverer: Christ.

Samson delivered Israel only for a moment before dying under the rubble himself; but Christ, through his own death, delivered his people once and for all, and rose again in victory. Every judge, every hero in the Old Testament, carries cracks, all crying out: we are not enough, you need a better Deliverer! Today, don’t place your hope in any gifted yet flawed person (including yourself), but look to the Lord whose name is “Wonderful.” And ask him to help you not repeat Samson’s mistake — letting character be worthy of the gift, letting holiness guard your strength.

Meditation: Do I value what I “can do” (gifts) more than “who I am” (character)? Is there an undealt-with lust in my life that will sooner or later trip me up?

Application: Today, honestly face a lust you’ve been indulging, thinking “it’s fine as long as I rely on my gifts,” and ask God to help you put it to death, so your character becomes worthy of the gift he has given you.

Prayer: Holy God, Samson had boundless strength, yet destroyed himself because he could not control his own lusts. Warn me: don’t let gifts become capital for my pride and indulgence, but let holiness and self-control guard everything you have given me. Thank you for sending the true Deliverer named “Wonderful” — through death and resurrection, he saved me forever. Let me not repeat Samson’s mistake, and let my character become worthy of your gifts. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你纵然失信,祂仍可信
entries.title_en: Even If You Are Faithless, He Remains Faithful
entries.content:
你纵然失信，祂仍可信

「我们纵然失信，他仍是可信的，因为他不能背乎自己。」(提摩太后书 2:13)

这一周,我们走过士师记那叫人叹息的循环——以色列一次次失信、悖逆、跌倒,神却一次次兴起拯救。人的故事满是反复,神的信实却始终如一。

这也是你的故事。你或许这一周也失信了、软弱了、跌倒了。但神的可信,不建立在你的忠心上,而在祂自己不改变的性情里。祂不能背乎自己。今天,安息在这不因你而动摇的信实里。

"If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself." (2 Timothy 2:13)
entries.content_en:
Even If You Are Faithless, He Remains Faithful

"If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself." (2 Timothy 2:13)

This week, we walked through Judges’s sigh-inducing cycle — Israel, again and again, breaking faith, rebelling, falling, and God, again and again, raising up deliverance. The human story is full of repetition, but God’s faithfulness remains constant.

This is your story too. You too may have broken faith, grown weak, fallen this week. But God’s faithfulness is not built on your loyalty, but on his own unchanging character. He cannot deny himself. Today, rest in this faithfulness that does not waver because of you.

"If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself." (2 Timothy 2:13)

entries.title: 各人任意而行——当人人都作自己的王
entries.title_en: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes — When Everyone Is Their Own King
entries.verse: 希伯来书十二章十六节
entries.content:
士师记以一片混乱作结:有人私设神像和祭司,有支派几乎被灭,有骇人听闻的暴行。作者反复用一句话为这一切下注脚:「那时,以色列中没有王,各人任意而行」(士21:25)。没有王,不只是政治上的无政府,更是属灵上的:人人都把自己当作最终的权威,凭自己觉得对的去行,再没有一个更高的标准约束人心。结果不是自由,而是失序与败坏。箴言早就点破这条路的结局:「有一条路,人以为正,至终成为死亡之路」(箴16:25)——任意而行的人,从不觉得自己在走向死亡,直到已经走到了尽头。

「各人任意而行」——这句话像极了我们这个时代的口号。「只要我喜欢,有什么不可以」「你有你的真理,我有我的真理」「谁也别来告诉我什么是对的」。人以为把神这位「王」赶下宝座,自己就自由了;殊不知,一个人人都作自己之王的世界,恰恰是最不安、最冷酷、最没有保障的世界。士师记末了的黑暗,正是「没有王」的必然结局。

希伯来书举了以扫作例子,警戒我们不可像他——「因一点食物把自己长子的名分卖了」(来12:16)。以扫就是「任意而行」的缩影:为了眼前一碗红豆汤的满足,轻看了那属天、长远、宝贵的名分。当人自己作王,判断的尺度就缩成了「此刻我想要什么」,于是一次次用永恒的东西,去换取眼前的一点欢愉。

唯一的出路,是让那位真正的王重新登基。我们需要的,不是一个「凡事任我」的人生,而是一位配得我们降服的主。当基督作王,人心才有真正的方向、真正的安息、真正的自由——因为我们本是为祂的国度而造的。今天,你生命中有没有一个「各人任意而行」的角落,你悄悄把自己立成了王?求主在那里重新登基,因为唯有祂作王,你才不至走向士师记的结局。

默想:我生命中有没有一个「各人任意而行」的角落,我把自己立成了最终的权威?我是否像以扫,常用长远宝贵的,去换眼前的一点满足?

应用:今天找出一处你一直「凭自己觉得对」而行、不肯让神作主的领域,把它交出来,让基督在那里重新登基。

祷告:掌权的主,士师时代「以色列中没有王,各人任意而行」,结局是失序与败坏,那看似正的路,至终成了死亡之路。我承认我心里也有许多角落,悄悄把自己立成了王,凭自己的喜好而行,甚至像以扫用宝贵的换取眼前的满足。求你在我生命的每一处重新登基,作我真正的王,叫我在降服你中,得着真正的方向与自由。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Judges ends in utter chaos: someone sets up his own idols and priest, a tribe is nearly wiped out, there is horrifying atrocity. The author repeatedly footnotes all of this with one sentence: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). No king was not merely political anarchy, but spiritual: everyone treated themselves as the final authority, acting according to what they themselves thought right, with no higher standard restraining the heart. The result was not freedom, but disorder and corruption. Proverbs had already exposed where this road ends: “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death” (Proverbs 16:25) — those who do as they please never feel they are heading toward death, until they have already reached the end.

“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” — this phrase sounds exactly like a slogan of our own age. “If it feels good, why not,” “you have your truth, I have mine,” “no one gets to tell me what’s right.” People think that once they’ve dethroned God the King, they become free; little do they know, a world where everyone is their own king is exactly the most anxious, coldest, most unprotected world of all. The darkness at the end of Judges is precisely the inevitable outcome of “no king.”

Hebrews uses Esau as an example, warning us not to be like him — “who sold his birthright for a single meal” (Hebrews 12:16). Esau is precisely a miniature of “doing what is right in one’s own eyes”: for the immediate satisfaction of a bowl of red stew, he despised his heavenly, lasting, precious birthright. When a person makes themselves king, the standard of judgment shrinks to “what I want right now,” and so, again and again, eternal things get traded for a moment’s pleasure.

The only way out is to let the true King take the throne again. What we need is not a life where “anything goes for me,” but a Lord worthy of our submission. When Christ reigns, the human heart finds its true direction, true rest, true freedom — because we were made for his kingdom. Today, is there a corner of your life where “everyone does what is right in their own eyes,” where you’ve quietly set yourself up as king? Ask the Lord to take the throne there again, because only when he reigns will you avoid the ending of Judges.

Meditation: Is there a corner of my life where “everyone does what is right in their own eyes,” where I’ve set myself up as the final authority? Am I, like Esau, often trading lasting, precious things for a moment’s satisfaction?

Application: Today, find an area where you’ve always acted “on what you think is right,” unwilling to let God be Lord, and hand it over, letting Christ take the throne there again.

Prayer: Reigning Lord, in the age of the judges, “there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes,” and the result was disorder and corruption — that way that seemed right ended as the way to death. I confess there are also many corners in my heart where I’ve quietly set myself up as king, acting on my own preference, even, like Esau, trading precious things for a moment’s satisfaction. Take the throne again in every part of my life, be my true King, and let me find true direction and freedom in submitting to you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你的神就是我的神——路得记里的救赎
entries.title_en: Your God Shall Be My God — Redemption in the Book of Ruth
entries.verse: 路得记一章十六至十七节
entries.content:
士师时代那样黑暗,神却在一个不起眼的角落,悄悄写着一个满有恩慈的故事。犹大妇人拿俄米,在饥荒中丧夫、丧子,带着摩押儿媳路得,两手空空地回到伯利恒。人间的苦几乎把她压垮;她甚至说,不要再叫我拿俄米(甜),要叫我玛拉(苦)。然而正是在这样的绝境里,神的救赎不动声色地展开了。

外邦女子路得说出了圣经中最动人的忠诚之一:「你往哪里去,我也往那里去……你的国就是我的国,你的神就是我的神」(得1:16)。她本可以回摩押、回娘家、另寻依靠;她却选择了拿俄米的神,把自己的命运,系在这位素不相识的耶和华身上。这份不离不弃的爱,正是神自己那信实慈爱(希伯来文所谓的 hesed)的映照。

故事的转折,在一位「至近的亲属」波阿斯身上。按律法,至近的亲属有权、也有责任救赎家人:替穷亲戚赎回卖掉的地,娶寡妇、为死者立后,使家族不至断绝。波阿斯甘愿付上代价,救赎了一无所有的路得与拿俄米。这位「救赎主」正是基督清晰的预表——祂成了我们的骨肉之亲,「藉这爱子的血得蒙救赎,过犯得以赦免」(弗1:7),甘愿付上自己性命的代价,救赎我们这些一无所有、走投无路的人。

而路得记的结尾更叫人惊叹:这外邦女子路得,竟成了大卫王的曾祖母,列在耶稣基督的家谱里(太1:5)。一个在饥荒与死亡中开始的破碎故事,神却把它编织进了祂救世的大计划。这告诉我们:你以为一败涂地、走投无路的境地,恰恰可能是神要施行救赎的地方。今天,把你的空虚与破碎,交给那位至近的救赎主;祂专会在玛拉(苦)之处,写出恩典的结局。

默想:我是否在破碎、空虚、走投无路之处,以为神已不在?波阿斯这「至近的救赎主」如何让我看见基督为我所付的代价?

应用:今天把一处你觉得「一败涂地、无可挽回」的境况,交在那位救赎主手里,求祂像救赎路得那样,在你的破碎中动工。

祷告:满有慈爱的救赎主,士师时代那样黑暗,你却在路得的破碎里写下救赎的故事。感谢你,波阿斯所预表的正是你——你成了我的骨肉之亲,藉你儿子的血救赎了我,赦免我的过犯。求你叫我在空虚与绝境中不再以为你已离开,而是把破碎交给你,深信你专在玛拉之处写出恩典的结局。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
As dark as the age of the judges was, God was quietly writing a story full of grace in an obscure corner. The Judahite woman Naomi, having lost her husband and sons in a famine, returned to Bethlehem empty-handed, bringing her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth. The suffering of this world had nearly crushed her; she even said, don’t call me Naomi (pleasant) anymore, call me Mara (bitter). Yet it was precisely in such desperate circumstances that God’s redemption quietly began to unfold.

The Gentile woman Ruth spoke one of Scripture’s most moving expressions of loyalty: “Where you go I will go... your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16). She could have returned to Moab, to her own family, to find security elsewhere; instead she chose Naomi’s God, tying her own destiny to this LORD she barely knew. This unrelenting, loyal love is exactly a reflection of God’s own faithful, steadfast love (the Hebrew hesed).

The turning point of the story comes with a “kinsman-redeemer,” Boaz. By law, the nearest kinsman had both the right and the responsibility to redeem family members: to buy back land a poor relative had sold, to marry the widow and raise up an heir for the deceased, so that the family line would not be cut off. Boaz was willing to pay the price, redeeming the utterly destitute Ruth and Naomi. This “redeemer” is a clear foreshadowing of Christ — he became our kinsman, and “through his blood we have redemption, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7), willing to pay the price of his own life to redeem us who had nothing, who had nowhere left to turn.

And the ending of Ruth is even more astonishing: this Gentile woman Ruth became the great-grandmother of King David, listed in the genealogy of Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:5). A broken story that began in famine and death — God wove it into his great plan of salvation. This tells us: the place you think is your utter, hopeless failure may be exactly the place God intends to bring about redemption. Today, hand your emptiness and brokenness to that near kinsman-Redeemer; he specializes in writing an ending of grace at exactly the place of Mara (bitterness).

Meditation: Do I, in brokenness, emptiness, at a dead end, think God has already left? How does Boaz, this “near kinsman-redeemer,” help me see the price Christ has paid for me?

Application: Today, hand over a situation you feel is “utterly ruined, beyond repair” to the Redeemer, asking him to work in your brokenness as he did in redeeming Ruth.

Prayer: Redeemer full of steadfast love, as dark as the age of the judges was, you wrote a story of redemption in Ruth’s brokenness. Thank you, Boaz foreshadows exactly you — you became my kinsman, redeeming me through your Son’s blood, forgiving my trespasses. Let me, in emptiness and desperate circumstances, no longer think you have left, but hand my brokenness to you, deeply believing you specialize in writing an ending of grace at the place of Mara. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我将这孩子归与耶和华——哈拿的奉献
entries.title_en: I Have Given This Child to the LORD — Hannah's Offering
entries.verse: 撒母耳记上一章廿七至廿八节
entries.content:
哈拿多年不孕,心里愁苦,在圣殿门口痛哭祷告,甚至被祭司误以为喝醉了。她向神许愿:若神赐她一个儿子,她就把这孩子终身归给神。神垂听了,赐下撒母耳。孩子断奶后,哈拿信守承诺,把这来之不易、朝思暮想的独子,亲手带到圣殿,交在祭司以利手中:「我将这孩子归与耶和华,使他终身归与耶和华」(撒上1:28)。

这是何等不易的奉献。撒母耳不是哈拿多余的、剩下的,而是她流泪求来的、最宝贵的。人之常情,越是来之不易的,越要牢牢抓在手里;哈拿却把最宝贝的,重新交回给那位赐下的神。这里藏着一个属灵的深理:我们从神所领受的一切恩赐——儿女、恩典、成就、机会——都不是要我们紧抓占有的,而是要我们捧在手心、随时可以交还给神的。

真正的敬虔,不在于我们能为神抓住多少,而在于我们肯为神松开多少手。哈拿松开了手,神并没有亏待她——撒母耳成了以色列一代的先知与士师,后来神也眷顾哈拿,再赐给她三个儿子、两个女儿(撒上2:21)。但这不是一场「交出就必得回报」的交易——神不欠我们,松手也不是换取更多的筹码。松手的意义,在于把最宝贝的放在最配得的手中,自己也从紧抓的辖制中得着释放。我们抓得越紧,越活在患得患失里;我们交得越彻底,越尝到那自由与安息。

你今天手里紧紧抓着的,是什么?是一个孩子、一段关系、一份成就、一个梦想?哈拿的榜样在邀请你,把它捧到神面前,像她那样说:主啊,这本是你赐的,如今我把它归还给你。这不是失去,而是把它放在最安全的地方——那位赐下它、也最爱它的神手中。学哈拿松开手,你会发现一种紧抓之人永远尝不到的自由。

默想:我从神领受的恩赐(儿女、成就、关系),是紧紧抓在手里占有,还是捧在手心、随时可以交还给神?

应用:今天把一样你一直紧抓、患得患失的恩赐,像哈拿一样在祷告中「归还」给神,宣告它属于祂,交在祂手中。

祷告:赐恩的神,哈拿把流泪求来的独子撒母耳,重新交还给你,终身归你。我承认我常把你所赐的恩赐紧紧抓在手里,患得患失,不肯松手。求你叫我学哈拿的功课:凡从你领受的,都捧在手心,随时可以交还给你。叫我在松开手中,尝到那紧抓之人永远得不着的自由与安息。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Hannah was barren for many years, her heart bitter with sorrow, weeping and praying at the door of the temple, so much so that the priest mistook her for drunk. She vowed to God: if he would give her a son, she would give the child back to God for his whole life. God heard, and gave Samuel. After the child was weaned, Hannah kept her promise, personally bringing this hard-won, long-cherished only son to the temple, handing him over to the priest Eli: “I have lent him to the LORD; as long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:28).

What a difficult offering this was. Samuel was not extra, not leftover, but the very thing Hannah had wept and prayed for, her most precious possession. Human nature is such that the harder-won something is, the more tightly we grip it; yet Hannah handed her most precious thing back to the very God who had given it. Hidden here is a deep spiritual truth: everything we receive from God — children, grace, achievement, opportunity — is not meant for us to clutch and possess, but to hold in an open hand, always ready to give back to God.

True godliness lies not in how much we can grasp for God, but in how much we’re willing to let go of for God. Hannah let go, and God did not shortchange her — Samuel became a prophet and judge for a generation of Israel, and later God also blessed Hannah, giving her three more sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21). But this is not a transaction of “give and you’ll get more back” — God owes us nothing, and letting go is not currency to trade for more. The meaning of letting go is placing the most precious thing in the most worthy hands, and being freed, ourselves, from the grip of clutching. The tighter we grip, the more we live in anxiety over gain and loss; the more completely we hand over, the more we taste freedom and rest.

What are you gripping tightly today? A child, a relationship, an achievement, a dream? Hannah’s example invites you to hold it up before God, and say as she did: Lord, this was always yours to give; now I give it back to you. This is not loss, but placing it in the safest place — in the hands of the God who gave it, and who loves it most. Learn to let go like Hannah, and you’ll discover a freedom those who grip tightly never taste.

Meditation: The gifts I’ve received from God (children, achievements, relationships) — am I gripping them tightly, possessing them, or holding them in an open hand, always ready to give them back to God?

Application: Today, take one gift you’ve been gripping tightly, anxious over gain and loss, and, like Hannah, “give it back” to God in prayer, declaring it belongs to him, placed in his hands.

Prayer: God of grace, Hannah gave back her only son Samuel, whom she had wept and prayed for, entirely to you, for his whole life. I confess I often grip your gifts tightly, anxious over gain and loss, unwilling to let go. Teach me Hannah’s lesson: everything received from you, held in an open hand, ready at any time to give back to you. Let me, in letting go, taste the freedom and rest that those who grip tightly never obtain. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
