entries.title: 不是倚靠势力——真正的得胜从何而来
entries.title_en: Not by Might — Where True Victory Comes From
entries.verse: 撒迦利亚书四章六节
entries.content:
以色列与非利士人交战,吃了败仗。他们想出一个「妙计」:把神的约柜从示罗抬到阵前,以为有了这圣物就能扭转战局。结果不但又大败,连约柜也被掳去,以利的两个儿子阵亡。以色列以为约柜是一件可以操控的护身符,能保证胜利;他们要的是神的「东西」,却不要神自己;要神为他们的计划背书,却不肯照神的心意而活。

这是一个深刻的提醒:我们常常也想把神当作达成目的的工具。我们祷告、聚会、奉献,骨子里却是想用这些「属灵操作」来换取自己想要的结果——仿佛只要按对了按钮,神就必须给我们成功。可是神不是护身符,祂是主。祂不受我们操控,也不为我们的野心效力。真正的得胜,从来不是靠我们抓住了什么「属灵法宝」,而是靠真正地降服于神、倚靠祂的灵。

撒迦利亚把这真理说得再清楚不过:「不是倚靠势力,不是倚靠才能,乃是倚靠我的灵方能成事」(亚4:6)。神的工,靠神的灵成就,不靠人的势力、才能、方法或资源。保罗后来也用一个朴素的比方说透了同一件事:「我们有这宝贝放在瓦器里,要显明这莫大的能力是出于神,不是出于我们」(林后4:7)。我们何等容易在服事与生活中,不知不觉地倚靠自己的聪明、人脉、经验、努力,把圣灵晾在一边,然后奇怪为什么使不上劲。属灵的果效,从不是人力堆出来的,而是圣灵作出来的。

后来神亲自出手,击败了非利士人。撒母耳立了一块石头,起名「以便以谢」,意思是「到如今耶和华都帮助我们」(撒上7:12)。得胜不是来自那被掳的约柜,而是来自那位施行拯救的神。今天,你在靠什么打你的仗?是靠自己的势力才能,还是靠神的灵?求神叫我们放下手中的「护身符」和自恃,单单倚靠祂——因为唯有祂的灵,能成就人力所不能成的事。

默想:我是否想把神当作达成目的的工具或护身符?我打属灵的仗,是靠自己的势力才能,还是真正倚靠神的灵?

应用:今天在一件你一向靠自己的聪明、人脉或努力硬撑的事上,刻意停下来,承认「不是倚靠势力,乃是倚靠神的灵」,先祷告寻求祂,再行动。

祷告:施行拯救的神,以色列想把约柜当护身符操控你,却大败而归。我承认我也常想把你当作达成目的的工具,或在服事中倚靠自己的势力才能,把你的灵晾在一边,忘了这宝贝原是放在瓦器里。求你叫我放下一切自恃,单单倚靠你的灵;叫我立起「以便以谢」的记号,承认到如今都是你帮助了我。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Israel fought the Philistines and was defeated. They came up with a “clever plan”: carry the ark of God’s covenant from Shiloh to the battle line, thinking that with this holy object they could turn the tide. The result was not only another crushing defeat, but the ark itself was captured, and Eli’s two sons were killed in battle. Israel thought the ark was a talisman they could manipulate, guaranteeing victory; what they wanted was God’s “thing,” not God himself; they wanted God to endorse their plan, but were unwilling to live according to God’s will.

This is a profound reminder: we too often want to treat God as a tool to achieve our purposes. We pray, gather, give, but at bottom we want to use these “spiritual operations” to trade for the outcome we want — as if pressing the right button obligates God to give us success. But God is not a talisman; he is Lord. He is not controlled by us, nor does he serve our ambitions. True victory has never come from grasping some “spiritual treasure,” but from truly submitting to God, relying on his Spirit.

Zechariah states this truth as clearly as possible: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). God’s work is accomplished by God’s Spirit, not by human power, ability, method, or resources. Paul later uses a plain metaphor to say the same thing: “we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). How easily we, in ministry and life, unconsciously rely on our own cleverness, connections, experience, effort, setting the Holy Spirit aside, and then wonder why we have no power. Spiritual fruit is never piled up by human effort, but produced by the Holy Spirit.

Later, God himself acted and defeated the Philistines. Samuel set up a stone, naming it Ebenezer, meaning “Till now the LORD has helped us” (1 Samuel 7:12). Victory did not come from that captured ark, but from the God who accomplishes salvation. Today, what are you relying on to fight your battle? Your own power and ability, or God’s Spirit? Ask God to let us lay down the “talismans” and self-reliance in our hands, relying on him alone — because only his Spirit can accomplish what human power cannot.

Meditation: Do I want to treat God as a tool or talisman to achieve my purposes? In fighting spiritual battles, do I rely on my own power and ability, or truly rely on God’s Spirit?

Application: Today, in a matter you’ve always powered through with your own cleverness, connections, or effort, deliberately stop, admit “not by might, but by God’s Spirit,” pray and seek him first, then act.

Prayer: God who accomplishes salvation, Israel wanted to treat the ark as a talisman to control you, but was badly defeated. I confess I too often want to treat you as a tool to achieve my purposes, or rely on my own power and ability in ministry, setting your Spirit aside, forgetting this treasure was always meant to be in jars of clay. Let me lay down all self-reliance, relying solely on your Spirit; let me set up an “Ebenezer” marker, acknowledging that till now you have helped me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 他们厌弃的是我——当人要一个别的王
entries.title_en: It Is Me They Have Rejected — When People Want a Different King
entries.verse: 箴言十八章十二节
entries.content:
撒母耳年老,以色列的长老来求他:「求你为我们立一个王治理我们,像列国一样」(撒上8:5)。他们要一个看得见的王,像周围的邦国那样。撒母耳听了很不喜悦,就祷告神。神的回答一针见血:「他们不是厌弃你,乃是厌弃我,不要我作他们的王」(撒上8:7)。以色列真正的问题,不是政治体制,而是他们心里,已经不要神作王了。

他们为什么要一个「像列国一样」的王?因为看得见的君王能带兵打仗、能给人安全感,比那位看不见的神更「靠得住」。这就是人心深处的挣扎:我们总想要一个能抓在手里、能满足我们期待、能照我们的意思行的「王」——事业、金钱、某个人、某种成就——来取代那位真正配作王、却常常不按我们剧本行事的神。厌弃神作王,往往不是公开的背叛,而是悄悄地把别的东西扶上了宝座。

耐人寻味的是,神竟应允了他们的要求,给了他们扫罗——一个身材高大、外表出众、正是他们想要的王。可这王后来成了他们的重担与祸患。这是一个严肃的提醒:神有时会把我们执意想要的给我们,好让我们尝到「拒绝神作王」的苦果。人以为找个别的王会更自由、更有保障,到头来才发现,离了那位真王,一切代替品都要辖制我们、叫我们失望。

然而神的恩典在于:祂没有因以色列的厌弃就撇下他们,反倒藉着这段曲折,最终引出那位真正的王——大卫的后裔,那位「可称颂、独有权能的万王之王、万主之主」(提前6:15)。祂才是我们的心一直在寻找、却又一再抗拒的王。今天,你的心里谁在作王?若你诚实检视,会不会发现有一个「扫罗」被你扶上了宝座,而那位真王被挤到了一旁?求神叫你甘心让祂作王——因为唯有祂作王,才是你真正的福气。

默想:我心里真正作王的是谁?我是否悄悄把某个东西(事业、人、成就)扶上宝座,厌弃了神作我的王?

应用:今天诚实检视你心中的「宝座」,指认一个被你扶上去代替神的「王」,把它请下来,让基督在你心中真正掌权。

祷告:配得作王的主,以色列要一个像列国的王,厌弃了你作他们的王;我心里也常悄悄把别的东西扶上宝座,不要你掌权。感谢你没有撇下悖逆的百姓,反倒藉着曲折,引出那位真王——万王之王、万主之主耶稣基督。求你叫我甘心让你作王,把一切代替品请下宝座,因为唯有你作王,才是我真正的福气。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Samuel was old, and the elders of Israel came asking him: “appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5). They wanted a visible king, like the surrounding nations. Samuel was displeased at this, and prayed to God. God’s answer cut straight to the point: “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7). Israel’s real problem was not the political system, but that, in their hearts, they no longer wanted God to be king.

Why did they want a king “like all the nations”? Because a visible king could lead an army into battle, could give a sense of security, seeming more “reliable” than the invisible God. This is exactly the struggle deep in the human heart: we always want a king we can grip in our hands, that satisfies our expectations, that acts according to our own will — a career, money, a certain person, some achievement — to replace the God who alone is truly worthy to be king, yet who often doesn’t act according to our script. Rejecting God as king is often not open rebellion, but quietly setting something else on the throne.

It’s intriguing that God actually granted their request, giving them Saul — a tall, outwardly impressive man, exactly the king they wanted. But this king later became their burden and calamity. This is a solemn reminder: God sometimes gives us what we insist on wanting, so that we would taste the bitter fruit of “rejecting God as king.” People think finding a different king will bring more freedom, more security, only to discover, in the end, that apart from the true King, every substitute will enslave them and disappoint them.

Yet God’s grace is this: he did not abandon Israel because of their rejection, but instead, through this winding road, ultimately brought forth the true King — David’s descendant, the one “who is blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). He is the King our hearts have always been searching for, yet also repeatedly resisting. Today, who is king in your heart? If you examine yourself honestly, might you find a “Saul” you’ve placed on the throne, while the true King has been pushed aside? Ask God to make you willing to let him be King — because only when he reigns is it truly your blessing.

Meditation: Who truly reigns in my heart? Have I quietly placed something (career, a person, achievement) on the throne, rejecting God as my King?

Application: Today, honestly examine the “throne” in your heart, name a “king” you’ve placed there in place of God, remove it, and let Christ truly reign in your heart.

Prayer: Lord worthy to be King, Israel wanted a king like the nations, rejecting you as their King; my heart too often quietly sets something else on the throne, unwilling to let you reign. Thank you for not abandoning your rebellious people, but instead, through this winding road, bringing forth the true King — Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords. Let me be willing to let you reign, removing every substitute from the throne, because only your reign is my true blessing. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 听命胜于献祭——神要的是顺服
entries.title_en: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice — What God Wants Is Obedience
entries.verse: 撒母耳记上十五章廿二节
entries.content:
扫罗作王后,两次在关键时刻违背了神的命令。一次是不等撒母耳,擅自献祭;一次是神吩咐他把亚玛力人和牲畜尽都灭绝,他却擅自留下上好的牛羊,说是要留着献给神。当撒母耳责问,扫罗一再辩解:我是为了献祭给耶和华啊!他把不顺服,包装成了敬虔。

撒母耳的回答,成了整本圣经中关乎顺服的经典宣告:「耶和华喜悦燔祭和平安祭,岂如喜悦人听从他的话呢?听命胜于献祭;顺从胜于公羊的脂油」(撒上15:22)。神所要的,首先不是我们轰轰烈烈的献祭与事奉,而是一颗单纯听命的心。再多的宗教活动,也不能弥补一次故意的悖逆;再好的祭物,也代替不了顺服。扫罗以为可以用「献祭」来抵消「不听命」,神却不接受这笔交易。

这话拆穿了我们许多人的属灵假象。我们常常在自己愿意的地方大发热心——多聚会、多奉献、多服事;却在神真正吩咐、而我们不情愿的地方,悄悄打折、绕道、留一手。然后我们用前者的热心,来安慰自己在后者上的不顺服,仿佛「我为神做了这么多」就可以了。但神看重的,不是我们挑自己喜欢的替祂做什么,而是我们肯不肯照祂所说的去顺服。撒母耳更把悖逆的严重,说到了极处:「悖逆的罪与行邪术的罪相等」(撒上15:23)。

顺服,尤其是在那些我们不情愿、不明白、要付代价的地方顺服,才是对神真实的敬拜。扫罗的悖逆,不过是亚当以来人类悖逆的又一个例证;而主耶稣自己「存心顺服,以至于死」(腓2:8),成了那真正的顺服者。保罗说:「因一人的悖逆,众人成为罪人;照样,因一人的顺从,众人也成为义了」(罗5:19)——基督的顺服,不只是给我们立下榜样,更是替我们成全了我们所不能的顺服,叫我们因祂得称为义。今天,神在哪一件事上清楚地吩咐了你,而你却一直用别的「热心」来回避?求神叫你放下扫罗式的辩解,在那一处真正地听命——因为听命,胜于一切献祭。

默想:我是否在自己喜欢的地方大发热心,却在神真正吩咐、我却不情愿的地方悄悄打折?我是否也想用「献祭」抵消「不听命」?

应用:今天指认一件神已清楚吩咐、你却一直用别的忙碌来回避的事,放下辩解,单纯地去顺服它。

祷告:圣洁的主,扫罗用献祭来包装他的不顺服,你却说听命胜于献祭。我承认我常在自己愿意的地方热心,却在你真正吩咐、我不情愿的地方打折绕道,还用忙碌来安慰自己。感谢主耶稣存心顺服以至于死,以祂一人的顺从,叫我这悖逆的人得称为义。求你叫我放下一切辩解,在你所吩咐的每一处单纯听命,因为这才是你所喜悦的敬拜。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
After Saul became king, he twice disobeyed God’s command at critical moments. Once he didn’t wait for Samuel, and offered a sacrifice on his own authority; another time, God commanded him to utterly destroy the Amalekites and their livestock, yet he kept the best of the sheep and cattle on his own authority, claiming he meant to sacrifice them to God. When Samuel confronted him, Saul kept defending himself: it was to sacrifice to the LORD! He dressed up disobedience as godliness.

Samuel’s answer became the classic statement in all of Scripture concerning obedience: “Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). What God wants, first of all, is not our dramatic sacrifices and service, but a heart that simply obeys. No amount of religious activity can make up for one deliberate act of rebellion; no offering, however good, can substitute for obedience. Saul thought he could use “sacrifice” to offset “not obeying,” but God does not accept this trade.

This word exposes the spiritual pretense many of us hold. We often show great zeal where we are willing — more meetings, more giving, more service — yet quietly discount, work around, or hold back where God has truly commanded and we are unwilling. Then we use the zeal of the former to console ourselves for the disobedience of the latter, as if “I’ve done so much for God” makes it fine. But what God values is not us choosing to do for him whatever we like, but whether we are willing to obey what he has actually said. Samuel takes the severity of rebellion to its utmost: “rebellion is as the sin of divination” (1 Samuel 15:23).

Obedience, especially obeying in places we are unwilling, don’t understand, and must pay a cost — this is true worship of God. Saul’s rebellion is just one more instance of humanity’s rebellion since Adam; but the Lord Jesus himself, “being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8), becoming the truly obedient one. Paul says: “as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19) — Christ’s obedience is not merely an example set for us, but fulfilled, in our place, the obedience we could not achieve, so that we are counted righteous through him. Today, in what matter has God clearly commanded you, yet you keep using other “zeal” to avoid it? Ask God to let you lay down Saul-style excuses, and truly obey in that one place — because obeying is better than every sacrifice.

Meditation: Do I show great zeal where I’m willing, but quietly discount where God has truly commanded and I’m unwilling? Am I too trying to use “sacrifice” to offset “not obeying”?

Application: Today, name something God has clearly commanded that you’ve always avoided with other busyness, lay down the excuses, and simply obey it.

Prayer: Holy Lord, Saul dressed up his disobedience with sacrifice, but you said obeying is better than sacrifice. I confess I’m often zealous where I’m willing, but discount and work around where you have truly commanded and I’m unwilling, even comforting myself with busyness. Thank you that the Lord Jesus was obedient to the point of death, so that through his one act of obedience, I, the rebellious one, am counted righteous. Let me lay down every excuse, and simply obey in every place you command, for this is the worship you delight in. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 到如今耶和华都帮助我们
entries.title_en: Till Now the LORD Has Helped Us
entries.content:
到如今耶和华都帮助我们

「撒母耳将一块石头立在 米斯巴 和 善 的中间，给石头起名叫 以便以谢 ，说：到如今耶和华都帮助我们。」(撒母耳记上 7:12)

这一周,我们走过士师的黑暗、路得的救赎、哈拿的奉献、以色列求王的曲折。回望这一路,你会发现一条不变的线:到如今,都是耶和华帮助了我们。

今天,为你的生命立一块「以便以谢」的石头。停下来,回望神一路的帮助——不是你的聪明、努力或运气,而是祂的手,一直扶持你到今天。数算它,然后安息在那必继续帮助你的神里。

"Thus far the LORD has helped us." (1 Samuel 7:12 — Ebenezer)
entries.content_en:
Till Now the LORD Has Helped Us

"Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer, saying, 'Till now the LORD has helped us.'" (1 Samuel 7:12)

This week, we walked through the darkness of the judges, Ruth’s redemption, Hannah’s offering, and the winding road of Israel demanding a king. Looking back over this road, you’ll find one unchanging thread: till now, it is the LORD who has helped us.

Today, set up an "Ebenezer" stone for your own life. Stop, and look back at God’s help along the way — not your own cleverness, effort, or luck, but his hand, holding you up all the way to today. Count it, then rest in the God who will surely keep helping you.

"Thus far the LORD has helped us." (1 Samuel 7:12 — Ebenezer)

entries.title: 神看的是内心——那位真正的大卫
entries.title_en: The LORD Looks on the Heart — The True David
entries.verse: 撒母耳记上十六章七节
entries.content:
撒母耳来到伯利恒膏王,耶西一个一个地把儿子领到他面前。以利押身材高大,撒母耳几乎脱口而出:这必是耶和华的受膏者了!神却拦住他:「不要看他的外貌和他身材高大,我不拣选他……耶和华是看内心。」(撒上16:7)最后被召来的,是那个连父亲都没想到要叫回来的、正在旷野放羊的小儿子大卫。神拣选的,从来不是人所高举的。

接下来的故事,我们太熟悉了:巨人歌利亚每日骂阵,扫罗和全军吓得胆战心惊,唯有这个牧童凭着对神的信心,一块石子就击倒了非利士的巨人。我们常把这段读成一则励志故事:你也要像大卫一样勇敢,去打倒你生命中的「歌利亚」。但请注意,当时以色列全军并没有一起上阵——他们站在山这边观战,由一位代表替他们争战;大卫得胜,全营的人就一同分享了他的得胜。

这正是福音的影子。大卫不是要我们效法的英雄,他是那位真正的大卫——耶稣基督——的预表。我们真正的仇敌是罪与死亡这两个我们绝无可能战胜的巨人;而神差来祂的爱子,独自下到战场,在十字架上迎战,用祂的死击倒了它们。祂得胜,凡信靠祂、与祂联合的人,就白白地分享了祂的得胜。

所以基督徒的信心,不是「我要靠意志力去砍倒我的巨人」,而是「那位真正的大卫已经替我砍倒了最大的巨人」。神看的是内心;而祂最终所喜悦、并且算作我们的,是基督那颗完全的心。今天,不要再逞强作自己的救主;安息在那已经为你得胜的救主里。

默想:我是不是常常想作「自己的大卫」,靠自己的刚强去砍倒生命中的巨人?我有没有看见那位替我争战、已经得胜的真大卫?

应用:指认一个你正独自苦战的「歌利亚」(某个惧怕、罪、难处),今天不靠自己硬撑,而是把它带到那已经得胜的基督面前,支取祂的得胜。

祷告:察看人心的主,谢谢你不看外貌,只看内心;更谢谢你差来那位真正的大卫,独自替我迎战了罪与死亡的巨人,并把祂的得胜算作我的。我承认我常想作自己的救主,靠血气去争战。求你叫我今天安息在基督已成就的得胜里,以祂的心为我的心。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint a king, and Jesse brought his sons before him one by one. Eliab was tall, and Samuel almost blurted out: this must be the LORD’s anointed! But God stopped him: “Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him... the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The one finally called in was the youngest son, out in the wilderness shepherding sheep, whom not even his father thought to call back. What God chooses has never been what people exalt.

The story that follows we know all too well: the giant Goliath taunted them daily, Saul and the whole army trembling in fear, and only this shepherd boy, on the strength of his faith in God, struck down the Philistine giant with a single stone. We often read this passage as an inspirational story: you too should be brave like David, and go strike down the “Goliath” in your life. But notice, at the time, the whole army of Israel did not go into battle together — they stood on the mountainside watching, with one representative fighting on their behalf; when David won, the whole camp shared in his victory together.

This is exactly a shadow of the gospel. David is not a hero for us to imitate — he is a foreshadowing of the true David, Jesus Christ. Our true enemies are the two giants of sin and death, which we could never possibly defeat; and God sent his beloved Son to go down to the battlefield alone, meeting them on the cross, striking them down through his death. He is victorious, and everyone who trusts in him, united to him, freely shares in his victory.

So a Christian’s faith is not “I must, by willpower, strike down my giant,” but “the true David has already struck down the greatest giant in my place.” The LORD looks on the heart; and what he ultimately delights in, and counts as ours, is Christ’s perfect heart. Today, stop trying to play the hero and be your own savior; rest in the Savior who has already won victory for you.

Meditation: Do I often try to be “my own David,” relying on my own strength to strike down the giants in my life? Have I seen the true David, who fought for me and has already won?

Application: Name a “Goliath” you’re fighting alone (some fear, sin, difficulty); today, instead of gritting your teeth on your own, bring it before the already-victorious Christ, and draw on his victory.

Prayer: Lord who examines the heart, thank you for not looking at appearance, but only at the heart; thank you even more for sending the true David, who alone fought the giants of sin and death in my place, and counted his victory as mine. I confess I often try to be my own savior, fighting by my own flesh and blood. Let me today rest in the victory Christ has already accomplished, making his heart my heart. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 旷野与山洞——神对付里面的人
entries.title_en: The Wilderness and the Cave — God Dealing With the Inner Man
entries.verse: 撒母耳记上廿三章十六节
entries.content:
大卫被膏立为王之后,并没有立刻登上宝座,反而开始了漫长的逃亡。他从王宫的宠臣,变成四处躲藏的亡命之徒,栖身于亚杜兰洞、西弗的旷野。膏油已经浇在他头上,神的应许清清楚楚,眼前的境遇却与应许完全相反。神为什么允许这样的旷野?

因为神所要的,不只是一个坐上宝座的大卫,更是一个里面被祂对付过、单单倚靠祂的大卫。宝座会叫人倚靠权势,旷野却叫人只能倚靠神自己。在山洞里,大卫失去了一切外面可倚靠的——地位、安全、前途,神就在那里,一点一点地拆毁他天然的刚强,把他带到只剩下神的地步。旷野不是神应许的中断,旷野正是神成全应许的学校。神先要得着这个人的里面,才把国交在他手里。

在这最黑暗的时候,神也没有撇下他。「扫罗的儿子约拿单起身,往那树林里去见大卫,使他倚靠神得以坚固。」(撒上23:16)约拿单没有为他解决扫罗的追杀,他做的是一件更深的事——扶助大卫的手,使他重新倚靠神。真正的属灵帮助,往往不是替人挪去环境,而是把人重新带回到神面前,叫他里面得以坚固。

你今天是否也在一个「应许」与「境遇」相反的旷野里?不要以为神忘了祂的话。祂正借着这隐藏的、被剥夺的日子,对付你里面那个不肯倚靠祂的旧人,好叫将来托付给你的,能真正荣耀祂。求神也差来一位「约拿单」,或叫你去作别人的约拿单——不是挪去他的难处,而是扶助他倚靠神得以坚固。

默想:我是否正处在应许与现实相反的旷野中?我在其中是抱怨环境,还是让神对付我里面那不肯倚靠祂的旧人?

应用:今天不求神立刻挪去你的难处,而是求祂在难处中「使你倚靠神得以坚固」;并找一个正在低谷中的人,作他的约拿单,把他带回到神面前。

祷告:主啊,我常盼望快快登上宝座,却不愿走过旷野;巴不得环境改变,却不愿里面被你对付。求你借着这隐藏的日子,拆毁我天然的倚靠,叫我单单倚靠你得以坚固;也求你使我成为别人的约拿单。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
After David was anointed king, he did not immediately ascend the throne — instead, a long exile began. He went from a favored courtier in the palace to a fugitive hiding here and there, taking shelter in the cave of Adullam, the wilderness of Ziph. The oil had already been poured on his head, God’s promise was crystal clear, yet his present circumstances were the complete opposite of that promise. Why did God allow such a wilderness?

Because what God wanted was not merely a David seated on the throne, but a David who had been dealt with within, who relied solely on him. The throne makes a person rely on power, but the wilderness makes a person able to rely only on God himself. In the cave, David lost every outward thing he could rely on — status, security, future — and there, God, bit by bit, tore down his natural strength, bringing him to the point where only God remained. The wilderness is not an interruption of God’s promise; the wilderness is precisely the school where God fulfills his promise. God must first take hold of this man’s inner being, before entrusting the kingdom to his hands.

In this darkest hour, God did not abandon him either. “And Jonathan, Saul’s son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). Jonathan did not solve the problem of Saul’s pursuit for him — what he did was something deeper — he strengthened David’s hand, so that he would again rely on God. True spiritual help is often not removing someone’s circumstances for them, but bringing them back before God, so that they are strengthened within.

Are you today also in a wilderness where “promise” and “circumstance” contradict each other? Don’t think God has forgotten his word. He is, through these hidden, stripped-away days, dealing with the old self in you that refuses to rely on him, so that what will be entrusted to you in the future can truly glorify him. Ask God to also send you a “Jonathan,” or to make you someone else’s Jonathan — not removing their difficulty, but strengthening their hand in God.

Meditation: Am I currently in a wilderness where promise and reality contradict each other? In it, am I complaining about circumstances, or letting God deal with the old self in me that refuses to rely on him?

Application: Today, don’t ask God to immediately remove your difficulty — instead ask him to “strengthen you in God” within the difficulty; and find someone in a low point, and be their Jonathan, bringing them back before God.

Prayer: Lord, I often hope to quickly ascend the throne, unwilling to walk through the wilderness; I long for my circumstances to change, yet am unwilling to be dealt with within. Through these hidden days, tear down my natural reliances, and let me be strengthened by relying on you alone; and make me someone else’s Jonathan. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.verse: 撒母耳记上廿六章廿三节
entries.content:
大卫有两次绝佳的机会可以杀掉扫罗:一次在隐基底的洞里,扫罗毫无防备地进来;一次在西弗的旷野,大卫夜入营中,扫罗正在熟睡。跟随他的人都说:这是神把仇敌交在你手里的日子,动手吧!按人的逻辑,这是自卫,是神开的路,更是他登上宝座的捷径。大卫却两次都停住了手,因为他不肯「伸手害耶和华的受膏者」。

大卫的自制,不是出于懦弱,而是出于一个坚定的信念:审判在于神,不在于我。他对扫罗说:「耶和华必照各人的公义诚实报应他。」(撒上26:23)他宁可把自己的冤屈、自己的前途,都交在那位公义的审判者手中,也不肯用自己的手去抢夺、去报复。他深知,神的应许若是真的,就不需要他用罪恶的手段去成就;凡需要靠犯罪才能得到的,都不是出于神。

这正是新约反复的教导:「不要自己伸冤……主说:伸冤在我,我必报应。」(罗12:19)我们受了亏待,里面立刻升起的,是抓住机会讨回公道、亲手了断的冲动。神却要我们松手,把那把「审判的刀」交回祂手中。这不是纵容不义,而是相信有一位比我们更公义、也更有能力的审判者,祂必不误事。

我们能这样松手,是因为主耶稣先这样行了。祂「被骂不还口……只将自己交托那按公义审判人的主」(彼前2:23)。祂在十字架上没有为自己伸冤,却成就了我们的救恩。今天,那个一直亏待你、你却时时想要「动手了断」的人或事,神要你放下自己的手,把审判交还给祂。

默想:有没有一个人亏待了我,而我心里一直握着一把「报复的刀」,只等机会?我是否相信神是公义的审判者,不需要我亲手了断?

应用:今天在祷告中,具体地把一件你受的亏待和那个亏待你的人,交在神公义的手中,松开你想报复的手,把伸冤的权柄交还给神。

祷告:公义的主,大卫两次不肯伸手害仇敌,只把审判交给你。我承认我受了亏待,里面就紧握着报复的刀,想亲手了断。谢谢主耶稣被骂不还口,只将自己交托那按公义审判人的主,替我成就了救恩。求你叫我今天放下自己的手,相信伸冤在你,你必报应。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
David had two excellent opportunities to kill Saul: once in the cave at En-gedi, when Saul, completely unaware, walked right in; once in the wilderness of Ziph, when David entered the camp by night, and Saul was sound asleep. Those following him all said: this is the day the LORD has given your enemy into your hand, act now! By human logic, this was self-defense, a door God had opened, even a shortcut to the throne. Yet twice David stayed his hand, because he refused to “stretch out his hand against the LORD’s anointed.”

David’s self-restraint did not come from cowardice, but from a firm conviction: judgment belongs to God, not to me. He said to Saul: “The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness” (1 Samuel 26:23). He would rather place his own grievance, his own future, entirely in the hands of that righteous Judge, than use his own hand to seize, to take revenge. He knew deeply: if God’s promise was true, it would not need him to use sinful means to accomplish it; whatever requires sin to obtain is not from God.

This is exactly the New Testament’s repeated teaching: “Never avenge yourselves... says the Lord, Vengeance is mine, I will repay” (Romans 12:19). When we are wronged, the impulse that immediately rises within us is to seize the chance to demand justice, to settle things with our own hands. But God wants us to let go, to hand that “sword of judgment” back into his hands. This is not tolerating injustice, but believing there is a Judge more righteous than us, more capable than us, who will surely not fail to act.

We can let go this way because the Lord Jesus did so first. He “when he was reviled, did not revile in return... but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). On the cross he did not seek justice for himself, yet he accomplished our salvation. Today, that person or matter that has always wronged you, that you keep wanting to “take care of” yourself — God wants you to lay down your own hand, and hand judgment back to him.

Meditation: Is there someone who wronged me, and I’ve been holding a “knife of revenge” in my heart, just waiting for the chance? Do I believe God is a righteous Judge, who doesn’t need me to settle things with my own hand?

Application: Today in prayer, concretely hand over a wrong you’ve suffered and the person who wronged you into God’s righteous hands, letting go of your hand of revenge, and returning the right of vindication to God.

Prayer: Righteous Lord, David twice refused to stretch out his hand against his enemy, handing judgment to you instead. I confess that when I’m wronged, I grip a knife of revenge inside, wanting to settle it myself. Thank you that the Lord Jesus, when reviled, did not revile in return, but entrusted himself to the Judge who judges justly, accomplishing salvation for me. Let me today lay down my own hand, believing that vengeance belongs to you, and you will repay. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 当神不再回答——悖逆的尽头
entries.title_en: When God No Longer Answers — The End of Rebellion
entries.verse: 撒母耳记上廿八章六节
entries.content:
扫罗的结局,是圣经中最令人战栗的画面之一。非利士大军压境,他心中惧怕,就去「求问耶和华」。经文却记着一句可怕的话:「耶和华却不藉梦,或乌陵,或先知回答他。」(撒上28:6)那位曾一次次向以色列说话的神,此刻沉默了。于是扫罗连夜乔装,去求问一个交鬼的妇人——他一生拒绝顺服神,末了竟去叩问阴间。次日,他就死在基利波山上。

神的沉默,不是一时的心血来潮,而是扫罗长年累月刚硬悖逆的尽头。他曾擅自献祭,曾违命留下亚玛力的牛羊,曾一次次追杀无辜的大卫,又用宗教的外壳包裹自己的不顺服。神多次借撒母耳向他说话,他却次次不听。到了这一天,不是神残忍地关上了门,而是扫罗自己,把心一次次地关上,直到再也听不见神的声音。这是一个严肃的警告:持续、故意地拒绝神的话,会让人的良心和耳朵渐渐麻木,直到落在神可怕的沉默里。

「你们今日若听他的话,就不可硬着心。」(来3:15)罪最大的欺骗,就是让我们以为「以后还有机会」。扫罗以为他随时可以回头,却不知每一次的不听,都在为那最后的沉默铺路。硬心是一寸一寸积累的,等到真需要听见神的时候,那扇门可能已经关上。

但这段黑暗的记载,也反衬出福音何等宝贵。对悔改的人,神从不沉默!祂已「藉着他儿子晓谕我们」(来1:2)。凡肯回转、谦卑求告的,神必不撇下;十字架上的基督,正是神向罪人所说的、最响亮的一句「我爱你,回来吧」。今天你若还听得见祂的声音,就不要硬着心;趁着还有「今日」,回到祂面前。

默想:神有没有借着祂的话、我的良心,一次次向我说某件事,而我一次次绕开、拖延?我是否在不知不觉中,正一寸寸地硬着自己的心?

应用:指认一件你一直听见、却一直不肯顺服的事,今天就不再拖延,趁着还是「今日」,回应神的声音,顺服祂。

祷告:说话的主,扫罗一生拒听你的话,末了落在你可怕的沉默里。我战兢地看见,硬心是一点一点积累的。求你叫我今日不硬着心,凡你所指出的,我就顺服。谢谢你对悔改的人从不沉默,已在你儿子里向我说尽了爱。趁我还听得见,求你领我回到你面前。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Saul’s end is one of the most chilling scenes in Scripture. The Philistine army pressed in, and, terrified, he went to “inquire of the LORD.” Yet the text records this terrifying sentence: “the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets” (1 Samuel 28:6). The God who had once spoken to Israel again and again was now silent. So Saul disguised himself that very night and went to consult a medium — he who had spent his life refusing to obey God now, in the end, sought counsel from the realm of the dead. The next day, he died on Mount Gilboa.

God’s silence was not a momentary whim, but the end result of Saul’s years of accumulated hardness and rebellion. He had once offered sacrifice on his own authority, disobeyed the command to destroy the Amalekites’ livestock, pursued the innocent David again and again, and wrapped his disobedience in a religious shell. God spoke to him many times through Samuel, yet each time he refused to listen. By this day, it was not God cruelly shutting the door — it was Saul himself, closing his own heart again and again, until he could no longer hear God’s voice at all. This is a solemn warning: persistent, deliberate rejection of God’s word gradually numbs a person’s conscience and ears, until they fall into God’s terrifying silence.

“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15). Sin’s greatest deception is letting us think “there will still be a chance later.” Saul thought he could turn back anytime, not knowing that every refusal to listen was paving the way toward that final silence. A hard heart accumulates inch by inch, and by the time you truly need to hear God, that door may already be closed.

But this dark record also, by contrast, shows how precious the gospel is. To the repentant, God is never silent! He “has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2). Whoever is willing to turn back and humbly cry out, God will surely not abandon; Christ on the cross is precisely God’s loudest word to sinners: “I love you, come back.” If you can still hear his voice today, don’t harden your heart; while it is still “today,” return to him.

Meditation: Has God, through his word, through my conscience, spoken to me about something again and again, while I keep going around it, delaying? Am I, unconsciously, hardening my own heart, inch by inch?

Application: Name something you’ve heard again and again but have always refused to obey; today, no more delay — while it is still “today,” respond to God’s voice and obey it.

Prayer: Lord who speaks, Saul spent his whole life refusing to hear your word, and in the end fell into your terrifying silence. I tremble to see that a hard heart accumulates little by little. Let me not harden my heart today; whatever you point out, let me obey. Thank you that to the repentant you are never silent, having already spoken your love fully in your Son. While I can still hear, lead me back before you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 为仇敌哀哭的心
entries.title_en: A Heart That Weeps for Its Enemy
entries.verse: 撒母耳记下三章一节
entries.content:
扫罗死了。这个追杀大卫多年、逼他流离旷野的人,终于倒下了。若换作我们,恐怕心里第一个反应是松一口气,甚至暗暗庆幸:压制我的那个人终于走了。大卫的反应却完全出人意料——他为扫罗和约拿单作哀歌,放声痛哭,又把那个自以为讨好、前来报告扫罗死讯的人治罪。大卫没有因仇敌的败亡而快乐。

这是一颗被神恩典改变了的心。世人的逻辑是:仇敌倒下,正是我扬眉吐气之时。大卫却看扫罗仍是「耶和华的受膏者」,为他的死真心哀伤。他没有把扫罗从「神所设立的王」贬为「我个人的敌人」,好让自己的报复心得着满足。恨一个人最容易的方法,就是先在心里把他非人化;而恩典所作的,恰恰相反——它让我们在最有理由记恨的人身上,仍看见一个神所造、值得为之哀哭的灵魂。

随后是扫罗家与大卫家漫长的争战,「大卫家日见强盛;扫罗家日见衰弱。」(撒下3:1)神没有让大卫用一场政变、一夜之间夺取王位,而是让他在漫长、缓慢、有时看似停滞的过程中,一步步被神高举。神的应许常常不是一步到位的闪电,而是「日见强盛」的黎明——慢,却真实,且不可阻挡。

这为仇敌哀哭、又肯耐心等候的心,从哪里来?它来自各各他。主耶稣在十字架上,为钉祂的人祷告说:「父啊,赦免他们」;祂爱仇敌,爱到为仇敌舍命——而那仇敌里,有你,有我。当我们真尝过「我这与神为敌的人,竟被祂如此深爱」的滋味,就再也无法用旧日那种幸灾乐祸的眼光,去看那亏待我们的人了。

默想:有没有一个「对头」,我巴不得看见他跌倒?我是否在心里把某个人非人化了,好让自己的记恨显得理直气壮?我等得起神那「日见强盛」的、缓慢的成全吗?

应用:为一个你曾视为「对头」的人祷告,求神让你能真心为他好;并在一件你巴望「立刻翻盘」的事上,选择耐心等候神缓慢却真实的成全。

祷告:爱仇敌的主,大卫竟为追杀他的扫罗放声痛哭。我承认,我常盼着对头跌倒,好叫自己称快。谢谢你在十字架上为仇敌代求、舍命,而那仇敌里就有我。求你用这被你深爱的经历,融化我里面幸灾乐祸的心,又叫我甘心等候你日见强盛的成全。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Saul was dead. The man who had pursued David for years, forcing him to wander the wilderness, had finally fallen. If it were us, our first reaction would probably be relief, even secret satisfaction: the one who oppressed me is finally gone. David’s reaction was completely unexpected — he composed a lament for Saul and Jonathan, wept aloud, and had the man who thought he was bringing welcome news of Saul’s death punished. David did not rejoice at his enemy’s downfall.

This is a heart changed by God’s grace. The world’s logic is: when the enemy falls, that’s my moment of triumph. But David still saw Saul as “the LORD’s anointed,” and genuinely grieved his death. He did not demote Saul from “the king God appointed” to “my personal enemy” in order to satisfy his own desire for revenge. The easiest way to hate someone is to first dehumanize them in your heart; and what grace does is exactly the opposite — it lets us still see, in the person we have every reason to resent, a soul made by God, worth weeping over.

What followed was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: “David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker” (2 Samuel 3:1). God did not let David seize the throne through a coup, overnight; instead he let him be exalted step by step, through a long, slow, sometimes seemingly stalled process. God’s promises are often not lightning that arrives all at once, but a dawn that “grows stronger and stronger” — slow, yet real, and unstoppable.

Where does this heart that weeps for its enemy, yet is willing to wait patiently, come from? It comes from Calvary. The Lord Jesus, on the cross, prayed for those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them”; he loved his enemies, loved them enough to lay down his life for them — and among those enemies were you, and me. When we have truly tasted what it means that “I, who was God’s enemy, was loved by him this deeply,” we can no longer look at those who have wronged us with that old gloating gaze.

Meditation: Is there an “enemy” whose downfall I long to see? Have I dehumanized someone in my heart, so that my resentment would feel justified? Can I wait for God’s slow, “growing stronger and stronger” fulfillment?

Application: Pray for someone you’ve considered an “enemy,” asking God to let you genuinely want good for them; and in a matter where you’re longing for an “immediate reversal,” choose to wait patiently for God’s slow but real fulfillment.

Prayer: Lord who loves his enemies, David actually wept aloud for Saul, who had pursued him. I confess I often hope for my enemy’s downfall, so that I can feel vindicated. Thank you for interceding for your enemies on the cross, laying down your life — and among those enemies was me. Use this experience of being deeply loved by you to melt the gloating in my heart, and make me willing to wait for your slow, growing fulfillment. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 神要为你建造一个家
entries.title_en: God Will Build You a House
entries.verse: 撒母耳记下七章十六节
entries.content:
大卫终于作王,统一了以色列,又把约柜迎进大卫城。安顿下来后,他心里生出一个美好的心愿:我住在香柏木的宫里,神的约柜却还在幔子里,我要为神建一座殿。这是何等虔诚的抱负!然而那一夜,神借先知拿单对大卫说的话,却把整件事彻底翻转了过来。

神说:不是你为我建殿,乃是「我必为你建立家室」。你的后裔要接续你,你的国、你的家、你的位「必在我面前永远坚立……直到永远。」(撒下7:16)大卫本想给神一样东西,神却回过头来,把无可比拟的大恩倾倒在他身上。这是恩典最核心的样式:我们捧着自己的一点心意来到神面前,以为要给祂什么,神却总是那位给得更多、给得先、给得完全的一位。

这也正是神之所以为神的荣耀所在。神从不亏欠人,也不需要人为祂添什么(徒17:25)。祂最深的荣耀,不在于接受,而在于施予;祂乐意作那位丰丰富富的赐予者。而我们最大的满足,恰恰在于放下「我要为神做点什么来换取什么」的心态,单单作一个空着手、被祂充满的领受者。神得荣耀,我们得满足,这两件事在恩典里从不冲突,反而合而为一。

更奇妙的是,这「永远坚立」的应许,大卫的肉身后裔无一人配得,唯独那位大卫的子孙——耶稣基督——成全了它。祂的国度没有尽头,祂的宝座直到永远(路1:32-33)。神向大卫所应许的那个永不倒塌的家,今天借着基督,也临到了每一个信祂的人:我们藉着祂,被建造成神永远的居所。你不必用一生的努力去为神「挣」一个位置;在基督里,神已经把永远的家白白赐给了你。

默想:我与神的关系,是不是常停在「我要为祂做什么来换祂的悦纳」?我有没有看见,祂总是那位给得更多、给得在先的神?

应用:今天暂时放下「为神做点什么」的忙碌,先安静领受祂在基督里已白白赐给你的一切;数算祂主动为你「建造的家」,以感恩回应,而非以交换回应。

祷告:丰富的主,大卫想为你建殿,你却说要为他建立永远的家。我承认,我常想用付出去换取你的悦纳,忘了你总是给得更多、给得在先的神。谢谢你借着大卫的子孙耶稣,把那永不倒塌的家白白赐给我。求你叫我今天以领受者的心,安息在你的恩典里,单单归荣耀给你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
David finally became king, united Israel, and brought the ark into the city of David. Once settled, a beautiful desire arose in his heart: I live in a house of cedar, yet God’s ark still dwells in a tent — I will build a temple for God. What a devout ambition! Yet that very night, through the words God spoke to David by the prophet Nathan, the whole thing was completely turned around.

God said: it is not you who will build me a house, but “I will make you a house.” Your offspring will succeed you, and your kingdom, your house, your throne “shall be established forever... forever” (2 Samuel 7:16). David had wanted to give God something, but God turned around and poured out incomparable grace upon him instead. This is the very core pattern of grace: we come before God holding our small offering, thinking we’re about to give him something, yet God is always the one who gives more, gives first, gives completely.

This is exactly where God’s glory as God shines through. God is never indebted to anyone, nor does he need anyone to add anything to him (Acts 17:25). His deepest glory lies not in receiving, but in giving; he delights to be the abundant Giver. And our greatest satisfaction lies precisely in laying down the mindset of “I want to do something for God to earn something,” and simply being an empty-handed receiver, filled by him. God is glorified, we are satisfied — these two things never conflict in grace; instead they become one.

More wonderful still, this promise of being “established forever” — no physical descendant of David was worthy of it, except that one descendant of David — Jesus Christ — who fulfilled it. His kingdom has no end, his throne is forever (Luke 1:32–33). The never-collapsing house God promised David has now, through Christ, come to everyone who believes in him too: through him, we are built into God’s eternal dwelling place. You don’t need to spend a lifetime of effort to “earn” a place with God; in Christ, God has already freely given you an eternal house.

Meditation: Does my relationship with God often stop at “what I need to do for him to earn his favor”? Have I seen that he is always the God who gives more, gives first?

Application: Today, temporarily lay down the busyness of “doing something for God,” and first quietly receive everything he has already freely given you in Christ; count the “house he has proactively built” for you, and respond with gratitude rather than transaction.

Prayer: Abundant Lord, David wanted to build you a temple, but you said you would build him an eternal house. I confess I often want to trade my giving for your favor, forgetting you are always the God who gives more, gives first. Thank you for freely giving me, through David’s descendant Jesus, that never-collapsing house. Let me today, as a receiver, rest in your grace, giving glory to you alone. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 牧童与宝座之间——安息与更新
entries.title_en: Between Shepherd Boy and Throne — Rest and Renewal
entries.content:
牧童与宝座之间——安息与更新

「你们要休息,要知道我是 神!」(诗篇 46:10)

这一周,我们陪着大卫走过被膏、逃亡、山洞、饶恕仇敌,直到登上宝座、领受永远的应许。回望这一路,你会看见一条安静的线:从牧童到君王的每一步,都不是大卫抢来的,而是神在祂自己的时候,一步步成全的。

他在旷野等候,神在暗中动工;他不肯伸手,神却亲自开路。今天,把你手中那件你一直想要「快快抓住」的事松一松。你不需要靠自己去夺取神已经应许要给你的;你只需要安息,并且知道——祂是神。

"Be still, and know that I am God." (Psalm 46:10)
entries.content_en:
Between Shepherd Boy and Throne — Rest and Renewal

"Be still, and know that I am God!" (Psalm 46:10)

This week, we walked with David through anointing, exile, caves, and forgiving his enemy, all the way to ascending the throne and receiving the eternal promise. Looking back over this road, you’ll see one quiet thread: every step from shepherd boy to king was never seized by David himself, but fulfilled, step by step, by God in his own time.

He waited in the wilderness, and God was at work in secret; he refused to lift his hand, and God himself opened the way. Today, loosen your grip a little on that thing you’ve always wanted to "quickly seize." You don’t need to rely on yourself to take hold of what God has already promised to give you; you need only rest, and know — he is God.

"Be still, and know that I am God." (Psalm 46:10)

entries.title: 瘸腿的人坐上王的筵席
entries.title_en: The Lame Man Seated at the King's Table
entries.verse: 撒母耳记下九章七节
entries.content:
大卫作王,国势日盛,四境扩张。就在权力的高峰,他忽然想起一件事:扫罗家还有剩下的人吗?我要因约拿单的缘故,向他施恩。按当时的政治常规,新王登基,巴不得斩草除根,把前朝的后裔一个不留;大卫却反其道而行,主动去寻找前王的骨肉,只为向他施恩。

他找到的,是约拿单的儿子米非波设——一个两脚都瘸了的人。这个本该继承王位、如今却隐姓埋名躲在罗底巴的人,一被带到大卫面前,就俯伏在地,自称是「死狗」。大卫对他说的第一句话是:「你不要惧怕,我必因你父亲约拿单的缘故施恩与你。」(撒下9:7)不是因为米非波设有什么可取,而是因着一份他毫无份儿、早已立定的盟约之爱;从此,这个瘸腿的人天天与王同席吃饭,如同王的儿子。

这几乎是整本圣经里最清晰的一幅恩典图画。我们本是与神为敌之人的后裔,灵里瘸腿、无力自救,躲在自己的罗底巴里,一见圣洁的君王就只配自称「死狗」。然而神却主动来寻找我们,不是因我们身上有什么配得的,而是因着祂儿子——那位真约拿单——所立的约,白白地接纳我们,叫我们这瘸腿的罪人,天天坐在王的筵席上,享用天父桌上的丰盛。

值得注意的是,米非波设的瘸腿,一生都没有得医治;他坐在王的席上,桌子遮住了他残缺的双脚。恩典不是先叫你变得体面才收纳你,而是照你残缺的原样收纳你,再用王的筵席遮盖你的不堪。今天,你若还在用「我不配」把自己关在罗底巴,请听王的呼唤:不要惧怕,来坐席吧——不是因为你配,而是因为约已经立定。

默想:我是否还躲在自己的「罗底巴」里,觉得自己太残缺、太不配,不敢坐上恩典的筵席?我有没有看见,王施恩的理由从来不在我,而在祂所立的约?

应用:今天不靠「我够好了没有」来到神面前,而是单单凭着基督所立的约支取接纳;并去向一个「不配你善待」的人主动施恩,让恩典借你流出去。

祷告:施恩的主,大卫因着约,把瘸腿的米非波设接到王的席上。我正是那灵里瘸腿、自称死狗的人,却蒙你因基督所立的约白白收纳,天天坐在你丰盛的筵席前。求你除去我「不配就不敢来」的惧怕,叫我安然坐席,也叫我照样向不配的人施恩。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
David was king, his kingdom growing ever stronger, his borders expanding. At the very peak of his power, he suddenly remembered something: is there still anyone left of Saul’s house? I want to show kindness to him for Jonathan’s sake. By the political conventions of the time, a new king would want to cut off every trace of the previous dynasty’s descendants; David instead did the opposite, proactively seeking out the former king’s remaining flesh and blood, solely to show him kindness.

The one he found was Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth — a man lame in both feet. This man, who should have inherited the throne, now hiding under an assumed name in Lo-debar, the moment he was brought before David, fell facedown, calling himself a “dead dog.” The first thing David said to him was: “Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan” (2 Samuel 9:7). Not because Mephibosheth had anything to commend him, but because of a covenant love he had no part in earning, already established long before; from then on, this lame man ate at the king’s table every day, as one of the king’s own sons.

This is almost the clearest picture of grace in the whole Bible. We were, by nature, descendants of those who were God’s enemies, lame in spirit, unable to save ourselves, hiding in our own Lo-debar, and at the sight of the holy King, fit only to call ourselves a “dead dog.” Yet God proactively came to seek us out, not because we had anything to commend us, but because of the covenant established by his Son — the true Jonathan — freely accepting us, so that we, lame sinners, would sit daily at the king’s table, enjoying the abundance of the Father’s table.

It’s worth noting that Mephibosheth’s lameness was never healed in his lifetime; he sat at the king’s table, and the table hid his crippled feet. Grace does not first require you to become presentable before it accepts you — it accepts you exactly as you are, crippled, and then covers your unpresentability with the king’s own table. Today, if you’re still shutting yourself in your own Lo-debar with “I don’t deserve it,” hear the king’s call: don’t be afraid, come sit at the table — not because you deserve it, but because the covenant has already been established.

Meditation: Am I still hiding in my own “Lo-debar,” feeling too crippled, too unworthy, to dare sit at the table of grace? Have I seen that the king’s reason for showing kindness was never in me, but in the covenant he established?

Application: Today, don’t come before God relying on “am I good enough yet” — draw on acceptance solely on the basis of the covenant Christ has established; and proactively show kindness to someone “undeserving of your kindness,” letting grace flow out through you.

Prayer: Gracious Lord, because of a covenant, David brought the lame Mephibosheth to the king’s table. I am exactly that one, lame in spirit, calling myself a dead dog, yet freely accepted because of the covenant you established in Christ, sitting daily before your abundant table. Remove my fear of “not daring to come because I don’t deserve it,” let me sit at your table in peace, and let me likewise show kindness to the undeserving. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 被拆穿的罪,与除罪的恩
entries.title_en: Sin Exposed, and Grace That Removes Sin
entries.verse: 撒母耳记下十二章十三节
entries.content:
这是大卫一生最黑暗的一章。一个本该出征的春天,他却留在宫中;一次不经意的观看,变成贪恋;贪恋生出奸淫,奸淫又用谋杀去遮盖。经文冷冷地记下一句:「大卫所行的这事,耶和华甚不喜悦。」罪从来不是一步到位的,它是一条滑坡:一次的放纵,若不对付,就必生出下一个更大的罪来遮盖前一个。而最可怕的是,大卫在事成之后,竟能若无其事地过了将近一年,良心仿佛被麻醉了一般。

直到神差先知拿单来。拿单没有一上来就定罪,他讲了一个穷人和小母羊羔的比喻,勾起大卫的义愤,然后一针见血:「你就是那人!」这一刀,划开了大卫用宗教与权力层层包裹的伪装。真正的悔改,就是从这一刻开始的——不是找借口,不是转移话题,而是俯首认罪:「我得罪耶和华了!」(撒下12:13)大卫后来在诗篇五十一篇里把这认罪倾倒出来:「我向你犯罪,惟独得罪了你。」

然而,就在他认罪的同一句话里,神惊人的恩典也临到了:拿单说:「耶和华已经除掉你的罪,你必不至于死。」(撒下12:13)神没有等大卫先做够多少补赎,才勉强赦免;认罪的话音刚落,除罪的宣告就随之而来。这就是福音:神不是先要我们变好,而是要我们诚实——凡真心认罪的,祂立时以基督的宝血除净。这血,足以洗净奸淫与谋杀这样滔天的罪。

但恩典赦免了罪,却不总是挪去罪在地上的后果。神虽除掉大卫的罪,刀剑却从此不离他的家:暗嫩、押沙龙、他玛……接下来几章的家庭悲剧,都是那一夜种下的苦果。这提醒我们:罪得赦免是白白的,却绝不是廉价的;被赦免的人,更当因着敬畏,远离一切引我们滑向深渊的第一步。今天,你有没有一个正在若无其事地遮盖、迟迟不肯认的罪?趁拿单的声音还临到你,俯首说:我得罪耶和华了。

默想:我生命中有没有一个「留在宫中」的松懈、一次没有对付的放纵,正在悄悄滑向更大的罪?我是在遮盖它,还是肯像大卫一样被拆穿、认罪?

应用:今天在神面前诚实指认一件你一直遮盖的罪,不找借口,照实认它;支取基督宝血的赦免,同时警醒远离那引你跌倒的「第一步」。

祷告:圣洁又满有怜悯的主,大卫的罪从一次放纵滑向奸淫与谋杀,又用近一年的时间麻醉良心。求你差你话语的拿单,拆穿我一切的遮盖。谢谢你在我认罪的那一刻,就凭基督的宝血除掉我的罪。求你叫我既蒙这样的赦免,就更敬畏你,远离那滑向深渊的第一步。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
This is the darkest chapter of David’s life. In a spring when he should have been at war, he stayed in the palace instead; a careless glance turned into lust; lust bred adultery, and adultery was covered up with murder. The text coldly records: “the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” Sin is never a single step — it is a slippery slope: one indulgence, if not dealt with, will surely give birth to a bigger sin to cover the previous one. And most terrifying of all, after it was done, David was able to go on as if nothing happened for nearly a year, his conscience seemingly numbed.

Until God sent the prophet Nathan. Nathan didn’t condemn him outright — he told a parable about a poor man and a little ewe lamb, stirring David’s righteous indignation, and then struck: “You are the man!” This one cut sliced open the disguise David had wrapped in layers of religion and power. True repentance began at this very moment — not making excuses, not changing the subject, but bowing the head and confessing: “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13). David later poured out this confession in Psalm 51: “Against you, you only, have I sinned.”

Yet in that very same sentence where he confessed, God’s astonishing grace also arrived: Nathan said, “The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Samuel 12:13). God did not wait for David to first do enough penance before reluctantly forgiving him; the words of confession had barely left his mouth when the declaration of removed sin followed immediately. This is the gospel: God doesn’t first require us to become good, but to be honest — whoever truly confesses, he immediately cleanses completely with Christ’s precious blood. This blood is sufficient to wash clean even monstrous sins like adultery and murder.

But grace forgives sin, yet does not always remove sin’s consequences on earth. Though God removed David’s sin, the sword never departed from his house from then on: Amnon, Absalom, Tamar... the family tragedies of the following chapters are all bitter fruit sown that one night. This reminds us: forgiveness of sin is free, but never cheap; those forgiven should, all the more, out of reverence, flee from every first step that slides us toward the abyss. Today, is there a sin you’re covering up as if nothing happened, that you’ve long refused to confess? While Nathan’s voice still comes to you, bow your head and say: I have sinned against the LORD.

Meditation: Is there a laxity of “staying in the palace,” an undealt-with indulgence in my life, quietly sliding toward a bigger sin? Am I covering it up, or willing, like David, to be exposed and confess?

Application: Today, honestly name before God a sin you’ve been covering up, without excuse, confessing it as it is; draw on the forgiveness of Christ’s blood, while staying watchful to flee the “first step” that leads you to fall.

Prayer: Holy and merciful Lord, David’s sin slid from one indulgence into adultery and murder, and he numbed his conscience for nearly a year. Send your Nathan of the word to expose all my cover-ups. Thank you that the moment I confess, you remove my sin by Christ’s precious blood. Because I have received such forgiveness, let me fear you all the more, fleeing the first step that slides toward the abyss. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 愿他凭自己的意旨待我——降服的功课
entries.title_en: Let Him Do to Me as Seems Good to Him — The Lesson of Submission
entries.verse: 撒母耳记下十五章廿六节
entries.content:
押沙龙的叛变,是大卫晚年最深的痛。他亲生的儿子谋夺他的王位,连他最倚重的谋士亚希多弗也倒戈相向。大卫赤着脚、蒙着头,哭着逃出耶路撒冷。这一路上,他所显出的,不是一个君王的挣扎与反扑,而是一个被神对付得极深的人的降服。

祭司要把约柜一同抬出城,大卫却叫他们把约柜抬回去,说了一句极深的话:神若喜悦我,必领我回来,再见约柜;「倘若他说:我不喜悦你,看哪,我在这里,愿他凭自己的意旨待我!」(撒下15:26)他没有把约柜当作护身符去操纵神,也没有要神必须照他的意思翻盘。他把自己整个交在神手里,连神「不喜悦」他、任凭他失去一切这样的可能,他都俯首接受了。这就是降服的极处——不是相信神一定会照我要的去成全,而是无论神怎样待我,我都说:愿你的旨意成就。

接着,示每一路跟着咒骂他、拿石头扔他。跟随的人要去取示每的命,大卫却拦住,说:由他咒骂吧,或者耶和华见我遭难,施恩与我。一个真被神破碎的人,不再急于为自己辩护、报复;他看一切临到的患难,甚至羞辱,都是从神手中经过、为要成全神在他身上的旨意。他不再挣扎着要掌控局面,只是安静地伏在神的手下。

神在我们身上最深的工作,往往不在顺境的高峰,而在这样众叛亲离、被剥夺净尽的低谷。祂要的,不是一个还在暗暗为自己筹算、随时准备反扑的人,而是一个肯说「愿你凭自己的意旨待我」的、彻底降服的人。你今天所受的,是否也像大卫这一段路?求神叫你不在其中挣扎自保,而是学会把双手完全松开,伏在祂美善的旨意之下。

默想:我对神的信靠,是「祂一定会照我要的成全」,还是「无论祂怎样待我,愿祂的旨意成就」?在被剥夺、被羞辱时,我是急于自保反扑,还是俯首降服?

应用:把一件你正紧紧抓住、想要掌控结局的事,今天在祷告中对神说出那句话:我在这里,愿你凭自己的意旨待我;然后把手松开。

祷告:掌管万有的主,大卫在众叛亲离中,竟能说出「愿他凭自己的意旨待我」。我承认,我的信靠常带着条件,总要你照我的意思翻盘。求你在我被剥夺、受羞辱的低谷里,作那更深的破碎,叫我不再挣扎自保,而是甘心伏在你美善的旨意之下。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Absalom’s rebellion was the deepest pain of David’s later years. His own son sought to seize his throne, and even Ahithophel, his most trusted counselor, turned against him. David, barefoot and with his head covered, fled Jerusalem weeping. Along this road, what he displayed was not a king’s struggle and counterattack, but the submission of a man deeply dealt with by God.

The priests wanted to carry the ark out of the city with him, but David told them to carry it back, saying something profoundly deep: if God delighted in him, he would bring him back to see the ark again; “but if he says, I have no pleasure in you, behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him” (2 Samuel 15:26). He did not treat the ark as a talisman to manipulate God, nor did he demand that God turn things around according to his own will. He handed his entire self over into God’s hands, even accepting the possibility that God might “not delight” in him, letting him lose everything. This is submission at its utmost — not believing God will surely fulfill what I want, but, no matter how God treats me, saying: let your will be done.

Then Shimei followed along the road, cursing him and throwing stones. Those following David wanted to take Shimei’s life, but David stopped them, saying: let him curse; perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good. A person truly broken by God no longer rushes to defend or avenge themselves; they see everything that comes upon them, even humiliation, as passing through God’s hand, meant to fulfill God’s purpose in them. He no longer struggles to control the situation, but quietly submits under God’s hand.

God’s deepest work in us often happens not at the peak of favorable circumstances, but in a low valley like this, deserted by everyone, stripped of everything. What he wants is not someone still secretly scheming for themselves, ready to counterattack anytime, but someone who is willing to say “let him do to me as seems good to him,” someone thoroughly submitted. Is what you’re going through today also like this stretch of David’s road? Ask God to let you not struggle to protect yourself within it, but learn to fully let go, submitting under his good will.

Meditation: Is my trust in God “he will surely fulfill what I want,” or “no matter how he treats me, let his will be done”? When stripped, humiliated, do I rush to protect and counterattack myself, or bow and submit?

Application: Take something you’re gripping tightly, wanting to control the outcome of, and today in prayer, say that sentence to God: here I am, let him do to me as seems good to him; then let go.

Prayer: Lord who governs all things, David, deserted by everyone, could still say “let him do to me as seems good to him.” I confess my trust often comes with conditions, always wanting you to turn things around according to my will. In the valley where I am stripped and humiliated, do that deeper breaking work in me, so that I no longer struggle to protect myself, but am willing to submit under your good will. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 只要我主我王平安——够了
entries.title_en: As Long as My Lord the King Is Safe — That Is Enough
entries.verse: 撒母耳记下十九章三十节
entries.content:
押沙龙死了,大卫得以回宫,但这个国仍在动荡中:以色列与犹大为「谁先迎王」争得面红耳赤,示巴又乘乱举旗叛乱。在这一片你争我夺、各为己利的乱局中,却有一个人的反应,格外扎心地干净。

他就是米非波设。他曾被仆人洗巴诬告、夺去了产业。如今王回来了,大卫说:你与洗巴均分那地吧。换作我们,一定要据理力争,把被夺的产业一寸不少地讨回来。米非波设却说:「我主我王既平平安安地回宫,就任凭洗巴都取了也可以。」(撒下19:30)他的意思是:王啊,你平平安安地回来,这就够了;至于田产,全给洗巴,我也甘心。对他而言,拥有王本身,已经胜过拥有王所能赐的一切。

这一句话,像一面镜子,照出我们信仰里一个致命的错位。我们太容易把神所赐的「产业」——健康、顺境、被人善待、事情如我所愿——看得比神自己更重。于是一旦这些被夺走、被误解、被亏待,我们就跟神算账、争产业,仿佛神欠了我们。米非波设却提醒我们:你真正拥有的,是王自己!若有了王,失了田产又何妨?若失了王,得了全世界又有何益?

主耶稣问过一句同样扎心的话:人若赚得全世界,赔上自己的生命,有什么益处呢?今天,神也许正让你失去某样你一直看得很重的「田产」。祂在问你:有我,够不够?求神把米非波设那颗心赐给你——不是抓着产业跟神讨价还价,而是说:主啊,有你,就够了;其余的,任凭拿去也可以。

默想:我是把神所赐的「产业」看得比神自己更重,还是真能说「有主就够了」?最近有没有一样被夺去的东西,叫我跟神争产、算账?

应用:指认一样你一直看得比神更重、失去就跟神闹的「田产」,今天在祷告中把它交出去,操练对神说:有你就够了,其余任凭你安排。

祷告:我的主我的王,米非波设说,只要你平安回宫,田产任凭洗巴取去也可以。我惭愧,我常把你所赐的看得比你自己更重,一失去就与你算账。求你叫我真看见,拥有你本身,已胜过一切;赐我一颗以你为满足的心,能坦然说:有你,就够了。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Absalom was dead, and David was able to return to the palace, but the kingdom was still in turmoil: Israel and Judah were red-faced arguing over “who gets to welcome the king first,” and Sheba raised a rebel flag amid the chaos. In this whole scene of everyone grabbing for themselves, each for their own interest, one man’s response stands out, strikingly clean.

It was Mephibosheth. He had once been falsely accused by his servant Ziba and stripped of his property. Now that the king had returned, David said: you and Ziba divide the land. In our place, we would surely argue our case, demanding back every last bit of the stolen property. But Mephibosheth said: “Since my lord the king has come safely home, let him take it all” (2 Samuel 19:30). What he meant was: my king, that you have come home safely — that alone is enough; as for the land, let Ziba have it all, and I am content. For him, having the king himself already surpassed having everything the king could give.

This one sentence is like a mirror, reflecting a fatal misplacement in our faith. We too easily value the “inheritance” God gives — health, favorable circumstances, being treated well, things going as I wish — more highly than God himself. So the moment these are taken away, misunderstood, or wronged, we settle accounts with God, fighting for our inheritance, as if God owed us. Mephibosheth reminds us: what you truly possess is the king himself! If you have the king, what does it matter if you lose the land? If you lose the king, what good is it to gain the whole world?

The Lord Jesus asked an equally piercing question: what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his own life? Today, God may be letting you lose some “land” you’ve always valued highly. He’s asking you: is having me enough? Ask God to give you Mephibosheth’s heart — not gripping your inheritance, haggling with God, but saying: Lord, having you is enough; take the rest, if you must.

Meditation: Do I value the “inheritance” God gives more than God himself, or can I truly say “having the Lord is enough”? Has something been taken from me recently that made me fight and settle accounts with God?

Application: Name a piece of “land” you’ve always valued more than God, and are ready to fight God over losing; today in prayer, hand it over, practicing saying to God: having you is enough, arrange the rest as you will.

Prayer: My Lord and my King, Mephibosheth said, as long as you return safely, let Ziba take the land. I am ashamed — I often value what you’ve given more than you yourself, and settle accounts with you the moment I lose it. Let me truly see that having you alone surpasses everything; give me a heart satisfied in you, able to say plainly: having you is enough. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我不献那不花代价的祭
entries.title_en: I Will Not Offer That Which Costs Me Nothing
entries.verse: 撒母耳记下廿四章廿四节
entries.content:
大卫晚年犯了一个我们不易看懂的罪:他数点百姓。这背后,是一颗渐渐倚靠军队数目、而非倚靠神的心。神降下瘟疫,大卫极其痛悔,在耶布斯人亚劳拿的禾场上看见管理者,就要在那里筑坛献祭。亚劳拿是个慷慨人,愿意把禾场、牛、器具全都白白送给王。这本是顺水人情——王不必破费,照样可以献祭。

大卫的回答,却成了整本圣经论敬拜的一句金句:「我必要按着价值向你买;我不肯用白得之物作燔祭献给耶和华我的神。」(撒下24:24)他坚持照价付了银子。为什么?因为大卫深知:那不花我一点代价的东西,根本称不上敬拜。真正的敬拜,必然触及我的所有、我的所爱、我的所惜;若我献给神的,是我反正不在乎、丢了也不心疼的,那不是敬拜,只是打发。

这句话直刺今天许多人的信仰。我们常想用「白得之物」来敬拜神:用我们的余暇、余钱、余力——反正是多出来、不影响自己的那一点。我们乐意在不需付代价的地方大方,却在真正触及所爱、所惜之处,悄悄留一手。但神所配得的,从来不是我们的剩余,而是我们最好、最宝贵、最舍不得的那一份。因为祂自己,正是那位没有向我们献「白得之物」的神。

这禾场后来成了所罗门圣殿的殿址——大卫肯付代价的敬拜之地,日后立起了神荣耀的居所。而所有献祭所指向的那一位,更是把祂独生的爱子,那最贵、最舍不得的一位,毫无保留地为我们舍了(罗8:32)。神既不用「白得之物」爱我们,我们又怎能用「白得之物」敬拜祂?今天,神在哪一处等你献上那真正花代价的祭?

默想:我献给神的,是我最好的、真触及所爱所惜的那一份,还是反正多出来、丢了也不心疼的「白得之物」?在时间、金钱、才干上,我是否总在不花代价处大方,在真需付代价处留一手?

应用:今天在一件真会花你代价的事上献给神——一段你舍不得的时间、一笔你会心疼的奉献、一个你不愿放下的主权,拒绝用「白得之物」敷衍祂。

祷告:配得一切的主,大卫说,我不肯用白得之物献给你。我承认,我常想用剩余的时间、精力、金钱来敬拜你,在不花代价处大方,在真宝贵处留一手。谢谢你没有用白得之物爱我,竟舍了你最爱的独生子。求你叫我甘心献上那真花代价的祭,把最好的归给你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In his later years, David committed a sin we don’t easily understand: he numbered the people. Behind this was a heart gradually coming to rely on the size of his army rather than on God. God sent a plague, and David, deeply grieved, saw the overseer at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, and wanted to build an altar there to offer sacrifice. Araunah was a generous man, willing to give the threshing floor, the oxen, and the equipment entirely for free to the king. This seemed like an easy favor to accept — the king wouldn’t need to spend anything, and could still offer the sacrifice.

David’s answer became a golden statement on worship in all of Scripture: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24). He insisted on paying full price in silver. Why? Because David knew deeply: something that costs me nothing simply cannot be called worship. True worship must touch what I have, what I love, what I treasure; if what I offer to God is something I don’t care about anyway, something I wouldn’t feel bad losing, that’s not worship, just going through the motions.

This statement pierces straight through many people’s faith today. We often want to worship God with “what costs nothing” — our spare time, spare money, spare energy — whatever is extra, doesn’t affect us anyway. We’re happy to be generous where no cost is required, but quietly hold back exactly where our love, our treasure, is truly touched. But what God deserves has never been our leftovers, but our best, most precious, most hard-to-give-up portion. Because he himself is the God who did not offer us something that “cost nothing.”

This threshing floor later became the site of Solomon’s temple — the place of costly worship that David was willing to pay for became, in time, the site where God’s glorious dwelling place was raised up. And the one to whom all sacrifices point gave his own beloved Son, the most costly, the hardest to give up, entirely without reserve, for us (Romans 8:32). Since God did not love us with “that which costs nothing,” how can we worship him with “that which costs nothing”? Today, where is God waiting for you to offer that truly costly sacrifice?

Meditation: What I offer to God — is it my best, the portion that truly touches what I love and treasure, or is it “something free,” extra anyway, that I wouldn’t feel bad losing? In time, money, and ability, am I always generous where no cost is required, holding back where real cost is needed?

Application: Today, offer God something that will truly cost you — time you’re reluctant to give, an offering that will pain you, control you’re unwilling to release — refusing to fob him off with “that which costs nothing.”

Prayer: Lord worthy of all, David said, I will not offer to you that which costs me nothing. I confess I often want to worship you with leftover time, energy, money, generous where no cost is required, holding back where it truly matters. Thank you for not loving me with that which cost nothing, but giving up your most beloved only Son. Let me be willing to offer that truly costly sacrifice, giving you my best. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 求智慧的王
entries.title_en: The King Who Asked for Wisdom
entries.verse: 列王纪上三章九节
entries.content:
所罗门继承王位,站在一生的起点上。那一夜,神在梦中向他显现,说了一句几乎能叫任何人心跳加速的话:「你愿我赐你什么?你可以求。」这是一张空白的支票,由全能的神亲自签发。若是我们,会填上什么?长寿?财富?仇敌的性命?名声?所罗门的选择,暴露出他里面真正看重的是什么。

他求的是智慧。他对神说:我不过是幼童,不知道应当怎样出入,求你赐仆人聪明,「可以判断你的民,能辨别是非。」(王上3:9)他没有为自己求,而是为着神交托给他的责任求;他所渴望的,是能按神的心意牧养神的百姓。这个祈求让神喜悦,神不但赐他所求的智慧,连他没有求的富足、尊荣也一并加给了他。这正应验了主的应许:你们要先求神的国和祂的义,这些东西都要加给你们了(太6:33)。

然而,我们要诚实地面对一个事实:这位求智慧的王,日后却在智慧上跌倒了。神所赐的智慧,若离开了那作智慧根基的「敬畏耶和华」(箴9:10),终必被众多的妃嫔、财富和骄傲蚕食殆尽。所罗门晚年的偏离提醒我们:一次美好的祈求、一份属天的恩赐,若不日日靠着敬畏神来持守,也会渐渐失落。恩赐不能替代与神持续的同行。

圣经说,如今有一位「比所罗门更大的」在这里(太12:42)。基督成了我们的智慧(林前1:30)——祂不仅赐下智慧,祂自己就是神的智慧;并且祂那求神旨意的心,始终没有跌倒,以至于死。所以我们求智慧,最终不是求一份能力使自己成功,而是求更深地认识、连于基督。今天,若神对你说「你愿我赐你什么」,你会求什么?这个答案,诚实地照出你的心。

默想:若神今天对我说「你愿我赐你什么」,我第一个想求的是什么?这答案照出我心里真正看重的,是神和祂的国,还是我自己的享受与安全?

应用:今天在祷告中,像所罗门一样,先为神交托给你的责任(家庭、工作、服事)求智慧与辨别力,而非先为自己的顺遂求;并求神赐你敬畏祂的心,好持守祂所赐的一切。

祷告:赐智慧的主,你让所罗门随意求,他却为牧养你的百姓求智慧,你就连他未求的也加给他。求你叫我也先求你的国,为你所交托的责任求辨别是非的智慧。我也从所罗门的跌倒学功课:求你赐我敬畏你的心,叫我日日连于那位比所罗门更大的基督,祂就是我的智慧。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Solomon inherited the throne, standing at the starting point of his life. That night, God appeared to him in a dream and said something that could make almost anyone’s heart race: “Ask what I shall give you.” This was a blank check, personally signed by the Almighty God. If it were us, what would we fill in? Long life? Wealth? The lives of our enemies? Fame? Solomon’s choice exposed what he truly valued within.

He asked for wisdom. He said to God: I am but a little child, I don’t know how to go out or come in; give your servant an understanding mind, “to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9). He did not ask for himself, but for the responsibility God had entrusted to him; what he longed for was to be able to shepherd God’s people according to God’s will. This request pleased God, and God not only gave him the wisdom he asked for, but added the riches and honor he had not asked for as well. This exactly fulfilled the Lord’s promise: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matthew 6:33).

Yet we must honestly face a fact: this king who asked for wisdom later stumbled precisely in wisdom. The wisdom God gave, if it departs from “the fear of the LORD,” the foundation of wisdom itself (Proverbs 9:10), will eventually be eaten away entirely by many wives, wealth, and pride. Solomon’s drift in his later years reminds us: a beautiful request, a heavenly gift, if not sustained daily by fearing God, will also gradually be lost. A gift cannot substitute for continually walking with God.

Scripture says there is now one here who is “greater than Solomon” (Matthew 12:42). Christ has become our wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:30) — he not only gives wisdom, he himself is the wisdom of God; and his heart, seeking God’s will, never once stumbled, even unto death. So when we ask for wisdom, ultimately we’re not asking for an ability to make ourselves succeed, but asking to know and be joined to Christ more deeply. Today, if God said to you, “what shall I give you,” what would you ask for? This answer honestly reflects your heart.

Meditation: If God said to me today, “what shall I give you,” what would be the first thing I’d want to ask for? Does this answer reflect that what I truly value is God and his kingdom, or my own enjoyment and security?

Application: Today in prayer, like Solomon, first ask for wisdom and discernment for the responsibilities God has entrusted to you (family, work, service), rather than first asking for your own success; and ask God to give you a heart that fears him, to keep everything he has given.

Prayer: Lord who gives wisdom, you let Solomon ask for anything, and he asked for wisdom to shepherd your people, so you added even what he did not ask for. Let me too seek your kingdom first, asking for wisdom to discern good and evil in the responsibilities you’ve entrusted to me. I also learn a lesson from Solomon’s fall: give me a heart that fears you, so that I am daily joined to that one greater than Solomon, Christ, who is my wisdom. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 祂看着一切所造的甚好——记念神的创造
entries.title_en: He Saw Everything He Had Made Was Very Good — Remembering God's Creation
entries.content:
祂看着一切所造的甚好——记念神的创造

「 神看着一切所造的都甚好。有晚上,有早晨,是第六日。」(创世记 1:31)

这一周,我们走过大卫的施恩、跌倒、降服与所罗门的求智慧,看尽了人的软弱与神的信实。今天安息日,把目光从人的故事挪开,抬头看那位创造万有、又在第七日安息的神。

祂造了光、海、飞鸟、繁星,又造了你;祂看着一切所造的,说「甚好」。你不是偶然,而是被这位甚好的神精心所造、也被祂看为宝贵。今天,停下你的劳碌,像神在第七日一样安息;在祂所造之物的美好里,重新认识这位又慈爱、又全能的创造主,并单单以祂为乐。

"And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." (Genesis 1:31)
entries.content_en:
He Saw Everything He Had Made Was Very Good — Remembering God’s Creation

"And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day." (Genesis 1:31)

This week, we walked through David’s kindness, his fall, his submission, and Solomon’s request for wisdom, seeing the full range of human weakness and God’s faithfulness. Today, on the Sabbath, turn your gaze away from the human story, and look up at the God who created all things, and rested on the seventh day.

He made light, sea, birds, stars, and he made you; he looked at everything he had made, and said "very good." You are not an accident, but carefully made by this very-good God, and precious in his sight. Today, stop your labor, and rest as God did on the seventh day; in the goodness of what he has made, know afresh this loving, almighty Creator, and delight in him alone.

"And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." (Genesis 1:31)

entries.title: 荣光充满了殿
entries.title_en: The Glory Filled the Temple
entries.verse: 列王纪上八章十一节
entries.content:
所罗门用了七年,倾全国之力,建成了那座辉煌的圣殿。金子、香柏木、精工的雕刻——一切都指向一个目的:为那不能被诸天所容的神,预备一个地上的居所。当约柜被抬进至圣所,祭司退出圣殿的那一刻,神以一件事回应了这一切筹备:「有云充满耶和华的殿……因为耶和华的荣光充满了殿。」(王上8:11)那荣耀何等浓密,以致祭司连站立供职都不能。

请注意这幅图画的重心。整场盛典的高潮,不是那金碧辉煌的建筑,不是所罗门的智慧与财富,而是神自己降临、以祂的荣光充满这殿。人所能献上最好的一切,若没有神的同在,不过是一座空壳。真正叫圣殿成为圣殿的,不是它的华美,而是那位住在其中的神。神从来不是要住进一座漂亮的房子,祂是要与祂的子民同住——这才是整本圣经跳动的心脏。

所罗门自己也在祷告中说出了这殿的吊诡:「神果真住在地上吗?看哪,天和天上的天尚且不足你居住的,何况我所建的这殿呢?」(王上8:27)是的,这殿盛不下神;它只是一个影子,一个应许,指向那更大的实体。及至日子满足,神的荣耀不再借一座石殿彰显,而是「道成了肉身,住在我们中间……我们也见过他的荣光」(约1:14)。基督,就是神荣光真正充满的圣殿;祂被拆毁,三日又建立起来(约2:19-21)。

而奇妙的是,如今这荣耀要住的地方,是你。「岂不知你们的身子就是圣灵的殿吗?」(林前6:19)神今天所寻求的,不是一座我们为祂盖的、精美却空洞的建筑,而是一颗被祂的同在充满的心。你我一切的服事、聚会、奉献,若没有神荣光的充满,也不过是华丽的空壳。今天最当祷告的,不是「主啊,悦纳我为你做的」,而是「主啊,求你的荣光充满这殿——充满我」。

默想:我是否常忙于为神「建造」漂亮的外壳(服事、活动、表现),却忽略了那真正使一切有意义的——神自己的同在?我的心,是被神的荣光充满,还是徒有敬虔的外表?

应用:今天暂停一切「为神做」的忙碌,单单安静在祂面前,求祂的荣光充满你;让你今天的每一件事,都从祂的同在里流出,而非只是空洞的外壳。

祷告:荣耀的主,所罗门倾全力建殿,你却以你的荣光充满它,叫一切华美都退居其后。我承认,我常忙着为你建造外壳,却忘了求你的同在。谢谢你差来那位真圣殿基督,又叫我的身子成为你灵的殿。求你的荣光今天充满我,叫我一切所作的,都因你的同在而有了意义。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Solomon spent seven years, pouring the whole nation’s strength, to build that magnificent temple. Gold, cedar wood, exquisite carvings — all pointed to one purpose: to prepare an earthly dwelling for the God whom the heavens cannot contain. When the ark was carried into the Most Holy Place, and the priests withdrew from the temple, God responded to all this preparation with one thing: “a cloud filled the house of the LORD... for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11). That glory was so dense that the priests could not even stand to minister.

Notice where the weight of this picture falls. The climax of the whole ceremony was not the gold-and-glory architecture, not Solomon’s wisdom and wealth, but God himself descending, filling this house with his glory. Everything people can offer their best, without God’s presence, is nothing but an empty shell. What truly makes a temple a temple is not its splendor, but the God who dwells within it. God has never wanted to move into a beautiful house — he wants to dwell with his people — this is the very heartbeat pulsing through the whole Bible.

Solomon himself, in his prayer, spoke the paradox of this temple: “will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27). Yes, this temple could not contain God; it was only a shadow, a promise, pointing to that greater reality. When the time was fulfilled, God’s glory was no longer displayed through a stone temple, but “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us... we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). Christ is the temple truly filled with God’s glory; he was torn down, and in three days raised up (John 2:19–21).

And wonderfully, the place where this glory now wants to dwell is you. “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Corinthians 6:19). What God seeks today is not a beautiful yet hollow building we build for him, but a heart filled with his presence. All our service, gatherings, and offerings, without the filling of God’s glory, are nothing but beautiful empty shells. The most important prayer today is not, “Lord, accept what I’ve done for you,” but, “Lord, let your glory fill this temple — fill me.”

Meditation: Am I often busy “building” beautiful shells for God (service, activities, performance), while neglecting what truly gives it all meaning — God’s own presence? Is my heart filled with God’s glory, or does it just have an outward form of godliness?

Application: Today, pause all the busyness of “doing for God,” and simply be still before him, asking his glory to fill you; let everything you do today flow from his presence, not just be an empty shell.

Prayer: Glorious Lord, Solomon poured all his strength into building the temple, yet you filled it with your glory, making all its splendor recede into the background. I confess I often busy myself building shells for you, forgetting to ask for your presence. Thank you for sending the true temple, Christ, and making my body a temple of your Spirit. Let your glory fill me today, so that everything I do has meaning because of your presence. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 渐渐偏离的心
entries.title_en: A Heart Gradually Drifting Away
entries.verse: 列王纪上十一章四节
entries.content:
没有人比所罗门有更好的开局。他见过神两次向他显现,建成了荣光充满的圣殿,智慧超过东方一切人,财富尊荣震动列国。若说这世上有谁绝不可能背弃神,那似乎非所罗门莫属。然而圣经却记下一句令人心惊的话:「所罗门年老的时候,他的妃嫔诱惑他的心去随从别神,不效法他父亲大卫诚诚实实地顺服耶和华他的神。」(王上11:4)

他不是一夜之间弃绝了神。请注意那几个字:「诱惑他的心」。这是一个缓慢的、几乎察觉不到的过程。他先是为政治联姻娶了外邦的女子——一点点的妥协,一点点的「情有可原」;每一步都不算太出格,却在他心的深处,一寸一寸地把对神的专一挪走。等他年老,那颗曾经火热的心,已经容得下别神的祭坛了。最可怕的堕落,往往不是悬崖式的一跃,而是斜坡式的滑行。

神真正在意的,不是我们外面的宗教成就有多辉煌,而是我们的心是否「诚诚实实地」向着祂。所罗门什么都有,唯独失了一颗完全的心。这正是主耶稣所警告的不冷不热——嘴唇尊敬神,心却远离神(太15:8);外面样样都在,里面却早已挪移。我们太容易一面维持着敬虔的外壳,一面在心里悄悄地为一个又一个「小小的别神」腾出地方:金钱、成就、某段关系、某种安全感。

今天,不要问「我有没有公然离弃神」,要问「我的心还完全向着祂吗」。有没有什么,正在一点一点地「诱惑我的心」,把我对神的专一挪走?趁着还是「渐渐」,而未成「年老」的定局,回转过来。求神鉴察你的心,把那些悄悄挤进来的别神一一挪去,重新夺回一颗对祂诚诚实实、完完全全的心。因为祂配得的,从来不是我们的一部分,而是我们的全心。

默想:我是否也在维持敬虔的外壳,心却渐渐偏离?有什么东西正一点一点「诱惑我的心」,把我对神的专一悄悄挪走?我的心还「诚诚实实」向着神吗?

应用:今天安静求神鉴察,具体指认一个正在分夺你心的「别神」(某样成就、关系、安逸或习惯),向神认它,并采取一个实际的行动,把心重新完全交还给神。

祷告:鉴察人心的主,所罗门什么都有,却在年老时失了一颗完全的心。我惧怕这样的堕落,因为它不是一跃,而是渐渐的滑行。求你照出我心里那些悄悄挤进来的别神,叫我不满足于敬虔的外壳,而是把整颗心诚诚实实地归还给你。你配得我的全心。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
No one had a better start than Solomon. He saw God appear to him twice, built the temple filled with glory, surpassed everyone in the East in wisdom, and shook the nations with his wealth and honor. If there were anyone in this world who could never possibly forsake God, it would seem to be Solomon. Yet Scripture records this heart-stopping sentence: “For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father” (1 Kings 11:4).

He did not reject God overnight. Notice those words: “turned away his heart.” This was a slow, almost imperceptible process. He first married foreign women for political alliances — a small compromise here, a small “excusable circumstance” there; each step didn’t seem too far out of line, yet deep in his heart, inch by inch, it removed his singular devotion to God. By the time he was old, that once-burning heart had room enough for the altars of other gods. The most terrifying downfall is often not a leap off a cliff, but a slide down a slope.

What God truly cares about is not how brilliant our outward religious achievements are, but whether our heart is “wholly true” toward him. Solomon had everything, yet lost the one thing — a whole heart. This is exactly the lukewarmness the Lord Jesus warned against — lips honoring God, while the heart is far from him (Matthew 15:8); everything intact outwardly, while inwardly it has already shifted. We too easily maintain a shell of godliness on the outside, while quietly making room, in our hearts, for one “small other god” after another: money, achievement, a certain relationship, a certain sense of security.

Today, don’t ask “have I openly forsaken God” — ask “is my heart still wholly toward him.” Is there something that’s, bit by bit, “turning away my heart,” removing my devotion to God? While it’s still “gradual,” and not yet a settled fact of “old age,” turn back. Ask God to search your heart, remove those other gods that have quietly crept in, one by one, and reclaim a heart wholly, completely true to him. Because what he deserves has never been a portion of us, but our whole heart.

Meditation: Am I too maintaining a shell of godliness while my heart gradually drifts away? Is something, bit by bit, “turning away my heart,” quietly removing my devotion to God? Is my heart still “wholly true” toward God?

Application: Today, quietly ask God to search you, concretely name an “other god” currently dividing your heart (some achievement, relationship, comfort, or habit), confess it to God, and take one practical action to hand your heart back to him completely.

Prayer: Lord who searches the heart, Solomon had everything, yet lost a whole heart in his old age. I fear this kind of downfall, because it is not a leap, but a gradual slide. Shine light on the other gods that have quietly crept into my heart; let me not be satisfied with a shell of godliness, but hand over my whole heart wholly to you. You deserve my entire heart. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 自己造的宗教
entries.title_en: A Religion of One's Own Making
entries.verse: 列王纪上十二章廿八节
entries.content:
所罗门死后,国就分裂了。北国以色列的第一个王耶罗波安,一坐上王位就面临一个难题:百姓每年仍要上耶路撒冷(南国)的圣殿守节献祭,他怕人心因此归回大卫家。于是他做了一个「聪明」的决定:铸造两个金牛犊,一个安在伯特利,一个安在但,对百姓说:「以色列人哪,……这就是领你们出埃及地的神。」(王上12:28)他又擅立祭司、擅定节期,搭建了一整套方便、就近、不必长途跋涉的宗教。

耶罗波安并没有公开叫百姓拜别的神,他声称这仍是敬拜那领他们出埃及的耶和华——只不过换了个方式、换了个地点、换了个更合人意的形式。这正是偶像最狡猾之处:它常常不是赤裸裸地否认真神,而是按着人的方便与喜好,重新塑造一个「更好用」的神。真正的问题不在于他是否虔诚,而在于:他所敬拜的,是照神所启示的样式,还是照自己所设计的样式?圣经反复用一句话为北国盖棺:他们行「耶罗波安使以色列人陷在罪里」的那事。

这警告直指今天的我们。我们也很容易造一个「自己的神」——一个专门肯定我、从不叫我为难、总是顺着我心意的神;一套挑我喜欢的信、避我不愿听的道、把敬拜改造成让我舒服的宗教。这种「量身定做」的信仰看似敬虔,实则是把神拉下宝座,让我自己坐上去。凡不是照着神在圣经中所启示的祂去敬拜,无论多热心、多方便,本质上都是在拜一个金牛犊。

真正的敬拜,是俯伏在神所是的那位面前,照祂所启示的去认识祂、顺服祂——哪怕那样不方便、不顺心、要付代价。我们不能重造神的形象来迁就自己;我们乃是被造,要被祂重塑成祂儿子的形象。今天,求神拆毁你心里一切「自己造的神」,叫你回到那位又真又活、按祂自己所是被敬拜的神面前。

默想:我心里那位神,是圣经所启示的真神,还是一个被我按喜好改造过、专门肯定我、从不叫我为难的「金牛犊」?我在信仰上是否总在挑方便、拣顺心的那部分?

应用:今天诚实检视:有没有一处真理是我一直回避、因为它叫我不舒服?选择在那一处顺服圣经所启示的神,而非我为自己量身定做的神。

祷告:又真又活的主,耶罗波安为着方便,造了金牛犊,还声称那就是领他们出埃及的神。我承认,我也常想造一个顺我心意、从不叫我为难的神。求你拆毁我心里一切自造的偶像,叫我照你在圣经中所启示的真实样式来认识你、敬拜你、顺服你,哪怕要付代价。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
After Solomon’s death, the kingdom split. Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel, faced a dilemma the moment he took the throne: the people still had to go up to the temple in Jerusalem (the southern kingdom) every year to keep the feasts and offer sacrifices, and he feared this would draw people’s hearts back to the house of David. So he made a “clever” decision: he cast two golden calves, setting one in Bethel and one in Dan, telling the people: “Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28). He also appointed his own priests and set his own feast days, building an entire religious system that was convenient, nearby, and required no long journey.

Jeroboam did not openly tell the people to worship a different god — he claimed this was still worship of the very LORD who had brought them out of Egypt — only in a different way, a different place, a more convenient form. This is precisely idolatry’s cunning: it often doesn’t openly deny the true God, but instead, according to human convenience and preference, reshapes a “more usable” god. The real question is not whether he was devout, but: was what he worshiped shaped according to what God had revealed, or according to what he himself designed? Scripture repeatedly seals the northern kingdom’s fate with one phrase: they walked in “the sin of Jeroboam, which he made Israel sin.”

This warning points directly at us today. We too easily make a “god of our own” — a god who exists purely to affirm me, who never makes things hard for me, who always goes along with my will; a faith of picking what we like to believe, avoiding what we don’t want to hear, remaking worship into a religion that makes us comfortable. This kind of “custom-tailored” faith looks devout, but in essence pulls God down from the throne, and puts myself on it instead. Whatever is not worshiped according to how God has revealed himself in Scripture, however zealous, however convenient, is essentially worshiping a golden calf.

True worship is bowing down before who God actually is, knowing him and obeying him according to how he has revealed himself — even when that’s inconvenient, unwelcome, and costly. We cannot remake God’s image to accommodate ourselves; we are the ones made, to be reshaped by him into the image of his Son. Today, ask God to tear down every “self-made god” in your heart, and let you return before the true and living God, worshiped according to who he himself actually is.

Meditation: Is the god in my heart the true God revealed in Scripture, or a “golden calf” I’ve reshaped to my own preference, one that only affirms me, never makes things hard for me? Do I always pick the convenient, agreeable parts of the faith?

Application: Today, honestly examine: is there a truth I’ve been avoiding because it makes me uncomfortable? Choose to obey the God revealed in Scripture in that one place, rather than the god custom-tailored to myself.

Prayer: True and living Lord, Jeroboam, for convenience, made golden calves, and even claimed that was the god who brought them out of Egypt. I confess I too often want to make a god who goes along with my will, who never makes things hard for me. Tear down every self-made idol in my heart, and let me know you, worship you, and obey you according to the true way you have revealed yourself in Scripture, even at a cost. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
