entries.title: 火后那微小的声音
entries.title_en: The Still Small Voice After the Fire
entries.verse: 列王纪上十九章十二节
entries.content:
就在迦密山上,以利亚刚刚经历了一生最辉煌的属灵高峰:他独自面对四百五十个巴力先知,向天求告,耶和华就降下火来,烧尽了燔祭。全民俯伏,高呼「耶和华是神」。你会以为,这样一场大胜之后,以利亚必定信心满满、勇往直前。谁知仅仅一个耶洗别的恐吓,就把他打垮了。他逃进旷野,坐在罗腾树下求死:「耶和华啊,罢了!求你取我的性命。」

这真实得叫人心疼。原来属灵的高峰之后,常常紧跟着深谷;越是刚烈、越是为神大发热心的人,越容易在事奉的燃烧后陷入枯干与绝望。以利亚不是不属灵,他是累垮了、也孤单透了(他一再说「只剩下我一个人」)。这提醒我们:属灵的低潮,未必是犯罪的结果,有时只是一个疲惫的仆人,燃尽了自己。

而神在何烈山上待祂这位仆人的方式,充满了温柔。神没有责备他的软弱,反倒先让他睡觉、吃饭——照顾他身体的需要。然后,烈风、地震、大火接连而过,「耶和华却不在其中」;直到最后,来了「微小的声音」(王上19:12)。那位曾在迦密山降下烈火的神,如今却用一个轻柔的声音,来医治一颗破碎枯干的心。神知道,有时我们需要的不是又一场烈火,而是祂贴近的、温柔的低语。

这正是福音里那位神的样式。祂正如经上所说,「压伤的芦苇,他不折断;将残的灯火,他不吹灭」(赛42:3);那位在客西马尼被压伤、又亲自体恤我们软弱的大祭司,最知道如何用祂微小而慈爱的声音,俯就一个精疲力竭的门徒。今天,你若正坐在自己的罗腾树下——疲惫、孤单、甚至想放弃,神未必立刻给你又一场轰轰烈烈的复兴;祂或许正俯身向你,用那微小的声音说:够了,孩子,先歇一歇,我还在这里。

默想:我是否也曾在属灵高峰之后跌入低谷?我在疲惫枯干时,是苛责自己不够属灵,还是肯让神像待以利亚一样温柔地照顾我?我能听见祂那「微小的声音」吗?

应用:如果你正枯干疲惫,今天不急着「再刚强起来」,而是像以利亚一样,先照顾好身体的歇息与饮食,再安静下来,专心聆听神微小而温柔的声音。

祷告:温柔的主,以利亚在大胜之后跌进求死的深谷,你却没有责备他,反而先给他歇息与饮食,又用微小的声音医治他。我承认,我也曾在事奉中燃尽、在高峰后枯干。谢谢你不折断压伤的芦苇。求你今天用你那微小而慈爱的声音贴近我,让我在你里面重新得力。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
On Mount Carmel, Elijah had just experienced the most glorious spiritual peak of his life: he alone faced four hundred fifty prophets of Baal, cried out to heaven, and the LORD sent down fire, consuming the burnt offering. The whole nation fell facedown, crying out, “The LORD, he is God.” You would think, after such a great victory, Elijah would surely be full of faith, pressing boldly forward. Yet a single threat from Jezebel was enough to crush him. He fled into the wilderness, sat under a broom tree, and asked to die: “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life.”

This is real enough to break your heart. It turns out that a spiritual peak is often closely followed by a deep valley; the more fierce, the more zealous for God a person is, the more easily they fall into dryness and despair after the fire of ministry burns out. Elijah wasn’t lacking in spirituality — he was exhausted, and utterly alone (he keeps saying, “I, even I only, am left”). This reminds us: a spiritual low is not necessarily the result of sin; sometimes it’s simply a weary servant who has burned himself out.

And the way God treated his servant on Mount Horeb is full of tenderness. God did not rebuke his weakness — instead he first let him sleep, and eat — tending to his body’s needs. Then, a great wind, an earthquake, a fire passed by in succession, “but the LORD was not in” them; until finally came “a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:12). The God who once sent down fire on Carmel now uses a gentle voice to heal a broken, dried-out heart. God knows that sometimes what we need is not another blazing fire, but his close, tender whisper.

This is exactly the pattern of the God in the gospel. As Scripture says, “a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench” (Isaiah 42:3); the High Priest who was crushed at Gethsemane, and who personally sympathizes with our weakness, knows best how to stoop down to an exhausted disciple with his small, loving voice. Today, if you’re sitting under your own broom tree — tired, alone, even wanting to give up — God may not immediately give you another blazing revival; he may be bending down toward you, saying in that small voice: enough, child, rest a while first, I am still here.

Meditation: Have I too fallen into a valley after a spiritual peak? When I’m exhausted and dry, do I harshly blame myself for not being spiritual enough, or am I willing to let God tenderly care for me as he did Elijah? Can I hear his “small voice”?

Application: If you’re dry and exhausted, don’t rush today to “be strong again” — instead, like Elijah, first tend to your body’s rest and food, then be still, and listen carefully for God’s small, tender voice.

Prayer: Tender Lord, Elijah, after a great victory, fell into a valley of wanting to die, yet you did not rebuke him — instead you first gave him rest and food, and healed him with a small voice. I confess I too have burned out in ministry, and grown dry after a peak. Thank you for not breaking the bruised reed. Draw near to me today with your small, loving voice, and let me be renewed in strength in you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title_en: Whatever the LORD Says, That I Will Speak
entries.verse: 列王纪上廿二章十四节
entries.content:
亚哈王想去攻取基列的拉末,便邀约沙法同去。约沙法要先求问耶和华。亚哈召来了四百个先知,他们异口同声:上去吧,主必将那城交在王手里!四百张嘴,一个声音,全是王爱听的话。可约沙法心里不安,问:这里不是还有一位耶和华的先知吗?亚哈答:还有一个米该雅,「只是我恨他;因为他指着我所说的预言,不说吉语,单说凶言。」

被召来之前,有人劝米该雅:先知们都说吉言,你也随和些吧,说些王爱听的。米该雅的回答,是每一个属神之人当有的骨气:「我指着永生的耶和华起誓,耶和华对我说什么,我就说什么。」(王上22:14)在四百比一的悬殊里,在王明摆着的厌恶里,在「随和一点就皆大欢喜」的诱惑里,他单单忠于一件事:神说什么,他就说什么——不加,不减,不为讨好谁而修饰。

这需要何等的信心。米该雅之所以能不惧四百人的声势、不顾王的脸色,是因为他深知:决定成败的,不是有多少人站在我这边,也不是掌权者喜不喜欢,而是耶和华的话必定成就。四百个先知的顺耳预言,一句也没有应验;米该雅所传那不受欢迎的真话,却字字成真——亚哈果然死在那场战役中。神的话,从不因传的人少、听的人厌而失去分毫效力。

我们活在一个「四百先知」的时代:随处都是迎合人心、只说吉语的声音,而忠于神的话往往不受欢迎、要付代价。求神赐我们米该雅的胆量——不是为了标新立异,而是因着敬畏那位说话的神,宁可孤单地站在真理这边,也不肯为了合群而稀释神的话。那位为真理作了美好见证、甚至为此舍命的基督(约18:37;提前6:13),是我们最终的榜样与力量。今天,在你被期待「随和一点」的地方,你能否也说:耶和华说什么,我就说什么?

默想:当忠于神的话会让我不受欢迎、要付代价时,我是选择「随和一点」去迎合众人,还是像米该雅一样单单忠于神所说的?我更在意人的脸色,还是神的话?

应用:指认一处你一直因怕不受欢迎而不敢照神的话去说、去行的地方,今天求神给你米该雅的胆量,在那里忠于真理,哪怕孤单。

祷告:说话的主,四百先知都说王爱听的话,唯有米该雅说「耶和华对我说什么,我就说什么」。我承认,我常怕不受欢迎,就把你的话稀释、修饰,去迎合人。求你赐我敬畏你、忠于你话语的胆量,叫我宁可孤单地站在真理这边。谢谢基督为真理作了美好的见证,作我的榜样与力量。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
King Ahab wanted to attack Ramoth-gilead, and invited Jehoshaphat to join him. Jehoshaphat wanted to inquire of the LORD first. Ahab summoned four hundred prophets, and they said with one voice: go up, the Lord will give it into the king’s hand! Four hundred mouths, one voice, all saying what the king wanted to hear. But Jehoshaphat felt uneasy, and asked: is there not still a prophet of the LORD here? Ahab answered: there is still one, Micaiah, “but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil.”

Before he was summoned, someone advised Micaiah: the prophets are all speaking favorably, you should go along too, and say what the king wants to hear. Micaiah’s answer is the backbone every person of God should have: “As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak” (1 Kings 22:14). Facing overwhelming odds of four hundred to one, facing the king’s obvious displeasure, facing the temptation of “just go along and everyone’s happy” — he was faithful to one thing alone: whatever God said, that he would speak — no adding, no subtracting, no polishing to please anyone.

What faith this required. Micaiah was able to not fear the sheer number of four hundred, not care about the king’s expression, because he knew deeply: what determines outcomes is not how many people stand on my side, nor whether those in power are pleased, but that the LORD’s word will surely come to pass. The four hundred prophets’ pleasant-sounding prophecy, not one word of it came true; Micaiah’s unwelcome truth came true word for word — Ahab indeed died in that battle. God’s word never loses one bit of its power because few proclaim it or many resent hearing it.

We live in an age of “four hundred prophets”: everywhere are voices that cater to people’s hearts, saying only pleasant things, while faithfulness to God’s word is often unwelcome, and costly. Ask God to give us Micaiah’s courage — not for the sake of being contrarian, but out of reverence for the God who speaks, willing to stand alone on the side of truth rather than dilute God’s word to fit in. Christ, who bore good witness to the truth, even laying down his life for it (John 18:37; 1 Timothy 6:13), is our ultimate example and strength. Today, in the place where you’re expected to “go along a bit,” can you too say: whatever the LORD says, that I will speak?

Meditation: When faithfulness to God’s word would make me unwelcome, cost me something, do I choose to “go along a bit” to please the crowd, or, like Micaiah, remain faithful solely to what God has said? Do I care more about people’s expressions, or God’s word?

Application: Name a place where you’ve been afraid to speak or act according to God’s word because you feared being unwelcome; today ask God for Micaiah’s courage, to be faithful to the truth there, even if alone.

Prayer: Lord who speaks, four hundred prophets all said what the king wanted to hear, but Micaiah alone said, “whatever the LORD says to me, that I will speak.” I confess I often fear being unwelcome, and so dilute and polish your word to please people. Give me courage to fear you and be faithful to your word, so that I would rather stand alone on the side of truth. Thank you that Christ bore good witness to the truth, as my example and strength. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 加倍的灵,与不止息的工
entries.title_en: A Double Portion of the Spirit, and a Work That Never Ceases
entries.verse: 列王纪下二章九节
entries.content:
以利亚要被接升天了。这位曾在迦密山呼风唤火的先知,即将退场。跟随他多年的门徒以利沙,一路紧紧相随,不肯离开。当以利亚问他:我未曾离开你以先,你要我为你做什么?以利沙的回答,道出了他心底最深的渴慕:「愿感动你的灵加倍地感动我。」(王下2:9)他所求的,不是以利亚的名声、地位或那件外袍本身,而是那使以利亚成为以利亚的——神的灵。

这是何等纯正的属灵胃口。人天然所贪求的,往往是外面的恩赐、能力、被人看重的地位;以利沙却越过这一切,单单渴慕那位赐能力的圣灵自己。他深知,一件从天落下的外袍,若没有那感动以利亚的灵,不过是一块布。属灵的传承,从来不是把职分、名号交接给下一个人,而是同一位神的灵,在一代又一代甘心倒空、切慕祂的器皿身上,继续作工。

以利亚被接去后,以利沙拾起那从天落下的外袍,走到约旦河边,打水,水就左右分开——正如当年以利亚所行的。神的工作,没有因那位伟大先知的离去而停顿一刻。这给我们极大的安慰与提醒:神的国度从不依赖某一个属灵伟人;那使工作有能力的,始终是神的灵,而非任何一个人。以利亚会过去,摩西会过去,你所敬佩的每一位属灵前辈都会过去,唯有神的灵长存,祂的工作永不止息。

所以今天真正当求的,不是「求神使我像某位属灵伟人那样有能力、有名声」,而是像以利沙一样,单单切慕神的灵充满、加倍地感动我。恩赐会朽坏,地位会更替,唯有被圣灵充满、单单倚靠祂的生命,才结出永存的果子。你今天心底最深的渴慕,是那件「外袍」,还是那感动人的「灵」?

默想:我心底最深的渴慕,是外面的恩赐、能力与被人看重的地位(那件「外袍」),还是那位赐下这一切的圣灵自己?我是否以为神的工作要靠某个属灵伟人,而非神的灵?

应用:今天像以利沙一样,把你的祷告从「求神使我有能力、被看重」调整为「求神的灵加倍地充满我、感动我」;并为着神的工作代祷,深信它不倚靠人,只倚靠神的灵。

祷告:赐圣灵的主,以利沙越过外袍、名声与地位,单单求那感动以利亚的灵加倍地感动他。我承认,我常贪求外面的恩赐与被看重,却忽略了那位赐下一切的圣灵自己。求你洁净我的渴慕,叫我单单切慕你的灵充满我;也叫我安息在一个真理里——你的工作永不倚靠人,只倚靠你的灵。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Elijah was about to be taken up to heaven. This prophet who had once called down fire on Mount Carmel was about to exit the stage. Elisha, who had followed him closely for years as a disciple, refused to leave his side. When Elijah asked him: before I am taken from you, what shall I do for you? Elisha’s answer revealed the deepest longing of his heart: “Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me” (2 Kings 2:9). What he asked for was not Elijah’s fame, status, or the outer cloak itself, but the very thing that made Elijah Elijah — the Spirit of God.

What a pure spiritual appetite this was. What people naturally covet is often the outward gift, ability, or the status of being esteemed by others; Elisha, however, passed beyond all this, longing solely for the very Spirit who gives power. He knew deeply: a cloak fallen from heaven, without the Spirit that moved Elijah, is nothing but a piece of cloth. Spiritual succession has never been handing off an office or title to the next person, but the same Spirit of God continuing to work, generation after generation, in vessels willing to be emptied and long for him.

After Elijah was taken up, Elisha picked up the cloak that had fallen from heaven, went to the Jordan, struck the water, and it parted to the left and right — just as Elijah had once done. God’s work did not stop for even a moment because that great prophet had left. This gives us enormous comfort and reminder: God’s kingdom has never depended on any one spiritual giant; what gives the work power has always been God’s Spirit, not any person. Elijah would pass, Moses would pass, every spiritual predecessor you admire will pass, but God’s Spirit alone remains forever, his work never ceasing.

So what we should truly ask for today is not, “ask God to make me powerful and famous like some spiritual giant,” but, like Elisha, to long solely for the Spirit’s filling, doubling upon me. Gifts decay, positions change hands, but only a life filled with the Spirit, relying on him alone, bears fruit that lasts forever. What is the deepest longing of your heart today — that “cloak,” or that moving “Spirit”?

Meditation: Is the deepest longing of my heart the outward gift, ability, and the status of being esteemed by others (that “cloak”), or the Holy Spirit who gives all of this? Do I think God’s work depends on some spiritual giant, rather than God’s Spirit?

Application: Today, like Elisha, adjust your prayer from “ask God to make me powerful and esteemed” to “ask God’s Spirit to fill me and move me, doubly”; and intercede for God’s work, deeply believing it depends not on people, but solely on God’s Spirit.

Prayer: Lord who gives the Holy Spirit, Elisha passed beyond the cloak, fame, and status, asking solely for a double portion of the spirit that moved Elijah. I confess I often covet outward gifts and esteem, while overlooking the Holy Spirit himself who gives all of it. Cleanse my longing, let me long solely for your Spirit to fill me; and let me rest in this truth: your work never depends on people, only on your Spirit. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 基督释放了我们——在主里得自由
entries.title_en: Christ Has Set Us Free — Freedom in the Lord
entries.content:
基督释放了我们——在主里得自由

「基督释放了我们,叫我们得以自由。所以要站立得稳,不要再被奴仆的轭挟制。」(加拉太书 5:1)

这一周,我们看见所罗门被别神诱惑了心、耶罗波安造了自己的神、亚哈被四百句顺耳的话捆绑。人心何等容易被各样的偶像与惧怕辖制,失去真自由。

今天安息日,记念一件事:你的自由,不是靠自己挣扎着摆脱这一切,而是基督已经在十字架上把你释放了。你不再需要靠别人的认可、靠成就、靠掌控来证明自己。在祂里面,你已经自由了。安息在这自由里,站立得稳,不要再回头戴上那已被除去的轭。

"For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore." (Galatians 5:1)
entries.content_en:
Christ Has Set Us Free — Freedom in the Lord

"For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery." (Galatians 5:1)

This week, we saw Solomon’s heart turned away by other gods, Jeroboam make a god of his own, and Ahab bound by four hundred pleasant-sounding words. How easily the human heart is enslaved by all kinds of idols and fears, losing true freedom.

Today, on the Sabbath, remember this: your freedom is not something you struggle to break free into on your own, but something Christ has already accomplished for you on the cross. You no longer need others’ approval, achievement, or control to prove yourself. In him, you are already free. Rest in this freedom, stand firm, and never turn back to put on the yoke that has already been removed.

"For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore." (Galatians 5:1)

entries.title: 在约旦河里放下自己
entries.title_en: Laying Yourself Down in the Jordan
entries.verse: 列王纪下五章十四节
entries.content:
乃缦是亚兰王的元帅,战功赫赫,位高权重,唯一的缺憾是他患了大麻风。他辗转听说以色列有一位先知能医治他,便带着重礼、带着王的荐书、带着大人物的排场,风尘仆仆地来到以利沙门前。他心里大概早已想好了医治的剧本:先知总该出来,恭恭敬敬地迎接他这位贵客,向他挥手祷告,治好他的病。

然而以利沙连门都没出,只打发一个仆人传话:去约旦河里沐浴七回,你的肉就必复原。乃缦大怒。他觉得受了羞辱:这算什么?我家乡的河不比这浑浊的约旦河强吗?他忿忿地要走。是他的仆人斗胆劝他:主人,先知若吩咐你做一件难事,你尚且要做;何况只是「沐浴就得洁净」呢?这句话点醒了他——真正拦阻他得医治的,不是那河太小,而是他的自尊太大。

最后,「乃缦下去,照着神人的话,在约旦河里沐浴七回;他的肉复原,好像小孩子的肉,他就洁净了。」(王下5:14)他必须先放下元帅的架子,像个无助的孩子一样,照着那看似「太简单、太失身份」的吩咐去做,才得着洁净。这正是福音叫每一个人为难的地方:神所开的救恩之路,不容我们带着功劳、身份和自我的排场进来;它只要求我们承认自己无力自救,像孩子一样,空手来接受。

我们的骄傲总在说:救恩不该这么简单,总得让我做点什么、贡献点什么、保留点尊严吧?但福音偏偏是:你什么都不能做,只能信靠基督为你成就的一切。那使乃缦洁净的,不是约旦河的水,而是他肯谦卑顺服的信心;那洗净我们的,也不是我们的功德,而是基督的宝血。今天,你是否还站在约旦河边,因着放不下的自尊,迟迟不肯下到那看似「太卑微」的恩典里?

默想:我是否也像乃缦,想按自己设想的、体面的方式得着神的恩?有什么「自尊」正拦阻我像孩子一样,空手谦卑地领受福音?

应用:今天在一件事上放下你的「元帅架子」,照着神话语中那看似简单、却触及你自尊的吩咐单纯地顺服;并操练像孩子一样,不靠功劳、只靠信心来到神面前。

祷告:施恩的主,乃缦必须放下元帅的尊严,像孩子一样下到约旦河,才得洁净。我承认,我的骄傲常嫌你的恩典太简单、太不给我留面子。求你除去我一切的自尊与排场,叫我空着手、像孩子一样,单单信靠基督的宝血得洁净。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Naaman was the commander of the army of the king of Aram, decorated with battle honors, high in rank and power, with only one flaw — he had leprosy. He heard, through a roundabout way, that there was a prophet in Israel who could heal him, and so, bringing rich gifts, a letter from the king, and the pomp of a great man, he traveled a long way to Elisha’s door. In his heart he had probably already scripted how the healing would go: the prophet would surely come out, respectfully receive this distinguished guest, wave his hand and pray over him, and heal his disease.

Yet Elisha didn’t even come to the door, only sending a servant with the message: go wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored. Naaman was furious. He felt insulted: what is this? Aren’t the rivers of my homeland better than this muddy Jordan? He turned to leave in a rage. It was his servants who dared to advise him: master, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it? How much more when he simply says, “Wash, and be clean”? This word woke him up — what was truly keeping him from healing was not that the river was too small, but that his pride was too great.

In the end, “he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean” (2 Kings 5:14). He had to first lay down his commander’s airs, and, like a helpless child, do what seemed “too simple, too undignified” — only then was he made clean. This is exactly where the gospel makes everyone uncomfortable: the road of salvation God has opened does not allow us to enter carrying our merit, status, and self-importance; it requires only that we admit we cannot save ourselves, and come, like a child, empty-handed, to receive.

Our pride keeps saying: salvation shouldn’t be this simple, surely I should do something, contribute something, retain some dignity? But the gospel insists: you can do nothing, you can only trust in everything Christ has accomplished for you. What cleansed Naaman was not the water of the Jordan, but his willingness to humbly obey in faith; what cleanses us is not our merit, but Christ’s precious blood. Today, are you still standing at the edge of the Jordan, unable, because of pride you can’t let go of, to step down into grace that seems “too humble”?

Meditation: Am I too, like Naaman, wanting to receive God’s grace in a way I’ve designed myself, a dignified way? What “pride” is keeping me from receiving the gospel humbly, empty-handed, like a child?

Application: Today, in one matter, lay down your “commander’s airs,” and simply obey a command in God’s word that seems simple, yet touches your pride; and practice coming before God like a child, relying not on merit, but on faith alone.

Prayer: Gracious Lord, Naaman had to lay down his commander’s dignity and go down to the Jordan like a child, before he was made clean. I confess my pride often complains that your grace is too simple, doesn’t let me save face. Remove all my pride and pretense, and let me, empty-handed, like a child, rely solely on Christ’s precious blood to be made clean. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 尽心,还是尽了一半
entries.title_en: Wholehearted, or Only Half
entries.verse: 列王纪下十章卅一节
entries.content:
耶户是神兴起来审判亚哈全家的器皿。他奉命行事,雷厉风行:击杀了背叛的约兰,处置了恶贯满盈的耶洗别,除灭了亚哈的众子,又铲平了拜巴力的党羽。单看这些,耶户简直是热心事奉神的典范;神也的确称许他行了在祂眼中看为正的事,应许他的子孙必坐以色列的国位到四代。然而,在这一片轰轰烈烈的「热心」背后,圣经却下了一句冷静而扎心的评语。

「只是耶户不尽心遵守耶和华以色列神的律法,不离开耶罗波安使以色列人陷在罪里的那罪。」(王下10:31)原来耶户除掉了巴力,却留下了金牛犊;他清除了别人的偶像,却不肯挪去自己的那一个。他的「热心」是有选择性的——凡是符合他政治利益、能巩固他王位的,他就大发热心去做;凡是触及他自己利益、要他真正付代价的,他就绕道而行。他事奉的,与其说是神,不如说是借着「事奉神」来成就自己。

这是何等真实、又何等危险的光景。我们也可能在许多事上大发热心,除掉一堆「看得见」的罪,活跃于各样属灵的争战与服事,却始终留着某一个自己心爱的偶像不肯对付。我们乐意在不需触及自己的地方为神火热,却在那真正要我们舍己的一处,悄悄地留一手。神所要的,从来不是选择性的、算计过的热心,而是一颗「尽心」——完完全全、毫无保留地归向祂的心。

「尽心」二字,是耶户所缺、也是我们所难的。唯有那位「尽心、尽性、尽意、尽力」爱父神,又存心顺服以至于死的基督(可12:30;腓2:8),成全了这全然的爱与顺服,并把它算作我们的,又借着祂的灵,把这样一颗完全的心,一点一点地作在我们里面。今天,求神照出你一直留着不肯对付的那个「金牛犊」,不再满足于选择性的热心,而是求祂得着你尽心的爱。

默想:我的热心是否是选择性的——在不触及自己的地方大发热心,却留着某一个心爱的偶像不肯对付?我是「尽心」归向神,还是只尽了对自己有利的那一半?

应用:今天求神指出你一直绕道、不肯挪去的那个「金牛犊」(某个你舍不得的罪或偶像),不再用别处的热心遮盖它,而是具体地在那一处向神降服。

祷告:鉴察人心的主,耶户除掉了巴力,却留下了金牛犊;他的热心是算计过的,不肯尽心。我承认,我也常在安全的地方火热,却留着一个心爱的偶像不肯对付。谢谢基督尽心爱你、顺服至死,替我成全了这全然的爱。求你的灵在我里面作成一颗尽心归向你的心。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Jehu was the vessel God raised up to judge the entire house of Ahab. He carried out his orders swiftly and decisively: he struck down the rebel Joram, dealt with the utterly wicked Jezebel, destroyed all of Ahab’s sons, and wiped out the followers of Baal worship. Looking at this alone, Jehu seems like a model of zealous service to God; God indeed commended him for doing what was right in his eyes, promising his descendants would sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. Yet, behind this blazing “zeal,” Scripture delivers a calm yet piercing verdict.

“But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin” (2 Kings 10:31). It turns out Jehu removed Baal, but left the golden calves; he cleared away others’ idols, but refused to remove his own. His “zeal” was selective — whatever aligned with his political interests, whatever could consolidate his throne, he threw himself into with zeal; whatever touched his own interests, whatever required him to truly pay a cost, he went around. What he served was, more accurately, himself, using “serving God” as the means.

How real, and how dangerous, this condition is. We too may be zealous in many things, removing a pile of “visible” sins, active in all kinds of spiritual battles and service, yet always keep one beloved idol of our own that we refuse to deal with. We’re happy to burn with zeal for God where it doesn’t touch ourselves, but quietly hold back exactly where we’re truly called to deny ourselves. What God wants has never been selective, calculated zeal, but a heart that is “wholehearted” — turning to him completely, without reservation.

“Wholehearted” is exactly what Jehu lacked, and what is hard for us too. Only Christ, who loved the Father “with all his heart, with all his soul, with all his mind, with all his strength,” and who was obedient even unto death (Mark 12:30; Philippians 2:8), fulfilled this complete love and obedience, counted it as ours, and, through his Spirit, is working such a whole heart into us, bit by bit. Today, ask God to shine light on the “golden calf” you’ve always left alone, refusing to deal with, no longer satisfied with selective zeal, but let him have your wholehearted love.

Meditation: Is my zeal selective — burning with zeal where it doesn’t touch myself, while leaving a beloved idol untouched? Am I turning to God “wholeheartedly,” or only fulfilling the half that benefits me?

Application: Today, ask God to point out the “golden calf” you’ve always gone around, refused to remove (some sin or idol you’re reluctant to give up), and no longer cover it with zeal elsewhere, but concretely submit to God in that one place.

Prayer: Lord who searches the heart, Jehu removed Baal, but left the golden calves; his zeal was calculated, not wholehearted. I confess I too am often zealous in safe places, while leaving a beloved idol untouched. Thank you, Christ loved you wholeheartedly and obeyed to the point of death, fulfilling this complete love in my place. Let your Spirit work in me a heart wholly turned to you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 硬着颈项的代价
entries.title_en: The Cost of a Stiff Neck
entries.verse: 列王纪下十七章十四节
entries.content:
北国以色列的历史,走到了尽头。亚述大军攻陷撒玛利亚,把以色列人掳到远方,北国就此灭亡,再未复国。圣经在记完这段亡国史后,罕见地停下来,用整整一章(王下十七章)郑重地追问一个问题:这一切,究竟是为什么?答案不在于亚述有多强,而在于以色列自己。

神并非没有警告。经文说,耶和华「借众先知、先见劝戒以色列人和犹大人」,一再差遣祂的仆人,苦口婆心地呼唤他们回转,离开恶行,谨守诫命。神何等有耐心,何等不愿他们灭亡!然而回应祂长久呼唤的,却是一句沉重的话:「他们却不听从,竟硬着颈项,效法他们列祖,不信服耶和华他们的神。」(王下17:14)亡国的根,不是一次突发的大罪,而是数百年如一日地、硬着颈项地拒绝听神的话。

「硬着颈项」是圣经形容悖逆最传神的一个词——像一头不肯被牵引的牛,神往东,它偏往西,任你怎样呼唤,它就是不回头。北国的悲剧提醒我们:神的审判从不是仓促的,它总是在长久的忍耐、一再的警告之后,才临到那始终不肯听的人。神的恒久忍耐,是要领人悔改(罗2:4);但人若把这忍耐误当作纵容,一次次地硬心,那忍耐的尽头,终必是公义的审判。

这段亡国史是一面镜子,照出我们里面同样的危险。神今天或许也借着祂的话、祂的灵、周围的提醒,一再向你说着同一件事;问题是,你是软化下来听从,还是又一次硬着颈项、绕了过去?「你们今日若听他的话,就不可硬着心。」(来3:15)不要试探神的忍耐,趁着祂还在呼唤、还在等候,低下你那刚硬的颈项,回到祂面前。祂的忍耐是恩典,不是可以无限透支的许可。

默想:神是否一再借着祂的话与周围的提醒,向我说着同一件事,而我一次次硬着颈项绕开?我是否把神的忍耐误当成了纵容,以为可以一直拖下去?

应用:指认一件神已长久提醒、你却始终硬心不听的事,今天不再拖延、不再绕道,趁祂还在呼唤,就软化下来顺服祂。

祷告:满有忍耐的主,以色列硬着颈项数百年,不听你借众先知的劝戒,终至亡国。我战兢地看见,你的忍耐不是可以无限透支的。求你软化我刚硬的颈项,凡你一再向我说的,我今天就听从,不再把你的恒久忍耐误当作纵容。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The history of the northern kingdom of Israel came to its end. The Assyrian army conquered Samaria, and carried the Israelites away to a distant land; the northern kingdom fell, never to be restored. After recording this history of national ruin, Scripture rarely pauses to solemnly ask, in an entire chapter (2 Kings 17), one question: why did all this happen? The answer lies not in how strong Assyria was, but in Israel itself.

God had not failed to warn them. The text says the LORD “warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer,” sending his servants again and again, pleading earnestly with them to turn back, to leave their evil ways, and keep his commandments. How patient God was, how unwilling he was for them to perish! Yet the response to his long-standing call is this heavy sentence: “they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God” (2 Kings 17:14). The root of the nation’s fall was not one sudden great sin, but centuries of, day after day, stubbornly refusing to hear God’s word.

“Stiff-necked” is one of Scripture’s most vivid words describing rebellion — like an ox that refuses to be led, God goes east, it insists on going west; however you call it, it simply won’t turn back. The northern kingdom’s tragedy reminds us: God’s judgment is never hasty; it always comes upon those who consistently refuse to listen only after long patience and repeated warnings. God’s enduring patience is meant to lead people to repentance (Romans 2:4); but if a person mistakes this patience for permission, hardening their heart again and again, the end of that patience will surely be righteous judgment.

This history of national ruin is a mirror, reflecting the same danger within us. God may today also, through his word, his Spirit, and the reminders around you, be saying the same thing to you again and again; the question is, will you soften and listen, or, once again, harden your neck and go around it? “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15). Don’t test God’s patience; while he is still calling, still waiting, lower your stiff neck, and return before him. His patience is grace, not a permit that can be drawn on without limit.

Meditation: Is God, again and again, through his word and the reminders around me, saying the same thing to me, while I, again and again, harden my neck and go around it? Have I mistaken God’s patience for permission, thinking I can keep delaying indefinitely?

Application: Name something God has long been reminding you of, that you’ve stubbornly refused to hear; today, no more delay, no more going around it — while he is still calling, soften and obey him.

Prayer: Lord of great patience, Israel hardened its neck for centuries, refusing to hear your admonition through the prophets, and finally the nation fell. I tremble to see that your patience is not something to be drawn on without limit. Soften my stiff neck; whatever you have said to me again and again, let me listen today, no longer mistaking your enduring patience for permission. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 把难处摊开在神面前
entries.title_en: Spreading Your Trouble Before God
entries.verse: 列王纪下十九章十九节
entries.content:
亚述王西拿基立的大军兵临耶路撒冷,他派人送来一封信,极尽羞辱与恐吓之能事:你所倚靠的神,救得了你吗?看看列国的神,哪一个从我手里救过他的百姓?这封信,是赤裸裸地向耶和华的名挑战。犹大王希西家读了信,他没有惊慌失措地去求埃及,也没有跪倒在人的权势之下。他做了一件极美的事:上到耶和华的殿,「将书信在耶和华面前展开」。

他把那封写满威吓的信,一字一句地摊开在神面前,然后祷告。而他祷告的重心,格外值得我们学习。他不是单单哀求「救我脱离亚述,好保住我的性命、我的城」;他祷告的最深处是:「现在求你救我们脱离亚述王的手,使天下万国都知道惟独你耶和华是神。」(王下19:19)希西家把自己的危难,连于了一件比自身安危更大的事——神的名要在万国面前得着荣耀。

这是祷告蒙垂听的一个奥秘。希西家不是把神当作满足自己需要的工具,求祂来成全「我的国泰民安」;他乃是把自己的难处,放进「神的名要得荣耀」这更大的心愿里。他求神拯救,最终是为了神的荣耀得彰显、神独一的神性被万国承认。那一夜,耶和华的使者出去,击杀亚述营中十八万五千人;神为祂自己的名,施行了大拯救。

今天,你也有你的「西拿基立的信」——那些威吓你、叫你惧怕的难处、诊断、账单、关系。学希西家吧:不要把它藏在心里独自焦虑,也不要拿去倚靠人的膀臂;把它摊开在神面前,一五一十地告诉祂。更要学他祷告的高度:不只求「救我脱离这难处」,更求「借着拯救我,叫你的名得荣耀」。当我们的祷告与神的荣耀连在一起,我们就摸着了那使万军之耶和华动工的把手。

默想:面对威吓我的难处,我是独自焦虑、四处倚靠人,还是把它摊开在神面前?我的祷告,是单单求「成全我的安逸」,还是也渴望「借此叫神的名得荣耀」?

应用:今天把一件正威吓你的难处,像希西家展开书信一样,具体地摊开在神面前祷告;并在祷告中加上一句真诚的渴望:主啊,求你借着帮助我,叫你的名得荣耀。

祷告:万军之耶和华,希西家把西拿基立的信展开在你面前,求你拯救,好叫天下万国都知道唯独你是神。我也把我正惧怕的难处摊开在你面前。求你救我,更求你借着救我,彰显你独一的荣耀与大能。叫我的祷告不只为自己的安逸,更为你的名。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The army of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, pressed in on Jerusalem, and he sent a letter, filled with the utmost insult and threat: can the god you rely on save you? Look at the gods of the nations — which one has ever saved his people from my hand? This letter was a naked challenge to the name of the LORD. King Hezekiah of Judah read the letter; he did not panic and rush to seek help from Egypt, nor did he fall to his knees before human power. He did an excellent thing: he went up to the house of the LORD, and “spread it before the LORD.”

He spread that letter, full of intimidation, word by word, before God, and then prayed. And the focus of his prayer is especially worth learning from. He did not merely plead “save me from Assyria, so I can keep my life, my city”; the deepest part of his prayer was: “So now, O LORD our God, save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone, O LORD, are God” (2 Kings 19:19). Hezekiah connected his own crisis to something greater than his own safety — that God’s name would be glorified before all the nations.

This is a mystery of answered prayer. Hezekiah did not treat God as a tool to satisfy his own needs, asking him to accomplish “my peace and prosperity”; instead he placed his own trouble within the greater desire that “God’s name be glorified.” He asked for salvation ultimately so that God’s glory would be displayed, and God’s unique deity acknowledged by all the nations. That night, the angel of the LORD went out and struck down a hundred eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians; God accomplished a great deliverance for his own name’s sake.

Today, you too have your own “Sennacherib’s letter” — those threatening things that make you afraid: difficulties, diagnoses, bills, relationships. Learn from Hezekiah: don’t hide it in your heart to worry over alone, and don’t take it to rely on human strength; spread it before God, and tell him everything, in detail. And learn the height of his prayer too: don’t just ask “save me from this trouble,” but also ask “through saving me, let your name be glorified.” When our prayers are connected to God’s glory, we touch the very handle that moves the LORD of hosts to act.

Meditation: Facing troubles that threaten me, do I worry alone, relying on people everywhere, or do I spread it before God? Is my prayer only asking “grant me comfort,” or also longing “that through this, God’s name would be glorified”?

Application: Today, take a difficulty currently threatening you, and, like Hezekiah spreading the letter, concretely spread it before God in prayer; and add a sincere longing in your prayer: Lord, through helping me, let your name be glorified.

Prayer: LORD of hosts, Hezekiah spread Sennacherib’s letter before you, asking for salvation, so that all the kingdoms of the earth would know you alone are God. I too spread the trouble I’m afraid of before you. Save me, and even more, through saving me, display your unique glory and power. Let my prayer be not only for my own comfort, but for your name. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 一卷失而复得的书
entries.title_en: A Scroll Lost and Found Again
entries.verse: 列王纪下廿三章廿五节
entries.content:
约西亚八岁登基,行耶和华眼中看为正的事。在他作王第十八年,吩咐修理荒废已久的圣殿,工人在殿里发现了一卷失落多年的「律法书」——神的话。当书记沙番在王面前把这书念出来,约西亚一听见其中的话,就撕裂衣服,深深战兢:原来他们列祖长久以来,根本没有听从、遵行这书上的话!整个国家在不知不觉中,已经离神的心意何等远。

值得深思的是:神的话一直都在,它并没有改变;改变的是,它被人遗忘了、封存了、荒废在殿的角落里。以色列的属灵败落,不是因为神停止了说话,而是因为神的话被人束之高阁,不再被诵读、被认真对待。而复兴的火种,恰恰是从这卷「重新被打开的书」燃起的。约西亚一旦真听见了神的话,立刻大刀阔斧地除偶像、洁净圣殿、重守逾越节,掀起了犹大末期最彻底的一场改革。

圣经这样评价他:「在约西亚以前没有王像他尽心、尽性、尽力地归向耶和华,遵行摩西的一切律法。」(王下23:25)真正的复兴,从来不是靠新奇的手段、火热的情绪堆出来的,而是神的话重新被打开、被听见、被认真遵行时,自然结出的果子。神的道一旦回到它当有的位置,人心就被光照,悔改就随之而来,改革就势不可挡。

今天,那卷「律法书」会不会也正荒废在你生命的某个角落——被更要紧的事挤到一边,许久不曾认真打开?属灵的荒凉,常常始于神的话在我们生活中失了位;属灵的复兴,也总是始于神的话重新被我们当作至宝来读、来信、来行。主耶稣就是那道成肉身的话(约1:1、14);认真回到圣经,就是回到祂面前。把那卷书重新打开吧——个人的复兴,往往从这里开始。

默想:神的话在我的生活里,是被珍视诵读的至宝,还是被更要紧的事挤到角落、久未打开的「律法书」?我属灵的荒凉,是否正源于神的话失了它当有的位置?

应用:今天重新为神的话腾出一个不被挤掉的固定位置——定下一个具体、可行的读经时间与计划,像约西亚一样,认真听见并遵行你所读到的。

祷告:说话的主,一卷失而复得的律法书,点燃了约西亚彻底的复兴。我承认,我常把你的话挤到生活的角落,久久不曾认真打开。求你叫我重新以你的话为至宝,认真地读、单纯地信、切实地行;叫你的道回到它当有的位置,在我里面燃起真实的悔改与复兴。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Josiah ascended the throne at eight years old, and did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. In the eighteenth year of his reign, he commanded the long-neglected temple to be repaired, and the workers discovered in the temple a “Book of the Law” — God’s word — lost for years. When the scribe Shaphan read this book before the king, the moment Josiah heard its words, he tore his clothes, deeply shaken: their ancestors, for so long, had simply not listened to and kept the words of this book! The whole nation, without realizing it, had drifted so far from God’s will.

What’s worth pondering is: God’s word had always been there, unchanged; what changed was that it had been forgotten by people, sealed away, left neglected in a corner of the temple. Israel’s spiritual decline was not because God stopped speaking, but because God’s word had been shelved by people, no longer read, no longer taken seriously. And the spark of revival was ignited precisely from this “newly reopened book.” The moment Josiah truly heard God’s word, he immediately, with sweeping resolve, removed idols, cleansed the temple, restored the keeping of Passover, launching the most thorough reformation of Judah’s final period.

Scripture assesses him this way: “Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might, according to all the Law of Moses” (2 Kings 23:25). True revival has never been piled up through novel methods or fervent emotion, but is the natural fruit borne when God’s word is reopened, heard, and taken seriously and obeyed. Once God’s word returns to its rightful place, hearts are illuminated, repentance follows, and reformation becomes unstoppable.

Today, might that “Book of the Law” also be lying neglected in some corner of your life — pushed aside by more urgent things, unopened for a long time? Spiritual desolation often begins when God’s word loses its place in our lives; spiritual revival always begins when God’s word is again treasured, read, believed, and obeyed by us. The Lord Jesus is that Word made flesh (John 1:1, 14); to earnestly return to Scripture is to return before him. Reopen that book — personal revival often begins right here.

Meditation: Is God’s word in my life a treasure I cherish and read, or a “Book of the Law” pushed to a corner by more urgent things, long unopened? Does my spiritual desolation stem precisely from God’s word losing its rightful place?

Application: Today, once again make a fixed, un-crowded-out place for God’s word — set a concrete, workable time and plan for Bible reading, and, like Josiah, earnestly hear and obey what you read.

Prayer: Lord who speaks, a Book of the Law, lost and found again, ignited Josiah’s thorough revival. I confess I often push your word into a corner of my life, unopened for a long time. Let me once again treasure your word, read it earnestly, believe it simply, and obey it faithfully; let your word return to its rightful place, igniting genuine repentance and revival within me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 神记得每一个名字
entries.title_en: God Remembers Every Name
entries.verse: 历代志上四章十节
entries.content:
历代志一开卷,就是长长的家谱——亚当、塞特、以挪士……一代又一代的名字,密密麻麻,读起来仿佛枯燥无味。我们的眼睛常常一扫而过,急着跳到「有故事」的地方。但请慢下来想一想:这几百个名字,对被掳归回、几乎要忘记自己是谁的以色列人而言,意味着什么?它意味着——神一个都没有忘记。在那些看似无名、平凡、被历史淹没的世代里,神始终记念着祂的百姓,一个名字接一个名字地,守着祂的约。

就在这一长串名字的中间,忽然插进了一个人短短的祷告。「雅比斯求告以色列的神说:甚愿你赐福与我,扩张我的境界,常与我同在,保佑我不遭患难,不受艰苦。」(代上4:10)雅比斯这名字的意思是「愁苦」——他一出生就带着母亲的痛。他本可以认命,活在名字所定的愁苦里;但他没有,他向神呼求,求神扩张他、与他同在。经文接着说:「神就应允他所求的。」在一片枯燥的名单里,神特意为这个不甘于愁苦、单单向祂呼求的人,留下了一处记念。

这两件事放在一起,说出一个极深的安慰:神看重的,从来不是你在世人眼中是否显赫、是否「有故事」。祂记念每一个属祂之人的名字,连那最平凡、最被忽略、一生仿佛只是家谱里一行小字的人,在祂那里都有名有姓、被祂看顾。你或许觉得自己的一生太平淡、太无足轻重,像家谱里转瞬即过的一个名字;但在那位守约的神眼中,你的名字被祂深深记念,你向祂的每一次呼求,祂都垂听。

主耶稣说,好牧人「按着名叫自己的羊」(约10:3);祂又要门徒欢喜,因为「你们的名记录在天上」(路10:20)。你不是茫茫人海中一个可有可无的编号;你是被那位守约的神按名认识、按名记念、按名呼召的。今天,像雅比斯一样,不必认命于你「名字」所定的愁苦,只管向那记得你名字的神呼求——祂听得见,也必按祂的美意应允。

默想:我是否觉得自己的一生太平凡、太无足轻重,像家谱里一行不起眼的小字?我是否真相信,那守约的神按名记念我、垂听我每一次的呼求?

应用:今天像雅比斯一样,不认命于你的「愁苦」,具体地向那记得你名字的神呼求一件事——求祂扩张你、与你同在;并为一个你身边「不起眼」的人代祷,记念神也记念他的名字。

祷告:守约的主,那长长的家谱告诉我,你一个名字都没有忘记;雅比斯的祷告告诉我,你垂听最平凡之人的呼求。我承认,我常觉得自己无足轻重。谢谢你这位好牧人,按着名认识我,把我的名字记在天上。求你叫我安息在被你记念的确据里,也像雅比斯一样,坦然向你呼求。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Chronicles opens with a long genealogy — Adam, Seth, Enosh... generation after generation of names, densely packed, seemingly dull to read. Our eyes often skim past, eager to jump to “the parts with a story.” But let’s slow down and think: what do these several hundred names mean to the exiled Israelites, returning home, nearly forgetting who they were? It means — God has not forgotten a single one. Throughout those seemingly nameless, ordinary generations, submerged by history, God continually remembered his people, name by name, keeping his covenant.

Right in the middle of this long list of names, a short prayer suddenly appears. “Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying, Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain!” (1 Chronicles 4:10). Jabez’s name means “sorrow” — he carried his mother’s pain from the moment of his birth. He could have accepted his fate, living within the sorrow his name determined; but he didn’t — he cried out to God, asking God to enlarge him, and be with him. The text goes on to say: “And God granted what he asked.” In the middle of a dull list, God specifically left a note of remembrance for this person who refused to settle for sorrow, and simply cried out to him.

These two things, placed together, speak a very deep comfort: what God values has never been whether you’re prominent in the world’s eyes, whether you have “a story.” He remembers the name of everyone who belongs to him, even the most ordinary, most overlooked, whose whole life seems to be only a single small line in a genealogy — with him, each has a name, and is watched over by him. You may feel your life is too plain, too insignificant, like a name that flashes by in a genealogy; but in the eyes of this covenant-keeping God, your name is deeply remembered by him, and every cry you make to him, he hears.

The Lord Jesus said the good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3); he also told his disciples to rejoice, because “your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). You are not a dispensable number lost in a sea of people; you are known by name, remembered by name, called by name by this covenant-keeping God. Today, like Jabez, don’t resign yourself to the sorrow your “name” determines — simply cry out to the God who remembers your name — he hears, and will surely answer according to his good will.

Meditation: Do I feel my life is too ordinary, too insignificant, like an unremarkable small line in a genealogy? Do I truly believe that this covenant-keeping God remembers me by name, and hears every cry I make to him?

Application: Today, like Jabez, don’t resign yourself to your “sorrow” — concretely cry out to the God who remembers your name for one thing — ask him to enlarge you, and be with you; and intercede for someone “unremarkable” near you, remembering that God remembers their name too.

Prayer: Covenant-keeping Lord, that long genealogy tells me you have not forgotten a single name; Jabez’s prayer tells me you hear the cry of the most ordinary person. I confess I often feel insignificant. Thank you, good Shepherd, for knowing me by name, and writing my name in heaven. Let me rest in the assurance of being remembered by you, and, like Jabez, cry out to you openly. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 等候耶和华的必重新得力——属灵的加油站
entries.title_en: Those Who Wait for the LORD Shall Renew Their Strength — A Spiritual Refueling Station
entries.content:
等候耶和华的必重新得力——属灵的加油站

「但那等候耶和华的必重新得力。他们必如鹰展翅上腾;他们奔跑却不困倦,行走却不疲乏。」(以赛亚书 40:31)

这一周,我们看见乃缦放下自尊得洁净、希西家把难处摊开在神面前、约西亚被神的话点燃。这些都不是靠人自己的力气挤出来的,而是从神那里支取的。

今天安息日,是你属灵的加油站。你或许已经奔跑得困倦、行走得疲乏。停下来,不是软弱,而是智慧。真正重新得力的秘诀,不是咬牙再撑一撑,而是「等候耶和华」——安静在祂面前,让祂重新充满你、更新你。今天就来,把空了的油箱交给祂加满。

"But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength." (Isaiah 40:31)
entries.content_en:
Those Who Wait for the LORD Shall Renew Their Strength — A Spiritual Refueling Station

"but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint." (Isaiah 40:31)

This week, we saw Naaman lay down his pride to be cleansed, Hezekiah spread his trouble before God, and Josiah ignited by God’s word. None of these came from squeezing out human strength, but from drawing on strength from God.

Today, the Sabbath, is your spiritual refueling station. You may already be weary from running, faint from walking. Stopping is not weakness — it’s wisdom. The true secret to renewed strength is not gritting your teeth to push a little further, but "waiting for the LORD" — being still before him, letting him fill you anew, renew you. Come today, and hand your empty tank to him to be filled.

"But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength." (Isaiah 40:31)

entries.title: 日见强盛的秘诀
entries.title_en: The Secret of Growing Ever Stronger
entries.verse: 历代志上十一章九节
entries.content:
历代志重新讲述大卫的故事,用的是一种「回望」的眼光。经历了亡国与被掳,归回的以色列人再读自己的历史,要问一个问题:我们的先祖大卫,他的国为什么能兴起、能强盛?世人会归功于大卫的军事天才、政治手腕,或是他麾下的勇士。但圣经给出的答案,却单单指向一处。

「大卫日见强盛,因为万军之耶和华与他同在。」(代上11:9)注意那个「因为」——它把大卫一切的强盛,归到了一个唯一的源头:不是他有多能干,而是神与他同在。大卫的勇士再骁勇,若没有神的同在,也不过是一群血气之勇的人;大卫的谋略再高明,若离了神,也终必落空。他之所以日见强盛,归根结底,是因为神在他身边。

这是我们极容易颠倒的一件事。当生命顺遂、事工兴旺、家庭和睦时,我们心里常悄悄地把功劳记在自己账上:是我努力、我聪明、我经营有方。历代志却提醒被掳归回、一无所有的百姓,也提醒今天的我们:你生命中一切真正的强盛、一切经得起时间的果子,都不是出于你自己,乃是出于「万军之耶和华与你同在」。离了祂的同在,一切成就都是沙上的楼阁。

所以,我们当追求的,从来不是「更强的自己」,而是「更近的神」。主耶稣说得再清楚不过:「离了我,你们就不能做什么。」(约15:5)真正叫我们刚强、结果、站立得住的,不是我们为神积攒了多少能力,而是那位与我们同在的神自己。今天,你若渴望生命有真实的强盛,不要先去追求本事与资源;先来亲近那位与你同在的主——祂的同在,才是一切强盛的源头。

默想:我是否把生命中的顺遂与成就,悄悄记在自己的聪明与努力账上?我真的相信,我一切真实的强盛,唯独来自「神与我同在」吗?

应用:今天在一件你正靠自己的能力硬撑的事上,停下来承认「离了你我就不能作什么」,把它交托给那位与你同在的神,先求祂的同在,而非先求更强的自己。

祷告:万军之耶和华,大卫日见强盛,唯一的秘诀是你与他同在。我承认,我常把成就归给自己的聪明与努力,忘了一切真实的强盛都出于你的同在。求你叫我不再追求「更强的自己」,而是渴慕「更近的你」;因为离了你,我就不能作什么。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Chronicles retells David’s story, using a “looking back” perspective. Having experienced the fall of the nation and exile, the returning Israelites, rereading their own history, want to ask a question: why was our ancestor David’s kingdom able to rise and grow strong? The world would credit David’s military genius, political skill, or the mighty men under his command. But Scripture’s answer points to one place alone.

“And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him” (1 Chronicles 11:9). Notice that “for” — it traces all of David’s strength back to a single source: not how capable he was, but that God was with him. However valiant David’s mighty men, without God’s presence they were nothing but a group of brave, flesh-and-blood men; however brilliant David’s strategy, apart from God it would ultimately come to nothing. That he grew ever stronger was, at bottom, because God was at his side.

This is something we easily get backwards. When life goes smoothly, ministry flourishes, family is at peace, we often quietly credit ourselves in our hearts: it’s because I worked hard, I’m clever, I managed things well. Yet Chronicles reminds the exiled, destitute people returning home, and reminds us today: everything truly strong in your life, every fruit that stands the test of time, comes not from yourself, but from “the LORD of hosts being with you.” Apart from his presence, every achievement is a castle built on sand.

So what we should pursue has never been “a stronger self,” but “a nearer God.” The Lord Jesus put it as clearly as possible: “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). What truly makes us strong, fruitful, and able to stand firm is not how much power we’ve accumulated for God, but the God who is with us himself. Today, if you long for true strength in your life, don’t first pursue ability and resources; first come near to the Lord who is with you — his presence is the source of all true strength.

Meditation: Do I quietly credit the smooth times and achievements in my life to my own cleverness and effort? Do I truly believe that all my true strength comes solely from “God being with me”?

Application: Today, in something you’re powering through on your own ability, stop and acknowledge “apart from you I can do nothing,” hand it over to the God who is with you, seeking his presence first, rather than a stronger self first.

Prayer: LORD of hosts, David grew ever stronger, and the only secret was that you were with him. I confess I often credit achievements to my own cleverness and effort, forgetting that all true strength comes from your presence. Let me no longer pursue “a stronger self,” but long for “a nearer you”; for apart from you, I can do nothing. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 按定例亲近圣洁的神
entries.title_en: Approaching the Holy God According to the Prescribed Order
entries.verse: 历代志上十五章十三节
entries.content:
大卫要把神的约柜接到耶路撒冷,这本是一件极美、极敬虔的事。第一次,他兴高采烈,把约柜放在一辆新车上运送——就照着当年非利士人的做法。一路上鼓乐喧天,气氛热烈。可当牛失前蹄,乌撒伸手扶住约柜,神的怒气就发作,乌撒当场死在约柜旁。大卫又惧怕又愁烦:亲近神,怎么会亲近出人命来?

问题不在于大卫的热心不够,而在于他没有照着神所定的方式来亲近神。神在律法中早已清楚吩咐:约柜当由利未人用杠抬着,不可触摸,不可用车拉。大卫凭着一腔热情,却忽略了神的话,用人自以为合适、甚至看起来更「先进」的方法来事奉。三个月后,大卫想通了,他对利未人说:「因你们先前没有抬这约柜,按定例求问耶和华我们的神,所以他刑罚我们。」(代上15:13)这一次,他们照着定例,用杠抬约柜,神就大大赐福。

这件事对今天热心却随性的我们,是一记重锤。我们太容易以为:只要我动机是好的、心是热的,神就必悦纳,方式无所谓。但神是圣洁的,祂不但看我们献上什么,也看我们怎样献上。敬拜不是我们凭喜好、凭热情随意设计的活动;它必须照着神所启示的方式,存着敬畏的心来到祂面前。热心若不受真理的约束,反可能变成冒犯。

我们能坦然亲近这位圣洁的神,不是因为我们够热心、够真诚,乃是因为基督为我们开了一条又新又活的路(来10:19-20)。祂用自己的血,使我们这些本不配近前的罪人,得以按着神所悦纳的唯一方式——藉着祂——坦然无惧地来到神面前。所以,真正的敬拜,是一面存着热切的心,一面存着战兢敬畏,照着神的话、藉着神的儿子来亲近祂。今天,你是凭自己的喜好设计敬拜,还是照着神所启示的方式敬畏地亲近祂?

默想:我亲近神,是否以为「只要我热心、动机好,方式就无所谓」?我是照自己的喜好设计敬拜,还是照神所启示的方式、存敬畏的心来到祂面前?

应用:今天检视一处你「凭热情随性而行」的属灵习惯,回到圣经,看神在这事上是怎样吩咐的,调整自己去照祂的话行,存敬畏的心亲近祂。

祷告:圣洁的主,大卫一腔热心,却因没有按定例抬约柜而受责罚。我承认,我常以为只要动机好,方式就无所谓,忘了你既圣洁,就在意我怎样亲近你。谢谢基督用祂的血,为我开了一条又新又活的路。求你叫我既热切、又敬畏,照你的话、藉你的儿子来到你面前。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
David wanted to bring the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem — a beautiful, deeply devout undertaking. The first time, filled with excitement, he had the ark carried on a new cart — exactly as the Philistines had once done. Music and rejoicing filled the whole way. But when the oxen stumbled and Uzzah reached out his hand to steady the ark, the anger of the LORD broke out, and Uzzah died on the spot beside the ark. David was both afraid and troubled: how could drawing near to God end in someone’s death?

The problem was not that David lacked zeal, but that he had not approached God in the way God himself had prescribed. God had already clearly commanded in the Law: the ark was to be carried on poles by the Levites, never touched, never hauled on a cart. Carrying a heartful of enthusiasm, David overlooked God’s word, using a method that seemed suitable to him, even more “advanced.” Three months later, David understood, and said to the Levites: “Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule” (1 Chronicles 15:13). This time, they carried the ark on poles according to the prescribed order, and God greatly blessed them.

This event is a heavy blow to us today, zealous yet careless. We too easily assume: as long as my motive is good, my heart is warm, God will surely accept it, and the method doesn’t matter. But God is holy — he looks not only at what we offer, but at how we offer it. Worship is not an activity we design casually according to our own preference and enthusiasm; it must come before him with reverence, according to the way he himself has revealed. Zeal unrestrained by truth can, instead, become an offense.

That we can boldly draw near to this holy God is not because we are zealous enough, sincere enough, but because Christ opened for us a new and living way (Hebrews 10:19-20). By his own blood, he has enabled us sinners, who were never worthy to draw near, to come before God without fear, in the one way God accepts — through him. So true worship holds both a fervent heart and a trembling reverence together, approaching him according to his word, through his Son. Today, are you designing worship according to your own preference, or drawing near to him with reverence, according to the way he has revealed?

Meditation: When I draw near to God, do I assume that as long as I’m zealous and my motive is good, the method doesn’t matter? Am I designing worship according to my own preference, or coming before him with reverence, according to the way he has revealed?

Application: Today, examine one spiritual habit you’ve been practicing “casually, on enthusiasm alone.” Return to Scripture, see how God has commanded in that matter, and adjust yourself to act according to his word, drawing near to him with reverence.

Prayer: Holy Lord, David’s heart was full of zeal, yet he was disciplined for not carrying the ark according to the prescribed order. I confess I often assume that as long as my motive is good, the method doesn’t matter, forgetting that because you are holy, you care how I draw near to you. Thank you that Christ, by his blood, opened for me a new and living way. Let me be both fervent and reverent, drawing near to you according to your word, through your Son. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 为自己看不见的殿预备
entries.title_en: Preparing for a Temple You Will Never See
entries.verse: 历代志上廿二章五节
entries.content:
大卫一生最深的心愿,是为神建一座圣殿。然而神明明地告诉他:建殿的,不是你,是你的儿子所罗门。对一个满腔热忱的人来说,这几乎是最难接受的答复:我一生所梦想的事,神却说,那不是给你做的。换作我们,或许就此心灰意冷,甚至暗自赌气——既然不让我建,那我便什么也不管了。

大卫却没有。他说:「我儿子所罗门还年幼娇嫩,要为耶和华建造的殿宇必须高大辉煌……所以我要为殿预备材料。」(代上22:5)于是他在未死之先,倾尽全力,预备了极多的金银、铜铁、石木——为着一座他自己此生绝不会亲眼看见落成的殿。他甘心退到幕后,把一切最好的都预备好,只为叫接续他的人能把神的工作完成得更美。

这是一种极其成熟、极其舍己的属灵生命。它已经从「我要亲手成就、我要看见果子、我要得着荣耀」的天然里被神释放出来,进到「只要神的工作被成全,谁去完成、谁得荣耀、我能否看见,都无关紧要」的地步。真正认识神心意的人,看重的是神的工作本身,而非自己在其中的角色与名分。他们甘心作铺路的人、预备材料的人、栽种而不必亲手收割的人。

神国度的工作,原是一棒接一棒的:「我栽种了,亚波罗浇灌了,惟有神叫他生长。」(林前3:6)有人撒种,有人收割;有人预备材料,有人建造殿宇。我们常盼望自己既撒种又收割、又建造又剪彩,好把功劳与荣耀都留给自己。但那更深的生命,是甘愿像大卫一样,默默为一座自己看不见的殿预备,把成全与荣耀,单单留给神和后来的人。今天,你是否愿意作这样一个甘心退到幕后、为神国度默默预备的人?

默想:我事奉神,是否总要亲手成就、亲眼看见果子、亲身得着荣耀?若神的工作要藉着别人、在我看不见的将来才成全,我甘心只作那默默预备材料的人吗?

应用:今天甘心作一件「为别人、为将来」而不为自己收割的服事——默默地为下一代、为接续你的人预备些什么,不求被看见、被记念。

祷告:主啊,大卫甘心为一座自己看不见的殿倾力预备,把建造与荣耀让给了后人。我承认,我事奉常想亲手成就、亲眼看见、亲身得荣耀。求你释放我脱离这天然的自我,叫我甘心作撒种、浇灌、预备材料的人,只要你的工作得成全、你的名得荣耀,就心满意足。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
David’s deepest longing throughout his life was to build a temple for God. Yet God told him plainly: the one who builds the temple will not be you, but your son Solomon. For a man burning with such passion, this was perhaps the hardest answer to accept: the very thing I have dreamed of my whole life, God says, is not for you to do. In our place, we might well grow discouraged, even secretly resentful — since I’m not allowed to build it, then let it be none of my concern.

But David did not do that. He said: “Solomon my son is young and inexperienced, and the house that is to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly magnificent... so I will make preparations for it” (1 Chronicles 22:5). So, before his death, he poured out all his strength to prepare vast quantities of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and timber — for a temple he himself would never live to see completed. He was willing to step back behind the scenes, preparing everything of the best, simply so that the one who followed him could complete God’s work more beautifully.

This is an extremely mature, extremely self-denying spiritual life. It has been freed by God from the natural instinct of “I must accomplish it with my own hands, I must see the fruit, I must receive the glory,” arriving at the place where “as long as God’s work is accomplished, it matters not who completes it, who receives the glory, or whether I get to see it.” Those who truly know God’s heart value God’s work itself, not their own role or credit within it. They are willing to be road-pavers, material-preparers, sowers who need not reap with their own hands.

The work of God’s kingdom has always been passed baton by baton: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Some sow, some reap; some prepare materials, some build the temple. We often hope to both sow and reap, both build and cut the ribbon, so that all the credit and glory stay with us. But that deeper life is willing, like David, to quietly prepare for a temple it will never see, leaving the completion and the glory solely to God and to those who come after. Today, are you willing to be such a person — willing to step back behind the scenes, quietly preparing for God’s kingdom?

Meditation: In serving God, do I always need to accomplish it with my own hands, see the fruit with my own eyes, receive the glory in my own person? If God’s work must be completed through others, in a future I will never see, am I willing to simply be the one who quietly prepares the materials?

Application: Today, be willing to do one act of service “for others, for the future” — one you will not reap yourself; quietly prepare something for the next generation, for those who will follow you, without seeking to be seen or remembered.

Prayer: Lord, David poured himself out preparing for a temple he would never see, leaving the building and the glory to those who came after. I confess that in serving I often want to accomplish it myself, see it myself, receive glory myself. Free me from this natural self, and let me be willing to sow, to water, to prepare materials — content as long as your work is accomplished and your name is glorified. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 无人看见的忠心
entries.title_en: Faithfulness No One Sees
entries.verse: 历代志上廿三章三十节
entries.content:
这几章,读起来像一份庞大的人事名册:大卫年老时,把利未人、祭司、歌唱的、守门的、管库房的,一一分派、编组、定班。密密麻麻的名字与职分,乍看枯燥,却藏着一幅动人的图画——在神的殿里,每一个岗位都有它的位置,每一份服事都被神看重,连那些一生默默无闻的,也都被一一记下。

其中有一句关于利未人的话,格外朴素:他们的职分之一,是「每日早晚,站立称谢赞美耶和华」(代上23:30)。这是何等平凡、又何等重复的工作:日复一日,早晚两次,站在那里称谢赞美,没有掌声,没有观众,不会被史书大书特书。守门的更是如此——一辈子守着一道门,谈不上什么轰轰烈烈。然而在神的账上,这些无人喝彩的忠心,与那些看得见的丰功伟绩,同样宝贵。

我们活在一个崇拜「被看见」的时代:仿佛唯有台前的、显眼的、能带来掌声与关注的服事才算数,而那些幕后的、琐碎的、无人知晓的忠心,不值一提。这种心态悄悄潜入教会,也潜入我们心里——我们渴望的,常常不是「忠心地服事神」,而是「被人看见我在服事神」。可神所看重的,从来不是舞台的大小、掌声的多少,而是那颗在无人处依然忠心的心。「无论做什么,都要从心里做,像是给主做的,不是给人做的。」(西3:23)

那位为我们「取了奴仆的形象」、甘心俯就卑微的主(腓2:7),最看重的,正是隐藏之处的忠心。祂应许:「你这又良善又忠心的仆人……可以进来享受你主人的快乐。」(太25:23)注意,祂称许的是「忠心」,不是「显赫」。今天,无论你的岗位多么不起眼、多么无人知晓——是那日复一日早晚的称谢,是那默默守着的一道门,是那没人看见的琐碎摆上——都要知道:在神眼中,无人看见的忠心,从不被埋没。

默想:我渴望的,是「忠心地服事神」,还是「被人看见我在服事神」?我是否轻看那些幕后、琐碎、无人知晓的服事,只想要台前显眼的岗位?

应用:今天甘心做一件无人会看见、无人会称赞的服事,单单「像是给主做的」;并去感谢一位在幕后默默摆上、少有人留意的弟兄姊妹。

祷告:鉴察隐秘的主,利未人日复一日早晚站立称谢你,守门的一生守着一道门,你却一一记念。我承认,我常渴望被看见,轻看那无人喝彩的忠心。谢谢主耶稣甘取奴仆的形象,最看重隐藏处的忠心。求你叫我无论作什么,都从心里做,像是给你做的,不是给人做的。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
These chapters read like an enormous personnel roster: as David grew old, he assigned, organized, and scheduled the Levites, priests, singers, gatekeepers, and treasury-keepers, one by one, into their divisions and duties. Row after row of names and offices — dry to read at first glance, yet hiding within it a moving picture: in God’s house, every position has its place, every act of service is valued by God, and even those who go entirely unnoticed their whole lives are recorded, one by one.

Among these, one line about the Levites stands out for its plainness: one of their duties was “to stand every morning, thanking and praising the LORD, and likewise at evening” (1 Chronicles 23:30). What an ordinary, repetitive work this was: day after day, morning and evening, standing there giving thanks and praise, with no applause, no audience, never to be recorded with fanfare in the history books. The gatekeepers were the same — spending a whole lifetime guarding a single door, nothing glamorous about it at all. Yet on God’s ledger, this unapplauded faithfulness is every bit as precious as visible, celebrated achievements.

We live in an age that worships being seen: as if only service that is up front, visible, capable of drawing applause and attention counts, while faithfulness behind the scenes, in trivial matters, unknown to anyone, is worth nothing. This mindset quietly creeps into the church, and into our hearts too — what we long for is often not “faithfully serving God,” but “being seen serving God.” But what God values has never been the size of the stage or the volume of the applause, but the heart that remains faithful where no one is watching. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).

The Lord, who “took the form of a servant” and willingly stooped to the lowest place (Philippians 2:7), values most of all faithfulness in hidden places. He promises: “Well done, good and faithful servant... Enter into the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:23). Notice — what he commends is “faithful,” not “famous.” Today, however unremarkable, however unknown your post — whether it’s that daily morning-and-evening thanksgiving, that quietly guarded door, that unseen, trivial offering — know this: faithfulness that no one sees is never buried in God’s sight.

Meditation: Do I long to “faithfully serve God,” or to “be seen serving God”? Do I look down on service that’s behind the scenes, trivial, unknown to anyone, wanting only the visible, prominent post?

Application: Today, willingly do one act of service that no one will see or praise, doing it solely “as for the Lord”; and go thank a brother or sister who quietly serves behind the scenes, seldom noticed.

Prayer: Lord who searches hidden things, the Levites stood day after day, morning and evening, giving thanks, the gatekeepers guarded one door their whole lives, yet you remembered every one. I confess I often long to be seen, and look down on unapplauded faithfulness. Thank you, Lord Jesus, for taking the form of a servant, valuing most of all faithfulness in hidden places. Let me do whatever I do heartily, as for you, and not for men. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 万物都从你而来
entries.title_en: All Things Come From You
entries.verse: 历代志上廿九章十四节
entries.content:
大卫一生走到尽头,他为圣殿预备了一切,又当着全会众的面,把自己私库中的金银也毫无保留地献上,百姓也大受感动,甘心乐意地奉献。财物堆积如山,气氛热烈感人。就在这全民踊跃奉献、最容易滋生「你看我们何等慷慨」这种自豪的时刻,大卫却发出了一篇令人震撼的祷告,把一切的荣耀彻底归还给了神。

他说:「我算什么,我的民算什么,竟能如此乐意奉献?因为万物都从你而来,我们把从你而得的献给你。」(代上29:14)这一句话,道破了一切奉献的真相。我们以为自己在「给神」,仿佛神欠了我们一份人情;大卫却看穿了:我们手中所有能献上的一切——金银、才干、时间、气力,甚至那颗肯奉献的心——没有一样不是先从神那里领受来的。所谓奉献,不过是把神先给我们的,再交回祂手中而已。我们从头到尾,都是领受者;神从头到尾,都是那位赐予者。

这个真相,一举斩断了骄傲的根。若我所献的原是我自己挣来的,我便有资格自夸、有资格向神邀功;可一旦看清「万物都从你而来」,一切自夸就烟消云散了——我还能夸什么呢?我不过是把你的东西还给你罢了。同时,它也斩断了另一头的重担:我们不必因「献得不够多」而焦虑自责,因为神从不缺乏,祂要的不是我们的补贴,而是我们甘心的心。奉献因此从一种交换、一种负担,变成了一种敬拜、一种喜乐。

这正是福音的回响。「你有什么不是领受的呢?」(林前4:7)连我们的救恩、我们的信心,也都是神白白的恩赐。所以基督徒的奉献,永远不是「我为神做了什么」,而是「神先为我做了一切,我满心感恩地把祂所赐的献回给祂」。今天,当你摆上金钱、时间或才干时,愿你也能存着大卫的心说:主啊,这本都是你的,我不过是把从你而得的,欢欢喜喜地献回给你。

默想:我奉献时,心里是「我在给神、神该记我的功」,还是「万物都从你而来,我不过把你的献回给你」?我手中有哪一样,不是先从神领受来的?

应用:今天在一次奉献(金钱、时间或才干)中,刻意存着「这本是你的」的心去献上,以感恩和敬拜的心,而非交换或邀功的心。

祷告:赐万物的主,大卫在全民踊跃奉献时,却说「万物都从你而来,我们把从你而得的献给你」。我承认,我奉献时常暗暗自夸,仿佛你欠了我。求你叫我看清,我手中一切能献的,连那颗肯献的心,都是先从你领受的。叫我的奉献成为感恩的敬拜,而非交换的负担。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
David had reached the end of his life. He had prepared everything for the temple, and before the whole assembly, he also gave, without reservation, the gold and silver from his own personal treasury. The people were deeply moved, and gave willingly and gladly too. Wealth piled up like a mountain; the atmosphere was warm and stirring. Right at this moment — when the whole nation’s eager giving could so easily breed the pride of “look how generous we are” — David instead offered a stunning prayer, returning all the glory completely to God.

He said: “But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you” (1 Chronicles 29:14). This one sentence exposes the truth behind all giving. We think we are “giving to God,” as if God owes us a favor in return; but David saw through it: everything in our hands that we could possibly offer — gold, silver, ability, time, strength, even the very heart willing to give — every bit of it was first received from God. So-called giving is nothing more than handing back to God what he first gave us. From beginning to end, we are only receivers; from beginning to end, God alone is the giver.

This truth cuts off the root of pride at a single stroke. If what I offer were something I earned myself, I would have grounds to boast, grounds to claim credit before God; but the moment we truly see that “all things come from you,” all boasting evaporates — what is there left to boast of? I am merely returning to you what is already yours. At the same time, it cuts off another burden: we need not be anxious and self-reproaching over “not having given enough,” because God is never in need — what he wants is not our supplement, but our willing heart. Giving is thus transformed from an exchange, a burden, into an act of worship, a joy.

This is exactly the echo of the gospel. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Even our salvation, even our faith, are gifts freely given by God. So a Christian’s giving is never “what I have done for God,” but “God first did everything for me, and I, overflowing with gratitude, give back to him what he has given.” Today, as you offer money, time, or ability, may you too, like David, say from the heart: Lord, this was always yours; I am merely giving back, joyfully, what I received from you.

Meditation: When I give, is my heart saying “I am giving to God, and he should credit me for it,” or “all things come from you, and I am merely returning what is yours”? What is there in my hands that I did not first receive from God?

Application: Today, in one act of giving (money, time, or ability), deliberately hold the attitude “this was always yours,” offering it with gratitude and worship, rather than as an exchange or a claim for credit.

Prayer: Giver of all things, as the whole nation gave eagerly, David said, “all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.” I confess that when I give, I often secretly take pride in it, as though you owed me something. Let me see clearly that everything in my hands that I could possibly offer, even the very heart willing to give, was first received from you. Let my giving become an act of grateful worship, not a burdensome exchange. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 声合为一的时候
entries.title_en: When the Sound Became One
entries.verse: 历代志下五章十三节
entries.content:
所罗门建成的圣殿终于要献给神了。当约柜被安放在至圣所,祭司与利未歌唱的都站在坛的东边,吹号的、歌唱的一同发声。历代志特意记下那一刻发生了什么:「吹号的、歌唱的都一齐发声,声合为一,赞美感谢耶和华。」(代下5:13)就在他们同心合一、扬声赞美的那一刻,耶和华的荣光如云彩充满了殿,以致祭司不能站立供职。

请留意荣耀降临的时机:不是在建筑落成时,不是在献祭最多时,而是在众人「声合为一」地赞美神时。这里有一个常被我们忽略的属灵真理:神格外喜悦、也格外亲近祂子民同心合一的敬拜。当神的百姓不再各唱各的调、各怀各的心,而是众人的口、众人的心融为一个声音,单单高举祂时,神的同在就以一种特别的方式彰显出来。合一的赞美,是神所悦纳、也是祂乐意居住的地方。

这话直指我们敬拜中一个真实的光景。我们常常人虽聚在一起,心却各在一方:有人在盘算下午的事,有人在暗暗比较,有人只是例行公事地开口。我们的敬拜之所以常常干涩、感受不到神的同在,未必是因为诗歌不够动人、程序不够精彩,而可能正是因为我们「声」在一处,「心」却四散,从未真正「合为一」。神所寻找的,不是技巧娴熟的表演,而是众心归一、单单向着祂的真实赞美。

主耶稣曾祷告,愿门徒「都合而为一……叫世人可以信」(约17:21);祂又应许,「无论在哪里,有两三个人奉我的名聚会,那里就有我在他们中间」(太18:20)。合一从不是可有可无的点缀,乃是神所喜悦的敬拜。但要记得:那充满圣殿的荣光,始终是神主权的恩赐,不是我们靠合一「催逼」或「换取」得来的;我们同心归向祂,不是要操纵神的同在,而是把当得的荣耀单单归还给祂。今天,当你与弟兄姊妹一同敬拜时,求神收回你四散的心,叫你不只是「在场」,而是真正投入那「声合为一」的赞美里——因为那正是神的荣光乐意充满的地方。

默想:我在敬拜中,是「声」在一处、「心」却四散,还是真正与众人「声合为一」地单单高举神?我的敬拜为何常常干涩、感受不到神的同在?

应用:下一次与弟兄姊妹一同敬拜时,刻意在开始前安静片刻,收回四散的心思,全人投入那同心合一的赞美中,不只是「在场」,而是真正与众人合一地高举神。

祷告:乐意与人同住的主,当以色列众人声合为一地赞美你时,你的荣光就充满了殿。我承认,我的敬拜常常人在心不在,与众人各怀各的心。求你收回我四散的心思,叫我真正投入同心合一的赞美里;因为那众心归一、单单高举你的地方,正是你荣光乐意充满之处。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The temple Solomon built was finally ready to be dedicated to God. As the ark was placed in the Most Holy Place, the priests and the Levite singers stood at the east side of the altar; the trumpeters and singers together raised one sound. Chronicles specifically records what happened at that moment: “the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD” (2 Chronicles 5:13). And it was in that very moment, as they were united in heart, raising their voices together in praise, that the glory of the LORD filled the house like a cloud, so that the priests could not stand to minister.

Notice the timing of that glory’s descent: not when the building was completed, not when the greatest number of sacrifices had been offered, but when the people’s sound became “as one” in praise. Here lies a spiritual truth we easily overlook: God is especially pleased, especially drawn near, by the united worship of his people. When God’s people no longer each sing their own tune, each hold their own private thoughts, but instead all mouths, all hearts, merge into a single voice, exalting him alone — God’s presence manifests in a special way. United praise is what God accepts, and what he delights to inhabit.

This speaks directly to a real condition in our own worship. We often gather bodily while our hearts are scattered in different directions: someone calculating their afternoon plans, someone quietly comparing themselves to others, someone merely going through the motions of opening their mouth. Our worship is often dry, unable to sense God’s presence, not necessarily because the songs aren’t moving enough or the program isn’t polished enough, but perhaps precisely because our “voices” are together while our “hearts” are scattered — never truly becoming “one.” What God seeks is not a technically polished performance, but a true praise where all hearts return to one, focused solely on him.

The Lord Jesus prayed that his disciples “may all be one... so that the world may believe” (John 17:21); he also promised, “where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20). Unity has never been an optional decoration — it is worship that God delights in. But remember: the glory that filled the temple was always a sovereign gift from God, not something we obtain by “forcing” or “trading for” through our unity; when we turn to him together in one heart, it is not to manipulate his presence, but simply to return to him alone the glory that is his due. Today, as you worship alongside brothers and sisters, ask God to gather in your scattered heart, so that you are not merely “present,” but truly given over to that praise where the sound becomes one — for that is exactly where God’s glory delights to fill.

Meditation: In worship, are my “voice” and my “heart” in different places, or am I truly, together with everyone else, raising one sound, exalting God alone? Why is my worship often dry, unable to sense God’s presence?

Application: The next time you worship together with brothers and sisters, deliberately be still for a moment before it begins, gather in your scattered thoughts, and give your whole self to that united praise — not merely “present,” but truly exalting God as one with everyone else.

Prayer: Lord who delights to dwell with your people, when all Israel raised one sound in praise to you, your glory filled the temple. I confess my worship is often bodily present while my heart is elsewhere, each holding their own private thoughts. Gather in my scattered heart, and let me truly give myself to united praise; for the place where all hearts return to one, exalting you alone, is exactly where your glory delights to fill. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 不可忘记祂的一切恩惠——数算恩典
entries.title_en: Forget Not All His Benefits — Counting Your Blessings
entries.content:
不可忘记祂的一切恩惠——数算恩典

「我的心哪,你要称颂耶和华!不可忘记他的一切恩惠!」(诗篇 103:2)

这一周,我们看见大卫一切的强盛因神与他同在、他一切的奉献都是从神而得。人最容易犯的毛病,就是健忘——顺境一久,便把神的恩惠当作理所当然,忘了这一切从何而来。

今天安息日,安静下来,对自己的心说话:我的心哪,不可忘记!回想神这一年、这一月、这一周,一件一件地待你何等好——你的一餐一饭、一次次的搭救、暗中的看顾。数算它们,不是为了交账,而是要重新看见那位赐恩的神,叫你的心重新被祂的爱融化,重新以祂为乐。

"Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." (Psalm 103:2)
entries.content_en:
Forget Not All His Benefits — Counting Your Blessings

"Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits!" (Psalm 103:2)

This week, we saw all of David’s strength come from God being with him, and all of his giving come from what he first received from God. The most common failing of humankind is forgetfulness — once things go well for a while, we take God’s benefits for granted, forgetting where they all came from.

Today, on the Sabbath, be still, and speak to your own soul: do not forget! Recall how good God has been to you this year, this month, this week, one thing at a time — your daily bread, your rescues time after time, his hidden watchful care. Count them, not to give an account, but to see the giving God afresh, letting your heart melt again in his love, delighting in him once more.

"Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." (Psalm 103:2)

entries.title: 回转的路,神早已开好
entries.title_en: The Road Back — Already Prepared by God
entries.verse: 历代志下七章十四节
entries.content:
所罗门献殿的祷告刚刚结束,火就从天上降下,烧尽了燔祭,耶和华的荣光充满了殿。当夜,神向所罗门显现,回应他的祷告。神知道,这荣耀的圣殿再宏伟,祂的百姓仍会犯罪、仍会悖逆、仍会招来天旱、瘟疫与刀兵。于是神在这荣耀的时刻,预先为将来必然跌倒的子民,指明了一条回转的路。

「这称为我名下的子民,若是自卑、祷告,寻求我的面,转离他们的恶行,我必从天上垂听,赦免他们的罪,医治他们的地。」(代下7:14)请细看神所指明的这条路,一步一步,毫不含糊:第一是「自卑」——放下自己的骄傲与理由,承认自己错了;第二是「祷告,寻求我的面」——不是求祂挪去后果,而是切切地寻求神自己;第三是「转离他们的恶行」——真实地离弃罪,而非只是口头认错。这三步之后,才是神那三重的应许:垂听、赦免、医治。

这段话里,藏着福音何等的怜悯。神大可以在百姓犯罪之后,就此撇弃他们、任凭他们灭亡;祂却在他们尚未跌倒之先,就把回家的路预先铺好了。神从不是那位站在远处、等着看我们跌倒好定我们罪的神;祂是那位早已为浪子留着灯、望着门、预备好回转之路的父亲。无论我们的地已荒凉到何等地步,只要肯照祂所指的路回转,祂垂听、赦免、医治的应许就依然有效。

值得我们警醒的是那第一步:「自卑」。回转最大的拦阻,从来不是罪太大、神不肯赦免,而是我们的骄傲太硬、不肯自卑。我们宁可辩解、宁可拖延、宁可假装无事,就是不肯低头承认「我错了」。今天,你生命中是否有一块「荒凉的地」——一段枯干的关系、一个反复的罪、一处迟迟不肯面对的光景?回转的路,神早已开好;所差的,只是你肯不肯走第一步——自卑下来,寻求祂的面,转离那恶行。祂垂听、赦免、医治的应许,正等着你回家。

默想:我生命中有没有一块「荒凉的地」,是我一直不肯面对的?拦阻我回转的,是罪太大,还是我的骄傲不肯「自卑」、不肯低头认错?

应用:今天照着神所指的路走第一步——在一件具体的罪或光景上真实地自卑下来,寻求神的面(而非只求挪去后果),并切实地转离那恶行。

祷告:满有怜悯的主,你在你百姓跌倒之先,就为他们预备了回转的路——自卑、祷告、寻求你的面、转离恶行。谢谢你不是等着定我罪的神,而是为浪子留灯望门的父。我承认,拦阻我回转的,常是我不肯自卑的骄傲。求你叫我今天低下头来,走上你早已开好的回家之路,支取你垂听、赦免、医治的应许。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Solomon had just finished his prayer of dedication for the temple, when fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering, and the glory of the LORD filled the house. That night, God appeared to Solomon, responding to his prayer. God knew that, however magnificent this glorious temple was, his people would still sin, still rebel, still bring drought, plague, and sword upon themselves. So in this very moment of glory, God laid out in advance, for a people certain to fall in the future, a road back.

“If my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14). Look closely at this road God has laid out, step by step, without ambiguity: first, “humble themselves” — laying down one’s own pride and excuses, admitting one is wrong; second, “pray and seek my face” — not asking him to remove the consequences, but earnestly seeking God himself; third, “turn from their wicked ways” — truly forsaking sin, not merely confessing it in words. Only after these three steps come God’s threefold promise: hear, forgive, heal.

What mercy of the gospel is hidden in this passage. God could easily have abandoned his people after they sinned, letting them perish; instead, before they had even fallen, he had already paved the road home. God has never been the one standing at a distance, waiting to watch us stumble so he can condemn us; he is the Father who has already left the lamp lit and is watching the road, with the way back already prepared, for the prodigal. However desolate our land has become, as long as we are willing to turn back according to the way he has shown, his promise to hear, forgive, and heal remains in force.

What deserves our alertness is that first step: “humble themselves.” The greatest obstacle to turning back has never been that our sin is too great for God to forgive, but that our pride is too hard to bow. We would rather make excuses, rather delay, rather pretend nothing is wrong, than bow our heads and admit “I was wrong.” Today, is there a “desolate land” in your life — a withered relationship, a recurring sin, a situation you keep refusing to face? The road back has already been prepared by God; what remains is only whether you are willing to take that first step — humbling yourself, seeking his face, turning from that wicked way. His promise to hear, forgive, and heal is waiting for you to come home.

Meditation: Is there a “desolate land” in my life that I keep refusing to face? What holds me back from turning back — is my sin too great, or is my pride too unwilling to “humble itself,” too unwilling to bow and admit I was wrong?

Application: Today, walk the first step of the road God has shown — genuinely humble yourself concerning one specific sin or situation, seek God’s face (rather than merely asking him to remove the consequences), and truly turn from that wicked way.

Prayer: Merciful Lord, before your people had even fallen, you prepared for them the road back — humbling themselves, praying, seeking your face, turning from their wicked way. Thank you that you are not a God waiting to condemn me, but a Father leaving the lamp lit and watching the road for the prodigal. I confess that what holds me back from turning back is often my unwillingness to humble myself in pride. Let me bow my head today, and walk the road home you have already prepared, laying hold of your promise to hear, forgive, and heal. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 强盛时最危险
entries.title_en: The Greatest Danger Comes in Strength
entries.verse: 历代志下十二章一节
entries.content:
罗波安是所罗门的儿子。他一登基就因刚愎自用,失去了北方十个支派,国土只剩下犹大和便雅悯。然而神施恩,让他在犹大渐渐站稳、国势坚立。按理说,神这样恩待他,他该更加倚靠神才对。可圣经记下的,却是一句令人心寒的转折。

「罗波安的国坚立,他强盛的时候就离弃耶和华的律法,以色列人也都随从他。」(代下12:1)请注意这句话里那个致命的因果:不是在软弱、患难、走投无路时离弃神,恰恰是在「国坚立」「强盛」的时候。顺境,竟成了他跌倒的温床。当他一无所有、四面楚歌时,他还知道抓住神;可一旦日子好过了、根基稳了、不再那么需要神了,他就悄悄地把神的律法放下了。

这是一个我们极少防备、却极其真实的属灵陷阱。我们总以为苦难才是信仰的最大威胁,其实顺境往往更凶险。患难会把我们逼到神面前,顺境却会把我们从神身边温柔地引开。当我们健康、顺利、丰足、诸事如意时,那份「非神不可」的迫切,会在不知不觉中被安逸慢慢腐蚀;我们照样忙碌、照样体面,却渐渐不再真正倚靠神——就像罗波安一样,在最强盛的时候,离神最远。

主耶稣警告过那种「不冷不热」的光景:「你说:我是富足,已经发了财,一样都不缺;却不知道你是那困苦、可怜、贫穷、瞎眼、赤身的。」(启3:17)真正的危险,不是你觉得自己缺了神,而是你觉得自己不再需要神。所以,越是顺境,越要警醒;越是强盛,越要谦卑地抓紧神。今天,回想你近来的光景:是不是日子越好过,与神却越疏远?求神叫你在强盛时,反而更深地倚靠祂,免得重蹈罗波安的覆辙。

默想:我是否以为苦难才是信仰最大的威胁,却低估了顺境的凶险?近来我日子越顺,与神是越亲,还是越疏远?我是否在「强盛」时,悄悄放下了对神的倚靠?

应用:今天诚实检视你正「顺利、丰足」的那个领域,警醒它是否正把你从神身边引开;刻意在那个你觉得「不再那么需要神」的地方,重新回到神面前,谦卑倚靠祂。

祷告:恒久信实的主,罗波安在国坚立、最强盛的时候,反倒离弃了你的律法。我战兢地看见,顺境竟比患难更能把我从你身边引开。求你叫我在健康、顺利、丰足时,不生出「不再需要你」的骄傲,反而更迫切、更谦卑地抓紧你;免得我在最强盛时,离你最远。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Rehoboam was Solomon’s son. As soon as he took the throne, his stubbornness cost him the ten northern tribes, leaving him only Judah and Benjamin. Yet God showed him grace, letting him gradually gain a firm footing and establish his strength in Judah. By all rights, such kindness from God should have made him rely on God even more. But Scripture records a chilling turn instead.

“When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him” (2 Chronicles 12:1). Notice the fatal cause-and-effect in this sentence: he did not abandon God in weakness, hardship, or a dead end — it was precisely when his “rule was established” and he “was strong.” Prosperity, of all things, became the breeding ground of his downfall. When he had nothing and was surrounded on every side, he still knew to cling to God; but once life grew comfortable, his foundation grew secure, and he no longer felt he needed God so urgently, he quietly set aside God’s law.

This is a spiritual trap we rarely guard against, yet it is extremely real. We always assume hardship is faith’s greatest threat, when in fact prosperity is often far more dangerous. Hardship drives us to God; prosperity gently draws us away from him. When we are healthy, thriving, well-off, and everything goes smoothly, that sense of desperate need for God quietly erodes under the corrosion of comfort; we stay just as busy, just as respectable, but gradually stop truly relying on God — just like Rehoboam, farthest from God at his strongest.

The Lord Jesus warned against exactly this lukewarm condition: “You say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). The true danger is not feeling that you lack God, but feeling that you no longer need him. So the more prosperous things become, the more alert we must be; the stronger we grow, the more humbly we must cling to God. Today, reflect on your recent condition: has life gone better while you’ve drifted further from God? Ask God to let you rely on him even more deeply in strength, lest you repeat Rehoboam’s fall.

Meditation: Do I assume hardship is faith’s greatest threat, while underestimating the danger of prosperity? Lately, as things go well for me, am I drawing nearer to God or further away? Have I, in “strength,” quietly set down my reliance on God?

Application: Today, honestly examine the area of your life that is currently “going well, well-off,” and watch whether it is quietly drawing you away from God; deliberately return to God’s presence in that very place where you feel you “no longer need him so much,” humbly relying on him.

Prayer: Ever-faithful Lord, Rehoboam abandoned your law precisely when his rule was established and he was strong. I tremble to see that prosperity can draw me away from you even more than hardship can. Let me not grow proud with a sense of “no longer needing you” when I am healthy, prosperous, and well-off, but instead cling to you more urgently, more humbly; lest I be farthest from you at my strongest. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
