entries.title: 神的眼目在寻找什么
entries.title_en: What God's Eyes Are Searching For
entries.verse: 历代志下十六章九节
entries.content:
亚撒是犹大一位好王,他曾大力除偶像、修祭坛,又在面对百万古实大军压境时,单单呼求耶和华:「耶和华啊,惟有你能帮助软弱的,胜过强盛的。」神就为他大大争战,使古实人败逃。那时的亚撒,深知自己一无所靠,唯独倚靠神。然而到了晚年,当北国的巴沙来犯,亚撒却不再求告神,反倒搬出圣殿和王宫的银子,去贿赂亚兰王来替他解围。

先见哈拿尼来责备他,说了一句震动人心的话:「耶和华的眼目遍察全地,要显大能帮助向他心存诚实的人。」(代下16:9)神在天上,并非冷眼旁观;祂的眼目正遍察全地,主动地、切切地在寻找。祂在寻找什么?不是寻找最有才干的人、最有资源的人、最成功的人;祂寻找的,是「向他心存诚实」——就是一颗完全向着祂、单单倚靠祂的心。祂一旦寻见这样的心,就乐意为他显出大能。

这话既是极大的安慰,也是极深的扎心。安慰的是:你不必样样都强、事事都行,神才肯帮你;祂所要的,只是一颗单纯倚靠祂的心。神的大能,从不临到那些自以为有办法、靠自己周旋的人,却临到那肯说「惟有你能帮助软弱的」的人。扎心的是:亚撒早年一无所靠时倚靠神,得着了神的大能;晚年有了办法、有了银子、有了外交手腕,反倒不再倚靠神了。原来拦阻我们经历神大能的,常常不是我们太软弱,而是我们「太有办法」。

神今天的眼目,仍在遍察全地,寻找一颗肯完全倚靠祂的心。问题是,当难处临到,你第一个转向的是什么?是像早年的亚撒那样呼求「惟有你能帮助」,还是像晚年的亚撒那样,忙着搬银子、找关系、想办法?神乐意向那心存诚实、单单仰赖祂的人显出大能——愿祂的眼目今天在你身上,寻见这样一颗心。

默想:当难处临到,我第一个转向的是神,还是自己的办法、资源与人脉?拦阻我经历神大能的,是我太软弱,还是我「太有办法」、不够倚靠祂?

应用:今天面对一个难处,刻意先转向神、单单倚靠祂,把「搬银子、找关系」的本能往后放;操练像早年的亚撒一样祷告:惟有你能帮助软弱的。

祷告:遍察全地的主,你的眼目在寻找一颗向你心存诚实、单单倚靠你的心。我承认,我常像晚年的亚撒,一有办法就不再倚靠你了。求你叫我不因自己「有办法」而离开你,乃在每一个难处中先转向你,单单仰赖你的大能。愿你的眼目在我身上,寻见一颗完全向你的心。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Asa was a good king of Judah. He worked hard to remove idols and repair the altars, and when facing an invading army of a million Cushites, he cried out to the LORD alone: “O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak.” God fought mightily for him, and the Cushites fled in defeat. At that time, Asa knew deeply that he had nothing else to rely on, and relied solely on God. But by his later years, when Baasha of the northern kingdom came against him, Asa no longer cried out to God — instead he took silver from the temple and the palace to bribe the king of Aram into rescuing him.

The seer Hanani came to rebuke him, speaking a sentence that shakes the heart: “The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (2 Chronicles 16:9). God in heaven is not coldly watching from a distance; his eyes are actively, earnestly searching the whole earth. What is he searching for? Not the most talented, not the most resourced, not the most successful; what he searches for is a heart “blameless toward him” — a heart wholly turned toward him, relying on him alone. Once he finds such a heart, he delights to show himself strong on its behalf.

This is both a great comfort and a deep conviction. The comfort: you don’t need to be strong in every way, capable in every matter, for God to be willing to help you; all he wants is a heart that simply relies on him. God’s power never comes to those who think they have their own resources, who manage things by their own maneuvering; it comes to those who are willing to say, “There is none like you to help.” The conviction: young Asa, with nothing else to rely on, relied on God and received his power; in his later years, having resources, silver, and diplomatic skill, he no longer relied on God. It turns out that what keeps us from experiencing God’s power is often not that we are too weak, but that we are “too resourceful.”

God’s eyes today are still running to and fro throughout the whole earth, searching for a heart wholly willing to rely on him. The question is: when trouble comes, what is the first thing you turn to? Do you cry out like the young Asa, “There is none like you to help,” or do you, like the older Asa, busy yourself moving silver, seeking connections, scheming solutions? God delights to show himself strong on behalf of the one whose heart is blameless, who relies on him alone — may his eyes find such a heart in you today.

Meditation: When trouble comes, is the first thing I turn to God, or my own resources, connections, and schemes? Is what keeps me from experiencing God’s power that I am too weak, or that I am “too resourceful,” not relying on him enough?

Application: Today, facing a difficulty, deliberately turn to God first, relying on him alone, setting aside the instinct to “move silver, seek connections”; practice praying like the young Asa: there is none like you to help the weak.

Prayer: Lord whose eyes run throughout the whole earth, you are searching for a heart blameless toward you, relying on you alone. I confess that, like the older Asa, I often stop relying on you the moment I have resources. Let me not leave you because I have “resources,” but turn to you first in every difficulty, relying solely on your power. May your eyes find in me a heart wholly given to you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我们的眼目单仰望你
entries.title_en: Our Eyes Are on You Alone
entries.verse: 历代志下二十章十二节
entries.content:
约沙法王面对的,是一场几乎必败的仗:摩押人、亚扪人联合起来,率领大军前来攻击犹大。消息传来,约沙法惧怕。但他所做的,不是急着调兵遣将、四处求援,而是「定意寻求耶和华」,又招聚全犹大的人一同禁食祷告。在圣殿的会众面前,他献上了一篇何等诚实、何等无助、又何等美的祷告。

祷告的结尾,是这样一句话:「我们也不知道怎样行,我们的眼目单仰望你。」(代下20:12)约沙法没有假装镇定,没有硬撑出一副胸有成竹的样子;他坦然承认:主啊,我们无力抵挡这大军,我们也不知道该怎么办——我们唯一能做的,就是把眼目单单仰望你。这不是信心的软弱,恰恰是信心的极处:走到了自己的尽头,才真正把全副的指望,转向了神。

我们常以为,信心就是「我心里有把握、有办法、能应付」;其实真正的信心,往往是从「我不知道怎样行」开始的。只要我们心里还盘算着自己的对策、还留着几分「实在不行我还有后手」的底气,我们就仍在倚靠自己,神还没有真正成为我们唯一的仰望。惟有当一切办法都用尽、一切倚靠都落空,我们才肯把眼目「单单」转向神——那个「单」字,是神一直在等候的。神往往要把我们逼到山穷水尽,不是要为难我们,而是要挪去我们一切别的倚靠,好叫我们的眼目,终于单单地仰望祂。

那一战,神叫他们不用争战——他们只管站着,唱诗赞美,神就使敌军自相击杀。当我们的眼目真正单单仰望神,争战就归了神,得胜也归了神。今天,你若正面对一场「不知道怎样行」的仗,不必为自己的无助羞愧;那正是你把眼目单单转向神的时刻。放下一切「后手」与盘算,像约沙法一样坦然向祂说:我不知道怎样行,我的眼目单仰望你。

默想:我的信心,是建立在「我有把握、有办法」之上,还是肯从「我不知道怎样行」开始?我是否总留着几分「后手」,以致眼目从未真正「单单」仰望神?

应用:今天在一件你正无力应对的事上,坦然向神承认「我不知道怎样行」,放下你暗暗留着的「后手」与盘算,把眼目单单转向祂,等候祂动工。

祷告:信实的主,约沙法在必败的仗前,坦然说「我们也不知道怎样行,我们的眼目单仰望你」。我承认,我的信心常建立在自己的办法上,总留着几分后手,以致从未单单仰望你。求你挪去我一切别的倚靠,叫我走到自己的尽头时,把眼目单单转向你;因为争战与得胜,都在乎你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
King Jehoshaphat faced a battle nearly impossible to win: the Moabites and Ammonites had joined forces, leading a great army against Judah. When the news arrived, Jehoshaphat was afraid. But what he did was not to rush about mustering troops and seeking allies — instead, he “set himself to seek the LORD,” and gathered all Judah together to fast and pray. Before the assembly at the temple, he offered a prayer of such honesty, such helplessness, and such beauty.

The prayer ends with this sentence: “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (2 Chronicles 20:12). Jehoshaphat did not pretend to be calm, did not force a confident, composed appearance; he candidly admitted: Lord, we are powerless against this great army, we don’t know what to do — the only thing we can do is fix our eyes on you alone. This is not weakness of faith — it is precisely faith at its furthest extremity: having reached the end of himself, he finally turned his whole hope, truly, toward God.

We often think faith means “I have confidence in my heart, I have a plan, I can handle it”; but true faith often begins from “I do not know what to do.” As long as we’re still scheming our own strategies in our hearts, still holding onto some “backup plan just in case,” we are still relying on ourselves, and God has not yet truly become our sole hope. Only when every method is exhausted, every other reliance has come up empty, are we willing to turn our eyes “alone” to God — that word “alone” is exactly what God has been waiting for. God often drives us to the utter end of our resources, not to make things hard for us, but to remove every other support, so that our eyes might, at last, be fixed on him alone.

In that battle, God told them there was no need to fight — they only needed to stand still, sing praises, and God caused the enemy armies to destroy one another. When our eyes are truly fixed on God alone, the battle becomes his, and the victory becomes his too. Today, if you’re facing a battle where you “don’t know what to do,” don’t be ashamed of your helplessness — that is exactly the moment your eyes turn wholly toward God. Set down every “backup plan” and scheme, and say to him openly, as Jehoshaphat did: I don’t know what to do, but my eyes are on you alone.

Meditation: Is my faith built on “I have confidence, I have a plan,” or am I willing to begin from “I do not know what to do”? Do I always keep some “backup plan,” so that my eyes have never truly been “alone” on God?

Application: Today, in a matter you are powerless to handle, candidly admit to God, “I do not know what to do,” set down the backup plans and schemes you’ve been secretly holding onto, and fix your eyes on him alone, waiting for him to act.

Prayer: Faithful Lord, facing a battle he could not win, Jehoshaphat openly said, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” I confess that my faith is often built on my own schemes, always keeping a backup plan, so that my eyes have never truly been on you alone. Remove every other reliance from me, so that when I reach the end of myself, my eyes turn wholly to you; for the battle and the victory both belong to you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 借来的信仰靠不住
entries.title_en: A Borrowed Faith Cannot Hold
entries.verse: 历代志下廿四章二节
entries.content:
约阿施的故事,起初读来令人振奋。他在婴孩时险遭杀害,被祭司耶何耶大夫妇冒死藏在圣殿里六年,才得以存活、登基。在耶何耶大的辅佐下,他行耶和华眼中看为正的事,还热心地修复了年久失修的圣殿。一切看起来都那么美好——直到那句意味深长的话浮现出来。

「祭司耶何耶大在世的时候,约阿施行耶和华眼中看为正的事。」(代下24:2)问题就藏在「在世的时候」这几个字里。耶何耶大一死,约阿施立刻变了:他听从了首领的谄媚,离弃耶和华的殿,去事奉偶像;甚至下令用石头打死了那位忠心劝诫他的、恩人耶何耶大的儿子撒迦利亚。原来,约阿施的敬虔,从头到尾都是「借来的」——那是耶何耶大的信仰,不是他自己的;是靠着一位属灵长者撑起来的,一旦这根支柱倒了,他里面竟一无所有。

这是一个我们都要认真面对的问题:你的信仰,是你自己的,还是借来的?许多人有信,是因为父母信、配偶信、牧者信,是因为身边有一位属灵的人在托着、带着、盯着;这固然是极大的祝福。但若我们始终只是靠着别人的信心而活,自己从未在神面前亲自认识祂、亲自与祂建立那不可替代的关系,那么当那位「耶何耶大」离开——搬走了、软弱了、或是离世了——我们的信仰就会像约阿施一样轰然倒塌。别人的信心可以扶持你一程,却永远不能代替你自己认识神。

神没有孙子,只有儿女。祂要的,是你亲自来认识祂,亲自尝到祂的恩慈,亲自在祂面前扎下自己的根。「你们亲近神,神就必亲近你们。」(雅4:8)属灵长者是恩典,但他们的角色是把你领到神面前,而不是永远代替你站在神面前。今天,求神使你的信仰从「借来的」变成「自己的」——不是靠着谁在托着你,而是你亲自认识、亲自倚靠这位又真又活的神。这样的根,才经得起任何一位「耶何耶大」的离去。

默想:我的信仰是我自己的,还是「借来的」——靠着父母、配偶、牧者或某位属灵长者在托着?若那个人离开了,我的信仰还站得住吗?我有没有亲自在神面前扎下自己的根?

应用:今天在无人陪伴、无人督促的情况下,亲自来到神面前——自己读祂的话、自己向祂祷告、自己与祂交通,操练一份不倚赖任何人、单单属于你和神之间的关系。

祷告:又真又活的主,约阿施的敬虔是借来的,耶何耶大一死,他就全然崩塌。我省察自己,我的信仰有多少是靠着别人托着的?求你叫我不再只靠别人的信心而活,而是亲自认识你、亲自倚靠你,在你面前扎下自己的根。因为你没有孙子,只有儿女;愿我亲自作你的儿女。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Joash’s story is exhilarating at first read. As an infant, he narrowly escaped being murdered, hidden in the temple for six years at the risk of the lives of the priest Jehoiada and his wife, until he could finally be enthroned. Under Jehoiada’s guidance, he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and zealously restored the long-neglected temple. Everything seemed wonderful — until that pregnant sentence surfaces.

“And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest” (2 Chronicles 24:2). The problem lies hidden in those words, “all the days of Jehoiada.” The moment Jehoiada died, Joash changed instantly: he listened to the flattery of the officials, abandoned the house of the LORD to serve idols, and even had Zechariah — son of his benefactor Jehoiada, the very man who faithfully rebuked him — stoned to death. It turns out Joash’s godliness had, from beginning to end, been “borrowed” — it was Jehoiada’s faith, not his own; it was propped up by a spiritual elder, and once that pillar fell, there was nothing left inside him at all.

This is a question we must all seriously face: is your faith your own, or borrowed? Many people believe because their parents believe, their spouse believes, their pastor believes — because there is a spiritual person nearby holding them up, guiding them, watching over them; this is certainly a tremendous blessing. But if we only ever live off someone else’s faith, never personally coming to know God for ourselves, never personally building that irreplaceable relationship with him, then when that “Jehoiada” departs — moves away, grows weak, or passes away — our faith will collapse like Joash’s did. Another’s faith can support you for a while, but it can never substitute for your own knowledge of God.

God has no grandchildren, only children. What he wants is for you to come to know him personally, to personally taste his kindness, to personally sink your own roots down before him. “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:8). A spiritual elder is a grace, but their role is to lead you to God, not to stand before God in your place forever. Today, ask God to turn your faith from “borrowed” into “your own” — not relying on someone else propping you up, but knowing personally and relying personally on this true and living God. Only such a root can withstand the departure of any “Jehoiada.”

Meditation: Is my faith my own, or “borrowed” — held up by my parents, spouse, pastor, or some spiritual elder? If that person left, would my faith still stand? Have I personally sunk my own roots down before God?

Application: Today, in a time of no companionship, no oversight, come personally before God — read his word yourself, pray to him yourself, commune with him yourself, practicing a relationship that depends on no one else, belonging solely to you and God.

Prayer: True and living Lord, Joash’s godliness was borrowed, and the moment Jehoiada died, it collapsed entirely. I examine myself — how much of my faith is held up by others? Let me no longer live only off others’ faith, but personally know you, personally rely on you, sinking my own roots down before you. For you have no grandchildren, only children; let me personally be your child. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 强盛之后的高傲
entries.title_en: Pride After Strength
entries.verse: 历代志下廿六章十六节
entries.content:
乌西雅是犹大又一位好王。他十六岁登基,寻求神,神就使他亨通。他南征北战、修筑城楼、发展农业、训练精兵,声名远播,极其强盛。这一切强盛的源头,经文说得清楚:「乌西雅的名声传到远方,因为他得了非常的帮助,甚是强盛。」(代下26:15)是神帮助了他,他才有这一切。然而,就在他最强盛的顶峰,悲剧发生了。

「他既强盛,就心高气傲,以致行事邪僻,干犯耶和华他的神,进耶和华的殿,要在香坛上烧香。」(代下26:16)烧香本是祭司才可作的事,乌西雅却仗着自己的权势与功业,擅闯圣所,要僭越神所设立的界限。当祭司拦阻他,他不但不听,反倒发怒;就在他向祭司发怒的当口,额上长出了大麻风,他成了终身的麻风病人,被隔离,直到死日。那使他跌倒的,不是外来的强敌,正是他自己里面那颗因强盛而膨胀的骄傲之心。

这里有一个反复出现、却总被我们轻忽的属灵规律:成功最大的危险,是它会悄悄地把我们的心喂养得高傲起来。乌西雅的悲剧,不在于他软弱,而在于他强盛;不在于他一无所成,而在于他成就太大,以致渐渐忘了这一切「非常的帮助」都是从神来的,开始以为自己有资格、有能力、可以不受约束。「骄傲在败坏以先;狂心在跌倒之前。」(箴16:18)神能赐给我们的最大恩典之一,有时正是不让我们太过顺利,免得我们像乌西雅一样,被自己的强盛毁掉。

你我或许没有王位,但同样的试探,潜伏在每一次的成功背后:一次被称赞、一次的顺利、一份亮眼的成绩,都可能悄悄地把「这是神的帮助」偷换成「这是我的本事」。真正的成熟,是越蒙神赐福、越强盛,就越谦卑、越敬畏、越承认「非常的帮助」都出于神。今天,在你正亨通的地方,格外要警醒你的心:它是越发谦卑地归荣耀给神,还是正在因强盛而悄悄高傲?

默想:在我正亨通、被称赞、有成就的地方,我的心是越发谦卑归荣耀给神,还是正因强盛而悄悄高傲?我是否把「神的帮助」偷换成了「我的本事」?

应用:今天在一件你做得好、被人称赞的事上,刻意把荣耀明确地归还给神,承认那是「祂非常的帮助」;并求神保守你不越过祂所定的界限、不生骄傲。

祷告:至高的主,乌西雅蒙你非常的帮助而强盛,却在顶峰因心高气傲而跌倒。我警醒地看见,成功最大的危险,是把我的心喂养得高傲。求你叫我越蒙你赐福,就越谦卑、越敬畏;拦阻我把你的帮助偷换成自己的本事,也拦阻我越过你所定的界限。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Uzziah was another good king of Judah. He took the throne at sixteen, sought God, and God made him prosper. He campaigned to the south and north, built towers, developed agriculture, trained elite troops — his fame spread far and wide, and he became extremely strong. Scripture states plainly the source of all this strength: “And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong” (2 Chronicles 26:15). It was God who had helped him — that was the source of all he had. Yet at the very peak of his strength, tragedy struck.

“But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense” (2 Chronicles 26:16). Burning incense was a duty only the priests could perform, yet Uzziah, relying on his own power and achievements, forced his way into the sanctuary, overstepping the boundary God had set. When the priests tried to stop him, not only did he refuse to listen, he grew furious; and at the very moment he raged at the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead — he became a leper for the rest of his life, isolated until the day he died. What brought him down was not an outside enemy, but the pride swelling within his own heart because of his strength.

Here is a spiritual pattern that recurs again and again, yet one we constantly overlook: success’s greatest danger is that it quietly feeds our hearts into pride. Uzziah’s tragedy was not that he was weak, but that he was strong; not that he had achieved nothing, but that he had achieved so much that he gradually forgot all this “marvelous help” came from God, and began to think he had the right, the ability, to act without restraint. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). One of the greatest graces God can give us is sometimes precisely not letting things go too smoothly for us, lest we, like Uzziah, be destroyed by our own strength.

You and I may not sit on a throne, but the same temptation lurks behind every success: one word of praise, one stroke of good fortune, one impressive accomplishment can quietly swap “this is God’s help” for “this is my own doing.” True maturity is this: the more blessed and strong we become, the more humble, the more reverent, the more we acknowledge that this “marvelous help” comes from God. Today, in the place where you are currently prospering, be especially watchful over your heart: is it growing more humble, giving glory to God, or is it quietly growing proud because of its strength?

Meditation: In the place where I am currently prospering, praised, and accomplished, is my heart growing more humble, giving glory to God, or is it quietly growing proud because of my strength? Have I swapped “God’s help” for “my own ability”?

Application: Today, in something you’ve done well and been praised for, deliberately give the glory back to God explicitly, acknowledging it was “his marvelous help”; and ask God to keep you from overstepping the boundaries he has set, and from growing proud.

Prayer: Most High Lord, Uzziah grew strong through your marvelous help, yet fell at his peak through pride. I watch with alertness — success’s greatest danger is that it feeds my heart into pride. Let me grow more humble, more reverent, the more you bless me; keep me from swapping your help for my own ability, and from overstepping the boundaries you have set. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 有一件事我曾求耶和华——专注于神
entries.title_en: One Thing Have I Asked of the LORD — Focused on God
entries.content:
有一件事我曾求耶和华——专注于神

「有一件事,我曾求耶和华,我仍要寻求:就是一生一世住在耶和华的殿中,瞻仰他的荣美,在他的殿里求问。」(诗篇 27:4)

这一周,我们看见一个又一个的王:有人在强盛时离弃神,有人靠别人的信心而活,有人因骄傲而跌倒。他们的心,都被太多的事分散了,唯独没有专注于神自己。

大卫却说,在千头万绪中,他心里其实「只有一件事」——就是住在神面前,瞻仰祂的荣美。今天安息日,让你被无数事务扯碎的心,重新归回这「一件事」。不是先求神为你解决十件难处,而是单单来瞻仰祂本身的荣美。当神在你心中重新成为那唯一的「一件事」,其余的一切,就都各归其位了。

"One thing have I asked of the LORD... to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD." (Psalm 27:4)
entries.content_en:
One Thing Have I Asked of the LORD — Focused on God

"One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple." (Psalm 27:4)

This week, we saw king after king: some abandoned God at the height of their strength, some lived off someone else’s faith, some fell through pride. Their hearts were all scattered by too many things, and none were focused on God himself.

Yet David said that, amid a thousand concerns, his heart truly held “one thing” — to dwell in God’s presence, gazing upon his beauty. Today, on the Sabbath, let your heart, torn apart by countless demands, return to this “one thing.” Don’t first ask God to solve your ten problems — simply come and gaze upon his own beauty. When God once again becomes that one thing in your heart, everything else falls into its rightful place.

"One thing have I asked of the LORD... to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD." (Psalm 27:4)

entries.title: 尽心去行的人生
entries.title_en: A Life Lived Wholeheartedly
entries.verse: 历代志下卅一章廿一节
entries.content:
希西家作王时,犹大的属灵光景已到谷底:圣殿的门关闭了,灯熄了,香也不烧了。希西家一登基,做的第一件事,就是重开圣殿的门,洁净它,恢复献祭与敬拜;接着又打发人走遍以色列,召聚众人回来守逾越节。这是一场彻底的复兴。而历代志为希西家所作的总评,道出了这一切的根源。

「凡他所行的,无论是办神殿的事,是遵律法守诫命,是寻求他的神,都是尽心去行,无不亨通。」(代下31:21)注意那个词——「尽心」。希西家的复兴,不是靠一时的情绪高涨,也不是靠精巧的方法,而是靠一颗「尽心」寻求神的心。无论是殿里的事、律法的事、还是寻求神本身,他都不是敷衍了事、不是尽了一半,而是全心全意地投入。

这里说他「尽心去行,无不亨通」,我们要小心,别把它读成一条「越爱神就越发财」的公式。这里的「亨通」,首先不是指外在的富足顺遂,而是指他所做的神的工作得以成全、结出真实的果子——一个尽心寻求神的人,他的生命与事奉是在神眼中真正「行得通」、真正丰盛的。神所看重、也所祝福的,从来不是我们做了多少件事,而是我们是否「尽心」地为祂而做。半心半意地做一百件事,不如尽心地做一件。

今天最扎心的问题,或许不是「我有没有服事神」,而是「我是不是尽心」。我们太容易活在一种「尽了一半」的信仰里:聚会去,但心不在;祷告有,但敷衍;服事做,但留一手。神却呼召我们像希西家一样,把整颗心投进去——尽心去爱、尽心去信、尽心去行。这也正是最大的诫命:「你要尽心、尽性、尽意爱主你的神。」(太22:37)因为祂已经尽心地、毫无保留地爱了我们,连独生子都舍了。今天,神在哪一件事上,等你不再尽一半,而是尽心去行?

默想:我的信仰是不是常「尽了一半」——聚会心不在、祷告敷衍、服事留一手?在神所交托我的事上,我是尽心去行,还是半心半意?

应用:今天挑一件你一向敷衍、半心半意在做的属灵功课(读经、祷告、某项服事),刻意「尽心」去做一次,全人投入,像是单单为神而做。

祷告:配得全心的主,希西家凡事尽心去行,你就使他所办的神的工作真实结果。我承认,我的信仰常尽了一半——心不在、留一手、敷衍了事。谢谢你先尽心地爱了我,连独生子都舍了。求你夺回我的整颗心,叫我尽心、尽性、尽意地爱你、信你、行你所吩咐的。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
When Hezekiah became king, Judah’s spiritual condition had hit rock bottom: the doors of the temple were shut, the lamps extinguished, no incense burned. The first thing Hezekiah did upon taking the throne was to reopen the temple doors, cleanse it, and restore the offerings and worship; he then sent men throughout Israel, calling the people back to keep the Passover. It was a thorough revival. And Chronicles’ overall assessment of Hezekiah reveals the root of it all.

“And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered” (2 Chronicles 31:21). Notice the word — “with all his heart.” Hezekiah’s revival did not come from a momentary surge of emotion, nor from clever methods, but from a heart that sought God “wholeheartedly.” Whether it was the affairs of the temple, the matters of the law, or the seeking of God himself, he did not go through the motions, did not do it halfway — he threw himself in fully, with his entire heart.

Here it says he “did it with all his heart, and prospered” — we should be careful not to read this as a formula: “the more you love God, the richer you get.” The “prosperity” here refers, first of all, not to outward wealth and ease, but to the fact that the work he undertook for God was accomplished, bearing real fruit — the life and service of one who seeks God wholeheartedly truly “works,” truly flourishes, in God’s eyes. What God values, and what he blesses, has never been how many things we do, but whether we do them “wholeheartedly.” Doing a hundred things half-heartedly is not worth doing one thing wholeheartedly.

Perhaps today’s most piercing question is not “am I serving God,” but “am I doing it wholeheartedly.” We too easily live a faith that’s “only half done”: attending gatherings with our minds elsewhere, praying but going through the motions, serving but holding something back. Yet God calls us, like Hezekiah, to throw our whole heart in — to love wholeheartedly, believe wholeheartedly, act wholeheartedly. This is exactly the greatest commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37). For he first loved us wholeheartedly, without reservation, even giving up his only Son. Today, in what matter is God waiting for you to stop doing it halfway, and instead do it wholeheartedly?

Meditation: Is my faith often “only half done” — attending with my mind elsewhere, praying perfunctorily, serving while holding something back? In what God has entrusted to me, am I acting wholeheartedly, or half-heartedly?

Application: Today, pick one spiritual discipline you’ve always done perfunctorily, half-heartedly (Bible reading, prayer, some service), and deliberately do it “wholeheartedly” once, giving your whole self, as though doing it for God alone.

Prayer: Lord worthy of the whole heart, Hezekiah did everything wholeheartedly, and you caused the work he undertook for God to truly bear fruit. I confess my faith is often only half done — my mind elsewhere, holding something back, going through the motions. Thank you for loving me wholeheartedly first, even giving up your only Son. Reclaim my whole heart, and let me love you, believe you, and obey what you command, wholeheartedly. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 最坏的人也有回头的路
entries.title_en: Even the Worst Person Has a Way Back
entries.verse: 历代志下卅三章十三节
entries.content:
玛拿西是犹大历史上最邪恶的王,没有之一。他在位五十五年,重建他父亲希西家拆毁的邱坛,为巴力筑坛,拜天上的万象,甚至使自己的儿子经火,又行邪术、交鬼,在圣殿里立偶像,并且流了许多无辜人的血,充满耶路撒冷。若说有谁的罪已恶贯满盈、绝无可赦,那似乎非玛拿西莫属。

然而,神使亚述王来攻击他,用铙钩钩住他,用铜链锁住他,把他掳到巴比伦。就在这极深的急难与羞辱中,这个恶王竟做了一件谁也想不到的事——他在他列祖的神面前「极其自卑」,恳求耶和华。接下来的经文,是全本圣经中最令人震撼的恩典宣告之一:「他祈祷耶和华,耶和华就允准他的祈求,垂听他的祷告,使他归回耶路撒冷,仍坐国位。玛拿西这才知道惟独耶和华是神。」(代下33:13)神竟然赦免了他,恢复了他。

这个故事,是给每一个觉得「我这样的人,神不可能要了」的人的。玛拿西的存在,像一记响亮的宣告:没有一个罪人,坏到神的恩典够不着的地步。你或许觉得自己的过去太不堪、罪太深、离神太远、回头太晚——但你再坏,能坏得过那个使儿子经火、让无辜人的血流满全城的玛拿西吗?若神的恩典能接纳、能赦免、能恢复玛拿西,祂的恩典也一样能够着你。神在意的,从来不是你过去有多坏,而是你此刻肯不肯像玛拿西一样「极其自卑」,回到祂面前。

这也正是十字架的逻辑。基督的宝血,不是只能洗净那些小小的、体面的罪;它是为着最深、最黑、最绝望的罪而流的。「罪在哪里显多,恩典就更显多了。」(罗5:20)那使我们不敢回头的,从来不是罪太大,而是我们不肯自卑、不肯相信神的恩典真有那么大。今天,若你心里藏着一个「连神也不会赦免」的念头,请看玛拿西——最坏的人也有回头的路,而那条路,今天也向你敞开。

默想:我心里是否藏着一个「我这样的人,神不可能要了」的念头?我是否以为自己某个罪太深、回头太晚,连神的恩典也够不着?玛拿西的故事如何回答我?

应用:今天把那件你一直觉得「太不堪、神不会赦免」的事,像玛拿西一样极其自卑地带到神面前,诚实认罪,支取那连玛拿西都能赦免的恩典。

祷告:满有恩典的主,玛拿西恶贯满盈,却在自卑恳求时蒙你垂听、赦免、恢复。这叫我看见,没有一个罪人坏到你的恩典够不着的地步。我承认,拦阻我回头的,常是我不肯相信你的恩典真有那么大。谢谢基督的宝血为最深的罪而流。求你叫我今天极其自卑地回到你面前。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Manasseh was the most evil king in Judah’s history, without question. He reigned fifty-five years, rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down, built altars for Baal, worshiped the host of heaven, even made his own son pass through the fire, practiced sorcery and divination, set up idols in the temple, and shed so much innocent blood that it filled Jerusalem from end to end. If there were ever someone whose sin seemed to have reached its full measure, beyond any possible forgiveness, it would seem to be Manasseh.

Yet God brought the king of Assyria against him, who caught him with hooks, bound him with bronze chains, and carried him off to Babylon. In the depths of this distress and humiliation, this wicked king did something no one would have expected — he “humbled himself greatly” before the God of his fathers, and pleaded with the LORD. What follows is one of the most stunning declarations of grace in the whole Bible: “He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God” (2 Chronicles 33:13). God actually forgave him, and restored him.

This story is for everyone who feels “someone like me — God could never want.” Manasseh’s existence stands as a loud declaration: no sinner is so bad that God’s grace cannot reach him. You may feel your past is too shameful, your sin too deep, you too far from God, too late to turn back — but however bad you are, could you be worse than Manasseh, who made his own son pass through the fire and filled a whole city with innocent blood? If God’s grace could receive, forgive, and restore Manasseh, his grace can reach you too. What God cares about has never been how bad your past is, but whether you, right now, are willing, like Manasseh, to “humble yourself greatly” and return to him.

This is exactly the logic of the cross. Christ’s precious blood was not shed only to cleanse small, respectable sins — it was shed for the deepest, darkest, most hopeless sin. “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). What keeps us from turning back has never been that our sin is too great, but that we are unwilling to humble ourselves, unwilling to believe God’s grace is truly that great. Today, if you’re carrying a thought that “even God couldn’t forgive this,” look at Manasseh — even the worst person has a way back, and that way is open to you too, today.

Meditation: Do I carry a thought that “someone like me — God could never want”? Do I think some sin of mine is too deep, my turning back too late, that even God’s grace can’t reach it? How does Manasseh’s story answer me?

Application: Today, bring that thing you’ve always felt was “too shameful, God would never forgive,” like Manasseh, in deep humility before God, honestly confessing it, and lay hold of the grace that could even forgive Manasseh.

Prayer: Lord full of grace, Manasseh’s sin reached its full measure, yet when he humbled himself and pleaded, you heard, forgave, and restored him. This shows me no sinner is so bad your grace cannot reach him. I confess that what keeps me from turning back is often my unwillingness to believe your grace is truly that great. Thank you that Christ’s precious blood was shed for the deepest sin. Let me humble myself greatly and return to you today. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 先筑坛的人
entries.title_en: Those Who Built the Altar First
entries.verse: 以斯拉记三章十一节
entries.content:
被掳七十年后,神感动波斯王古列下诏,容许犹大人归回,重建耶路撒冷的圣殿。第一批归回的人,面对的是一片废墟:城墙塌了,圣殿毁了,四围还有仇敌环伺。百废待兴,千头万绪,他们最先做的是什么?不是先修城墙保护自己,不是先盖房子安顿自己,而是「在原有的根基上筑坛」——先重建祭坛,恢复献祭与敬拜。他们在惧怕中,仍把神摆在了第一位。

这个次序,极有属灵的分量。人在重建、在忙乱、在危机四伏时,天然的反应总是先顾自己的安全与需要,把敬拜神放到「等一切安顿好再说」。这批归回的人却反其道而行:在最没有安全感的时候,先为神筑坛。因为他们深知,若不先恢复与神的关系、先把神放回中心,城墙盖得再牢、房子建得再好,也不过是没有神的空城。真正的重建,永远是从祭坛开始,从敬拜开始,从神重新居首位开始。

更美的是,当圣殿的根基立定,他们就一同赞美称谢耶和华:「他们彼此唱和,赞美称谢耶和华说:他本为善,他向以色列人永发慈爱。」(拉3:11)房子还只是个地基,墙还没影儿,他们却已经在废墟上放声歌唱神的恩慈了。他们的喜乐,不是建立在工程完成之上,而是建立在「神本为善」这不变的事实之上。只要神仍在,只要祭坛已立,即便四围仍是残垣断壁,也足以叫人歌唱。

你今天的生命里,是否也有一片需要重建的「废墟」——一段破碎的关系、一个跌倒后的重来、一处荒凉的光景?不要先急着修补外面的城墙。先筑坛。先把神重新放回你生命的中心,恢复那被荒废的敬拜与亲近。当神重新居首位,其余的重建,自会在祂的次序里一一立起。真正的复兴,永远从祭坛开始。

默想:在我忙乱、危机、重建的时候,我是先顾自己的安全与需要,还是先「筑坛」——先把神放回中心、恢复敬拜?我的喜乐,是建立在事情完成上,还是建立在「神本为善」上?

应用:今天在你生命需要重建的那片「废墟」上,先做「筑坛」的事——恢复一项被你荒废的敬拜或亲近神的操练,把神重新放回首位,再谈其余的重建。

祷告:本为善的主,归回的百姓在惧怕与废墟中,仍先为你筑坛、恢复敬拜。我承认,我在忙乱危机中,总把亲近你放到「等安顿好再说」。求你叫我学会先筑坛——在一切重建之先,先把你放回我生命的中心;叫我的喜乐不系于事情的成败,而系于你本为善、永发慈爱。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
After seventy years of exile, God moved King Cyrus of Persia to issue a decree allowing the people of Judah to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. The first group to return faced a scene of ruins: the walls collapsed, the temple destroyed, enemies surrounding them on every side. With everything in disrepair and a thousand pressing needs, what did they do first? Not repairing the walls to protect themselves first, not building houses to settle themselves first, but “building the altar on its foundation” — rebuilding the altar first, restoring sacrifice and worship. Even in their fear, they still put God first.

This order carries tremendous spiritual weight. When people are rebuilding, busy, surrounded by crisis, the natural response is always to attend to one’s own safety and needs first, putting worship of God off until “everything is settled.” These returning exiles did the opposite: at the moment they had the least security, they built the altar for God first. Because they knew deeply: if the relationship with God was not restored first, if God was not put back at the center first, however sturdy the walls, however well-built the houses, it would still be nothing but an empty city without God. True rebuilding always begins from the altar, from worship, from God being restored to first place.

More beautifully still, once the temple’s foundation was laid, they praised and gave thanks to the LORD together: “And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, ‘For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel’” (Ezra 3:11). The house was still just a foundation, the walls not even a hint yet, and yet they were already singing aloud, celebrating God’s steadfast love, amid the ruins. Their joy was not built upon the completion of the project, but upon the unchanging fact that “God is good.” As long as God remained, as long as the altar was set up, even if the ruined walls still stood all around, it was enough to make them sing.

Is there a “ruin” in your life today that needs rebuilding — a broken relationship, a fresh start after a fall, a desolate situation? Don’t rush to repair the outer walls first. Build the altar first. Put God back at the center of your life first, restore the worship and closeness that had fallen into disrepair. When God is restored to first place, the rest of the rebuilding will rise up, one by one, in his own order. True revival always begins at the altar.

Meditation: In my busyness, crisis, and rebuilding, do I attend to my own safety and needs first, or do I “build the altar” first — putting God back at the center, restoring worship? Is my joy built upon things being completed, or upon “God is good”?

Application: Today, on that “ruin” in your life that needs rebuilding, do the work of “building the altar” first — restore some worship practice or way of drawing near to God that you’ve let fall into disrepair, putting God back in first place before addressing the rest of the rebuilding.

Prayer: Good Lord, the returning exiles, even in fear and amid ruins, still built the altar for you first, restoring worship. I confess that in busyness and crisis, I always put drawing near to you off until “things are settled.” Teach me to build the altar first — before all rebuilding, put you back at the center of my life; let my joy not depend on how things turn out, but rest on the fact that you are good, and your steadfast love endures forever. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 工程停了,神的话叫它再动
entries.title_en: The Work Stopped — God's Word Set It Moving Again
entries.verse: 以斯拉记六章十四节
entries.content:
重建圣殿的工程,起头轰轰烈烈,却很快遇上了拦阻。四围的仇敌先是假意要参与,被拒绝后就转为公开的敌对:他们贿赂官员、上书控告、使计骚扰,叫百姓灰心丧胆。工程就这样停了——一停,竟停了约十五年之久。起初的热心冷了,人们退回各自的生活,那半途而废的地基,荒凉地晾在那里。

是什么叫停摆多年的工程重新动起来的?不是新的资金,不是有力的靠山,而是神的话。神兴起两位先知——哈该和撒迦利亚——向灰心的百姓传讲神的话,责备、激励、应许。神的话像一把火,重新点燃了那颗冷却的心。「犹大长老因先知哈该和易多的孙子撒迦利亚所说劝勉的话就建造这殿,凡事亨通。」(拉6:14)百姓一重新听进神的话,手就重新拿起了工具,停摆的工程就再次向前,直到完工。

这幅图画,像极了我们许多人的属灵光景。我们的生命里,也常有一些「停了工的圣殿」:曾经立志要建立的读经祷告习惯、曾经领受要去做的一件事、曾经火热却因拦阻和灰心而半途搁下的服事。它们就像那荒凉的地基,晾在那里,成了我们心中隐隐的亏欠。拦阻是真的,灰心也是真的,但工程停摆最深的原因,往往是我们不再听神的话了——一旦神的话在我们心中沉寂,手上的工也就停了。

好消息是:那使停摆的工程重新动起来的力量,今天依然有效——就是神的话。当我们重新回到神的话面前,认真地听、让它责备我们的灰心、点燃我们的心,那搁置已久的「圣殿」,就有可能重新动工。你生命中有没有一件「停了工」的事,是神曾清楚感动你去做的?今天不要靠自己咬牙硬撑,回到神的话面前,让祂的话重新点燃你——然后,重新拿起工具。

默想:我生命中有没有一座「停了工的圣殿」——曾经立志、却因拦阻和灰心而半途搁下的事?它停摆,是否正因为我不再认真听神的话了?

应用:今天指认一件你曾被神感动、却半途搁下的事,回到神的话面前,让祂的话重新点燃你的心,并采取一个具体的小步,重新「动工」。

祷告:用话语点火的主,停摆十五年的圣殿,因先知所传你的话就重新动工。我承认,我生命里也有搁下的工,而它停摆最深的原因,是我不再认真听你的话。求你的话今天重新临到我,责备我的灰心,点燃我冷却的心,叫我重新拿起工具,把你所托付的建造下去。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The work of rebuilding the temple began with great fervor, but soon met obstacles. The surrounding enemies first pretended to want to help, and when refused, turned to open hostility: they bribed officials, filed accusations, and harassed the people with schemes, discouraging them until their hands grew weak. The work simply stopped — and stopped for about fifteen years. The initial zeal cooled, people retreated to their own lives, and that half-finished foundation lay there, desolate.

What got the stalled work moving again after all those years? Not new funding, not a powerful patron, but the word of God. God raised up two prophets — Haggai and Zechariah — to speak God’s word to the discouraged people: rebuking, encouraging, promising. God’s word was like fire, rekindling that cooled heart. “And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo” (Ezra 6:14). The moment the people took God’s word to heart again, their hands picked up the tools again, and the stalled work moved forward again, all the way to completion.

This picture closely resembles the spiritual condition of so many of us. In our lives, too, there are often “temples whose work has stopped”: a Bible-reading and prayer habit we once resolved to build, a task we once felt called to do, a service that was once on fire but was set aside halfway through, because of obstacles and discouragement. They lie there like that desolate foundation, becoming a quiet debt in our hearts. The obstacles are real, the discouragement is real, but the deepest reason the work stalls is often that we’ve stopped listening to God’s word — once God’s word grows silent in our hearts, the work in our hands stops too.

The good news is: the power that got the stalled work moving again is still effective today — the word of God. When we return to God’s word again, listen carefully, let it rebuke our discouragement, let it kindle our hearts, that long-abandoned “temple” may well start moving again. Is there something in your life that has “stopped work,” something God once clearly moved you to do? Don’t try to grit your teeth and force it through on your own strength today. Return to God’s word, let his word rekindle you — then, pick up the tools again.

Meditation: Is there a “temple whose work has stopped” in my life — something I once resolved to do, but set aside halfway through because of obstacles and discouragement? Has it stalled precisely because I’ve stopped listening carefully to God’s word?

Application: Today, identify one thing God once moved you toward that you’ve abandoned halfway; return to God’s word, let it rekindle your heart, and take one concrete small step to “get back to work.”

Prayer: Lord who kindles with your word, the temple, stalled for fifteen years, began moving again through the word you spoke through the prophets. I confess that I too have abandoned work in my life, and the deepest reason it stalled is that I stopped listening carefully to your word. Let your word come to me afresh today, rebuke my discouragement, kindle my cooled heart, and let me pick up the tools again and continue building what you’ve entrusted to me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 定志:考究、遵行、教导
entries.title_en: Resolved: Study, Practice, Teach
entries.verse: 以斯拉记七章十节
entries.content:
以斯拉是一位文士,一位精通神律法的教师。当他带着第二批被掳的人从巴比伦归回,面对的是一群灵性松散、律法荒废、甚至与外邦人混杂通婚的百姓。以斯拉如何带来真正的改变?圣经用一句话总结了他一生事奉的根基,而这句话为一切想服事神、想影响别人的人,立下了永远的次序。

「以斯拉定志考究遵行耶和华的律法,又将律例典章教训以色列人。」(拉7:10)请细看这句话里三个动词的顺序:先是「考究」——他下定决心,认真地研读、明白神的话;接着是「遵行」——他先把所明白的,行在自己身上;最后才是「教训」别人。考究、遵行、教导,这个次序,一个也不能颠倒。

我们常想跳过前两步,直接到第三步。我们渴望能教导人、影响人、纠正人,却不肯先花功夫认真考究神的话,更不肯先让神的话在自己身上生根、结果。结果就是:讲的是一套,活的是另一套;要求别人的,自己却做不到。这样的「教导」,没有能力,也没有说服力,因为它是空的。以斯拉带来复兴的秘诀,不在于他口才多好,而在于他所教导的,是他自己先认真考究、又切实遵行了的——他的生命,先被神的话建造,然后他的话才有分量。

注意那两个字:「定志」。考究、遵行、教导神的话,从来不是自然而然发生的,它需要一个坚定的心志、一个刻意的委身。神今天寻找的,不是能言善道的人,而是像以斯拉一样「定志」的人——先让神的话在自己心里扎根、在自己生命里成形,然后才从一个被神的话充满的生命里,自然地流向别人。你想影响你的家人、同事、教会吗?次序永远是:先考究,再遵行,后教导。今天,你在哪一步上,想抄近路?

默想:在「考究、遵行、教导」这三步中,我是否总想跳过前两步、直接去教导纠正别人?我讲的和我活的,是否一致?我有没有「定志」让神的话先在自己身上扎根?

应用:今天在你想去劝勉、纠正、教导别人(家人、同事、弟兄姊妹)的一件事上,先回到神的话认真考究,并先切实地行在自己身上,再去影响别人。

祷告:赐下真理的主,以斯拉定志考究、遵行,然后才教导,你就借他带来复兴。我承认,我常想跳过前两步,直接去教导纠正别人,以致讲的和活的不一样。求你赐我以斯拉那样定志的心,让你的话先在我里面扎根、结果,再借我流向别人。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezra was a scribe, a teacher well-versed in God’s law. When he led the second group of exiles back from Babylon, he faced a people spiritually slack, careless of the law, even intermarried with foreign nations. How did Ezra bring about real change? Scripture summarizes the foundation of his entire ministry in one sentence — a sentence that establishes a permanent order for everyone who wants to serve God and influence others.

“For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel” (Ezra 7:10). Look closely at the order of the three verbs in this sentence: first, “study” — he resolved to seriously research and understand God’s word; next, “do it” — he first put into practice in his own life what he had understood; only then, “teach” others. Study, practice, teach — this order cannot be reversed, not even one step.

We often want to skip the first two steps and go straight to the third. We long to teach, influence, correct people, yet we’re unwilling to first put in the effort to seriously study God’s word, and even more unwilling to let God’s word first take root and bear fruit in our own lives. The result: preaching one thing, living another; demanding of others what we cannot do ourselves. Such “teaching” has no power, no persuasiveness, because it’s hollow. The secret to Ezra’s revival was not his eloquence, but that what he taught was what he himself had first seriously studied and truly practiced — his life was built by God’s word first, and only then did his words carry weight.

Notice those two words: “set his heart.” Studying, practicing, and teaching God’s word has never happened naturally on its own — it requires a firm resolve, a deliberate commitment. What God seeks today is not the eloquent, but people like Ezra who have “set their heart” — letting God’s word take root and take shape in their own hearts first, then naturally flowing out from a life filled with God’s word to others. Do you want to influence your family, coworkers, church? The order is always: study first, practice next, teach last. Today, at which step are you tempted to take a shortcut?

Meditation: In these three steps — study, practice, teach — do I always want to skip the first two and go straight to teaching and correcting others? Are what I preach and what I live consistent? Have I “set my heart” to let God’s word take root in myself first?

Application: Today, in something you want to exhort, correct, or teach someone (family, coworker, brother or sister), first return to God’s word and seriously study it, first truly practice it in your own life, and only then go on to influence others.

Prayer: Lord who gives truth, Ezra set his heart to study, to practice, and only then to teach, and you brought revival through him. I confess I often want to skip the first two steps and go straight to teaching and correcting others, so that what I preach and what I live don’t match. Give me Ezra’s resolved heart, let your word take root and bear fruit in me first, and then flow through me to others. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 先跪下,再动工
entries.title_en: Kneel First, Then Get to Work
entries.verse: 尼希米记二章八节
entries.content:
尼希米在波斯王宫中作酒政,地位优渥。当他听见耶路撒冷城墙拆毁、城门被火焚烧、余民大遭凌辱的消息,他没有耸耸肩说「那太远了,与我无关」。经文说,他一听见,就坐下哭泣,悲哀了几日,在神面前禁食祈祷。一个身在异乡、生活安稳的人,竟为着神百姓的荒凉,心痛到如此地步。真正的负担,是从一颗被神的事所触动的心开始的。

但尼希米不是只会流泪。他为这事禁食祷告了约四个月,才在合宜的时机,向王开口求准他回去重建。而当王应允时,尼希米把这一切的成就,归给了一个源头:「王就允准我,因我神施恩的手帮助我。」(尼2:8)他清楚知道:打动王心的,不是他的口才或运气,乃是神施恩的手在背后动工。他先在神面前跪了几个月,才在王面前站起来说话。

这里有一个我们最容易失衡的功课:祷告与行动的次序。有人只祷告,却从不采取任何行动,把「交托神」当成不负责任的借口;也有人一有负担就立刻冲出去做,忙得团团转,却从不先跪下寻求神。尼希米两样都做,而且次序分明:先跪下,再动工。他的行动不是取代祷告,而是从祷告里长出来的;他的祷告也不是取代行动,而是要托住行动。深深地祷告,然后勇敢地行动——这两者从不矛盾,乃是一体。

更要紧的是尼希米那句话背后的信念:一切真实的成就,都是「因神施恩的手帮助」。他即将开始的,是一项浩大艰难、四面受敌的工程;支撑他往前的,不是他自己的能力与筹划,而是深信有一只施恩的手在他之先、在他之上动工。今天,你心里是否也有一个神所给的负担?不要只是流泪叹息,也不要贸然冲动。学尼希米:先为它深深地跪下,寻求那施恩的手;然后,凭着信心,勇敢地动工。

默想:面对神放在我心上的负担,我是只叹息却从不行动,还是一冲动就忙着做、却从不先跪下?我是否相信,一切真实的成就都在乎「神施恩的手」,而非我自己的能力?

应用:今天为一个神放在你心上的负担(一个人、一件事、一处需要),先像尼希米一样认真地跪下祷告寻求神,再凭信心迈出一个具体、勇敢的行动。

祷告:施恩的主,尼希米为你百姓的荒凉哭泣、禁食祷告数月,才在王前开口;他深知成就他的,是你施恩的手。我承认,我常在祷告与行动上失衡——要么只叹息不动,要么只忙碌不祷告。求你赐我尼希米的心:先深深跪下,再勇敢动工,并始终倚靠你那在我之先动工的施恩之手。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Nehemiah served as cupbearer in the Persian palace, a position of comfort and privilege. When he heard that Jerusalem’s walls were torn down, its gates burned with fire, and the remnant left in great distress and disgrace, he did not shrug and say, “that’s too far away, not my concern.” Scripture says that as soon as he heard, he sat down and wept, mourned for days, and fasted and prayed before God. A man living securely in a foreign land, so pierced with grief over the desolation of God’s people. True burden always begins with a heart moved by the things of God.

But Nehemiah did not merely weep. He fasted and prayed about this for about four months before, at the right moment, asking the king’s permission to return and rebuild. And when the king granted it, Nehemiah traced this whole accomplishment back to a single source: “And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me” (Nehemiah 2:8). He knew clearly: what moved the king’s heart was not his eloquence or luck, but the good hand of God working behind the scenes. He knelt before God for months before he stood before the king to speak.

Here is a lesson we most easily get out of balance: the order of prayer and action. Some only pray, yet never take any action, using “entrusting it to God” as an excuse for irresponsibility; others, the moment they feel a burden, rush out to act, busying themselves endlessly, yet never kneel first to seek God. Nehemiah did both, and in clear order: kneel first, then get to work. His action did not replace prayer — it grew out of prayer; his prayer did not replace action — it was meant to undergird action. Pray deeply, then act boldly — these two are never in conflict; they are one whole.

Even more crucial is the conviction behind Nehemiah’s words: every true accomplishment comes “because the good hand of my God was upon me.” The task he was about to begin was vast, difficult, opposed on every side; what sustained him was not his own ability and planning, but his deep conviction that a gracious hand was at work ahead of him, above him. Do you too carry a burden today that God has given you? Don’t just sigh and weep, and don’t act rashly either. Learn from Nehemiah: kneel deeply for it first, seeking that gracious hand; then, in faith, get to work boldly.

Meditation: Facing a burden God has placed on my heart, do I only sigh without acting, or do I rush to act impulsively, never kneeling first? Do I believe every true accomplishment depends on “the good hand of God,” rather than my own ability?

Application: Today, for a burden God has placed on your heart (a person, a matter, a need), first seriously kneel and pray to seek God, like Nehemiah, then step out in one concrete, courageous act of faith.

Prayer: Gracious Lord, Nehemiah wept and fasted for months over the desolation of your people before he spoke to the king; he knew deeply that what accomplished it was your gracious hand. I confess I’m often out of balance between prayer and action — either only sighing without moving, or only busying myself without praying. Give me Nehemiah’s heart: to kneel deeply first, then act boldly, always relying on your gracious hand that works ahead of me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 到我这里来得安息——安息与更新
entries.title_en: Come to Me and Find Rest — Rest and Renewal
entries.content:
到我这里来得安息——安息与更新

「凡劳苦担重担的人可以到我这里来,我就使你们得安息。」(马太福音 11:28)

这一周,我们看见希西家尽心的复兴、玛拿西回头的恩典、归回百姓在废墟上先筑坛的敬拜。这一切的重建,都极耗心力。你或许也正劳苦、也正担着重担。

今天安息日,请听主最温柔的邀请:祂没有说「凡够刚强的人到我这里来」,而是说「凡劳苦担重担的人」。你不必先把自己收拾好、先把重担卸下,才够资格来;你只管带着那份劳苦与重担,原原本本地来到祂面前。真正的安息,不是一个地方,也不是一段假期,而是一位——就是主自己。到祂这里来,祂必亲自使你得安息。

"Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28)
entries.content_en:
Come to Me and Find Rest — Rest and Renewal

"Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28)

This week, we saw Hezekiah’s wholehearted revival, Manasseh’s grace of turning back, and the returning people building the altar first amid the ruins. All this rebuilding takes enormous toll. You too may be laboring, carrying a heavy burden.

Today, on the Sabbath, hear the Lord’s most tender invitation: he did not say “all who are strong enough, come to me,” but “all who labor and are heavy laden.” You don’t need to get yourself in order first, or set down your burden first, to qualify to come; you simply bring that labor and that burden, exactly as they are, into his presence. True rest is not a place, nor a vacation, but a person — the Lord himself. Come to him, and he himself will give you rest.

"Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28)

entries.title: 我办理大工,不能下去
entries.title_en: I Am Doing a Great Work; I Cannot Come Down
entries.verse: 尼希米记六章三节
entries.content:
尼希米带领百姓修造耶路撒冷的城墙,仇敌参巴拉和多比雅想尽办法拦阻。硬的不行,就来软的:他们四次差人来请尼希米,说「你来,我们在阿挪平原相会吧」,言语间客客气气,实则暗藏杀机——要把他从工作上引开,好加害于他。这是一个极狡猾的试探:不是叫你去犯罪作恶,只是叫你「离开岗位一下下」,去处理些看似要紧、实则要把你从神的工作上拉下来的事。

尼希米的回答,斩钉截铁,成了每一个想专心事奉神之人的座右铭:「我现在办理大工,不能下去。焉能停工下去见你们呢?」(尼6:3)他看得极清楚:我手上的,是神的大工;任何要把我从这大工上引开的邀请,无论听起来多合理、多诱人,我都不下去。他不是没有别的事可做,而是他分得清什么是「大工」、什么是会叫大工停摆的「下去」。

我们这个时代最擅长的,不是叫人公然背弃神,而是叫人「分心」。数不清的邀请、通知、机会、消遣,每一样单独看都不算坏,却合力把我们一次次从那真正要紧的「大工」上引下来——引离与神亲近的时间,引离神托付我们的呼召,引离我们本该专心去建造的。魔鬼未必需要你去做什么大恶,它只需要让你一直「忙于别的」,让那城墙永远修不完。分心,是这世代最有效的拦阻。

问题的关键,是你有没有认定手上的「大工」——那件神呼召你、此刻最当专心去做的事。一旦认定了,你就有底气对无数「下去一下」的邀请说不。主耶稣一生都专注于父交给祂的工,以致祂能说「我在地上已经荣耀你,你所托付我的事,我已成全了」(约17:4)。今天,什么是神交给你的「大工」?又有什么「阿挪平原的邀请」,正想把你从其上引下来?学尼希米,定睛在大工上,坦然地说:我不能下去。

默想:我认定神此刻交给我的「大工」是什么吗?有哪些看似合理、实则叫我分心的「邀请」,正一次次把我从这大工上引下来?我是否被「忙于别的」拦阻,以致该建造的城墙迟迟修不完?

应用:今天认定一件神此刻呼召你专心去做的「大工」,并对一个一直在分你心的「阿挪平原的邀请」(某个消遣、某件次要的忙碌)清楚地说「不」,守住你的岗位。

祷告:呼召我的主,尼希米认定手上是你的大工,任凭仇敌怎样引诱,都坚定地说「我不能下去」。我承认,这世代最能拦阻我的,不是大恶,而是无数叫我分心的忙碌。求你叫我认清你此刻交托我的大工,赐我定睛其上的专一,能对一切把我引下来的邀请坦然说不。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Nehemiah led the people in rebuilding Jerusalem’s walls, and the enemies Sanballat and Tobiah tried every scheme to stop him. When force didn’t work, they turned soft: four times they sent word to Nehemiah, saying, “Come, let us meet together at Kephirim in the plain of Ono” — polite words on the surface, but murderous intent hidden beneath — to lure him away from the work so they could harm him. This was an extremely cunning temptation: not tempting you to sin outright, but simply to “step away from your post for just a bit,” to attend to something that seems important but would actually pull you off God’s work.

Nehemiah’s answer was decisive, and has become the motto for everyone who wants to serve God single-mindedly: “I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?” (Nehemiah 6:3). He saw with perfect clarity: what is in my hands is God’s great work; any invitation to pull me away from this great work, however reasonable, however enticing it sounds, I will not go down for it. It wasn’t that he had nothing else he could possibly do — it was that he could distinguish clearly what was the “great work,” and what was the “coming down” that would stall it.

What our age is best at is not making people openly forsake God, but making them “distracted.” Countless invitations, notifications, opportunities, diversions — each one, taken alone, doesn’t look so bad, yet together they repeatedly pull us away from the truly important “great work” — away from time close to God, away from the calling God has entrusted to us, away from what we ought to be single-mindedly building. The devil doesn’t necessarily need you to commit some great evil; it only needs to keep you constantly “busy with other things,” so that the wall never gets finished. Distraction is this age’s most effective obstacle.

The crux of the matter is whether you have identified the “great work” in your hands — the thing God has called you to, the thing that most deserves your undivided focus right now. Once identified, you have the grounds to say no to countless invitations to “come down for a bit.” The Lord Jesus spent his whole life focused on the work the Father gave him, so that he could say, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Today, what is the “great work” God has entrusted to you? And what “plain of Ono invitations” are trying to pull you away from it? Learn from Nehemiah — fix your eyes on the great work, and say plainly: I cannot come down.

Meditation: Have I identified the “great work” God has entrusted to me right now? What seemingly reasonable, actually distracting “invitations” keep pulling me away from this great work, again and again? Am I so hindered by being “busy with other things” that the wall I should be building remains unfinished?

Application: Today, identify one “great work” God is calling you to focus on right now, and clearly say “no” to one “plain of Ono invitation” that keeps distracting you (some diversion, some secondary busyness), guarding your post.

Prayer: Lord who calls me, Nehemiah identified God’s great work in his hands, and no matter how the enemy tempted him, he firmly said, “I cannot come down.” I confess that what most hinders me in this age is not great evil, but the countless distracting busyness. Let me clearly recognize the great work you’ve entrusted to me now, give me single-minded focus upon it, and let me plainly say no to every invitation that would pull me down from it. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 靠耶和华而得的喜乐
entries.title_en: The Joy of the LORD
entries.verse: 尼希米记八章十节
entries.content:
城墙修完了,百姓聚集在水门前的宽阔处。文士以斯拉站在木台上,从清晨到晌午,把神的律法书念给众人听。这是被掳归回后,神的话第一次这样公开、完整地向全民宣读。当百姓听明白律法的话,他们做的第一件事,是放声大哭——因为他们看见了自己长久以来何等偏离神的心意,心中充满了懊悔与自责。

然而,尼希米、以斯拉和利未人却制止了他们的哭泣,对他们说了一句出人意料的话:今日是耶和华的圣日,「不要忧愁,因靠耶和华而得的喜乐是你们的力量。」(尼8:10)神的话固然照出了他们的罪,叫他们忧伤;但神在那一刻要给他们的,不是让他们停在自责的忧愁里,而是要他们进入一种更深的喜乐——一种「靠耶和华而得的」、以神自己为满足的喜乐。而这喜乐,正是他们重建生命、走下去的力量。

这里有一个极重要、却常被我们弄反的真理。我们常以为,力量来自咬紧牙关、来自更多的自责与努力;圣经却说,真正的力量,来自「喜乐」——而且是特定的一种喜乐:靠耶和华而得的喜乐。不是靠环境顺遂而来的高兴,不是靠自己表现良好而来的自满,乃是单单以神自己为乐、因祂是我的神而生的喜乐。当一个人真正以神为他心中最深的喜乐,他就有了任何忧愁、任何重担都夺不去的力量。反过来,一个失了神里喜乐的人,无论怎样咬牙硬撑,都是软弱的。

这正是福音要给我们的。认罪之后,神不要我们永远停在懊悔的眼泪里,自我惩罚;祂要我们抬起头,重新在祂里面欢喜——因为在基督里,我们的罪已被赦免,神已成了我们的神。你今天觉得软弱、无力、被重担压得喘不过气吗?或许你缺的不是更多的自责与努力,而是重新回到神面前,支取那「靠耶和华而得的喜乐」。以祂为乐,你就重新有了力量。

默想:我以为力量来自咬牙硬撑、来自更多的自责,还是来自「靠耶和华而得的喜乐」?认罪之后,我是停在自我惩罚的忧愁里,还是进入以神为乐的喜乐?我心中最深的喜乐,是靠环境,还是靠神自己?

应用:今天当你感到软弱无力时,不靠加倍的自责与硬撑,而是刻意回到神面前,数算祂是谁、祂为你做了什么,操练「以神为乐」,从这喜乐里支取力量。

祷告:我的喜乐、我的力量的主,百姓因你的话忧伤痛哭,你却叫他们进入「靠耶和华而得的喜乐」,并说这喜乐是他们的力量。我承认,我常以为力量来自自责与硬撑,以致越发软弱。谢谢你在基督里赦免了我、作了我的神。求你叫我重新以你为乐,从这不能被夺去的喜乐里得着力量。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The wall was finished, and the people gathered in the square before the Water Gate. Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform, and from early morning until midday, read the Book of the Law of God aloud to all the people. This was the first time, since the return from exile, that God’s word was publicly and completely read to the whole nation. When the people understood the words of the Law, the first thing they did was weep aloud — because they saw how far they had long strayed from God’s will, and their hearts were filled with regret and self-reproach.

But Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites stopped their weeping, saying an unexpected word to them: this day is holy to the LORD, “do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10). God’s word had certainly exposed their sin and grieved them; but what God wanted to give them at that moment was not for them to stay stuck in self-reproachful sorrow — he wanted them to enter into a deeper joy — a joy “of the LORD,” a joy satisfied in God himself. And this joy was exactly the strength by which they would rebuild their lives and keep going.

Here is a crucial truth we often get backwards. We often think strength comes from gritting our teeth, from more self-reproach and effort; but Scripture says true strength comes from “joy” — and a specific kind of joy: the joy of the LORD. Not happiness that comes from favorable circumstances, not self-satisfaction from performing well, but joy that comes solely from delighting in God himself, because he is my God. When a person truly makes God his deepest joy, he possesses a strength that no sorrow, no burden, can take away. Conversely, a person who has lost the joy of the Lord, however much he grits his teeth, remains weak.

This is exactly what the gospel wants to give us. After confessing sin, God does not want us to stay forever in tears of regret, punishing ourselves; he wants us to lift our heads and rejoice again in him — because in Christ, our sins are forgiven, and God has become our God. Do you feel weak, powerless, crushed under a burden today? Perhaps what you lack is not more self-reproach and effort, but returning to God again, laying hold of “the joy of the LORD.” Delight in him, and you will have strength again.

Meditation: Do I think strength comes from gritting my teeth, from more self-reproach, or from “the joy of the LORD”? After confessing sin, do I stay stuck in self-punishing sorrow, or enter into the joy of delighting in God? Is my deepest joy dependent on circumstances, or on God himself?

Application: Today, when you feel weak and powerless, instead of doubling down on self-reproach and gritting your teeth, deliberately return to God’s presence, count who he is and what he has done for you, practicing “delighting in God,” and drawing strength from that joy.

Prayer: Lord who is my joy and my strength, the people wept in grief over your word, yet you led them into “the joy of the LORD,” and said this joy was their strength. I confess I often think strength comes from self-reproach and gritting my teeth, only to grow weaker. Thank you for forgiving me in Christ and becoming my God. Let me delight in you again, and draw strength from this joy that can never be taken away. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 守住神所重建的
entries.title_en: Guarding What God Has Rebuilt
entries.verse: 尼希米记十三章十四节
entries.content:
城墙建好了,百姓也立了约,要遵行神的律法,气象一新。故事似乎该在这里画上圆满的句号。然而尼希米记的最后一章,却给我们看见一幅现实得叫人心沉的画面:尼希米因事离开耶路撒冷一段时间,再回来时,发现一切又走了样——圣殿的库房被外人占用,利未人因得不到供应而离散,安息日照样有人做买卖,百姓又与外邦人通婚。他辛苦重建的一切,竟在他一转身之间,悄悄地滑回了老样子。

这提醒我们一个常被忽略的属灵真相:建造难,守住更难。神在我们身上动了工、给了我们复兴、重建了某个荒废的领域,这固然宝贵;但属灵的生命不是一次建成、就永远稳固的。人心有一种可怕的下坠力,总在不知不觉中往回滑——你一松手、一疏忽、一离开,那些好不容易建立起来的,就会慢慢地荒废、变质、回到从前。得着,需要恩典;守住所得着的,同样需要天天的儆醒与看守。

尼希米面对这一切,没有灰心撒手,而是再一次挺身而出,大刀阔斧地重整:洁净库房、召回利未人、严守安息日、责备通婚。他一面认真地对付,一面反复向神祷告:「我的神啊,求你因这事记念我,不要涂抹我为神的殿与其中的礼节所行的善。」(尼13:14)他知道,守护神的家、守护那被重建的圣洁,是一场不能松懈的持久战;而在这场持久战里,他所倚靠、所仰望的,始终是那位记念他的神。

你的生命中,是否也有一处神曾重建、如今却又在悄悄回滑的领域?一个曾经戒掉、如今又冒头的旧习;一段曾经修复、如今又冷淡的关系;一个曾经火热、如今又松懈的属灵操练?不要以为「建好了就一劳永逸」。求神给你尼希米那样的儆醒与勇气,一面靠祂的恩典天天看守你已得着的,一面在滑落之处再次挺身重整;并像他一样,把这场持久的守护,天天交托给那位始终记念你的神。

默想:我是否以为属灵的建造「一次建好就永远稳固」,而忽略了守住所得着的同样需要天天儆醒?我生命中有没有一处神曾重建、如今却在悄悄回滑的领域?

应用:今天指认一个你曾靠神得胜、如今却在松懈回滑的领域(一个旧习、一段关系、一项操练),像尼希米一样再次挺身重整它,并把这守护交托给那记念你的神。

祷告:记念我的主,尼希米重建的一切,一转身竟又滑回老样子;他却再次挺身重整,并求你记念。我承认,我常以为建好就一劳永逸,忽略了人心可怕的下坠力。求你赐我儆醒与勇气,靠你的恩典天天看守你在我身上所重建的,在滑落之处再次挺身;这场持久战,我天天交托给记念我的你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The wall was built, and the people had made a covenant to keep God’s law — everything looked fresh and renewed. The story seems like it should end here, on a perfect note. Yet the final chapter of Nehemiah shows us a picture heavy enough to sink the heart: Nehemiah left Jerusalem for a time on business, and when he returned, he found everything had slipped out of shape again — the temple storerooms had been taken over by outsiders, the Levites had scattered for lack of provision, people were doing business on the Sabbath as usual, and the people had intermarried with foreigners again. Everything he had worked so hard to rebuild had quietly slid back to its old state the moment he turned his back.

This reminds us of a spiritual truth we easily overlook: building is hard, but guarding what’s built is harder. That God has worked in us, given us revival, rebuilt some desolate area of our lives — this is certainly precious; but the spiritual life is not something built once and settled forever. There is a fearsome pull of gravity in the human heart, always sliding backward without our noticing — the moment you let go, grow careless, or step away, all that was so hard-won will slowly fall into disrepair, degenerate, and return to how it was. Gaining requires grace; guarding what has been gained requires just as much daily watchfulness.

Facing all this, Nehemiah did not give up in discouragement — he rose up once more, decisively reordering everything: cleansing the storerooms, recalling the Levites, strictly keeping the Sabbath, rebuking the intermarriages. As he seriously dealt with it, he also repeatedly prayed to God: “Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and do not wipe out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God and for his service” (Nehemiah 13:14). He knew that guarding God’s house, guarding the holiness that had been rebuilt, was a long war that could not be relaxed for a moment; and in this long war, what he relied on, what he looked to, was always the God who remembered him.

Is there an area in your life, too, that God once rebuilt, but is now quietly sliding back? An old habit you once broke, now resurfacing; a relationship once repaired, now growing cold again; a spiritual discipline once on fire, now slack again? Don’t assume “once built, it’s settled forever.” Ask God to give you Nehemiah’s watchfulness and courage — relying on his grace to guard daily what you’ve already gained, and rising up again to reorder whatever is slipping; and like him, entrust this ongoing guardianship, day after day, to the God who always remembers you.

Meditation: Do I assume that spiritual building “once done is settled forever,” overlooking that guarding what’s been gained requires just as much daily watchfulness? Is there an area in my life that God once rebuilt, but is now quietly sliding back?

Application: Today, identify one area where you once had victory in God but are now slackening and sliding back (an old habit, a relationship, a discipline); like Nehemiah, rise up again to reorder it, and entrust this guardianship to the God who remembers you.

Prayer: Lord who remembers me, everything Nehemiah rebuilt slipped back the moment he turned away; yet he rose up again to reorder it, and asked you to remember him. I confess I often assume that once built, things are settled forever, overlooking the fearsome pull of the human heart to slide backward. Give me watchfulness and courage, relying on your grace to guard daily what you’ve rebuilt in me, rising up again wherever it’s slipping; I entrust this long war, day after day, to you who remember me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 为了现今的机会
entries.title_en: For Such a Time as This
entries.verse: 以斯帖记四章十四节
entries.content:
以斯帖记是圣经中一卷奇特的书:从头到尾,没有出现过一次「神」的名字。没有神迹,没有先知,没有直接的启示,读起来仿佛只是波斯宫廷里一连串的巧合——一个犹大孤女意外被选为王后,一个太监的密谋恰好被记下,一个王恰好在某夜失眠。然而,正是在这看似「神隐身」的故事里,我们看见了神最真实、最深刻的一种作为:祂在幕后,借着环境、时机、人的选择,一步一步地成就祂的救赎。

当灭族的危机临到,末底改对王后以斯帖说出了那句震撼千古的话:「此时你若闭口不言,犹大人必从别处得解脱,蒙拯救……焉知你得了王后的位分,不是为现今的机会吗?」(斯4:14)这句话里有两个惊人的信念。其一:神的拯救必不落空——你若沉默,神会从别处兴起拯救,祂的计划不倚赖你。其二:然而神却把「你」放在了这个位分、这个时刻,绝非偶然——你的处境、你的身份、你此刻所在的地方,都是神精心的安排,为要借你成就祂的美意。

这正是神对待我们每一个人的方式。你今天所在的位置——你的家庭、你的职场、你的人际圈、你所处的这个时代与难处——都不是随机掉落的,而是神有意的安排。你或许常觉得自己平凡、无足轻重,处境也不过是偶然;但神却在问你:焉知你被放在这个位分、这个时刻,不正是「为了现今的机会」吗?祂把你放在那里,是要借着你,在那个别人到不了的角落,成就祂的心意。

神的主权与你的责任,在这里奇妙地交汇:一面,拯救全在于神,祂的计划断不落空,这除去了我们的重担与惧怕;另一面,神偏偏拣选借着你去成就,这赋予了我们的人生真实的意义与呼召。那位最终「为了现今的机会」而来、甘愿为拯救我们舍命的,正是基督自己。今天,求神开你的眼,看见你被放在何处、为着何等的机会;不要闭口不言,乃要为着神所交托你的那一处,勇敢地站出来。

默想:我是否觉得自己的处境、身份不过是偶然,自己平凡得无足轻重?我能否相信,神把我放在现今的位分与时刻,是「为了现今的机会」、要借我成就祂的心意?

应用:今天求神让你看见,祂把你放在你的家庭、职场或人际圈中,是为了什么「现今的机会」;并在那一处,勇敢地迈出一步去回应,不再闭口不言、袖手旁观。

祷告:在暗中掌权的主,以斯帖记里虽不见你的名,却处处是你的手。谢谢你借末底改提醒:拯救不落空,而我却被放在这位分,是为了现今的机会。我承认,我常小看自己的处境,以为不过是偶然。求你开我的眼,看见你把我放在何处、为何而放,叫我不闭口不言,勇敢地为你所托付的站出来。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Esther is a peculiar book in Scripture: from beginning to end, the name “God” never once appears. No miracles, no prophets, no direct revelation — reading it feels like nothing more than a string of coincidences in the Persian court: an orphaned Jewish girl unexpectedly chosen as queen, a eunuch’s plot happening to be recorded, a king happening to suffer insomnia on a certain night. Yet it is precisely in this story where God seems to hide, that we see one of God’s most real, most profound ways of working: he works behind the scenes, through circumstances, timing, and human choices, accomplishing his redemption step by step.

When the crisis of annihilation came, Mordecai spoke these words to Queen Esther, words that have echoed through the ages: “For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place... And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14). Two astonishing convictions are held in this sentence. First: God’s deliverance will surely not fail — if you stay silent, God will raise up deliverance from elsewhere; his plan does not depend on you. Second: yet God placed “you” in this position, at this moment, by no means by accident — your circumstances, your identity, the place where you now stand, are all God’s deliberate arrangement, so that through you he might accomplish his good purpose.

This is exactly how God deals with each of us. Where you stand today — your family, your workplace, your circle of relationships, this era and these difficulties you find yourself in — none of it fell there at random; it is God’s deliberate arrangement. You may often feel yourself ordinary, insignificant, your circumstances merely coincidental; but God is asking you: who knows whether you have been placed in this position, at this moment, not precisely “for such a time as this”? He has placed you there so that, through you, in a corner others cannot reach, he might accomplish his purpose.

God’s sovereignty and your responsibility meet wonderfully here: on one hand, deliverance rests entirely with God, his plan will surely not fail — this removes our burden and fear; on the other hand, God has specifically chosen to accomplish it through you — this gives our lives real meaning and calling. The one who ultimately came “for such a time as this,” willingly laying down his life to save us, is Christ himself. Today, ask God to open your eyes, to see where you’ve been placed and for what opportunity; don’t stay silent — stand up boldly for the place God has entrusted to you.

Meditation: Do I feel my circumstances and identity are merely coincidental, myself too ordinary to matter? Can I believe that God has placed me in my present position and moment “for such a time as this,” to accomplish his purpose through me?

Application: Today, ask God to show you what “opportunity for such a time as this” he has placed you in your family, workplace, or circle of relationships for; and in that place, boldly take one step to respond, no longer staying silent or standing idly by.

Prayer: Lord who reigns in secret, though your name never appears in Esther, your hand is everywhere in it. Thank you for reminding me, through Mordecai, that deliverance will not fail, yet I have been placed in this position for such a time as this. I confess I often belittle my own circumstances, thinking them merely coincidental. Open my eyes to see where and why you have placed me, and let me not stay silent, but boldly stand up for what you have entrusted to me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 那夜,王睡不着觉
entries.title_en: That Night, the King Could Not Sleep
entries.verse: 以斯帖记六章一节
entries.content:
哈曼的阴谋眼看就要得逞。他因末底改不肯向他跪拜,怒火中烧,不但要杀末底改,更要灭绝波斯全国的犹大人;他甚至已经竖起了一座五丈高的木架,专为吊死末底改而预备。局势看起来对神的百姓极其不利:权势、诏书、木架,全都在恶人这一边。然而,神却借着一件极小、极不起眼的事,让整个局面彻底翻转。

「那夜,王睡不着觉,就吩咐人取历史来,念给他听。」(斯6:1)就是这么一件小事——王失眠了。他叫人念宫廷的历史,恰好念到末底改从前揭发刺王阴谋、救过王命、却一直未得赏赐的记载。于是就在哈曼进宫、想求王吊死末底改的那个清晨,王反倒问哈曼:「王所喜悦尊荣的人,当如何待他呢?」结局众所周知:哈曼被迫牵着马,让末底改尊荣游街;不久,他自己被挂在了那为末底改预备的木架上。

请留意神翻转全局的「手段」:不是一场地震,不是一位天使显现,而仅仅是一个王在某一夜的失眠。圣经在这里没有提神的名字,但每一个信的人都看得见——那使王睡不着觉的,是谁?那叫人恰好念到那一段历史的,又是谁?神掌管万有,大到列国的兴衰,小到一个人某一夜的睡与不睡;祂能用最微不足道的一件小事,来成就祂拯救的大计,来翻转看似无可挽回的绝境。恶人自以为稳操胜券,却不知道有一位在暗中,连他仇敌的失眠都在使用。

这给一切正处在「哈曼的木架」阴影下的人极大的安慰。当邪恶看似占尽上风、当局势看似全然不利、当你觉得神仿佛缺席时,请记得那个睡不着觉的夜晚:神从未缺席,祂正借着你看不见的、微小的、看似偶然的方式,在幕后一步步翻转全局。「义人多有苦难,但耶和华救他脱离这一切。」(诗34:19)你的神,连一个王的失眠都在祂手中——你还有什么绝境,是祂翻转不了的呢?

默想:当邪恶看似占上风、局势全然不利、神仿佛缺席时,我是绝望,还是相信神正借着我看不见的方式在幕后动工?我是否小看了神,以为祂只能借「大神迹」、而不能借一件小事来翻转全局?

应用:今天把一个你觉得「已成定局、无可挽回」的难处,重新交在那位连王的失眠都掌管的神手中;拒绝绝望,凭信心等候祂在暗中翻转,并留意祂借小事施行的作为。

祷告:掌管万有的主,你借着一个王某夜的失眠,就翻转了灭族的绝境。我承认,当邪恶占上风、你仿佛缺席时,我常绝望,又小看你只能借大神迹动工。求你叫我看见,大到列国、小到一夜的睡与不睡,都在你手中;叫我把一切绝境交给你,凭信心等候你在暗中翻转全局。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Haman’s plot was about to succeed. Enraged that Mordecai would not bow to him, he intended not only to kill Mordecai but to annihilate all the Jews throughout the Persian empire; he had even erected a gallows fifty cubits high, prepared specifically to hang Mordecai. The situation looked extremely unfavorable for God’s people: power, decree, gallows — all on the side of the wicked. Yet God, through one extremely small, extremely unremarkable event, completely reversed the entire situation.

“On that night the king could not sleep, and he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king” (Esther 6:1). It was just such a small thing — the king had insomnia. He had someone read the court records to him, and it happened to land on the account of how Mordecai had once exposed a plot to assassinate the king, saving his life, yet had never been rewarded. So, on the very morning Haman entered the palace hoping to ask the king to hang Mordecai, the king instead asked Haman: “What should be done for the man whom the king delights to honor?” The outcome is well known: Haman was forced to lead Mordecai through the streets in honor; not long after, he himself was hanged on the very gallows he had prepared for Mordecai.

Notice the “means” by which God reversed the entire situation: not an earthquake, not an angel’s appearance, but simply a king’s insomnia on one particular night. Scripture never mentions God’s name here, but every believer can see it — who kept the king awake that night? Who made them happen to read that particular passage of history? God governs all things, from the rise and fall of nations down to whether one man sleeps or wakes on a given night; he can use the most insignificant small thing to accomplish his great plan of salvation, to reverse what seems like an irreversible dead end. The wicked thought themselves assured of victory, never knowing that One works in secret, using even his enemy’s insomnia.

This gives tremendous comfort to everyone currently living under the shadow of “Haman’s gallows.” When evil seems to have the upper hand, when the situation seems entirely unfavorable, when you feel as though God is absent, remember that sleepless night: God was never absent — he is, through ways you cannot see, small, seemingly coincidental means, turning the whole situation around, step by step, behind the scenes. “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all” (Psalm 34:19). Your God holds even a king’s insomnia in his hand — what dead end is there that he cannot reverse?

Meditation: When evil seems to have the upper hand, the situation entirely unfavorable, and God seems absent, do I despair, or believe that God is working behind the scenes through means I cannot see? Have I underestimated God, thinking he can only work through “great miracles,” not through some small thing, to turn the whole situation around?

Application: Today, hand over a difficulty you feel is “a foregone conclusion, beyond hope” once again to the God who governs even a king’s insomnia; refuse despair, wait in faith for him to turn things around in secret, and watch for how he works through small things.

Prayer: Lord who governs all things, you turned around a plot of annihilation through a king’s insomnia on one particular night. I confess that when evil has the upper hand and you seem absent, I often despair, and underestimate you, thinking you can only work through great miracles. Let me see that from nations to a single night’s sleep, everything is in your hand; let me hand every dead end over to you, and wait in faith for you to turn the whole situation around in secret. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 为本族的人求好处
entries.title_en: Seeking the Good of His People
entries.verse: 以斯帖记十章三节
entries.content:
危机解除了。哈曼被除,末底改被高升为宰相,犹大人不但脱离灭族之祸,还得胜有余。这是一个大团圆的结局。而在故事的最后,圣经为末底改留下了一句意味深长的总评——不是称赞他官做得多大、权势多显赫,而是记下他如何使用他的地位。

「犹大人末底改作亚哈随鲁王的宰相,在犹大人中为大,得他众弟兄的喜悦,为本族的人求好处,向他们说和平的话。」(斯10:3)注意这后半句:他「为本族的人求好处」。末底改爬到了一人之下、万人之上的高位,他却没有用这权势来谋自己的享受、巩固自己的地位、报复自己的仇敌;他用它来为神的百姓谋福、为他们说和平的话。他把神所赐的地位,当作服事他人的器皿,而非满足自己的资本。

这一句总评,是对我们每一个「有点什么」的人的拷问。你我或许没有宰相之位,但我们各自都握着某种「地位」——一份影响力、一点资源、一些人脉、一个职分、一份在家庭或群体中的分量。问题是:我们拿这些来做什么?人的天性,是用一切所拥有的来为自己谋好处——更多的舒适、更大的名声、更稳的地位。神却呼召我们,像末底改一样,把手中所有的,转过来「为别人求好处」。地位越高,越是服事的机会,而非享受的资本。

这正是主耶稣自己的样式。祂本有神的形象,却虚己,取了奴仆的样式,不是要受人的服事,乃是要服事人,并且为我们舍命(可10:45)。祂拥有至高的地位,却完完全全地用来「为我们求好处」——甚至舍了自己的命。今天,神放在你手中的那一点地位、影响力、资源,你是拿来为自己谋好处,还是像末底改、像你的主一样,拿来为别人求好处、向人说和平的话?

默想:神放在我手中的「地位」(影响力、资源、人脉、职分),我是拿来为自己谋好处,还是「为别人求好处」?我是否把所拥有的当作享受的资本,而非服事他人的器皿?

应用:今天在你所在的一个「有点分量」的位置上(家庭、职场、群体),刻意用你的影响力或资源去为某个人求好处、说一句和平的话,而非只为自己谋利。

祷告:为我舍命的主,末底改身居高位,却用它为本族的人求好处、说和平的话。我省察自己,我总想用手中所有的为自己谋好处。谢谢你本有神的形象,却虚己作仆人,为我求好处,甚至舍命。求你叫我效法你,把你放在我手中的一切地位与资源,转过来为别人求好处、向人说和平的话。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The crisis was averted. Haman was removed, Mordecai was promoted to prime minister, and the Jews were not only delivered from annihilation, but triumphed with abundance. It was a grand, happy ending. And at the very end of the story, Scripture leaves a pregnant final assessment of Mordecai — not praising how high his office was, how prominent his power, but recording how he used his position.

“For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people” (Esther 10:3). Notice the second half of this sentence: he “sought the welfare of his people.” Mordecai climbed to a position second only to the king himself, yet he did not use that power to pursue his own enjoyment, consolidate his own status, or take revenge on his own enemies; he used it to seek the good of God’s people, to speak peace to them. He treated the position God gave him as a vessel for serving others, not as capital for satisfying himself.

This single assessment is a searching question for every one of us who has “a bit of something.” You and I may hold no office of prime minister, but each of us holds some kind of “position” — a measure of influence, a bit of resources, some connections, a role, a certain weight within a family or group. The question is: what do we do with these? Human nature is to use everything we have to seek our own good — more comfort, greater fame, more secure status. Yet God calls us, like Mordecai, to turn what’s in our hands around to “seek the good of others.” The higher the position, the greater the opportunity for service, not for enjoyment.

This is exactly the pattern of the Lord Jesus himself. Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life for us (Mark 10:45). He held the highest position, yet used it completely to “seek our good” — even to the giving up of his own life. Today, that bit of position, influence, or resource God has placed in your hands — are you using it to seek good for yourself, or, like Mordecai, like your Lord, to seek good for others and speak a word of peace?

Meditation: The “position” God has placed in my hands (influence, resources, connections, role) — am I using it to seek good for myself, or “to seek good for others”? Do I treat what I have as capital for my own enjoyment, rather than as a vessel for serving others?

Application: Today, in some position of “a bit of weight” you hold (family, workplace, group), deliberately use your influence or resources to seek good for someone, to speak a word of peace, rather than only pursuing benefit for yourself.

Prayer: Lord who gave your life for me, Mordecai held a high position, yet used it to seek good for his people and speak peace. I examine myself, and I always want to use what’s in my hands to seek good for myself. Thank you that though you were in the form of God, you emptied yourself as a servant, sought my good, and even gave your life. Let me follow your example, turning every position and resource you’ve placed in my hands around to seek good for others, and to speak a word of peace. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
