entries.title: 用智慧建立世界的主——记念神的创造
entries.title_en: The Lord Who Established the World by Wisdom — Remembering God's Creation
entries.content:
用智慧建立世界的主——记念神的创造

「耶和华用能力创造大地,用智慧建立世界,用聪明铺张穹苍。」(耶利米书 10:12)

这一周,我们随耶利米走过审判、被掳、又看见新约的应许。就在斥责偶像的虚假时,耶利米抬起头,把独一真神与那些不能行、不能救的偶像相比——祂是用能力、智慧、聪明创造并托住万有的主。

今天安息日,默想这三个词:能力、智慧、聪明。神造这世界,不是随手而成的,乃是以祂无穷的「能力」立定根基、以祂深不可测的「智慧」精心设计、以祂的「聪明」铺张浩瀚的诸天。你抬头所见的每一颗星、低头所见的每一片叶,都出自这位又有能力、又有智慧的创造主之手。那用如此的智慧造了、又托住了整个宇宙的神,岂会没有智慧安排你这一生的每一个细节呢?在祂能力与智慧的创造里,安息、敬拜、并且放心地把你的一生交托给祂。

"It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom." (Jeremiah 10:12)
entries.content_en:
The Lord Who Established the World by Wisdom — Remembering God's Creation

"It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens." (Jeremiah 10:12)

This week, we walked with Jeremiah through judgment, exile, and glimpsed the promise of the new covenant. Right in the middle of rebuking the falseness of idols, Jeremiah looked up, and compared the one true God to those idols that cannot act, cannot save — he is the Lord who created and sustains all things by power, wisdom, and understanding.

Today, on the Sabbath, meditate on these three words: power, wisdom, understanding. God did not make this world offhandedly — he laid its foundation with his boundless "power," designed it carefully with his unfathomable "wisdom," and stretched out the vast heavens with his "understanding." Every star you see when you look up, every leaf you see when you look down, comes from the hand of this Creator, both powerful and wise. The God who made, and sustains, the entire universe with such wisdom — would he lack the wisdom to arrange every detail of your life? Rest, worship, and confidently entrust your whole life to him, in this creation of his power and wisdom.

"It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom." (Jeremiah 10:12)

entries.title: 他们的救赎主大有能力
entries.title_en: Their Redeemer Is Strong
entries.verse: 耶利米书五十章卅四节
entries.content:
耶利米书的末了,神把审判的目光,转向了那个曾被祂用来管教犹大的国——巴比伦。这个不可一世的帝国,以为自己的强盛出于自己,便肆意欺压、掳掠神的百姓;神却宣告,它的日子到了,它必要倾覆。而在宣告巴比伦倾覆的同时,神对祂那被掳、被欺压、看似被撇弃的百姓,说了一句满有安慰的话。

「他们的救赎主大有能力,万军之耶和华是他的名。他必伸清他们的冤,好使全地得平安。」(耶50:34)在被掳之地,神的百姓大概觉得自己孤苦无告:强敌当前,无人替他们说话,无人替他们伸冤,仿佛神也忘了他们。神却宣告:你们的「救赎主大有能力」!「救赎主」——原文指那位有权、有责为落难的至亲赎回产业、伸冤报仇的近亲;神说,祂就是以色列的救赎主,而且祂「大有能力」,是「万军之耶和华」。你们不是孤苦无告的;有一位大能的至亲,已经站在你们这边,祂必亲自替你们伸冤、为你们争战。

这真理,对每一个觉得自己被欺压、被亏待、无处申冤的人,是极大的安慰。我们受了冤屈,常常最痛苦的,不是那冤屈本身,而是那种「无人替我说话、无处讨公道」的孤立无助。我们要么忍气吞声、暗自苦毒,要么想亲手报复、讨回公道,结果把自己也拖进罪里。神却提醒我们:你有一位「大有能力」的救赎主;你不必自己去伸冤,也不必绝望地忍受不义——把你的冤屈,交在这位大能的救赎主手中,祂必亲自为你伸清。「伸冤在我,我必报应」(罗12:19)——这不是叫我们纵容不义,而是把讨公道的权柄,从我们无力的手中,交回给那位大有能力、绝不误事的神。

以色列的这位救赎主,最终有了一个名字。祂就是耶稣基督——那位不但要在末日审判一切不义、为祂受苦的百姓伸尽冤屈的大能君王,更是那位付上自己性命的赎价、把我们从罪与死的辖制中赎回来的大救赎主。「你们……不是凭着能坏的金银……乃是凭着基督的宝血」(彼前1:18-19)被赎的。今天,你若正被某种不义欺压、觉得无人替你说话、无处申冤,不要独自苦毒,也不要亲手报复;抬起头来,你有一位大有能力的救赎主,万军之耶和华是祂的名。把你的冤屈交给祂,祂必伸清。

默想:我受了冤屈时,最深的痛苦是否是那种「无人替我说话、无处讨公道」的孤立无助?我是忍气吞声暗自苦毒,还是想亲手报复?我是否真相信,我有一位「大有能力」的救赎主,祂必亲自为我伸清冤屈?

应用:今天把一件你受的冤屈、觉得无处申冤的事,交在那位大能的救赎主手中;放下亲手报复的冲动、也放下暗自的苦毒,把讨公道的权柄交还给那位「必伸清你冤」、绝不误事的神。

祷告:大有能力的救赎主,你向被掳受欺的百姓宣告:他们的救赎主大有能力,必伸清他们的冤。我承认,我受冤屈时,常暗自苦毒、或想亲手报复,把自己拖进罪里。谢谢你不但要在末日为我伸尽冤屈,更用基督的宝血把我从罪与死中赎回。求你叫我把一切冤屈交在你手中,信靠你必伸清,不再独自苦毒或报复。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
At the end of the book of Jeremiah, God turns his gaze of judgment toward the very nation he had once used to discipline Judah — Babylon. This unrivaled empire, thinking its strength came from itself, wantonly oppressed and plundered God’s people; yet God declares that its day has come, and it must fall. And in the very act of declaring Babylon’s downfall, God speaks a sentence full of comfort to his people — exiled, oppressed, seemingly forsaken.

“Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth” (Jeremiah 50:34). In the land of exile, God’s people probably felt themselves utterly helpless: facing a mighty enemy, no one to speak for them, no one to plead their cause, as though even God had forgotten them. Yet God declares: your “Redeemer is strong”! “Redeemer” — in the original, refers to that close relative with the right and duty to redeem the inheritance of a fallen kin, to plead their cause and avenge them; God says he himself is Israel’s Redeemer, and he is “strong,” “the LORD of hosts.” You are not helpless and alone; a mighty kinsman has already stood on your side, and he will personally plead your cause, fight for you.

This truth is such great comfort to everyone who feels oppressed, wronged, with nowhere to seek justice. When we’ve suffered injustice, often the most painful part is not the injustice itself, but that isolated helplessness of “no one speaks for me, nowhere to seek justice.” We either swallow our anger and grow secretly bitter, or want to take revenge with our own hands, and end up dragging ourselves into sin too. But God reminds us: you have a Redeemer who is “strong”; you don’t need to plead your own cause, nor despairingly endure injustice — hand your grievance into the hands of this mighty Redeemer, and he will personally set it right for you. “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19) — this doesn’t call us to condone injustice, but to hand the authority to seek justice, from our powerless hands, back to the God who is mighty and never fails.

This Redeemer of Israel ultimately has a name. He is Jesus Christ — not only the mighty King who will, on the last day, judge all injustice and fully vindicate his suffering people, but also the great Redeemer who paid the ransom with his own life, redeeming us from the dominion of sin and death. “You... were ransomed... not with perishable things such as silver or gold... but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18-19). Today, if you’re being oppressed by some injustice, feeling that no one speaks for you, nowhere to seek justice, don’t grow bitter alone, and don’t take revenge with your own hands; lift up your head — you have a Redeemer who is strong, the LORD of hosts is his name. Hand your grievance to him, and he will surely set it right.

Meditation: When I’ve suffered injustice, is my deepest pain that isolated helplessness of “no one speaks for me, nowhere to seek justice”? Do I swallow my anger and grow secretly bitter, or want to take revenge with my own hands? Do I truly believe I have a Redeemer who is “strong,” who will personally set my grievance right?

Application: Today, hand an injustice you’ve suffered, something you feel has nowhere to seek justice, into the hands of this mighty Redeemer; lay down the impulse to take revenge with your own hands, and lay down secret bitterness too, handing the authority to seek justice back to the God who “will surely set your wrong right” and never fails.

Prayer: Mighty Redeemer, you declared to your exiled, oppressed people: their Redeemer is strong, and will surely plead their cause. I confess that when I’ve suffered injustice, I often grow secretly bitter, or want to take revenge with my own hands, dragging myself into sin. Thank you that you will not only fully vindicate me on the last day, but have also redeemed me from sin and death with Christ’s precious blood. Let me hand all my grievances into your hands, trusting you will surely set them right, no longer bitter or vengeful alone. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 每早晨都是新的
entries.title_en: New Every Morning
entries.verse: 耶利米哀歌三章廿二节
entries.content:
耶利米哀歌,是耶利米为耶路撒冷的倾覆所写的一卷挽歌。字里行间,是撕心裂肺的哀恸:圣城成了废墟,圣殿被焚,百姓被掳,饥荒中连母亲都吃了自己的孩子。这是一卷从最深的痛苦、最黑的绝境中流出的书。然而,恰恰在全书的正中央、在这一片废墟与眼泪的最深处,忽然迸发出一段全本圣经中论神信实最灿烂的宣告。

「我们不致消灭,是出于耶和华诸般的慈爱;是因他的怜悯不致断绝。每早晨,这都是新的;你的诚实极其广大!」(哀3:22-23)请留意这宣告的处境:它不是在春风得意时唱出的,而是在国破家亡、万念俱灰的废墟上迸发的。耶利米环顾四周,满目疮痍;可他抬起头,却看见了一件比废墟更真实的事:我们竟然还没有被灭绝净尽——这本身,就是神的慈爱与怜悯还在的铁证!在一片「一切都失去了」的哀恸中,他抓住了那「不致断绝」的一样:神的怜悯。

而他形容这怜悯的方式,格外美:「每早晨,这都是新的。」神的怜悯,不是一笔会用完的存款,不是昨天用了今天就少一点的东西;它像每天清晨的日出,每一个早晨,都是崭新的、充足的、重新临到的。无论昨天你如何失败、如何跌倒、如何耗尽,当新的一天破晓,神的怜悯又是全新的、丰满的,在那里等着你。你无法用尽神的怜悯,因为它每早晨都重新供应;你昨天的罪与失败,拦不住今晨神向你重新涌流的慈爱。这对每一个被过去缠累、觉得「我已经把神的耐心耗尽了」的人,是何等的福音。

耶利米何以能在废墟上,如此确信神的怜悯每早晨都是新的?他所凭的,是神的「诚实(信实)极其广大」——神必守约、必不改变的性情。而这份信实,在基督里得着了最终、最确凿的印证:神向我们的慈爱,已经在十字架上一次而永远地证明了;基督的复活,更是那「永远的早晨」,保证了神的怜悯永不断绝。所以,无论你正站在怎样的「废墟」上——一段失败、一场失丧、一个看似一切都毁了的境地——请抓住耶利米在废墟上所抓住的:神的慈爱不致断绝,祂的怜悯每早晨都是新的。今晨,它又重新临到你了。

默想:我是否正站在某种「废墟」上,觉得一切都失去了、都毁了?在这境地里,我能否像耶利米一样,抓住那「不致断绝」的一样——神的怜悯?我是否觉得自己已把神的耐心耗尽,却忘了祂的怜悯「每早晨都是新的」、无法被我用尽?

应用:今天早晨(或此刻),刻意支取「神的怜悯每早晨都是新的」这一应许——把昨天的失败、跌倒、耗尽交给神,不让它拦阻你;领受今晨神向你重新涌流的、全新充足的慈爱,重新起来。

祷告:信实的主,耶利米在国破家亡的废墟上,却抓住了你不致断绝的怜悯——「每早晨,这都是新的」。我承认,我常被过去的失败缠累,以为已把你的耐心耗尽。谢谢你的慈爱在十字架上一次而永远地证明了,你的怜悯每早晨都重新临到,无法被我用尽。求你叫我在自己的废墟上,抓住你不改变的信实,领受今晨你向我重新涌流的慈爱。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Lamentations is a book of dirges Jeremiah wrote for Jerusalem’s downfall. Every line is heart-wrenching grief: the holy city reduced to ruins, the temple burned, the people carried away, and in the famine, even mothers ate their own children. This is a book flowing out of the deepest pain, the darkest dead end. Yet right in the very middle of the book, at the deepest point of this ruin and these tears, one of the most brilliant declarations in all of Scripture about God’s faithfulness suddenly bursts forth.

“The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22-23). Notice the circumstances of this declaration: it was not sung in a season of ease and success, but burst forth on the ruins of a nation destroyed, a family shattered, in utter despair. Jeremiah looked around and saw devastation everywhere; yet he lifted his head and saw something more real than the ruins: we have not yet been utterly consumed — this itself is ironclad proof that God’s steadfast love and mercy are still there! Amid the mourning of “everything is lost,” he grasped hold of the one thing that “never ends”: God’s mercy.

And the way he describes this mercy is especially beautiful: “they are new every morning.” God’s mercy is not a savings account that could run out, not something that dwindles bit by bit as it’s used up each day; it’s like the sunrise every morning — every single morning, it is brand new, sufficient, arriving afresh. However you failed yesterday, however you stumbled, however exhausted you are, when the new day breaks, God’s mercy is again completely new and full, waiting there for you. You cannot exhaust God’s mercy, because it is supplied afresh every morning; your sin and failure yesterday cannot hold back the steadfast love flowing afresh toward you this morning. What good news this is for anyone burdened by the past, feeling “I’ve already used up God’s patience.”

How could Jeremiah, amid the ruins, be so certain that God’s mercy is new every morning? What he relied on was that God’s “faithfulness is great” — God’s unchanging character, that he must keep his covenant. And this faithfulness has received its final, most certain confirmation in Christ: God’s steadfast love toward us has already been proven, once and for all, on the cross; Christ’s resurrection is even more that “eternal morning,” guaranteeing that God’s mercy never ceases. So whatever kind of “ruins” you’re standing on today — a failure, a loss, a situation that seems utterly destroyed — hold onto what Jeremiah held onto amid the ruins: God’s steadfast love never ceases, his mercies are new every morning. This morning, they have come to you afresh again.

Meditation: Am I standing on some kind of “ruins,” feeling everything is lost, everything destroyed? In this situation, can I, like Jeremiah, hold onto the one thing that “never ceases” — God’s mercy? Do I feel I’ve already used up God’s patience, forgetting that his mercy is “new every morning,” something I could never exhaust?

Application: This morning (or right now), deliberately draw on the promise that “God’s mercy is new every morning” — hand yesterday’s failure, stumbling, and exhaustion over to God, refusing to let it hinder you; receive the fresh, completely sufficient steadfast love flowing toward you this morning, and rise again.

Prayer: Faithful Lord, Jeremiah, amid the ruins of national destruction and family collapse, held onto your never-ceasing mercy — “they are new every morning.” I confess I’m often burdened by past failures, thinking I’ve already used up your patience. Thank you that your steadfast love was proven once and for all on the cross, and your mercy arrives afresh every morning, something I could never exhaust. Let me, on my own ruins, hold onto your unchanging faithfulness, and receive the steadfast love flowing toward me afresh this morning. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我一看见就俯伏在地
entries.title_en: When I Saw It, I Fell on My Face
entries.verse: 以西结书一章廿八节
entries.content:
以西结是被掳到巴比伦的祭司。就在异乡的迦巴鲁河边,神向他显现了一个极其奇异、极其荣耀的异象:狂风、大云、闪烁的火、四个活物、旋转的轮子,轮辋周围满了眼睛;活物头上有穹苍,穹苍之上有宝座的形象;宝座上,有仿佛人的形状,周围有光辉环绕,如同雨中的彩虹。以西结用尽了「仿佛」「好像」「如同」这些词,竭力去描述那超乎言语的荣耀——因为人的语言,根本承载不了神荣耀的实体。

当这一切荣耀的异象临到顶点,以西结说:「这就是耶和华荣耀的形象。我一看见就俯伏在地,又听见一位说话的声音。」(结1:28)请注意以西结的反应——「我一看见就俯伏在地」。他没有好奇地端详,没有兴奋地分析,没有从容地记录;他一看见神的荣耀,整个人就仆倒在地。这是每一个真正瞥见神荣耀之人,唯一可能的反应。神的荣耀,是祂一切的美善、圣洁、威严、大能所发出的、可见的光辉;人一旦真看见它,就再也站立不住,只能俯伏。

这幅「一看见就俯伏」的画面,量出了我们敬拜的真伪与深浅。我们今天的「敬拜」,常常太随便、太轻慢、太以自我为中心:我们来「敬拜」,却仍能谈笑自若、心思游荡、评头论足,仿佛来赴一场社交聚会,而非来到那位荣耀之神的面前。为什么?因为我们从未真正看见祂的荣耀。一个真看见了神荣耀的人,不可能还那样随便;他会像以西结、像以赛亚、像使徒约翰见了荣耀的基督一样,仆倒在地。我们敬拜的轻慢,归根究底,暴露的是我们对神荣耀之看见的贫乏。

而这位使以西结俯伏在地的荣耀之神,在新约里,把祂的荣耀向我们显明得更近、更亲。约翰说:「道成了肉身,住在我们中间……我们也见过他的荣光」(约1:14);保罗说,神的荣耀「显在耶稣基督的面上」(林后4:6)。以西结在异象中远远瞥见、竟仆倒在地的那荣耀,如今在基督的脸上,向我们敞开了。今天,求神开你的眼,叫你不只是「知道」神荣耀的道理,而是真实地「看见」祂的荣耀——因为那真看见的人,他的敬拜、他的生命,必被这荣耀彻底地折服、俯伏、更新。

默想:我的敬拜,是否太随便、太轻慢、太以自我为中心——能谈笑自若、心思游荡,仿佛来赴社交聚会,而非来到荣耀之神面前?这轻慢,是否正暴露了我从未真正「看见」神的荣耀?我是只「知道」神荣耀的道理,还是真实地看见过、以致俯伏?

应用:今天在敬拜、祷告、读经之前,刻意求神开你的眼,叫你真看见祂的荣耀(默想以西结书一章或启示录一章那荣耀的基督);带着「一看见就俯伏」的敬畏,而非随便轻慢的心,来到祂面前。

祷告:荣耀的主,以西结一看见你荣耀的形像,就俯伏在地。我惭愧,我的敬拜常常随便轻慢、以自我为中心,正暴露了我从未真正看见你的荣耀。谢谢你在基督的脸上,把你的荣耀向我显明。求你开我的眼,叫我不只知道你荣耀的道理,而是真实地看见你的荣耀,以致我的敬拜与生命,被你彻底折服、俯伏、更新。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel was a priest carried into exile in Babylon. Right by the river Chebar in a foreign land, God appeared to him in an extremely strange, extremely glorious vision: a stormy wind, a great cloud, flashing fire, four living creatures, whirling wheels, their rims full of eyes; above the heads of the living creatures was an expanse, and above the expanse was the likeness of a throne; on the throne was a figure like that of a man, with radiance around it like a rainbow in the rain. Ezekiel exhausted words like “as it were,” “like,” “appearance of,” straining to describe a glory beyond words — because human language simply cannot bear the reality of God’s glory.

When all this glorious vision reached its peak, Ezekiel said: “Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking” (Ezekiel 1:28). Notice Ezekiel’s reaction — “when I saw it, I fell on my face.” He did not curiously examine it, did not excitedly analyze it, did not calmly record it; the moment he saw God’s glory, his whole self collapsed to the ground. This is the only possible reaction of anyone who truly glimpses God’s glory. God’s glory is the visible radiance emanating from all his goodness, holiness, majesty, and power; once a person truly sees it, they can no longer stand — they can only fall prostrate.

This picture of “falling prostrate the moment you see it” measures the authenticity and depth of our worship. Our “worship” today is often too casual, too careless, too self-centered: we come to “worship,” yet can still chat freely, let our minds wander, criticize this and that, as though attending a social gathering rather than coming before that glorious God. Why? Because we have never truly seen his glory. A person who has truly seen God’s glory cannot possibly stay that casual; they will, like Ezekiel, like Isaiah, like the apostle John who saw the glorified Christ, fall prostrate on the ground. Our careless worship, traced to its root, exposes our poverty in having seen God’s glory.

And this glorious God who made Ezekiel fall prostrate has, in the New Testament, revealed his glory to us more closely, more intimately. John said: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us... we have seen his glory” (John 1:14); Paul said God’s glory is “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). That glory Ezekiel glimpsed from afar in a vision, which made him fall prostrate, is now opened to us in Christ’s very face. Today, ask God to open your eyes, so that you would not merely “know” the doctrine of God’s glory, but truly “see” his glory — because the one who truly sees will have their worship, their whole life, thoroughly conquered, made to bow down, and renewed by this glory.

Meditation: Is my worship too casual, too careless, too self-centered — able to chat freely, let my mind wander, as though attending a social gathering rather than coming before the glorious God? Does this carelessness expose that I have never truly “seen” God’s glory? Do I merely “know” the doctrine of God’s glory, or have I truly seen it, so as to fall prostrate?

Application: Today, before worship, prayer, and Bible reading, deliberately ask God to open your eyes, to let you truly see his glory (meditate on Ezekiel 1 or the glorified Christ in Revelation 1); come before him with the reverence of “falling prostrate the moment you see it,” rather than a casual, careless heart.

Prayer: Glorious Lord, the moment Ezekiel saw the likeness of your glory, he fell on his face. I am ashamed that my worship is often casual and careless, self-centered, exposing that I have never truly seen your glory. Thank you for revealing your glory to me in Christ’s face. Open my eyes, so that I would not only know the doctrine of your glory, but truly see your glory, so that my worship and my life would be thoroughly conquered, made to bow down, and renewed by you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我因他们的心伤破
entries.title_en: I Am Brokenhearted Over Their Whoring Heart
entries.verse: 以西结书六章九节
entries.content:
以西结奉命向以色列宣告审判:因着他们长久的拜偶像、行可憎的事,刀剑、饥荒、瘟疫必要临到。这是一段极其沉重的审判信息。然而,就在这一片审判的宣告中,神忽然向我们敞开了祂的心——原来,在祂公义的忿怒背后,是一颗被祂百姓的背弃深深「伤破」的心。

神论到那些将来被掳、终于回想起祂的人,说:「那脱离刀剑的人必在所掳到的各国中记念我,为他们心中何等伤破,是因他们起淫心,远离我,眼对偶像行邪淫。」(结6:9)请注意「伤破」这个词——中文和合本这里说的,是神因他们「起淫心、远离我」而心中伤破。神在这里把祂百姓的拜偶像、离弃祂,比作婚姻中的「行淫」;而祂对这背弃的反应,不是一位无动于衷的审判官冷冷地定罪,而是一位被深爱之人背叛了的丈夫,心被伤透了。原来,我们的罪,不只是触犯了神的律法,更是伤了神的心。

这幅图画,把「罪」从一个抽象的「违规」,还原成了一件极其个人、极其痛的事——它伤的是一位爱我们的神的心。我们常把罪看得很轻:不过是犯了个规、做了件不该做的事,认个错、改一改就好了。可神却告诉我们:你的罪,在我眼中,如同婚姻里的背叛;当你转向别的「偶像」——无论是钱财、情欲、名声、还是任何被你放在神之上的东西——你不只是「犯了错」,你是伤了那位以专一之爱爱你的神的心。真正认识罪的严重,不是先看它违犯了多少条规,而是先看它伤了神何等深的爱。

而这位「心被伤破」的神,最叫人震撼的,是祂并没有因被伤而弃绝我们。祂反倒差来祂的儿子,亲自为我们这些伤祂心的人,舍了命。十字架是神受伤之爱的极致:祂被我们的罪伤透了心,却没有转身离去,反而张开双臂,担当了我们背叛的罪,只为把我们这些「行淫」的心,重新赢回到祂的爱里。今天,你是否把自己的罪看得太轻,忘了它伤的是神的心?求神叫你看见你偶像背后神那伤破的心;这份被伤却仍不离弃的爱,比一切审判的威吓,更能叫我们真正回转。

默想:我是否把自己的罪看得太轻——不过是犯规、做错事,认个错就好?我是否看见,我的罪(尤其是把某样东西放在神之上的「属灵行淫」),伤的是那位以专一之爱爱我之神的心?什么「偶像」正叫神为我心中伤破?

应用:今天不把罪只当作「违规」来对付,而是看见它伤了神的心;为一个你一直放在神之上的「偶像」向神真诚悔改——不只因为它是「错的」,更因为它伤了那位深爱你之神的心,回转归向祂专一的爱。

祷告:被我伤心、却仍爱我的主,你把我的拜偶像看作婚姻里的背叛,为我「起淫心、远离你」而心中伤破。我承认,我常把罪看得太轻,忘了它伤的是你的心。谢谢你被我的罪伤透了心,却没有离去,反而差爱子为我这背叛的人舍命。求你叫我看见偶像背后你伤破的心,以这被伤却不离弃的爱,叫我真正回转,归向你专一的爱。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel was commanded to declare judgment against Israel: because of their long-standing idolatry and abominable acts, sword, famine, and plague must come. This is an extremely heavy message of judgment. Yet right in the midst of this pronouncement of judgment, God suddenly opens his heart to us — it turns out that behind his righteous wrath is a heart deeply “brokenhearted” over his people’s betrayal.

Speaking of those who would later be exiled and would finally remember him, God says: “And those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols” (Ezekiel 6:9). Notice the word “broken.” God here likens his people’s idolatry and forsaking of him to “whoring” within a marriage; and his response to this betrayal is not that of a cold judge indifferently pronouncing condemnation, but that of a husband whose heart has been broken by the betrayal of the one he deeply loved. It turns out our sin doesn’t merely violate God’s law — it wounds God’s heart.

This picture restores “sin” from an abstract “violation” back to something extremely personal, extremely painful — it wounds the heart of a God who loves us. We often take sin too lightly: as though it’s just breaking a rule, doing something we shouldn’t have, that we can apologize for and change and be fine. But God tells us: your sin, in my eyes, is like betrayal within a marriage; when you turn to other “idols” — whether money, lust, fame, or anything you’ve placed above God — you’re not just “making a mistake,” you’re wounding the heart of a God who loves you with an exclusive love. Truly recognizing sin’s seriousness means seeing not first how many rules it violated, but how deeply it wounded God’s love.

And what’s most astonishing about this God whose “heart was broken” is that he did not reject us for being wounded. Instead, he sent his Son, to personally give his life for us who have wounded his heart. The cross is the ultimate expression of God’s wounded love: he was heartbroken by our sin, yet did not turn away — instead he opened his arms wide, bearing the sin of our betrayal, all to win back these “whoring” hearts of ours into his love. Today, are you taking your sin too lightly, forgetting that it wounds God’s heart? Ask God to let you see the broken heart of God behind your idols; this wounded yet never-forsaking love can turn us back more truly than any threat of judgment.

Meditation: Am I taking my sin too lightly — just breaking a rule, doing something wrong, that I can apologize for and be fine? Do I see that my sin (especially the “spiritual whoring” of placing something above God) wounds the heart of a God who loves me with an exclusive love? What “idol” is currently breaking God’s heart over me?

Application: Today, don’t just deal with sin as a “violation” — see that it wounds God’s heart; genuinely repent to God over an “idol” you’ve always placed above him — not only because it’s “wrong,” but because it wounds the heart of a God who deeply loves you, and turn back to his exclusive love.

Prayer: Lord who I have wounded, yet who still loves me, you liken my idolatry to betrayal within a marriage, brokenhearted over my “whoring heart, departed from you.” I confess I often take sin too lightly, forgetting it wounds your heart. Thank you for being heartbroken by my sin, yet not turning away, instead sending your beloved Son to die for me, this betrayer. Let me see the broken heart behind my idols, and let this wounded yet never-forsaking love truly turn me back, to your exclusive love. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 除掉石心,赐给肉心
entries.title_en: I Will Remove the Heart of Stone and Give a Heart of Flesh
entries.verse: 以西结书十一章十九节
entries.content:
以西结在异象中,看见神的荣耀,因着圣殿中可憎的偶像,一步一步地离开了圣殿——这是何等沉重的一幕。然而,就在审判与荣耀离去的黑暗中,神却应许了一件将来复兴时要成就的、极其深刻的工作。这工作,触及的不是外面的行为,而是人里面那颗心的根本。

「我要使他们有合一的心,也要将新灵放在他们里面,又从他们肉体中除掉石心,赐给他们肉心。」(结11:19)请注意神所要作的,是一个「换心」的手术。人的问题,归根究底,不在外面的行为,而在里面那颗「石心」——一颗刚硬、冷漠、不能感应神、不肯顺服神的心。律法可以规范人外面的行为,却无法软化人里面那颗石头一样的心;人可以靠意志力勉强守一阵规条,但那颗石心一日不换,他就一日无法真正地爱神、亲近神、顺服神。神深知这一点,所以祂应许的,不是给人一套更严的规条、或更强的意志力,而是从根本上「除掉石心,赐给肉心」——把那不能感应的石头,换成一颗柔软、能爱、能顺服、向神跳动的心。

这就道破了一个我们常常弄错的属灵真理:真正的改变,是「从里到外」的,不是「从外到内」的。我们常常拼命地想改自己外面的行为——想更爱神、想戒掉某个罪、想变得更顺服——却发现无论怎样努力,里面那颗心还是硬的、还是不情愿的、还是使不上劲。原因就在于:我们想靠自己去「修理」行为,神却知道问题在「心」,而心是我们自己换不了的。你无法靠自己把一颗石心变成肉心;这是一个只有神能作的、创造性的、「换心」的神迹。

而这「除掉石心、赐给肉心」的应许,在新约里,借着基督与圣灵完全成就了。神应许:「我必将我的灵放在你们里面,使你们……谨守遵行我的典章」(结36:27);凡在基督里的,就是「新造的人」,神已经把一颗新心、新灵赐给了他。所以基督徒的生命,不是靠自己咬牙去改硬心,而是先来到神面前,求祂作这「换心」的工作——把我里面的石心除去,赐我一颗向祂柔软的肉心。今天,你是否一直在靠自己「修理」外面的行为,却始终改不动里面那颗石心?停下这徒劳的努力;来求那位唯一能换心的神,把你的石心换成肉心。

默想:我是否一直在靠自己「从外到内」地修理行为——想更爱神、戒某个罪、更顺服,却发现里面那颗心还是硬的、使不上劲?我是否看见,真正的问题在「石心」,而这是我自己换不了、唯有神能作的「换心」神迹?

应用:今天停止靠自己咬牙去「修理」外面的行为;转而来到神面前,为你里面某一处的刚硬(对某人、某事、某个命令的硬心),求神作那「除掉石心、赐给肉心」的工作,把你的心从里到外地更新。

祷告:换心的主,你应许要除掉你百姓里面的石心,赐给他们肉心,把新灵放在他们里面。我承认,我一直靠自己修理外面的行为,却改不动里面那颗刚硬、不能感应你的石心。谢谢你借着基督与圣灵,已把一颗新心赐给我。求你继续作这换心的工作,除去我一切的刚硬,赐我一颗向你柔软、能爱、能顺服的肉心。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In a vision, Ezekiel saw God’s glory, because of the abominable idols in the temple, departing step by step from the temple — what a heavy scene this is. Yet right in this darkness of judgment and departing glory, God promises an extremely profound work he will accomplish at the time of future restoration. This work touches not outward behavior, but the very root of the human heart within.

“And I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19). Notice that what God will do is a “heart transplant” surgery. Humanity’s problem, traced to its root, lies not in outward behavior, but in the “heart of stone” within — a hard, cold heart, unresponsive to God, unwilling to obey God. The law can regulate a person’s outward behavior, but it cannot soften that stone-like heart within; a person can, by willpower, force themselves to keep rules for a while, but as long as that heart of stone is not replaced, they cannot truly love God, draw near to God, obey God. God knows this deeply, so what he promises is not giving people a stricter set of rules, or stronger willpower, but fundamentally “removing the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh” — exchanging that unresponsive stone for a soft heart, able to love, able to obey, beating toward God.

This reveals a spiritual truth we often get wrong: true change is “from the inside out,” not “from the outside in.” We often work desperately to change our outward behavior — wanting to love God more, wanting to quit some sin, wanting to become more obedient — only to discover that however hard we try, the heart within is still hard, still unwilling, still without strength. The reason is: we’re trying to “repair” behavior by ourselves, but God knows the problem is in the “heart,” and the heart is something we cannot replace ourselves. You cannot, by your own strength, turn a heart of stone into a heart of flesh; this is a creative “heart transplant” miracle only God can perform.

And this promise of “removing the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh” has, in the New Testament, been completely fulfilled through Christ and the Holy Spirit. God promises: “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27); everyone in Christ is a “new creation” — God has already given them a new heart, a new spirit. So the Christian life is not gritting your teeth to change a hard heart by yourself, but first coming before God, asking him to perform this “heart transplant” work — removing the heart of stone within me, giving me a heart of flesh soft toward him. Today, have you been trying to “repair” your outward behavior by yourself, “from the outside in,” yet still unable to move that heart of stone within? Stop this futile effort; come and ask the only God who can transplant hearts to exchange your heart of stone for a heart of flesh.

Meditation: Have I been trying to repair behavior by myself, “from the outside in” — wanting to love God more, quit some sin, be more obedient — only to find the heart within still hard, without strength? Do I see that the real problem is the “heart of stone,” something I cannot replace myself, a “heart transplant” miracle only God can perform?

Application: Today, stop gritting your teeth trying to “repair” outward behavior by yourself; instead come before God, and for some hardness within you (a hard heart toward a person, a matter, a command), ask God to perform the work of “removing the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh,” renewing your heart from the inside out.

Prayer: Lord who transplants hearts, you promise to remove the heart of stone within your people and give them a heart of flesh, putting a new spirit within them. I confess I have been trying to repair my outward behavior by myself, yet unable to move the hard, unresponsive heart of stone within. Thank you for already giving me a new heart through Christ and the Holy Spirit. Continue this heart-transplanting work, removing all my hardness, and give me a heart of flesh soft toward you, able to love, able to obey. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 回头吧,离开你们的偶像
entries.title_en: Repent and Turn Away from Your Idols
entries.verse: 以西结书十四章六节
entries.content:
以西结继续宣告审判。以色列的长老们外面来求问神,心里却仍「将偶像接到心里」。神一针见血地拆穿了这种表里不一的敬虔:你们一面来到我面前求问,一面却在心里给偶像留着地位。对这样的心,神发出了一个清清楚楚、毫不含糊的呼召。

「所以你要告诉以色列家说:主耶和华如此说:回头吧!离开你们的偶像,转脸莫从你们一切可憎的事。」(结14:6)请注意神呼召中的两个动作:「回头」与「离开」。真正的悔改,不是一个模糊的、感觉上的「我错了」,而是一个明确的、方向性的转身:从偶像那里「回头」,「离开」它,「转脸」不再跟从它。悔改的本质,是「转向」——转离罪与偶像,转向神。它不只是为罪难过、流泪、懊悔;那些若没有带来实际的「转身」与「离开」,就还不是圣经所说的悔改。神要的,不是我们一面守着偶像、一面向祂掉眼泪;而是我们真实地、决绝地,离开那偶像,转回到祂面前。

这拆穿了我们许多人「悔改」里的自欺。我们常常为某个罪难过、自责、甚至在神面前痛哭,决心「以后不再这样了」;可我们的心,却仍旧「将偶像接到心里」——我们从未真正下决心离开它、与它了断,我们只是为它带来的痛苦而懊恼,却舍不得那偶像本身。于是我们在同一个罪里,一次次地跌倒、一次次地「悔改」、又一次次地回去,循环不息。因为我们的「悔改」,停在了「难过」,却从未走到「回头、离开」。神今天向我们发出的,仍是同样清楚的呼召:不是叫你再多难过一点,而是叫你「回头、离开」——真正地转身,与那偶像了断。

而这「回头、离开」的力量,不是靠我们自己的决心硬挤出来的。神呼召我们回转,同时也在基督里赐下回转的恩典:祂赦免我们过去偏行的路,又借着圣灵,赐我们离开偶像、转向祂的心与力。真正的悔改,始终源于神的恩慈——「他的恩慈是领你悔改」(罗2:4)——是先看见神那被我们背弃、却仍向我们敞开的爱,我们才生出真实回转的心。今天,你心里是否也「将偶像接到心里」,一面求问神,一面舍不得离开某样占据你心的东西?听神清楚的呼召:回头吧,离开你们的偶像。不要只停在难过里;真正地转身,回到神面前。

默想:我的「悔改」,是否常常停在「为罪难过、自责、流泪」,却从未真正「回头、离开」那罪与偶像?我是否一面求问神,一面却仍「将偶像接到心里」,舍不得与它了断?这是否正是我在同一个罪里循环跌倒的原因?

应用:今天对一个你一直「难过、却舍不得离开」的偶像或罪,采取真实的「回头、离开」——不只是再难过一次,而是具体地、决绝地与它了断(挪去引诱、切断途径、向人求问守望),靠着神所赐回转的恩典,真正转身回到神面前。

祷告:呼召我回转的主,你拆穿了那一面求问你、一面把偶像接到心里的假敬虔,清楚地呼召:回头吧,离开你们的偶像。我承认,我的悔改常停在难过里,却从未真正回头、离开,以致在同一个罪里循环跌倒。谢谢你的恩慈领我悔改,又在基督里赐我回转的力量。求你叫我不只难过,而是真实地转身,与偶像了断,回到你面前。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel continues to declare judgment. Israel’s elders came outwardly to inquire of God, yet in their hearts they still “set up their idols in their hearts.” God plainly exposes this inconsistent godliness: you come before me to inquire, yet in your hearts you still give idols a place. To such a heart, God issues a clear, unambiguous call.

“Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Repent and turn away from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your abominations” (Ezekiel 14:6). Notice the two actions in God’s call: “repent” and “turn away.” True repentance is not a vague, emotional “I was wrong,” but a definite, directional turning: turning back from idols, turning away from them, turning your face no longer to follow them. The essence of repentance is “turning” — turning from sin and idols, turning to God. It is not merely being sorrowful, weeping, and regretting over sin; if these do not bring an actual “turning” and “departing,” they are not yet the repentance Scripture speaks of. What God wants is not for us to keep our idols while shedding tears before him; it is for us to truly, resolutely leave that idol, and turn back before him.

This exposes the self-deception within many of our “repentances.” We often feel sorrowful, self-reproach, even weep bitterly before God over some sin, resolving “I won’t do this again” — yet our hearts still “set up idols within.” We never truly resolve to leave it, to break with it; we’re only distressed over the pain it brings, but unwilling to give up the idol itself. So we stumble again and again in the same sin, “repent” again and again, and go back again and again, an endless cycle. Because our “repentance” stops at “being sorrowful,” never reaching “turning back, departing.” What God calls us to today is still the same clear calling: not to be a bit more sorrowful, but to “turn back, depart” — truly turn around, and break with that idol.

And the power for this “turning back, departing” is not squeezed out by our own resolve alone. God calls us to turn back, and at the same time gives, in Christ, the grace of turning back: he forgives our past wayward paths, and through the Holy Spirit, gives us the heart and strength to leave idols and turn to him. True repentance always originates in God’s kindness — “God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4) — it is first seeing God’s love, forsaken by us yet still open to us, that gives rise in us to a true turning heart. Today, does your heart too “set up idols within,” inquiring of God on one hand, yet unwilling to leave something occupying your heart on the other? Hear God’s clear calling: repent, and turn away from your idols. Don’t just stay in sorrow; truly turn around, and return before God.

Meditation: Does my “repentance” often stop at “being sorrowful over sin, self-reproach, tears,” yet never truly “turn back, depart” from that sin and idol? Do I inquire of God on one hand, yet “set up idols within my heart” on the other, unwilling to break with it? Is this exactly why I keep stumbling in a cycle in the same sin?

Application: Today, toward an idol or sin you’ve always “felt sorrowful over, yet unwilling to leave,” take real action to “turn back, depart” — not just being sorrowful once more, but concretely, resolutely breaking with it (removing the temptation, cutting off the means, asking someone to hold you accountable), truly turning around and returning before God, relying on the grace of turning back he gives.

Prayer: Lord who calls me to turn back, you exposed the false godliness of inquiring of you on one hand while setting up idols in the heart on the other, clearly calling: repent, and turn away from your idols. I confess my repentance often stops at sorrow, never truly turning back and departing, so I stumble in a cycle in the same sin. Thank you that your kindness leads me to repentance, and gives me, in Christ, the strength to turn back. Let me not only be sorrowful, but truly turn around, break with idols, and return before you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 在基督里释放了我——在主里得自由
entries.title_en: Set Me Free in Christ Jesus — Freedom in the Lord
entries.content:
在基督里释放了我——在主里得自由

「因为赐生命圣灵的律,在基督耶稣里释放了我,使我脱离罪和死的律了。」(罗马书 8:2)

这一周,我们看见神因百姓的偶像而心中伤破,又应许要除掉石心、赐下肉心,呼召人回头离开偶像。这一切的核心,都是神要把祂的百姓,从罪的辖制里释放出来。

今天安息日,请听这自由的宣告。我们里面原有一条「罪和死的律」——像地心引力一样,一股压不住的力,把我们不断往下拉,拉向罪、拉向死。靠自己挣扎,是挣不脱这引力的。但神赐下了一条更强的律——「赐生命圣灵的律」;正如飞机靠更强的升力胜过地心引力而飞起,圣灵的大能在基督里,把你从罪和死那压不住的引力中,释放了出来。你的自由,不是靠自己更用力地挣扎,而是靠里面那位圣灵更强的托举。今天,安息在这自由里:在基督耶稣里,你已经被释放了。

"For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death." (Romans 8:2)
entries.content_en:
Set Me Free in Christ Jesus — Freedom in the Lord

"For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death." (Romans 8:2)

This week, we saw God brokenhearted over his people’s idols, promising to remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, calling people to turn back and leave their idols. At the center of all of it is God’s desire to set his people free from sin’s dominion.

Today, on the Sabbath, hear this declaration of freedom. There was once a "law of sin and death" within us — like gravity, an unstoppable force, constantly pulling us downward, pulling us toward sin, pulling us toward death. Struggling by our own effort, we could never break free of this pull. But God has given a stronger law — "the law of the Spirit of life"; just as a plane overcomes gravity through greater lift and flies, the Holy Spirit’s power in Christ Jesus has set you free from that unstoppable pull of sin and death. Your freedom does not come from struggling harder on your own, but from the stronger lifting power of the Spirit within you. Today, rest in this freedom: in Christ Jesus, you have already been set free.

"For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death." (Romans 8:2)

entries.title: 神不喜悦恶人死亡
entries.title_en: I Have No Pleasure in the Death of the Wicked
entries.verse: 以西结书十八章廿三节
entries.content:
以西结书十八章,回应了当时百姓一句流行的怨言。他们说:「父亲吃了酸葡萄,儿子的牙酸倒了」——意思是,我们受苦,是替列祖背黑锅,神这样审判不公平。神借以西结,郑重地纠正了他们:各人要为自己的罪负责;义人必因义存活,恶人必因罪死亡。然而,在这严肃的审判宣告中,神却忽然向我们敞开了祂的心肠——原来在这位审判者的公义背后,是一颗何等不愿人灭亡的心。

「主耶和华说:恶人死亡,岂是我喜悦的吗?不是喜悦他回头离开所行的道存活吗?」(结18:23)请深深默想这一问。神是公义的审判者,祂必不以有罪的为无罪;然而,当祂不得不审判恶人时,祂的心并不以此为「喜悦」。祂宣告审判,却不喜悦审判;祂能定罪,心却渴望人回头存活。这与我们对神的印象,常常大相径庭。我们心里的神,往往是一位冷酷的、随时准备定罪的、甚至乐于降罚的审判官;神却在这里亲口剖白:恶人的死亡,不是我所喜悦的;我所喜悦的,是他回头、离开恶道、得以存活。

这句话,揭示了神心肠最深处的渴望。祂不是一位「巴不得抓住你的错、好定你罪」的神;祂是一位「巴不得你回头、好叫你存活」的神。祂发出审判的警告,恰恰是出于这份不愿人灭亡的爱——警告,是为要挽回,而非为要毁灭。这就是为什么,神的审判信息里,总是同时响着一个恳切的呼召:「你们转回,转回吧!离开恶道,何必死亡呢?」(结33:11)神不是站在远处冷眼等你跌倒;祂是张开双臂,切切盼你回头的父。

神这份「不喜悦恶人死亡」的心肠,在基督里得到了最终、最有力的证明。「神爱世人,甚至将他的独生子赐给他们」(约3:16);又说,神「不愿有一人沉沦,乃愿人人都悔改」(彼后3:9)。一位真愿人灭亡的神,断不会差祂的儿子来,为罪人死。十字架,是神「不喜悦恶人死亡、只喜悦他回头存活」这心肠的极致宣告。今天,你是否把神想成了一位冷酷、乐于定罪的审判官,以致不敢回头、不敢近前?听祂亲口的剖白:恶人的死亡,不是我喜悦的;我巴不得你回头,得以存活。带着你的罪,回到这位切切盼你回头的神面前。

默想:我心里的神,是一位冷酷的、随时准备定罪、甚至乐于降罚的审判官,还是那位亲口说「恶人死亡不是我所喜悦」、切切盼我回头存活的神?这幅画像的差别,如何影响我肯不肯带着罪回到祂面前?

应用:今天若你因把神想成冷酷的审判官,而一直不敢带着某个罪回到祂面前;就支取祂亲口的剖白——祂不喜悦你死亡,只喜悦你回头存活;坦然回转,离开那恶道,来到这位盼你回头的神面前。

祷告:不喜悦恶人死亡的主,你亲口剖白:恶人的死亡不是你所喜悦的,你喜悦的是他回头、离开恶道、得以存活。我承认,我常把你想成冷酷、乐于定罪的审判官,以致不敢回头近前。谢谢你差爱子为我死,证明你何等不愿我灭亡。求你叫我看见你切切盼我回头的心肠,坦然带着我的罪,回到你面前得以存活。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel 18 responds to a popular complaint of the people at the time. They said: “The fathers eat sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” — meaning, we suffer for carrying the blame of our ancestors, and God’s judgment like this is unfair. Through Ezekiel, God solemnly corrects them: each person is responsible for their own sin; the righteous shall surely live because of his righteousness, and the wicked shall surely die because of his sin. Yet in the midst of this solemn pronouncement of judgment, God suddenly opens his innermost heart to us — it turns out that behind this Judge’s justice is a heart that so utterly does not want anyone to perish.

“Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). Ponder this question deeply. God is a righteous Judge, and he will surely not acquit the guilty; yet when he must judge the wicked, his heart does not take “pleasure” in it. He pronounces judgment, yet does not delight in judgment; he is able to condemn, yet his heart longs for people to turn back and live. This is often quite different from our impression of God. The God in our hearts is often a cold judge, always ready to condemn, even one who delights in inflicting punishment; yet here God personally bares his heart: the death of the wicked is not what I delight in; what I delight in is that he would turn back, leave his wicked way, and live.

This sentence reveals the deepest longing of God’s heart. He is not a God who “can’t wait to catch your fault so he can condemn you”; he is a God who “can’t wait for you to turn back so he can let you live.” He issues the warning of judgment precisely out of this love that does not want anyone to perish — the warning is meant to reclaim, not to destroy. This is why, in God’s messages of judgment, there always sounds, at the same time, an earnest calling: “Turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die?” (Ezekiel 33:11). God is not standing at a distance, coldly waiting for you to stumble; he is the Father with arms wide open, earnestly hoping you will turn back.

This heart of God’s, that “takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked,” has received its final, most powerful proof in Christ. “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16); it also says God “is not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). A God who truly wanted people to perish would never send his Son to die for sinners. The cross is the ultimate declaration of God’s heart, that he “takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but only in his turning back to live.” Today, have you imagined God as a cold, condemnation-loving judge, so that you dare not turn back, dare not draw near? Hear his own confession: the death of the wicked is not what I delight in; I long for you to turn back, and live. Bring your sin, and return before this God who earnestly longs for you to turn back.

Meditation: Is the God in my heart a cold judge, always ready to condemn, even one who delights in inflicting punishment, or the God who personally says “the death of the wicked is not what I delight in,” earnestly longing for me to turn back and live? How does the difference between these two pictures affect whether I dare to bring my sin back before him?

Application: Today, if you’ve been too afraid to bring some sin back before God because you’ve imagined him as a cold judge, draw on his own confession — he does not delight in your death, only in your turning back to live; candidly turn back, leave that wicked way, and come before this God who longs for you to turn back.

Prayer: Lord who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, you personally confess: the death of the wicked is not what you delight in; what you delight in is that he would turn back, leave his wicked way, and live. I confess I often imagine you as a cold, condemnation-loving judge, so that I dare not turn back and draw near. Thank you for sending your beloved Son to die for me, proving how much you do not want me to perish. Let me see your heart earnestly longing for me to turn back, and candidly bring my sin, returning before you to live. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 为我名的缘故
entries.title_en: For My Name's Sake
entries.verse: 以西结书二十章四十四节
entries.content:
以西结书二十章,是神对以色列历史的一次回顾。神一幕一幕地数算:祂如何领他们出埃及、在旷野养育他们;而他们又如何一次次地悖逆、拜偶像、干犯祂的安息日。按他们的行为,神大可以在旷野就把他们灭尽。然而,经文里反复出现一句话,道破了神为什么一次次地忍耐、没有灭绝他们——不是因为他们配,而是因为一个更高的缘由。

「主耶和华说:以色列家啊,我为我名的缘故,不照着你们的恶行和你们的坏事待你们;你们就知道我是耶和华。」(结20:44)请留意「为我名的缘故」这几个字,它像一条主线,贯穿了整章。神没有照他们的恶行待他们,不是因为他们的恶行不严重,也不是因为他们后来变好了、配得了;乃是「为我名的缘故」——为要在列国面前,彰显祂自己名的圣洁、信实与荣耀。神施恩、忍耐、不灭绝他们,归根究底,是为了祂自己名的荣耀。

这真理,乍看似乎叫人不适:难道神施恩不是为了爱我们,而是为了祂自己吗?但请深想:这恰恰是我们救恩最坚固的保障。倘若神拯救我、忍耐我、不弃绝我,是「因为我配」「因为我够好」「因为我表现得不错」,那么我的救恩就建立在我这变幻无常的表现上,随时可能因我的失败而崩塌。可神说,祂待我们「为祂名的缘故」——那么我的救恩,就不再建立在我的可靠上,而建立在神对祂自己名之荣耀的看重上。而神的名、神的荣耀,是永不改变、永不落空的。神救我,是为叫祂的名得荣耀;祂断不会让祂拯救的工作半途而废、叫祂的名蒙羞。这就是我们最深的安全感所在。

神「为自己名的缘故」施行拯救,在福音里达到了顶峰。基督为我们死,叫我们「得蒙救赎……使他荣耀的恩典得着称赞」(弗1:6-7);神赦免我们的罪,也是「为自己的缘故」「因你的名」(赛43:25;诗25:11)。这意味着:你的得救、你的蒙保守、你最终的得荣耀,不是押在你善变的表现上,而是押在神对祂自己荣耀那永不动摇的委身上。所以当你软弱、失败、觉得自己不配时,你的盼望不在于「我够不够好」,而在于「神必为祂名的缘故,成全祂在我身上的救恩」。今天,把你救恩的根基,从你自己身上,挪到神对祂自己名之荣耀的看重上——那才是永不动摇的磐石。

默想:我救恩的根基,是押在「我够不够好、表现得可不可靠」上,还是押在「神必为祂自己名的荣耀成全我」上?若神待我「为祂名的缘故」而非「因我配」,这如何在我软弱失败、觉得自己不配时,成为我最深的安全感?

应用:今天当你因自己的软弱、失败而怀疑「神还会不会要我」时,不去自己的表现里找答案;而是支取「神为祂自己名的缘故必成全我」这一根基,把救恩的确据钉在神对祂荣耀那永不动摇的委身上。

祷告:为你名的缘故施恩的主,以色列一再悖逆,你却为你名的缘故没有照他们的恶行待他们。谢谢你待我,也不是因我配,而是为你自己名的荣耀。我承认,我常把救恩的根基押在自己善变的表现上,一失败就怀疑你还要不要我。求你叫我把根基挪到你对自己荣耀那永不动摇的委身上;你救我,是为你的名,你断不叫这工作半途而废。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel 20 is a review of Israel’s history that God gives. God counts, scene by scene: how he led them out of Egypt, nourished them in the wilderness; and how they, again and again, rebelled, worshiped idols, and violated his Sabbaths. By their actions, God could well have wiped them out in the wilderness. Yet a sentence recurs again and again throughout the text, revealing why God endured them, time after time, without destroying them — not because they deserved it, but for a higher reason.

“And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I deal with you for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt deeds, O house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 20:44). Notice the phrase “for my name’s sake” — it runs like a main thread through the whole chapter. God did not deal with them according to their evil deeds, not because their evil deeds weren’t serious, and not because they later became good enough, deserving of it; it was “for my name’s sake” — to display, before the nations, the holiness, faithfulness, and glory of his own name. God’s showing grace, patience, and not destroying them, traced to its root, was for the glory of his own name.

This truth seems, at first, uncomfortable: does God’s grace exist not for love of us, but for himself? But consider deeply: this is exactly the firmest guarantee of our salvation. If God’s saving me, enduring me, not rejecting me, were “because I deserve it,” “because I’m good enough,” “because I perform well,” then my salvation would be built on my own fickle performance, liable to collapse at any moment due to my failure. But God says he deals with us “for the sake of his name” — then my salvation is no longer built on my own reliability, but on God’s regard for the glory of his own name. And God’s name, God’s glory, never changes, never comes to nothing. God saves me so that his name would be glorified; he will by no means let his work of salvation be abandoned halfway, letting his name be put to shame. This is where our deepest security lies.

God’s working salvation “for his own name’s sake” reaches its peak in the gospel. Christ died for us, so that we would “be redeemed... to the praise of his glorious grace” (Ephesians 1:6-7); God forgives our sins likewise “for his own sake,” “for his name’s sake” (Isaiah 43:25; Psalm 25:11). This means: your salvation, your being kept, your final glorification, is not staked on your fickle performance, but staked on God’s never-shaking commitment to his own glory. So when you’re weak, failing, feeling unworthy, your hope lies not in “am I good enough,” but in “God will surely, for his name’s sake, accomplish his salvation in me.” Today, move the foundation of your salvation from yourself onto God’s regard for the glory of his own name — that is the never-shaking rock.

Meditation: Is the foundation of my salvation staked on “am I good enough, reliable enough in performance,” or staked on “God will surely accomplish it in me for the glory of his own name”? If God deals with me “for his name’s sake” rather than “because I deserve it,” how does this become my deepest security when I’m weak, failing, feeling unworthy?

Application: Today, when you doubt “whether God still wants me” because of your own weakness and failure, don’t look for the answer in your own performance; instead draw on the foundation that “God will surely accomplish it in me for the glory of his own name,” anchoring the assurance of your salvation on God’s never-shaking commitment to his own glory.

Prayer: Lord who shows grace for your name’s sake, Israel rebelled again and again, yet you, for your name’s sake, did not deal with them according to their evil ways. Thank you that you deal with me too, not because I deserve it, but for the glory of your own name. I confess I often stake the foundation of my salvation on my own fickle performance, doubting whether you still want me the moment I fail. Let me move the foundation onto your never-shaking commitment to your own glory; you save me for your name’s sake, and you will by no means let this work be abandoned halfway. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 因美丽而高傲的心
entries.title_en: A Heart Proud Because of Its Beauty
entries.verse: 以西结书廿八章十七节
entries.content:
以西结书二十八章,是对推罗王的一段审判预言。推罗是当时地中海一带首屈一指的贸易强国,富甲天下,繁荣无比。推罗王也因此心高气傲,竟自称为神,说「我是神,我在海中坐神之位」。神借以西结,拆穿了他的狂妄,并道出了他败亡的根源——那也是一切骄傲之败亡共同的根源。

「你因美丽心中高傲,又因荣光败坏智慧,我已将你摔倒在地。」(结28:17)请看骄傲是怎样运作的。推罗王所拥有的美丽、荣光、智慧、财富,本都是好的、本都是神所赐的;问题出在他「因」这些而「心中高傲」。他把神所赐的恩赐,当成了自己夸耀、自高、甚至自封为神的资本;他忘了这一切从何而来,以为是自己挣得的、是自己配得的、是自己了不起。于是那本该叫他谦卑感恩、归荣耀给神的美丽与荣光,反倒「败坏」了他的智慧,叫他昏了头、忘了自己不过是受造的、有限的、必朽的人。骄傲,就是把神的恩赐据为己有,又用它来把自己抬到神的位置上。

这是一个我们都当警惕的、极隐蔽的危险。神所赐给我们的每一样好东西——才干、美貌、成就、财富、地位、甚至属灵的恩赐与经历——都可能成为我们「心中高傲」的资本。我们太容易在得着这些之后,渐渐忘了它们的源头,把「这是神白白赐的」偷换成「这是我努力挣的、我本事大、我了不起」;然后,那本该叫我们更谦卑、更感恩、更荣耀神的恩赐,反倒「败坏」了我们,叫我们自高自大、目中无神。越是蒙福、越是有恩赐的人,越要在这一点上警醒——因为骄傲最爱附着在人的长处与恩赐上。

破解这骄傲的,唯有一个问题:「你有什么不是领受的呢?若是领受的,为何自夸,仿佛不是领受的呢?」(林前4:7)你所夸口的一切,没有一样不是从神白白领受的;既是领受的,就没有一样是你可以据为己有、用来自高的。而那位本有神的形象、却「反倒虚己,取了奴仆的形象」、自甘卑微以至于死的基督(腓2:6-8),是与推罗王截然相反的榜样:祂是真神,却极其谦卑;推罗王是受造之人,却自封为神。今天,神所赐给你的美丽、荣光、成就,是叫你更谦卑地归荣耀给祂,还是正悄悄成为你「心中高傲」的资本?求神叫你在蒙福之处,格外警醒你的心。

默想:神所赐给我的好东西(才干、美貌、成就、财富、地位、属灵恩赐),是叫我更谦卑感恩、更归荣耀给神,还是正悄悄成为我「心中高傲」的资本?我是否把「这是神白白赐的」,偷换成了「这是我挣的、我了不起」?

应用:今天在一样你最引以为傲、最容易自高的长处或恩赐上,刻意把它明确地归还给神——承认「我有的没有一样不是领受的」;并求神保守你,叫这恩赐不成为你骄傲的资本,而成为你谦卑事奉、荣耀神的器皿。

祷告:至高的主,推罗王因美丽、荣光而心中高傲,竟自封为神,你就将他摔倒在地。我警醒地看见,你所赐我的每一样好东西,都可能成为我骄傲的资本。我承认,我常把你白白的恩赐,偷换成自己的本事来自高。谢谢基督本是真神,却虚己谦卑至死。求你叫我在蒙福之处格外警醒,把一切恩赐归还给你,单单归荣耀给你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel 28 is a judgment prophecy against the king of Tyre. Tyre was, at the time, the foremost trading power along the Mediterranean, wealthier and more prosperous than any other. Because of this, the king of Tyre grew arrogant, even claiming to be a god, saying “I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas.” Through Ezekiel, God exposes his arrogance, and lays bare the root of his downfall — which is also the common root of the downfall of all pride.

“Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. I cast you to the ground” (Ezekiel 28:17). Look at how pride operates. The beauty, splendor, wisdom, and wealth the king of Tyre possessed were all, in themselves, good, all gifts from God; the problem arose in that his heart became “proud” “because of” these things. He treated the gifts God gave as his own capital for boasting, self-exaltation, even claiming to be a god; he forgot where all of it came from, thinking he had earned it, deserved it, that he himself was remarkable. So what should have made him humbly grateful, giving glory to God — his beauty and splendor — instead “corrupted” his wisdom, going to his head, making him forget he was nothing but a created, finite, mortal being. Pride is exactly taking God’s gifts as one’s own possession, and using them to raise oneself to God’s place.

This is an extremely hidden danger we should all be alert to. Every good thing God gives us — talent, beauty, achievement, wealth, status, even spiritual gifts and experiences — can become capital for our “proud heart.” We too easily, after receiving these, gradually forget their source, exchanging “this was freely given by God” for “this is what I worked hard for, I’m skilled, I’m remarkable”; and then, what should have made us more humble, more grateful, more glorifying to God instead “corrupts” us, making us arrogant, self-important, indifferent to God. The more blessed, the more gifted a person is, the more they need to be watchful on this point — because pride most loves to attach itself to a person’s strengths and gifts.

There is only one question that can dismantle this pride: “What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). There is nothing you boast of that was not freely received from God; since it was received, there is nothing you can claim as your own to exalt yourself with. And Christ, who was in the form of God, yet “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant,” willingly humbling himself to death (Philippians 2:6-8), is a pattern utterly opposite to the king of Tyre: he was truly God, yet extremely humble; the king of Tyre was a created man, yet claimed to be a god. Today, are the beauty, splendor, and achievements God has given you making you more humbly give glory to him, or quietly becoming capital for your “proud heart”? Ask God to make you especially watchful over your heart in the places where you are blessed.

Meditation: Are the good things God has given me (talent, beauty, achievement, wealth, status, spiritual gifts) making me more humbly grateful, more glorifying to God, or quietly becoming capital for my “proud heart”? Have I exchanged “this was freely given by God” for “this is what I worked hard for, I’m remarkable”?

Application: Today, in a strength or gift you’re most proud of, most easily made arrogant by, deliberately give it back to God explicitly — acknowledging “there is nothing I have that was not received”; and ask God to keep you, so that this gift does not become your capital for pride, but a vessel for humble service and glorifying God.

Prayer: Most High Lord, the king of Tyre’s heart grew proud because of his beauty and splendor, even claiming to be a god, and you cast him to the ground. I watch with alertness that every good thing you give me could become my capital for pride. I confess I often exchange your freely given gifts for my own boasted ability. Thank you that Christ, truly God, humbled himself to death. Let me be especially watchful in the places where I am blessed, giving all gifts back to you, and giving glory to you alone. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 压伤的芦苇杖
entries.title_en: A Bruised Reed of a Staff
entries.verse: 以西结书廿九章七节
entries.content:
以西结书二十九至三十二章,是对埃及的一连串审判预言。埃及,是当时的一大强国,也是以色列人屡屡想要倚靠、结盟的对象。每当亚述或巴比伦的威胁临到,犹大的领袖们第一个想到的,往往不是倚靠神,而是南下求助于埃及。神借以西结,用一个极其生动的比喻,拆穿了倚靠埃及的愚昧。

「他们用手持住你,你就断折,伤了他们的肩;他们倚靠你,你就断折,闪了他们的腰。」(结29:7)神把埃及比作一根「芦苇杖」。芦苇看起来像根可以拄的手杖,可它是空心的、脆弱的;人若真把全身的重量压上去,倚靠它,它非但撑不住,反而会应声断折,那断裂的尖头还会刺伤倚靠者的手、扎进他的肩。这就是一切「倚靠受造之物」的下场:你越是把生命的重量全然压上去,它越是撑不住,不但帮不了你,反而在断裂时反过来伤你。

这「压伤的芦苇杖」,是我们每个人都要认清的一课。我们的生命,总在寻找可以「拄靠」的手杖——某样能给我们安全感、能在难处中托住我们的东西:或是金钱,或是人脉,或是自己的才干,或是某段关系,或是健康、地位。这些东西,像埃及一样,看起来结实可靠,值得倚靠;可它们本质上,都是「芦苇杖」——都是有限的、会变的、终必朽坏的受造之物。你若把生命全部的重量压在它们身上,把它们当作终极的倚靠,它们迟早会断折;而它们断折之时,往往正是你最需要它们的时候,那断裂反过来会深深地刺伤你。

神拆穿埃及这根芦苇杖,不是要我们绝望,而是要把我们的倚靠,从会断折的芦苇杖,转向那永不断折的磐石——神自己。「你们当倚靠耶和华直到永远,因为耶和华是永久的磐石」(赛26:4)。唯有神,是那压上全身重量也永不断折、永不叫倚靠祂的人蒙羞的倚靠;而祂在基督里,已经证明祂是这样一位可靠的神——祂连自己的儿子都为我们舍了。今天,你正把生命的重量,压在哪一根「芦苇杖」上?趁它还没断折、还没反过来刺伤你,把你的倚靠,从这脆弱的芦苇,转到那永久的磐石上。

默想:我正把生命的重量、我的安全感,压在哪一根「芦苇杖」上——金钱、人脉、才干、某段关系、健康、地位?我是否以为它结实可靠,却忘了它不过是有限、会变、终必断折的受造之物?当它断折时,是否正会反过来刺伤我?

应用:今天诚实指认一根你一直全然倚靠的「芦苇杖」;把压在它身上的生命重量,一点一点地转移到神——那永久的磐石——身上,操练在难处中先倚靠神,而非先倚靠那会断折的东西。

祷告:永久磐石的主,你把埃及比作压伤的芦苇杖——人越倚靠它,它越断折,还反过来刺伤倚靠的人。我承认,我常把生命的重量压在金钱、人脉、才干、关系这些芦苇杖上,以为它们可靠。谢谢你拆穿它们,是要把我的倚靠转向你这永不断折的磐石;你连爱子都为我舍了,证明你何等可靠。求你叫我把生命的重量,从芦苇杖转到你身上。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel 29–32 is a series of judgment prophecies against Egypt. Egypt was a great power of the time, and also the object Israel repeatedly wanted to rely on and ally with. Whenever the threat of Assyria or Babylon came, the leaders of Judah’s first thought was often not to rely on God, but to go south seeking help from Egypt. Through Ezekiel, God uses an extremely vivid metaphor to expose the folly of relying on Egypt.

“When they grasped you with the hand, you broke and tore all their shoulders; and when they leaned on you, you broke and made all their loins to shake” (Ezekiel 29:7). God likens Egypt to a “staff of reed.” A reed looks like a staff one could lean on, but it is hollow and fragile; if a person truly puts their full weight on it, leaning on it, it not only fails to hold, but snaps at the touch, and the broken, splintered end pierces the hand of the one leaning on it, digging into their shoulder. This is the fate of everything “relying on created things”: the more fully you put the weight of your life on it, the less it can hold, not only failing to help you, but wounding you instead when it breaks.

This “bruised reed of a staff” is a lesson every one of us needs to recognize clearly. Our lives are always searching for a staff to “lean on” — something that can give us security, that can hold us up in difficulty: whether money, connections, our own ability, a certain relationship, health, or status. These things, like Egypt, look sturdy and reliable, worth leaning on; but in essence, they are all “reeds of staffs” — all finite, changeable, created things that must ultimately decay. If you put the full weight of your life on them, treating them as your ultimate reliance, they will sooner or later break; and the moment they break is often exactly when you need them most, and that break will, in turn, deeply wound you.

God exposes Egypt as this reed of a staff not to make us despair, but to turn our reliance from the breakable reed, to the never-breaking rock — God himself. “Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock” (Isaiah 26:4). Only God is a reliance that never breaks, that never puts to shame those who put their full weight on him and rely on him; and in Christ, he has already proven he is exactly such a reliable God — he even gave up his own Son for us. Today, on which “reed of a staff” are you putting the weight of your life? Before it breaks, before it turns and pierces you, move your reliance from this fragile reed onto that everlasting rock.

Meditation: On which “reed of a staff” am I putting the weight of my life, my sense of security — money, connections, ability, a certain relationship, health, status? Do I think it’s sturdy and reliable, forgetting it’s nothing but a finite, changeable created thing that must ultimately break? When it breaks, will it turn and pierce me?

Application: Today, honestly identify a “reed of a staff” you’ve always fully relied on; move the weight of your life resting on it, bit by bit, onto God — that everlasting rock; practice relying on God first in difficulty, rather than that breakable thing first.

Prayer: Everlasting rock, Lord, you likened Egypt to a bruised reed of a staff — the more one relies on it, the more it breaks, wounding the one relying on it in turn. I confess I often put the weight of my life on reeds of staffs like money, connections, ability, and relationships, thinking them reliable. Thank you for exposing them, to turn my reliance to you, this never-breaking rock; you even gave up your beloved Son for me, proving how reliable you are. Let me move the weight of my life from the reed of a staff onto you. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我必亲自寻找我的羊
entries.title_en: I Myself Will Search for My Sheep
entries.verse: 以西结书卅四章十六节
entries.content:
以西结书三十四章,神严厉地责备了以色列的「牧人」——那些本该牧养神百姓的领袖。他们只顾自己:吃羊的脂油、穿羊的羊毛、宰肥壮的,却不牧养群羊;瘦弱的没有养壮,有病的没有医治,受伤的没有缠裹,被逐的没有领回,失丧的没有寻找。群羊因无人牧养,四散、被掳、成了野兽的食物。面对这失职的光景,神宣告了一件震动人心的事:既然这些牧人不肯牧养,「我必亲自」来作群羊的牧人。

「失丧的,我必寻找;被逐的,我必领回;受伤的,我必缠裹;有病的,我必医治。」(结34:16)请细品这一连串「我必」。神没有说「我会派更好的牧人去」,祂说「我必亲自」:失丧的,我亲自去寻找;被逐的,我亲自去领回;受伤的,我亲自去缠裹;有病的,我亲自去医治。这位至高的神,竟俯下身来,亲自作那寻找一只迷羊、缠裹一只伤羊、医治一只病羊的牧人。祂对祂每一只羊——尤其是那失丧的、被逐的、受伤的、有病的——的看顾,是何等地亲自、何等地细致、何等地温柔。

这幅图画,是给每一只自觉「失丧、被逐、受伤、有病」之羊的极大安慰。我们里面常有一个惧怕:我这样软弱、这样跌倒、这样满身是伤、这样失丧,神大概早已放弃我了吧?可神在这里宣告的,恰恰相反:祂所特别要亲自寻找、领回、缠裹、医治的,正是那失丧的、被逐的、受伤的、有病的羊!你的软弱与失丧,不是叫神放弃你的理由,反倒正是祂要亲自俯身来寻找你、医治你的地方。祂不是嫌弃软弱之羊的牧人,祂是专门俯身照顾软弱之羊的牧人。

这位说「我必亲自」寻羊的神,后来真的亲自来了。主耶稣说:「我是好牧人,好牧人为羊舍命」(约10:11);祂又说,祂来「为要寻找、拯救失丧的人」(路19:10)。以西结所预言那位「亲自」寻羊的神,就是道成肉身、为羊舍命的基督;祂撇下九十九只,去寻找那一只迷失的,寻见了就欢欢喜喜地扛在肩上(路15:4-5)。今天,你若正自觉失丧、受伤、有病、被逐,以为神早已放弃了你——听神的「我必亲自」:祂正俯身寻找你、要缠裹你、医治你。让这位亲自寻羊的牧人寻见你。

默想:我里面是否有一个惧怕——「我这样软弱、跌倒、满身是伤、失丧,神大概早放弃我了」?神却说,祂所特别要「亲自」寻找、领回、缠裹、医治的,正是失丧、被逐、受伤、有病的羊——这如何改变我?我的软弱,是叫神放弃我的理由,还是祂要亲自俯身来医治我的地方?

应用:今天不因自己的软弱、失丧、受伤而躲避神、以为祂放弃了你;而是把你最软弱、最受伤、最失丧的那一处,坦然带到这位「必亲自寻找、缠裹、医治」的牧人面前,让祂寻见你、医治你。

祷告:亲自寻羊的好牧人,那些牧人不顾群羊,你却说「我必亲自」:失丧的我寻找,受伤的我缠裹,有病的我医治。我承认,我常因自己的软弱、跌倒、满身是伤,以为你早已放弃了我。谢谢你,主耶稣,你亲自来为羊舍命,寻找拯救失丧的人。求你叫我不再躲避,把我最软弱失丧的一处带到你面前,让你这亲自寻羊的牧人寻见我、医治我。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Ezekiel 34 has God severely rebuking Israel’s “shepherds” — the leaders who should have been shepherding God’s people. They cared only for themselves: eating the fat of the sheep, wearing the wool, slaughtering the fattest, but not shepherding the flock; the weak were not strengthened, the sick were not healed, the injured were not bound up, the strayed were not brought back, the lost were not sought. The flock, having no one to shepherd them, scattered, were carried away, and became food for wild beasts. Facing this derelict scene, God declares something that shakes the heart: since these shepherds refuse to shepherd, “I myself” will come and be the shepherd of the flock.

“I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16). Consider carefully this succession of “I will”s. God did not say “I will send better shepherds”; he said “I myself”: the lost, I myself will seek; the strayed, I myself will bring back; the injured, I myself will bind up; the sick, I myself will heal. This Most High God actually stoops down, to personally be the shepherd who seeks a stray sheep, binds up a wounded sheep, heals a sick sheep. How personal, how meticulous, how tender his care is for each of his sheep — especially the lost, strayed, injured, and sick.

This picture is a tremendous comfort to every sheep who feels itself “lost, strayed, injured, sick.” We often carry a fear within: I’m so weak, I’ve stumbled so much, I’m so covered in wounds, I’m so lost — God has probably already given up on me. But what God declares here is exactly the opposite: what he especially wants to personally seek, bring back, bind up, and heal is precisely the lost, strayed, injured, sick sheep! Your weakness and loss are not reasons for God to give up on you — they are exactly the place where he wants to personally stoop down and seek you, heal you. He is not a shepherd who disdains weak sheep; he is a shepherd who specializes in stooping down to care for weak sheep.

This God who says “I myself” will seek the sheep later truly came in person. The Lord Jesus said: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11); he also said he came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). That God Ezekiel foretold who would “personally” seek the sheep is exactly Christ, who became flesh and gave his life for the sheep; he leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one lost sheep, and when he finds it, joyfully carries it on his shoulders (Luke 15:4-5). Today, if you feel yourself lost, injured, sick, cast out, thinking God has already given up on you — hear God’s “I myself will”: he is stooping down to seek you, wanting to bind up your wounds, to heal you. Let this shepherd who personally seeks the sheep find you.

Meditation: Is there a fear within me — “I’m so weak, I’ve stumbled so much, I’m so covered in wounds, I’m so lost, God has probably already given up on me”? Yet God says what he especially wants to “personally” seek, bring back, bind up, and heal is precisely the lost, strayed, injured, sick sheep — how does this change me? Is my weakness a reason for God to give up on me, or the place where he wants to personally stoop down and heal me?

Application: Today, don’t hide from God because of your own weakness, loss, or injury, thinking he has given up on you; instead bring your weakest, most injured, most lost place candidly before this shepherd who “will personally seek, bind up, and heal,” and let him find you and heal you.

Prayer: Good shepherd who personally seeks the sheep, those shepherds cared nothing for the flock, yet you say “I myself will”: the lost, I will seek; the injured, I will bind up; the sick, I will heal. I confess I often think, because of my weakness, stumbling, and wounds, that you have already given up on me. Thank you, Lord Jesus, for personally coming to give your life for the sheep, seeking and saving the lost. Let me no longer hide, but bring my weakest, most lost place before you, and let you, this shepherd who personally seeks the sheep, find me and heal me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 这些骸骨能复活吗
entries.title_en: Can These Bones Live?
entries.verse: 以西结书卅七章五节
entries.content:
神把以西结带到一个平原,那里遍满了骸骨——不是刚死的、还有血肉的尸体,而是「甚多」「极其枯干」的骸骨。这是死亡最彻底、最绝望的图景:不只是死了,而是死了很久,连血肉都已朽尽,只剩下一地白骨。神问以西结一个几乎不可能有正面答案的问题:「人子啊,这些骸骨能复活吗?」以西结不敢说能,也不敢说不能,只答:「主耶和华啊,你是知道的。」

然后,神吩咐以西结向这些枯骨说预言;神宣告:「主耶和华对这些骸骨如此说:『我必使气息进入你们里面,你们就要活了。』」(结37:5)于是骸骨彼此连接,长出筋、肉、皮;神的气息(灵)一进入,这一大批极其枯干的骸骨,竟站立起来,成为一支极大的军队。那彻底死透、毫无指望的,竟因神的话与神的灵,重新活了过来。这异象,首先是应许那看似「已死无望」的以色列必要复兴、归回;但它更深地宣告了一个真理——唯有神,能叫死人复活。

这枯骨复活的异象,正是每一个属灵生命的写照。圣经说,我们未信主之前,「死在过犯罪恶之中」(弗2:1)——不是「病了」「弱了」,而是「死了」;在属灵的意义上,我们正如那平原上极其枯干的骸骨,毫无自救的能力,也毫无自活的指望。一个死人,无法叫自己复活;正如枯骨无法靠自己长出筋肉、无法靠自己吹进气息。所以,属灵的重生,从来不是死人自己努力「活过来」的结果,乃是神的话临到、神的灵吹入,把死的变成活的——这是一个彻头彻尾、唯独出于神的创造性神迹。这也叫我们对那些看似「无可救药」的灵魂、那些死透了的光景,不再绝望:因为叫人复活的,不是人的努力,而是神的灵。

那使枯骨复活的「气息」「灵」,新约把它的名字向我们说明了:是神的圣灵,借着复活的基督所赐下的。「叫耶稣从死里复活者的灵,若住在你们心里,那叫基督耶稣从死里复活的,也必藉着住在你们心里的圣灵,使你们必死的身体又活过来」(罗8:11)。那位叫基督从死里复活的大能,也正是叫我们从灵性的死亡中复活、并要在末日叫我们身体复活的大能。今天,你若正为自己里面某处「死透了」的光景、或某个「无可救药」的灵魂而绝望,记得这平原上的枯骨:在人这是不能的,在神凡事都能;祂的灵一吹入,极枯干的骸骨也必复活。

默想:我是否真明白,人未重生之前是「死在过犯罪恶中」——不是病了、弱了,而是死了,如那极枯干的骸骨,毫无自救之力?我的重生,是我努力「活过来」的,还是神的话与灵吹入的创造性神迹?面对某个「死透了、无可救药」的光景或灵魂,我是绝望,还是相信神的灵能叫枯骨复活?

应用:今天为一个你觉得「已经死透、无可救药」的光景或灵魂(某个远离神的亲友、某处你以为再无指望的境地)祷告——不靠人的努力,而是求那使枯骨复活的圣灵吹入,凭信心把它交给那位叫死人复活的神。

祷告:叫死人复活的主,你在遍满极枯干骸骨的平原上,凭你的话与你的灵,叫它们复活成为大军。我承认,我未信之前死在过犯罪恶中,如那枯骨毫无自活之力;是你的灵吹入,叫我重生。谢谢那叫基督从死里复活的大能,也住在我里面。求你叫我不为任何「死透、无可救药」的光景绝望,深信你的灵一吹入,枯骨也必复活。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
God brought Ezekiel to a valley, full of bones everywhere — not freshly dead bodies still with flesh, but bones “very many” and “very dry.” This is the most complete, most hopeless picture of death: not merely dead, but dead a long time, even the flesh long since decayed, leaving nothing but a field of white bones. God asks Ezekiel a question that seems almost impossible to answer positively: “Son of man, can these bones live?” Ezekiel dared not say yes, nor dared say no, only answering: “O Lord GOD, you know.”

Then God commanded Ezekiel to prophesy to these dry bones; God declared: “Thus says the Lord GOD to these bones: Behold, I will cause breath to enter you, and you shall live” (Ezekiel 37:5). So the bones connected to one another, and sinews, flesh, and skin grew; when God’s breath (Spirit) entered, this vast multitude of extremely dry bones actually stood up, becoming an exceedingly great army. That which was utterly, completely dead, without any hope, actually came back to life through God’s word and God’s Spirit. This vision, first of all, promises that Israel, seemingly “already dead, without hope,” would surely be restored and returned; but more deeply, it declares a truth — only God can raise the dead.

This vision of the bones coming to life is exactly a portrait of every spiritual life. Scripture says that before we believed in the Lord, we were “dead in the trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1) — not “sick,” “weak,” but “dead”; in a spiritual sense, we were exactly like those extremely dry bones on that plain, with no ability to save ourselves, no hope of coming alive on our own. A dead person cannot raise themselves to life; just as dry bones cannot, by themselves, grow sinews and flesh, cannot breathe life into themselves by themselves. So spiritual rebirth has never been the result of a dead person’s own effort to “come alive”; it is God’s word arriving, God’s Spirit breathing in, turning the dead into the living — this is a thoroughgoing, creative miracle originating solely from God. This also keeps us from despairing over those souls that seem “beyond saving,” those thoroughly dead situations: because what raises people to life is not human effort, but God’s Spirit.

That “breath,” that “spirit,” which raised the dry bones to life — the New Testament makes its name known to us: it is the Holy Spirit of God, given through the risen Christ. “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). The same power that raised Christ from the dead is exactly the power that raises us from spiritual death, and will raise our bodies on the last day. Today, if you’re in despair over some “thoroughly dead” condition within yourself, or over some “beyond saving” soul, remember this valley of bones: what is impossible with man is possible with God; the moment his Spirit breathes in, even the most withered bones will surely live.

Meditation: Do I truly understand that man before rebirth is “dead in trespasses and sins” — not sick, not weak, but dead, like those extremely dry bones, with no ability to save myself? Was my rebirth the result of my own effort to “come alive,” or a creative miracle of God’s word and Spirit breathing in? Facing some “thoroughly dead, beyond saving” situation or soul, do I despair, or believe God’s Spirit can raise dry bones to life?

Application: Today, pray for a situation or soul you feel is “already thoroughly dead, beyond saving” (some loved one far from God, some place you thought had no hope left) — not relying on human effort, but asking the Holy Spirit who raises dry bones to life to breathe in, handing it over by faith to the God who raises the dead.

Prayer: Lord who raises the dead, on that plain full of extremely dry bones, you, by your word and your Spirit, raised them to life as a great army. I confess that before I believed, I was dead in trespasses and sins, like those bones, with no ability to come alive myself; it was your Spirit breathing in that raised me to life. Thank you that the same power that raised Christ from the dead also dwells in me. Let me not despair over any “thoroughly dead, beyond saving” situation, deeply believing that the moment your Spirit breathes in, even dry bones will surely live. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你们是我草场上的羊——数算恩典
entries.title_en: You Are My Sheep, the Sheep of My Pasture — Counting Your Blessings
entries.content:
你们是我草场上的羊——数算恩典

「你们作我的羊,我草场上的羊,乃是 以色列 人,我也是你们的 神。这是主耶和华说的。」(以西结书 34:31)

这一周,我们看见神不喜悦恶人死亡、为自己名的缘故施恩、亲自寻找失丧的羊、又叫枯骨复活。这一切的核心,是一句满有归属感的宣告:你是我的羊,我是你的神。

今天安息日,安静地把这句话反复咀嚼:「你们作我的羊……我也是你们的神。」这是一份双向的、立定的归属——你属于祂,祂也属于你。数算这归属所带来的一切:一位亲自寻你、缠裹你、医治你的牧人;一位以祂名的荣耀担保你救恩的神;一位能叫你枯干之处重新复活的主。你不是一只无人认领、无人看顾的野羊;你是祂草场上的羊,有名有姓,被祂昼夜看顾。在这份归属里,安息、感恩、并且放心。

"And you are my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, and I am your God, declares the Lord GOD." (Ezekiel 34:31)
entries.content_en:
You Are My Sheep, the Sheep of My Pasture — Counting Your Blessings

"And you are my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, and I am your God, declares the Lord GOD." (Ezekiel 34:31)

This week, we saw that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, that he shows grace for his own name’s sake, that he personally seeks the lost sheep, and that he raises dry bones to life. At the center of it all is a declaration full of belonging: you are my sheep, and I am your God.

Today, on the Sabbath, quietly chew on this sentence again and again: "you are my sheep... and I am your God." This is a mutual, settled belonging — you belong to him, and he belongs to you. Count everything this belonging brings: a shepherd who personally seeks you, binds up your wounds, and heals you; a God who guarantees your salvation by the glory of his own name; a Lord who can raise your withered places back to life. You are not a stray sheep that no one claims, that no one watches over; you are the sheep of his pasture, known by name, cared for by him day and night. Rest, give thanks, and be at ease in this belonging.

"And you are my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, and I am your God, declares the Lord GOD." (Ezekiel 34:31)

entries.title: 神要住在他们中间,直到永远
entries.title_en: I Will Dwell in Their Midst Forever
entries.verse: 以西结书四十三章七节
entries.content:
以西结书的末了几章,神向被掳的以西结,展示了一座宏伟的新殿的异象。之前,以西结曾亲眼看见神的荣耀,因百姓的罪,一步步地离开了旧的圣殿——那是何等沉痛的一幕。而如今,在这新殿的异象里,以西结看见了那令他心跳加速的一幕:耶和华的荣光,从东门回来了,充满了这殿。荣耀回来了!而神接着说的话,道出了整本圣经跳动的心脏。

「他对我说:人子啊,这是我宝座之地,是我脚掌所踏之地。我要在这里住,在以色列人中直到永远。」(结43:7)请听这应许的核心——「我要在这里住,在以色列人中直到永远」。神一切救赎工作的目标,归根究底,不是叫我们得着某些好处,而是叫神自己能与祂的百姓同住;不是暂时的造访,而是「直到永远」的居住。从伊甸园里神与人同行,到会幕、圣殿中神的荣耀充满,到这新殿的异象,神的心意始终如一:祂渴望与祂所造、所赎的百姓,永永远远地住在一起。这,就是圣经从创世记到启示录,那一条贯穿始终的主线。

这真理,校正了我们对救恩、对天堂常有的、以自我为中心的理解。我们常把救恩想成「神赐给我的种种好处」——赦罪、平安、永生、天堂的福乐;把天堂想成一个「没有眼泪、街道是金的美好地方」。这些都不错,但它们都还不是那颗跳动的心脏。救恩最深、最荣耀的祝福,不是神所赐的任何礼物,而是神自己;天堂之所以是天堂,不是因为那里的街道是金的,而是因为「神要与他们同在,作他们的神」。若一个「天堂」里有一切的福乐、却没有神,那对真爱神的人来说,根本算不得天堂。神就是那福;与神同住,就是那终极的赏赐。

而神「要与人同住直到永远」的这个心愿,在基督里,一步步地成就了。那位名叫「以马内利——神与我们同在」的基督,道成肉身,「住在我们中间」(约1:14)——「住」字原文有「支搭帐棚、居住」之意;祂又赐下圣灵,使信徒的身体成为「神藉着圣灵居住的所在」(弗2:22);而这一切,都指向那最终的成全——在新天新地,「神的帐幕在人间。他要与人同住,他们要作他的子民……神要亲自与他们同在,作他们的神」(启21:3)。今天,你渴望的,是神所赐的种种好处,还是神自己?救恩的核心、天堂的核心,是那位渴望与你永远同住的神。愿这成为你心中最深的渴望。

默想:我对救恩、对天堂的理解,是否停在「神所赐给我的种种好处」上,却错过了那颗跳动的心脏——神自己要与我永远同住?我心里最深渴望的,是神所赐的礼物,还是神自己?一个有一切福乐、却没有神的「天堂」,对我还算不算天堂?

应用:今天在你向神的祷告与渴望中,刻意把重心从「求神赐我种种好处」,转向「渴慕神自己、渴慕祂的同在」;操练以「有神与我同在」本身为你最深的满足与赏赐,而非只把神当作赐福的来源。

祷告:渴望与人同住的主,你一切救赎的目标,是「我要住在他们中间,直到永远」。我承认,我常把救恩想成你赐我的种种好处,把天堂想成美好的地方,却错过了那核心——你自己。谢谢你在基督里道成肉身、住在我们中间,又要在新天新地永远与我同住。求你叫我渴慕的不是你的礼物,而是你自己;以有你同在,为我最深的满足。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The final chapters of Ezekiel show the exiled Ezekiel a vision of a magnificent new temple. Earlier, Ezekiel had personally watched God’s glory, because of the people’s sin, depart step by step from the old temple — what a painful scene that was. And now, in this vision of the new temple, Ezekiel sees the scene that made his heart race: the glory of the LORD returned, from the east gate, filling this temple. The glory has returned! And what God says next reveals the beating heart of the entire Bible.

“He said to me, Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever” (Ezekiel 43:7). Hear the core of this promise — “I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever.” The goal of all God’s redemptive work, traced to its root, is not to give us certain benefits, but for God himself to be able to dwell with his people; not a temporary visit, but a dwelling “forever.” From God walking with man in Eden, to God’s glory filling the tabernacle and the temple, to this vision of the new temple, God’s intention has remained unchanged all along: he longs to dwell forever with the people he made and redeemed. This is the thread that runs from Genesis to Revelation, beating at the heart of Scripture.

This truth corrects the self-centered understanding we often hold about salvation, about heaven. We often think of salvation as “the various benefits God gives me” — forgiveness of sin, peace, eternal life, the blessings of heaven; we think of heaven as a “wonderful place with no tears, where the streets are gold.” These are all correct, but none of them are yet that beating heart. The deepest, most glorious blessing of salvation is not any gift God gives, but God himself; heaven is heaven not because its streets are gold, but because “God will dwell with them, and be their God.” If a “heaven” had every blessing, but no God, then to someone who truly loves God, it would hardly count as heaven at all. God himself is the blessing; dwelling with God is the ultimate reward.

And this longing of God’s “to dwell with man forever” has, in Christ, been accomplished step by step. That Christ, named “Immanuel — God with us,” became flesh, and “dwelt among us” (John 1:14) — the word “dwelt” in the original carries the sense of “pitching a tent, taking up residence”; he also gave the Holy Spirit, making believers’ bodies “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22); and all of this points to that final fulfillment — in the new heaven and new earth, “the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people... God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). Today, what do you long for — the various benefits God gives, or God himself? The core of salvation, the core of heaven, is that God who longs to dwell with you forever. May this become the deepest longing of your heart.

Meditation: Does my understanding of salvation, of heaven, stay at “the various benefits God gives me,” missing the beating heart — that God himself wants to dwell with me forever? What do I long for most deeply — the gifts God gives, or God himself? Would a “heaven” with every blessing, but no God, still count as heaven to me?

Application: Today, in your prayers and longings toward God, deliberately shift the focus from “asking God to give me various good things” toward “longing for God himself, longing for his presence”; practice treating “having God with me” itself as your deepest satisfaction and reward, rather than only treating God as a source of blessings.

Prayer: Lord who longs to dwell with man, the goal of all your redemptive work is “I will dwell in their midst forever.” I confess I often think of salvation as the various benefits you give me, and think of heaven as a wonderful place, missing the core — you yourself. Thank you for becoming flesh in Christ and dwelling among us, and for wanting to dwell with me forever in the new heaven and new earth. Let me long not for your gifts, but for you yourself; let having you with me be my deepest satisfaction. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
