entries.title: 你竟这样爱那城
entries.title_en: Should Not I Pity That Great City
entries.verse: 约拿书四章二节
entries.content:
约拿的故事,我们耳熟能详:神差他去向尼尼微城宣告审判,他却往相反的方向逃跑;神用大鱼把他追了回来;他终于去传道,尼尼微竟全城悔改,神就不降所说的灾。故事本该在这里皆大欢喜地结束。然而,约拿书没有停在这里;它最深刻、也最扎心的部分,恰恰是最后一章——约拿对神施怜悯,大大地发怒了。

约拿向神吐露了他一开始就逃跑的真实原因:「耶和华啊,我在本国的时候岂不是这样说吗?……我知道你是有恩典、有怜悯的神,不轻易发怒,有丰盛的慈爱,并且后悔不降所说的灾。」(约拿书4:2)何等讽刺!约拿逃跑,不是因为他不认识神,恰恰是因为他太认识神了——他知道神有恩典、有怜悯;他就是怕神真的怜悯尼尼微。尼尼微是亚述的都城,是以色列凶残的仇敌;约拿宁可这仇敌被灭,也不愿看见神向他们施恩。他信一位有怜悯的神,却无法忍受这怜悯临到他所恨恶的人身上。

这就是约拿书那面照人的镜子。约拿的问题,不是不信神的怜悯,而是他希望这怜悯只临到「像我这样的人」、只临到「我们这一边」,却不要临到「他们」——那些我看不惯的、与我为敌的、我觉得不配的人。我们里面,常藏着一个同样的「约拿」:我们乐意领受神向自己的怜悯,却在心里悄悄地划出一条界线,巴不得神的审判(而非怜悯)临到那些我们所厌恶、所鄙视、所论断的人。当神的恩典临到一个「那种人」——一个我们认定不配、甚至该受报应的人——我们里面竟会像约拿一样,不是欢喜,而是不满、甚至发怒。这暴露出:我们并没有真正被恩典折服;我们只是喜欢「对自己有利」的恩典。

约拿书以神一个满有怜悯的问题结束:「这尼尼微大城……我岂能不爱惜呢?」神的心,比约拿宽广得多;祂的怜悯,越过了一切我们所划的界线,临到那最不配、最凶残、最像仇敌的人。而这份越过界线的爱,在基督里达到了顶峰——祂为「仇敌」死,而那仇敌里,有你,有我;祂差门徒去,把福音传到「地极」,传给每一个「尼尼微」。今天,你心里是否也藏着一个约拿——乐意领受神对自己的怜悯,却不愿神的恩典临到某些「那种人」?求神把祂那越过一切界线的怜悯之心,赐给你。

默想:我里面是否藏着一个「约拿」——乐意领受神对自己的怜悯,却在心里划出界线,巴不得神的审判(而非怜悯)临到那些我厌恶、鄙视、认定不配的「那种人」?当神的恩典临到一个我觉得「不配」的人,我是欢喜,还是像约拿一样不满?

应用:今天为一个你一直厌恶、鄙视、认定「不配蒙恩」的人(或一类人)祷告——求神让你有祂那越过界线的怜悯之心,真心盼望神的恩典也临到他;省察并悔改你心里那条划分「我们」与「他们」的界线。

祷告:怜悯越过界线的主,约拿宁可仇敌被灭,也不愿你向他们施恩;他信你有怜悯,却不愿这怜悯临到他所恨的人。我承认,我里面也藏着这样一个约拿,乐意领受你对我的怜悯,却给你的恩典划界线。谢谢你的爱越过一切界线,为仇敌(包括我)舍命。求你把你那宽广、越过界线的怜悯之心赐给我,拆毁我心里「我们」与「他们」的界线。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Jonah’s story is one we know well: God sent him to declare judgment on Nineveh, but he fled in the opposite direction; God pursued him back with a great fish; he finally went and preached, and the whole city of Nineveh actually repented, so God did not bring the disaster he had spoken of. The story should end here, happily ever after. Yet Jonah does not stop here; its most profound, most piercing part is exactly the last chapter — Jonah, at God’s showing mercy, becomes greatly angry.

Jonah pours out to God the real reason he fled in the first place: “O LORD, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country?... I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster” (Jonah 4:2). What irony! Jonah fled not because he didn’t know God, but precisely because he knew God too well — he knew God was gracious and merciful; he was afraid God would truly show mercy to Nineveh. Nineveh was Assyria’s capital, Israel’s savage enemy; Jonah would rather this enemy be destroyed than see God show them grace. He believed in a merciful God, yet could not bear that mercy coming upon those he hated.

This is exactly the mirror that shows us ourselves in the book of Jonah. Jonah’s problem was not disbelief in God’s mercy, but that he hoped this mercy would only come upon “people like me,” only upon “my side,” but not upon “them” — those he couldn’t stand, who were his enemies, whom he felt undeserving. Within us, there is often a similar “Jonah”: we’re happy to receive God’s mercy toward ourselves, yet secretly draw a line in our hearts, hoping God’s judgment (not mercy) would come upon those we detest, despise, and condemn. When God’s grace comes upon “that kind of person” — someone we’ve decided is undeserving, even deserving of retribution — within us, like Jonah, arises not joy, but resentment, even anger. This exposes: we haven’t truly been conquered by grace; we only like grace that “benefits ourselves.”

The book of Jonah ends with a question of God’s, full of compassion: “should not I pity Nineveh, that great city?” God’s heart is far wider than Jonah’s; his mercy crosses every line we draw, reaching the most undeserving, the most savage, the most enemy-like people. And this boundary-crossing love reached its peak in Christ — he died for “enemies,” and among those enemies are you, and me; he sent his disciples out, to bring the gospel to “the ends of the earth,” to every “Nineveh.” Today, is there a Jonah hidden in your heart too — happy to receive God’s mercy toward yourself, yet unwilling for God’s grace to come upon some “kind of people”? Ask God to give you his mercy that crosses every line.

Meditation: Is there a “Jonah” hidden within me — happy to receive God’s mercy toward myself, yet drawing a line in my heart, hoping God’s judgment (not mercy) would come upon those I detest, despise, and have decided are undeserving, “that kind of people”? When God’s grace comes upon someone I feel is “undeserving,” am I joyful, or, like Jonah, resentful?

Application: Today, pray for someone (or a group of people) you’ve always detested, despised, decided is “undeserving of grace” — ask God to give you his boundary-crossing mercy, truly hoping God’s grace would come upon them too; examine and repent of the line in your heart dividing “us” from “them.”

Prayer: Lord whose mercy crosses every line, Jonah would rather his enemy be destroyed than have you show them grace; he believed you had mercy, yet was unwilling for that mercy to come upon those he hated. I confess there is also such a Jonah hidden within me, happy to receive your mercy toward myself, yet drawing lines around your grace. Thank you that your love crosses every line, giving your life for enemies (including me). Give me your wide, boundary-crossing mercy, and tear down the line in my heart dividing “us” from “them.” In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 因手有能力就行出来
entries.title_en: Because It Is in the Power of Their Hand
entries.verse: 弥迦书二章一节
entries.content:
弥迦与以赛亚、阿摩司同时代,他向犹大和以色列的权贵发出审判。他所揭露的,是当时社会一种普遍的罪恶——有权有势的人,如何利用他们的权势,去欺压、盘剥那些无力还手的平民。弥迦一针见血地描绘了这种罪的运作方式。

「祸哉,那些在床上图谋罪孽、造作奸恶的!天一发亮,因手有能力就行出来。」(弥迦书2:1)请留意这罪的两个阶段。第一阶段,是「在床上图谋」——他们夜里躺在床上,不是安息,而是处心积虑地盘算怎样贪占别人的田地、房屋、产业;罪,是从心里的图谋开始的。第二阶段,是「天一发亮就行出来」,而他们之所以敢明目张胆地行出来,是「因手有能力」——因为他们有权、有势、有办法,料定没人能拦阻他们、没人敢追究他们。他们把神所给的「能力」,变成了行恶、欺压、贪占的工具。

这里揭露了一个极深的属灵试探:权力对人心的腐蚀。当一个人「手有能力」——有了权柄、地位、资源、或对某人某事的掌控力——他就面临一个试探:把这能力用来为自己谋利、去占那些无力还手之人的便宜,并且料定「反正没人能把我怎么样」。这罪之所以隐蔽,是因为「手有能力」的人,往往能把欺压包装得合法、合理、体面;他们不必动刀动枪,只需利用规则、利用地位、利用别人的无助,就能「合法地」盘剥人。而神所看的,不是这行为在人前多么体面,而是那颗「因手有能力就行出来」的、欺压弱者的心。

神特别看顾那些「无力还手」的人;凡利用权势欺压他们的,就是与神为敌。而神所赐的能力、权柄、资源,原不是要我们用来欺压人、为自己谋利的,乃是要我们用来服事人、保护弱者、行公义的。那位「本有神的形象」、拥有至高权柄的基督,却用祂的能力,不是来辖制我们,而是来服事我们、为我们舍命(可10:45);祂是与「因手有能力就行出来」截然相反的榜样——祂手握一切能力,却用来舍己爱人。今天,你「手中的能力」——你的权柄、地位、资源、或对某人的影响力——是用来欺压、占便宜、为自己谋利,还是用来服事、保护、造福那些比你弱小的人?

默想:我「手中的能力」(权柄、地位、资源、对某人某事的掌控力),是用来为自己谋利、占那些无力还手之人的便宜,还是用来服事、保护弱者?我是否曾「因手有能力」,就把欺压包装得合法体面,料定没人敢追究?

应用:今天在一处你「手有能力」、可以占人便宜或为己谋利的地方(职权、家庭角色、某种掌控力),刻意拒绝用它欺压或占便宜;反而效法基督,用这能力去服事、保护、造福一个比你弱小的人。

祷告:看顾弱者的主,你责备那些「因手有能力就行出来」、欺压无力还手之人的权贵。我省察自己,我手中的能力,是否也曾用来为自己谋利、占人便宜,还包装得合法体面?谢谢基督手握至高的能力,却用来服事我、为我舍命。求你叫我不用能力欺压人,而是效法基督,用它去服事、保护、造福那比我弱小的人。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Micah, a contemporary of Isaiah and Amos, issued judgment against the powerful in Judah and Israel. What he exposed was a common evil in society at the time — how those with power and status used their power to oppress and exploit ordinary people who couldn’t fight back. Micah, with piercing precision, describes how this sin operates.

“Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand” (Micah 2:1). Notice the two stages of this sin. The first stage is “devising on their beds” — at night, lying in bed, not resting but scheming how to seize others’ fields, houses, and property; sin begins with scheming in the heart. The second stage is “when the morning dawns, they perform it,” and the reason they dare to do it so openly is “because it is in the power of their hand” — because they have power, status, means, and are confident no one can stop them, no one dares hold them accountable. They turned the “power” God gave them into a tool for doing evil, oppressing, and grasping.

This exposes an extremely deep spiritual temptation: the corrosive effect of power on the human heart. When a person has “power in their hand” — has gained authority, status, resources, or control over some person or matter — they face a temptation: to use this power to profit themselves, to take advantage of those who cannot fight back, confident that “no one can do anything to me anyway.” This sin is so hidden precisely because those with “power in hand” can often package their oppression as legal, reasonable, respectable; they need not wield a sword or gun — they need only use rules, use status, use others’ helplessness, to “legally” exploit people. And what God looks at is not how respectable this behavior appears before others, but the heart that “performs it because it is in the power of their hand,” oppressing the weak.

God especially watches over those who “cannot fight back”; whoever uses power to oppress them is at enmity with God. And the power, authority, and resources God gives were never meant for us to use to oppress people, to profit ourselves; they were meant for us to serve people, protect the weak, and act justly. That Christ, who “was in the form of God” and held supreme authority, used his power not to dominate us, but to serve us and give his life for us (Mark 10:45); he is a pattern utterly opposite to those who “perform evil because it is in the power of their hand” — he held all power in hand, yet used it to deny himself and love others. Today, is the “power in your hand” — your authority, status, resources, or influence over someone — being used to oppress, take advantage, profit yourself, or to serve, protect, and benefit those weaker than you?

Meditation: Is the “power in my hand” (authority, status, resources, control over some person or matter) being used to profit myself, take advantage of those who cannot fight back, or to serve and protect the weak? Have I ever, “because it is in the power of my hand,” packaged oppression as legal and respectable, confident no one would dare hold me accountable?

Application: Today, in a place where you “have power in hand,” able to take advantage or profit yourself (workplace authority, family role, some form of control), deliberately refuse to use it to oppress or take advantage; instead, following Christ’s example, use this power to serve, protect, and benefit someone weaker than you.

Prayer: Lord who watches over the weak, you rebuked those in power who “perform evil because it is in the power of their hand,” oppressing those who cannot fight back. I examine myself — has the power in my hand also been used to profit myself, take advantage of others, and packaged as legal and respectable? Thank you that Christ held supreme power in hand, yet used it to serve me and give his life for me. Let me not use power to oppress people, but, following Christ’s example, use it to serve, protect, and benefit those weaker than me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 从伯利恒出来的那一位
entries.title_en: The One Who Comes Out of Bethlehem
entries.verse: 弥迦书五章二节
entries.content:
弥迦在宣告审判的黑暗中,忽然射出一道极其明亮的弥赛亚预言之光。当时,大卫的王朝已日渐衰微,犹大即将被掳,君王的荣耀似乎要熄灭了。就在这看似绝望的时刻,神却借弥迦,指着一个毫不起眼的小城,宣告了那位要来的君王的降生之地。

「伯利恒的以法他啊,你在犹大诸城中为小,将来必有一位从你那里出来,在以色列中为我作掌权的;他的根源从亘古,从太初就有。」(弥迦书5:2)请深思这节预言里那惊人的张力。一面,是极卑微的:伯利恒,是犹大诸城中「为小」的一座小城,毫不起眼、无足轻重;这位掌权者,竟要从这样一个不起眼的地方出来。另一面,却是极崇高的:这位要从伯利恒出来的掌权者,「他的根源从亘古,从太初就有」——祂不是一个在伯利恒才开始存在的婴孩,祂是那位从亘古、从永恒里就已存在的一位!这一节,把这位弥赛亚的「永恒神性」与「卑微降生」,并列在了一起。

七百年后,这预言一字一句地应验了。当东方的博士来寻找那生下来作犹太人之王的,希律王的文士,正是引用弥迦书这节经文,指出基督当生在伯利恒(太2:5-6)。那位「根源从亘古、从太初就有」的永恒之子,竟真的降生在伯利恒那卑微的马槽里。这就是道成肉身的奥秘,也是福音最叫人惊叹俯伏之处:那位创造万有、从亘古就有、本是永恒之神的一位,竟为我们的缘故,虚己、降卑,取了肉身,生在最卑微之处。祂本可以带着天上的荣耀君临,却选择从一座「为小」的城、一个卑微的马槽,悄悄地进入了人类的历史。

这位从亘古就有、却降生伯利恒的掌权者,祂掌权的方式,也与地上的君王截然不同。地上的王,靠权势、靠武力辖制人;祂却像牧人一样牧养群羊(弥5:4),最终更以牧人为羊舍命的方式,得着了祂的国。祂的伟大,不在于祂高高在上,而在于祂甘愿降卑;祂的掌权,不是靠压制,而是靠舍己的爱。今天,当你默想这位「根源从亘古、却降生伯利恒」的基督时,愿你的心被这样一位神折服:祂是何等的崇高,又是何等的谦卑;祂本配得一切,却为你降卑至此。这样一位主,值得你俯伏敬拜、倾心跟随。

默想:我是否真默想过这惊人的奥秘——那位「根源从亘古、从太初就有」的永恒之神,竟为我降生在伯利恒那卑微的马槽里?祂的崇高(永恒神性)与祂的谦卑(卑微降生)并列在一起,如何叫我的心俯伏敬拜?祂靠舍己的爱、而非压制来掌权,这对我意味着什么?

应用:今天默想基督「从亘古就有、却降生伯利恒」的崇高与谦卑;为这位本配得一切、却为你降卑至马槽的永恒之子,向祂献上俯伏的敬拜与倾心的跟随;并效法祂,在一处你可以「高高在上」的地方,选择降卑、服事。

祷告:从亘古就有、却降生伯利恒的主,弥迦预言那从最小之城出来的掌权者,根源从太初就有——而这正是道成肉身的你。我俯伏惊叹:你是何等崇高,又何等谦卑;你本配得一切,却为我降卑到马槽。谢谢你不靠压制、而靠舍己的爱掌权,为羊舍命。求你叫我的心被你折服,俯伏敬拜、倾心跟随你,也效法你的降卑。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In the midst of pronouncing judgment, Micah suddenly shoots out an extremely bright ray of messianic prophecy. At the time, the Davidic dynasty was in decline, Judah was about to be exiled, and the glory of the kingship seemed about to be extinguished. Right at this seemingly hopeless moment, God, through Micah, pointed to an insignificant small town, declaring the birthplace of the coming King.

“But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” (Micah 5:2). Consider deeply the astonishing tension in this prophecy. On one hand, it is extremely lowly: Bethlehem was a small town, “too little” among the towns of Judah, insignificant, of no account; this ruler would actually come forth from such an unremarkable place. On the other hand, it is extremely exalted: this ruler who would come from Bethlehem, “whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” — he is not a baby who began to exist only in Bethlehem; he is the one who has existed from of old, from eternity! This verse sets side by side this Messiah’s “eternal deity” and “lowly birth.”

Seven hundred years later, this prophecy was fulfilled word for word. When the wise men from the East came seeking the one born to be king of the Jews, it was exactly this verse in Micah that Herod’s scribes quoted, pointing out that Christ was to be born in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:5-6). That eternal Son, “whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days,” actually was born in that lowly manger in Bethlehem. This is the mystery of the incarnation, and also the place where the gospel most astonishes us into worship: that one who created all things, who has existed from of old, who is truly the eternal God, for our sake, emptied himself, humbled himself, took on flesh, and was born in the lowliest place. He could have come with heavenly glory, reigning; instead he chose to quietly enter human history from a “too little” town, a lowly manger.

This ruler, who has existed from of old yet was born in Bethlehem, rules in a way utterly different from earthly kings too. Earthly kings rely on power, on force, to dominate people; he instead, like a shepherd, shepherds his flock (Micah 5:4), and ultimately obtains his kingdom by the way of a shepherd giving his life for the sheep. His greatness lies not in being high above, but in his willingness to humble himself; his rule is not by suppression, but by self-giving love. Today, as you meditate on this Christ “whose coming forth is from of old, yet was born in Bethlehem,” may your heart be conquered by such a God: how exalted he is, and how humble; he deserved everything, yet humbled himself this far for you. Such a Lord deserves your prostrate worship and wholehearted following.

Meditation: Have I truly meditated on this astonishing mystery — that the eternal God, “whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days,” was born for me in that lowly manger in Bethlehem? How does his exaltation (eternal deity) set side by side with his humility (lowly birth) move my heart to fall down in worship? What does it mean for me that he rules by self-giving love, not by suppression?

Application: Today, meditate on Christ’s exaltation and humility — “existing from of old, yet born in Bethlehem”; offer prostrate worship and wholehearted following to this eternal Son who deserved everything, yet humbled himself for you to the manger; and, following his example, in a place where you could be “high above,” choose instead to humble yourself and serve.

Prayer: Lord who has existed from of old, yet was born in Bethlehem, Micah prophesied that the ruler who would come from the smallest town has existed from ancient days — and this is exactly you, incarnate. I fall prostrate in wonder: how exalted you are, and how humble; you deserved everything, yet humbled yourself for me to the manger. Thank you for ruling not by suppression, but by self-giving love, giving your life for the sheep. Let my heart be conquered by you, falling prostrate in worship, following you wholeheartedly, and following your example of humility. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 我要仰望那救我的神——安息与更新
entries.title_en: I Will Look to the God of My Salvation — Rest and Renewal
entries.content:
我要仰望那救我的神——安息与更新

「至于我,我要仰望耶和华,要等候那救我的 神;我的 神必应允我。」(弥迦书 7:7)

这一周,我们走过审判的信息:听不见神话语的饥荒、以东的幸灾乐祸、约拿的怨怒、权贵的欺压。四围满是黑暗与不义,叫人容易灰心、焦躁、失了指望。

今天安息日,请听弥迦在满目疮痍中所立定的心志。他说「至于我」——无论四围怎样黑暗、别人怎样行,至于我,我要单单「仰望」耶和华,「等候」那救我的神。仰望与等候,是安息的两个动作:仰望,是把眼目从纷乱的环境挪向神;等候,是安静地信靠祂的时候。而这仰望等候,从不落空——「我的神必应允我」。今天,把你被环境搅扰的眼目,重新仰望这位救你的神;在等候中安息,深信祂必应允。

"But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me." (Micah 7:7)
entries.content_en:
I Will Look to the God of My Salvation — Rest and Renewal

"But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me." (Micah 7:7)

This week, we walked through messages of judgment: the famine of not hearing God’s word, Edom’s gloating, Jonah’s resentment, the oppression of the powerful. Darkness and injustice surrounded on every side, easily leading to discouragement, restlessness, and loss of hope.

Today, on the Sabbath, hear the resolve Micah set amid the devastation. He says "but as for me" — however dark things are all around, however others act, as for me, I will simply "look" to the LORD, and "wait" for the God who saves me. Looking and waiting are the two movements of rest: looking moves the eyes from the chaotic circumstances to God; waiting is the time when we quietly trust him. And this looking and waiting never comes to nothing — "my God will hear me." Today, turn your eyes, so stirred up by circumstances, back to look upon this God who saves you; rest in the waiting, deeply believing he will surely hear you.

"But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me." (Micah 7:7)

entries.title: 行公义,好怜悯,存谦卑
entries.title_en: Do Justice, Love Kindness, Walk Humbly
entries.verse: 弥迦书六章八节
entries.content:
弥迦书里,神与祂的百姓「争辩」。百姓以为,只要献上足够多、足够贵的祭物,神就满意了——他们甚至问:难道要献上千千的公羊、万万的油河,或是献上头生的儿女,来赎我的罪吗?他们把与神的关系,想成了一场「用祭物换取神悦纳」的交易。神却借弥迦,把祂真正所要的,简明扼要地告诉了他们。

「世人哪,耶和华已指示你何为善。他向你所要的是什么呢?只要你行公义,好怜悯,存谦卑的心,与你的神同行。」(弥迦书6:8)神所要的,不是堆积如山的祭物,而是三样朴素、却触及生命核心的东西:行公义——在待人接物上公正、正直,不欺压、不亏负人;好怜悯——以慈爱、恩慈待人,尤其是待那些软弱、有需要的人;存谦卑的心与神同行——在神面前谦卑,不自义、不自恃,天天与祂亲密同行。这三样,概括了一个真正敬虔之人的全貌:对人公义、怜悯,对神谦卑同行。神所要的,从来不是我们「为祂做的事」,而是我们「成为怎样的人」、怎样「与祂同行」。

然而,我们要小心,别把这节经文读成一张「靠行为讨神喜悦」的清单——仿佛只要我努力做到公义、怜悯、谦卑,就能赚得神的悦纳。若这样读,它就变成了最重的律法、最压人的重担;因为凭我们自己,没有一个人能真正地、完全地行公义、好怜悯、存谦卑。恰恰相反,这节经文,是写给那些已经蒙神恩典、已经与神立约的百姓的;它不是「得救的条件」,而是「蒙恩之人的生命样式」。次序至关重要:不是我们先行公义、好怜悯,神才与我们同行;而是神先以恩典与我们立约、与我们同行,我们才被这恩典改变,活出公义、怜悯与谦卑。

而这「行公义、好怜悯、存谦卑与神同行」的生命,唯有那位完全的义者基督,完全活了出来。祂行尽了公义,祂满有怜悯,祂存心谦卑以至于死(腓2:8);祂又把祂所成就的义,赐给了我们,并借着祂的灵,把公义、怜悯、谦卑,一点一点地作在我们里面。所以,当我们读这节经文,不是绝望地看着一张自己达不到的清单,而是一面因基督替我们成全了它而感恩,一面靠着祂的灵,渐渐活出这蒙恩者的样式。今天,神向你所要的,不是更多的「祭物」与忙碌,而是一个被祂恩典改变、以致行公义、好怜悯、存谦卑与祂同行的生命。

默想:我是否把与神的关系,想成了一场「用祭物、用忙碌的事奉换取神悦纳」的交易?神所要的,却是「行公义、好怜悯、存谦卑与祂同行」——一个被恩典改变的生命。我是把这节读成压人的律法清单,还是蒙恩之人自然流露的样式?

应用:今天不用「为神多做些什么」来讨祂喜悦;而是靠着基督的恩典,在一处具体的事上活出这三样中的一样——待某人更公义(不亏负)、更怜悯(施恩慈),或在神面前更谦卑(放下自义),操练「与神同行」的生命。

祷告:与我同行的主,你所要的不是堆积如山的祭物,而是我行公义、好怜悯、存谦卑与你同行。我承认,我常想用忙碌的事奉换取你的悦纳,又靠自己达不到这三样。谢谢基督完全行尽了公义、怜悯、谦卑,又把祂的义赐给我。求你先以恩典与我同行,再借你的灵,叫我活出这蒙恩者公义、怜悯、谦卑的生命。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In Micah, God “contends” with his people. The people thought that as long as they offered enough, costly enough sacrifices, God would be satisfied — they even asked: shall I offer thousands of rams, ten thousand rivers of oil, or shall I offer my firstborn children, to atone for my sin? They had thought of their relationship with God as a transaction of “buying God’s favor with sacrifices.” Through Micah, God told them, plainly and concisely, what he truly wanted.

“He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). What God wants is not a mountain of sacrifices, but three plain, yet life-touching-the-core things: doing justice — being fair and upright in dealing with people, not oppressing, not wronging others; loving kindness — treating people with love and grace, especially the weak and needy; and walking humbly with God — being humble before God, not self-righteous, not self-reliant, walking closely with him daily. These three summarize the whole picture of a truly godly person: justice and mercy toward people, humble walking with God. What God wants has never been “what we do for him,” but “what kind of person we become,” and how we “walk with him.”

Yet we must be careful not to read this verse as a checklist for “earning God’s favor through works” — as though as long as I work hard to achieve justice, kindness, and humility, I could earn God’s favor. Read this way, it becomes the heaviest law, the most crushing burden; because none of us, by ourselves, can truly, perfectly do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly. Quite the opposite, this verse is written to a people who have already received God’s grace, who have already entered a covenant with God; it is not “the condition of salvation,” but “the pattern of life for those who have received grace.” The order matters greatly: it’s not that we first do justice and love kindness, and only then does God walk with us; rather, God first enters into covenant with us by grace, walks with us, and only then, changed by this grace, do we live out justice, kindness, and humility.

And this life of “doing justice, loving kindness, walking humbly with God” has been fully lived out only by Christ, the perfectly righteous One. He fully did justice, was full of kindness, humbled himself even to death (Philippians 2:8); and he gave the righteousness he accomplished to us, and through his Spirit, works justice, kindness, and humility into us, bit by bit. So when we read this verse, we’re not despairingly looking at a checklist we can’t reach, but, on one hand, grateful that Christ fulfilled it in our place, and on the other, gradually living out this recipient’s pattern of life by relying on his Spirit. Today, what God wants from you is not more “sacrifices” and busyness, but a life changed by his grace, so as to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with him.

Meditation: Have I thought of my relationship with God as a transaction of “buying God’s favor with sacrifices, busy service”? Yet what God wants is “doing justice, loving kindness, walking humbly with him” — a life changed by grace. Do I read this verse as a crushing legal checklist, or as the natural overflow of a recipient of grace?

Application: Today, don’t try to please God by “doing more for God”; instead, relying on Christ’s grace, live out one of these three in a concrete matter — treat someone more justly (not wronging them), more mercifully (showing kindness), or be more humble before God (laying down self-righteousness), practicing a life of “walking with God.”

Prayer: Lord who walks with me, what you want is not a mountain of sacrifices, but that I do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with you. I confess I often try to buy your favor with busy service, and rely on myself to reach these three, unable. Thank you, Christ, for fully doing justice, kindness, and humility, and giving me your righteousness. Walk with me first by grace, and then, through your Spirit, let me live out this recipient’s life of justice, kindness, and humility. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 他认得那些投靠他的人
entries.title_en: He Knows Those Who Take Refuge in Him
entries.verse: 那鸿书一章七节
entries.content:
那鸿书,是对尼尼微(亚述帝国的都城)所发的审判预言。亚述是当时最凶残、最不可一世的强权,曾灭了北国以色列,又威胁犹大。那鸿宣告:这个仗势欺人、看似坚不可摧的帝国,神必要将它倾覆。整卷书,满是对恶者审判的雷霆之声。然而,就在这一片审判的宣告中,神却插进了一句无比温柔的话,如同雷雨中的一道暖光。

「耶和华本为善,在患难的日子为人的保障,并且认得那些投靠他的人。」(那鸿书1:7)请看神在这里如何自我启示。祂一面是那位向仗势欺人的恶者施行审判、大而可畏的神;祂另一面,却是那位「本为善」、在患难的日子作祂子民「保障(避难所)」、并且「认得」那些投靠祂之人的神。同一位神,对硬着心欺压人的恶者,是烈火般的审判;对那在患难中投靠祂的人,却是温柔的避难所。神的公义与祂的良善,从不矛盾;正是因为祂良善、祂看顾受欺压的,祂才必审判那欺压人的。

请特别默想「他认得那些投靠他的人」这一句。在一个大帝国倾覆、天下动荡的宏大背景下,神竟然「认得」——祂认识、记念、看顾——每一个投靠祂的、微小的个人。你或许觉得自己太渺小,在这翻腾的世界、这些庞大的势力面前,自己不过是无人理会的一粒微尘;可神说,祂「认得」你——只要你投靠祂,你就不是茫茫人海中一个无名无姓的路人,而是被这位掌管万有的神,亲自认识、亲自看顾、亲自记念的人。当审判临到骄傲的强权时,那些投靠神的人,却被祂稳稳地藏在祂的保障之中。

这位「在患难的日子为人保障、认得投靠祂之人」的神,在基督里,成了我们随时可进的避难所。诗人说「神是我们的避难所,是我们的力量,是我们在患难中随时的帮助」(诗46:1);而主耶稣更亲自发出邀请:「凡劳苦担重担的人可以到我这里来」。祂又是那位「按着名叫自己的羊」的好牧人——祂「认得」祂每一只羊。今天,你若正在患难中、在动荡里、在惧怕下,不要以为自己太渺小、无人理会;投靠这位本为善的神,祂必作你的保障,因为祂认得每一个投靠祂的人。

默想:我是否觉得自己太渺小,在动荡的世界、庞大的势力面前,不过是无人理会的一粒微尘?神却说祂「认得那些投靠他的人」——只要我投靠祂,我就被这掌管万有的神亲自认识、看顾、记念。当患难临到,我是投靠这位「本为善」的保障,还是独自惧怕?

应用:今天在一件正叫你惧怕、觉得自己渺小无助的患难中,刻意「投靠」神——把它带到祂面前,以祂为你的避难所;支取「祂认得我、看顾我」的确据,不再以为自己太渺小、无人理会。

祷告:本为善的主,在向恶者施行审判之中,你却是患难日子的保障,认得每一个投靠你的人。我承认,我常觉得自己太渺小,在动荡与庞大的势力前无人理会,便独自惧怕。谢谢你,你认得我;谢谢主耶稣邀我到你这里来得安息。求你叫我在患难中投靠你,以你为我的避难所,安息在「你认得我」的确据里。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Nahum is a judgment prophecy against Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian empire. Assyria was the most savage, unrivaled power of the time, having destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel, and threatening Judah. Nahum declares: this bullying, seemingly indestructible empire, God will surely overturn. The whole book is full of the thunder of judgment against the wicked. Yet right in the midst of this pronouncement of judgment, God inserts an incomparably tender sentence, like a warm ray of light amid the thunderstorm.

“The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him” (Nahum 1:7). Look at how God reveals himself here. On one hand, he is the great and awesome God who executes judgment on the bullying wicked; on the other hand, he is the God who “is good,” who is a “stronghold (refuge)” for his people in the day of trouble, and who “knows” those who take refuge in him. The same God, to the hard-hearted wicked who oppress others, is a fire of judgment; to those who take refuge in him in trouble, he is a tender refuge. God’s justice and his goodness are never contradictory; it is precisely because he is good, because he watches over the oppressed, that he must judge the oppressor.

Meditate especially on this sentence: “he knows those who take refuge in him.” Against the vast backdrop of a great empire overturning, the whole world in turmoil, God actually “knows” — knows, remembers, watches over — every small individual who takes refuge in him. You may feel yourself too small, before this churning world, these massive powers, nothing but an unnoticed speck of dust; but God says he “knows” you — as long as you take refuge in him, you are not an anonymous, faceless passerby in the vast sea of humanity, but one personally known, personally watched over, personally remembered by this God who governs all things. When judgment comes upon the proud powers, those who take refuge in God are held securely, hidden within his stronghold.

This God, who “is a stronghold in the day of trouble, who knows those who take refuge in him,” has, in Christ, become the refuge we can enter at any time. The psalmist says “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1); and the Lord Jesus himself personally issues the invitation: “come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden.” He is also the good shepherd who “calls his own sheep by name” — he “knows” each of his sheep. Today, if you’re in trouble, in turmoil, under fear, don’t think yourself too small, unnoticed; take refuge in this good God — he will surely be your stronghold, because he knows everyone who takes refuge in him.

Meditation: Do I feel myself too small, before this turbulent world, these massive powers, nothing but an unnoticed speck of dust? Yet God says he “knows those who take refuge in him” — as long as I take refuge in him, I am personally known, watched over, remembered by this God who governs all things. When trouble comes, do I take refuge in this God who “is good” as my stronghold, or fear alone?

Application: Today, in a trouble currently making you afraid, feeling yourself small and helpless, deliberately “take refuge” in God — bring it before him, making him your refuge; draw on the assurance that “he knows me, watches over me,” no longer thinking yourself too small, unnoticed.

Prayer: Good Lord, in the midst of judging the wicked, you are the stronghold in the day of trouble, who knows everyone who takes refuge in you. I confess I often feel myself too small, unnoticed before turmoil and massive powers, and so fear alone. Thank you, for you know me; thank you, Lord Jesus, for inviting me to come to you and find rest. Let me take refuge in you in trouble, making you my stronghold, resting in the assurance that “you know me.” In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 虽然...我仍要因耶和华喜乐
entries.title_en: Yet I Will Rejoice in the LORD
entries.verse: 哈巴谷书三章十八节
entries.content:
哈巴谷书,是一卷「从怀疑到相信」的书。先知一开始,是满腹的疑问与抱怨:神啊,为什么你容让不义横行?为什么你用比犹大更恶的巴比伦来刑罚犹大?他把这些尖锐的问题,坦然地向神倾吐。然而,经过与神的对话,到了全书的末了,哈巴谷的心,已经从怀疑与惧怕,升华到了一个惊人的高度——他唱出了圣经中论喜乐最不可思议的一段。

他说:「虽然无花果树不发旺,葡萄树不结果,橄榄树也不效力,田地不出粮食,圈中绝了羊,棚内也没有牛;然而,我要因耶和华欢欣,因救我的神喜乐。」(哈巴谷书3:17-18)请细数哈巴谷所列的,是一个农业社会里,一个人所能拥有的一切生计与保障——果树、葡萄、橄榄、粮食、牛羊。他假设:即使这一切全都落空了,即使我一无所有、颗粒无收、血本无归、走投无路——「然而」,他说,我仍要因耶和华欢欣,因救我的神喜乐。

这里藏着基督徒喜乐最深、也最坚固的秘密。世人的喜乐,是建立在「所拥有的」之上的:有果子、有收成、有牛羊、诸事顺遂,就喜乐;一旦这些落空,喜乐也随之崩塌。这种喜乐,像建在沙土上的房子,经不起风浪。哈巴谷却让我们看见一种建在磐石上的喜乐:它的根基,不在「神所赐的东西」,而在「神自己」——「因耶和华欢欣,因救我的神喜乐」。当一个人喜乐的根基,是神自己,而非神所赐的任何礼物,那么无论这些礼物如何被夺去,他的喜乐都夺不走;因为那作他喜乐之源的神,永不改变、永不落空。「虽然」万物皆失,「然而」神仍是我的神——这就够了,这就足以叫人喜乐。

这「虽然...然而」的喜乐,唯有在福音里,才有最坚实的根基。因为神已经在十字架上,把祂最大的礼物——祂的儿子——赐给了我们;「神既不爱惜自己的儿子,为我们众人舍了,岂不也把万物和他一同白白地赐给我们吗?」(罗8:32)一位连爱子都为你舍了的神,就是你在失去一切时,仍然拥有的、那夺不走的至宝。所以,基督徒可以在最深的患难、最彻底的失去中,仍然唱出「然而,我要因救我的神喜乐」——因为我们所拥有的神自己,比我们所失去的一切,都无限地宝贵。今天,你的喜乐,是建在「所拥有的」之上,还是建在「神自己」之上?愿你也能在「虽然」之后,唱出那「然而」的喜乐。

默想:我的喜乐,是建在「所拥有的」(收成、顺遂、健康、成就)之上,一旦落空就崩塌,还是建在「神自己」之上,夺不走?我能否像哈巴谷一样,在「虽然」万物皆失之后,仍唱出「然而,我要因救我的神喜乐」?我所拥有的神自己,在我心中,是否比我所能失去的一切更宝贵?

应用:今天在一件你正失去、或惧怕失去的事上(某样保障、收成、顺遂),操练哈巴谷的「虽然...然而」——承认这失去是真实的痛,却刻意把喜乐的根基从「这样东西」挪到「神自己」身上,向神宣告:然而,我仍要因救我的神喜乐。

祷告:作我喜乐之源的主,哈巴谷在一无所有的假设中,仍唱出「然而,我要因救我的神喜乐」。我承认,我的喜乐常建在所拥有的东西上,一落空就崩塌。谢谢你连爱子都为我舍了,你自己就是我失去一切时仍拥有的至宝。求你把我喜乐的根基,从你所赐的礼物,挪到你自己身上,叫我在「虽然」之后,也唱得出「然而」的喜乐。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Habakkuk is a book of “from doubt to faith.” The prophet begins full of questions and complaints: God, why do you allow injustice to run rampant? Why do you use Babylon, more wicked than Judah, to punish Judah? He candidly pours out these sharp questions to God. Yet through his dialogue with God, by the end of the book, Habakkuk’s heart has been lifted from doubt and fear to an astonishing height — he sings one of the most unbelievable passages on joy in all of Scripture.

He says: “Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation” (Habakkuk 3:17-18). Consider carefully the list Habakkuk gives — it is, in an agricultural society, everything a person could have for livelihood and security — fruit trees, vines, olives, food, flocks. He assumes: even if all of this came to nothing, even if I had nothing left, no harvest, no return, no way out — “yet,” he says, I will still rejoice in the LORD, take joy in the God of my salvation.

Here lies the deepest, most solid secret of Christian joy. The world’s joy is built upon “what one has”: having fruit, having harvest, having flocks, everything going smoothly — that’s when there’s joy; once these come to nothing, joy collapses along with them. This kind of joy, like a house built on sand, cannot withstand storms. Habakkuk instead shows us a joy built on rock: its foundation is not “what God gives,” but “God himself” — “I will rejoice in the LORD, take joy in the God of my salvation.” When a person’s foundation of joy is God himself, not any gift God gives, then however these gifts are taken away, his joy cannot be taken away; because the God who is the source of his joy never changes, never comes to nothing. “Though” everything is lost, “yet” God is still my God — that is enough, that is enough to make a person rejoice.

This “though... yet” joy has its most solid foundation only in the gospel. Because God has already, on the cross, given us his greatest gift — his Son; “he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). A God who even gave up his beloved Son for you is exactly the treasure you still possess, that cannot be taken away, when you lose everything else. So a Christian can, in the deepest hardship, the most complete loss, still sing out “yet I will rejoice in the God of my salvation” — because the God we possess is infinitely more precious than everything we’ve lost. Today, is your joy built on “what you have,” or on “God himself”? May you too, after the “though,” be able to sing that “yet” of joy.

Meditation: Is my joy built on “what I have” (harvest, smooth circumstances, health, achievement), collapsing the moment it comes to nothing, or built on “God himself,” something that cannot be taken away? Can I, like Habakkuk, after “though” everything is lost, still sing “yet I will rejoice in the God of my salvation”? Is God himself, whom I possess, more precious in my heart than everything I could possibly lose?

Application: Today, in something you’re currently losing, or afraid of losing (some security, harvest, smooth circumstance), practice Habakkuk’s “though... yet” — acknowledge this loss is real pain, yet deliberately move the foundation of joy from “this thing” onto “God himself,” declaring to God: yet I will still rejoice in the God of my salvation.

Prayer: Lord who is the source of my joy, Habakkuk, in the hypothetical of having nothing, still sang “yet I will rejoice in the God of my salvation.” I confess my joy is often built on what I have, collapsing the moment it comes to nothing. Thank you for giving up even your beloved Son for me; you yourself are the treasure I still possess when I lose everything. Move the foundation of my joy from your gifts onto you yourself, so that after “though,” I too can sing the joy of “yet.” In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 他因你欢欣喜乐
entries.title_en: He Will Rejoice Over You with Gladness
entries.verse: 西番雅书三章十七节
entries.content:
西番雅书,大部分是对「耶和华的日子」——那大而可畏的审判之日——的宣告。然而,到了全书的末了,笔锋一转,神向那蒙拯救、被洁净的余民,发出了一段满有慈爱的话。而这段话里,有一个几乎叫人不敢相信的启示:神竟然会「因祂的百姓而欢喜歌唱」。

「耶和华你的神是施行拯救、大有能力的主。他在你中间必因你欢欣喜乐,默然爱你,且因你喜乐而欢呼。」(西番雅书3:17)请慢慢地、逐字地默想这一句,因为它所描绘的,超乎我们对神的一切想象。我们通常想象的神,是威严的、审判的、至多是「勉强容忍」我们的;我们很难想象,神会「因我」欢欣喜乐。可这节经文明明地说:神「在你中间,必因你欢欣喜乐」——祂看着你,心里涌起喜乐;祂「默然爱你」——祂的爱深到一个地步,以致安静、无言;祂甚至「因你喜乐而欢呼(歌唱)」——那位创造诸天的神,竟像一个得着所爱之人的新郎,为你放声歌唱。

这个启示,医治我们许多人心底一个最深的伤:我们总觉得,神对我们,顶多是「接纳」「容忍」,却谈不上「喜悦」「欢喜」;我们总以为,自己这样软弱、这样不堪、这样常常失败,神看着我,大概只有失望和无奈。可西番雅书三章告诉我们:那位施行拯救、洁净了你的神,看着祂在基督里所救赎、所洁净的你,不是勉强容忍,而是欢欣喜乐、甚至为你歌唱!这不是因为你表现得多好、多可爱,而是因为祂以拯救的大爱爱你——祂看你,是透过祂爱子的宝血,看你为祂所宝贝、所欢喜的儿女。

这正是福音带给我们最深的安慰。主耶稣曾用一个牧人寻回迷羊的比喻说,牧人寻见了那只羊,「就欢欢喜喜地扛在肩上,回到家里」,又请朋友一同欢喜(路15:5-6);祂又说,「一个罪人悔改,在天上也要这样为他欢喜」(路15:7)。神对祂所救赎之人的态度,从来不是冷淡的容忍,而是失而复得的欢喜。今天,你是否总以为神对你只是勉强接纳、甚至满心失望?听西番雅的启示:那位救你的神,正在你中间因你欢欣喜乐,默然爱你,且因你喜乐而歌唱。安息在这被神欢喜的爱里。

默想:我是否总觉得,神对我顶多是「接纳、容忍」,却谈不上「喜悦、欢喜」,甚至以为祂看着软弱不堪的我只有失望?西番雅书三章17节说神「因你欢欣喜乐,默然爱你,且因你喜乐而欢呼」——这如何医治我心底「神对我只是勉强容忍」的伤?

应用:今天当你因自己的软弱、失败而觉得「神大概对我失望透了」时,刻意默想并支取西番雅书3:17——那救你的神,正因你欢欣喜乐、为你歌唱;不靠自己的表现,而是凭祂在基督里对你的欢喜,坦然安息在祂面前。

祷告:因我欢喜歌唱的主,西番雅说你在你百姓中间必因他们欢欣喜乐,默然爱他们,且因他们喜乐而欢呼。我承认,我总以为你对我顶多是勉强容忍,看着不堪的我满心失望。谢谢你透过爱子的宝血看我,不是容忍,而是欢喜,甚至为我歌唱,像牧人寻回迷羊。求你医治我心底的伤,叫我安息在这被你欢喜的爱里。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Zephaniah is, for the most part, a pronouncement of “the day of the LORD” — that great and dreadful day of judgment. Yet by the end of the book, the pen turns, and God speaks a passage full of love to the delivered, cleansed remnant. And in this passage is a revelation almost too astonishing to believe: God actually “rejoices and sings” over his people.

“The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17). Meditate slowly, word by word, on this sentence, because what it describes is beyond all our imaginings about God. We usually imagine God as majestic, judging, at most “grudgingly tolerating” us; we can hardly imagine God “rejoicing with gladness” over me. But this verse plainly says: God, “in your midst, will rejoice over you with gladness” — he looks at you, and joy wells up in his heart; he “quiets you by his love” — his love is so deep that it becomes still, wordless; he even “exults over you with loud singing” — the God who created the heavens actually, like a bridegroom who has found his beloved, sings aloud for you.

This revelation heals one of the deepest wounds in many of our hearts: we always feel that God, toward us, is at most “acceptance,” “tolerance,” but hardly “delight,” “gladness”; we always think that being this weak, this unworthy, this often failing, God, looking at me, probably feels only disappointment and helplessness. But Zephaniah 3 tells us: that God who works salvation, who has cleansed you, looking at you — whom he has redeemed and cleansed in Christ — is not grudging tolerance, but rejoicing gladness, even singing for you! This is not because you perform so well, are so lovable, but because he loves you with the great love of salvation — he looks at you through the blood of his beloved Son, seeing you as a child he treasures, delights in.

This is exactly the deepest comfort the gospel brings us. The Lord Jesus once used a parable of a shepherd finding a lost sheep, saying that when the shepherd found the sheep, “he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing,” returns home, and invites friends to rejoice together (Luke 15:5-6); he also said, “there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7). God’s attitude toward those he has redeemed has never been cold tolerance, but the joy of finding what was lost. Today, do you always think God’s attitude toward you is merely grudging acceptance, even utter disappointment? Hear Zephaniah’s revelation: that God who saves you is, right now, in your midst, rejoicing over you with gladness, quieting you with his love, and exulting over you with singing. Rest in this love that delights in you.

Meditation: Do I always feel that God, toward me, is at most “acceptance, tolerance,” hardly “delight, gladness,” even thinking that looking at my weak, unworthy self, he feels only disappointment? Zephaniah 3:17 says God “will rejoice over you with gladness, quiet you by his love, and exult over you with loud singing” — how does this heal that wound deep within me, of thinking “God merely tolerates me”?

Application: Today, when you feel “God is probably utterly disappointed in me” because of your own weakness and failure, deliberately meditate on and draw on Zephaniah 3:17 — that God who saves you is, right now, rejoicing over you with gladness, singing for you; not relying on your own performance, but on his gladness toward you in Christ, resting candidly in his presence.

Prayer: Lord who sings with joy over me, Zephaniah says you, in the midst of your people, will rejoice over them with gladness, quiet them by your love, and exult over them with loud singing. I confess I always think you, toward me, are at most grudging tolerance, looking at my unworthy self with utter disappointment. Thank you for looking at me through the blood of your beloved Son, not with tolerance, but with gladness, even singing for me, like a shepherd who has found his lost sheep. Heal the wound deep in my heart, and let me rest in this love that delights in me. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 省察你们的行为
entries.title_en: Consider Your Ways
entries.verse: 哈该书一章五节
entries.content:
被掳归回的犹大人,起初热心地动工重建圣殿;可遇到拦阻之后,工程停了,一停就是许多年。这些年里,他们并没有闲着——他们忙着建造自己的房子、经营自己的生活,把神的殿撂在一旁,任它荒凉。他们心里的盘算是:「建造耶和华殿的时候尚未来到。」神借先知哈该,向这样一群人,发出了一个叫他们停下来反省的呼召。

「现在万军之耶和华如此说:你们要省察自己的行为。」(哈该书1:5)神接着叫他们看一个奇怪的现象:他们撒的种多,收的却少;吃,却不得饱;喝,却不得足;赚钱的,却像把钱装在破漏的囊中。他们越忙,越觉得空;越经营,越留不住。为什么?神点破了:「因我的殿荒凉,你们各人却顾自己的房屋。」他们把神的事撂在一边,一心先顾自己的享受与经营;结果,神就叫他们所忙的一切,都像破漏的囊,留不住、也不得满足。

「省察自己的行为」——这是神向每一个忙碌却空虚之人发出的呼召。我们的生活,常常和这些归回的犹大人一模一样:我们把大把的时间、精力、心思,都投在了「建造自己的房屋」上——事业、享受、财富、安逸;而神的事、与神的关系、祂托付我们的、永恒的,却被我们一再地往后排,想着「等我先把自己安顿好、忙完这一阵,再来顾神的事」。结果呢?我们越忙,里面越空;越是拼命经营,越觉得不得满足——正如把钱装在破漏的囊中。这份挥之不去的空虚,恰恰是神在叫我们「省察自己的行为」:你把什么放在了第一位?

问题的核心,是「次序」。主耶稣说得再清楚不过:「你们要先求他的国和他的义,这些东西都要加给你们了」(太6:33)。神并不是不让我们顾自己的生活;祂是要我们把「先后次序」摆正——先求神的国,先顾与神的关系、先把祂放在生命的中心,其余的,神必看顾。当神被撂在一旁、被排在末位时,我们所忙的一切,都成了破漏的囊;当神被放回中心、被摆在首位时,生命才重新有了根基与满足。今天,神也在叫你「省察自己的行为」:在你的时间、精力、心思里,神被排在了第几位?

默想:我是否也像归回的犹大人,把大把时间、精力都投在「建造自己的房屋」上,却把神的事、与神的关系一再往后排,想着「等我忙完再说」?我越忙越空、越经营越不满足,是否正是神在叫我「省察自己的行为」——看我把什么放在了第一位?

应用:今天认真「省察」一次:在你的时间、精力、金钱、心思的实际分配上,神被排在了第几位?据此调整一个具体的次序——把一样你一直「等忙完再说」的属灵优先(读经、祷告、事奉、与神亲近),重新摆回它当有的首位。

祷告:当居首位的主,归回的百姓忙着建造自己的房屋,却任你的殿荒凉,你就叫他们所忙的都像破漏的囊,并呼召他们省察自己的行为。我承认,我也常把你的事往后排,一心先顾自己的经营与享受,以致越忙越空。谢谢你应许,先求你的国,这些都要加给我。求你叫我省察自己的行为,把你重新放回我生命的首位。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The Judeans who returned from exile had, at first, zealously begun rebuilding the temple; but after meeting obstacles, the work stopped, and stopped for many years. During these years, they were not idle — they were busy building their own houses, managing their own lives, setting God’s temple aside, letting it lie desolate. Their reasoning was: “the time has not yet come to build the house of the LORD.” Through the prophet Haggai, God issued to such a people a call to stop and reflect.

“Now, therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways” (Haggai 1:5). God then has them look at a strange phenomenon: they sowed much, but harvested little; they ate, but were not satisfied; they drank, but were not filled; whoever earned wages earned wages to put them into a bag with holes. The busier they were, the emptier they felt; the more they managed, the less they could hold onto. Why? God reveals it plainly: “because my house lies in ruins, while each of you busies himself with his own house.” They set God’s affairs aside, focused solely on their own enjoyment and management first; as a result, God let everything they were busy with become like a bag with holes — unable to hold anything, never satisfying.

“Consider your ways” — this is the call God issues to every busy yet empty person. Our lives are often exactly like these returning Judeans: we invest vast amounts of time, energy, and thought into “building our own house” — career, pleasure, wealth, comfort; while God’s affairs, our relationship with God, what he has entrusted to us, that which is eternal, we keep pushing back, thinking “once I’ve settled myself, once I’m through this busy stretch, then I’ll attend to God’s affairs.” And the result? The busier we are, the emptier we feel within; the more desperately we manage, the less satisfied we feel — exactly like putting money into a bag with holes. This lingering emptiness is exactly God calling us to “consider our ways”: what have you put first?

The core of the problem is “order.” The Lord Jesus could not have said it more clearly: “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). God isn’t forbidding us from attending to our own lives; he wants us to get the “priority” right — seek God’s kingdom first, attend to our relationship with God first, put him at the center of life first, and God will surely take care of the rest. When God is set aside, put last, everything we’re busy with becomes a bag with holes; when God is put back at the center, placed first, life finds its foundation and satisfaction again. Today, God is also calling you to “consider your ways”: in your time, energy, and thoughts, where does God rank?

Meditation: Am I too, like the returning Judeans, investing vast time and energy into “building my own house,” while pushing God’s affairs, my relationship with him, back again and again, thinking “I’ll attend to it once I’m through being busy”? Is my growing emptiness the busier I get, my growing dissatisfaction the more I manage, exactly God calling me to “consider my ways” — to see what I’ve put first?

Application: Today, seriously “consider” once: in the actual distribution of your time, energy, money, and thoughts, where does God rank? Based on this, adjust one concrete order — put a spiritual priority you’ve always said “I’ll get to once I’m through being busy” (Bible reading, prayer, service, drawing near to God) back into its rightful first place.

Prayer: Lord who deserves first place, the returning people busied themselves building their own houses, while letting your temple lie desolate, so you let everything they were busy with become like a bag with holes, and called them to consider their ways. I confess I too often push your affairs back, focused solely on my own management and enjoyment first, so the busier I get, the emptier I feel. Thank you for promising that if I seek your kingdom first, all these things will be added to me. Let me consider my ways, and put you back in the first place of my life. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 脱去污秽,穿上华美
entries.title_en: Take Off the Filthy Garments, Put On Pure Vestments
entries.verse: 撒迦利亚书三章四节
entries.content:
撒迦利亚在异象中,看见了一幅极其生动、也极其深刻的图画。大祭司约书亚,站在耶和华的使者面前;而撒但也站在旁边,要控告他。约书亚身上,「穿着污秽的衣服」——这污秽的衣服,象征着他和百姓的罪孽与不洁。在圣洁的神面前,一个穿着污秽衣服的大祭司,本该被定罪、被赶出去。然而,接下来发生的事,是整本圣经里最清晰的一幅「称义」的图画。

「使者吩咐站在面前的说:你们要脱去他污秽的衣服;又对约书亚说:我使你脱离罪孽,要给你穿上华美的衣服。」(撒迦利亚书3:4)请看神在这里所做的两件事。第一,是「脱去」——祂主动地、亲自地,把约书亚身上那污秽的、代表罪孽的衣服脱去了;第二,是「穿上」——祂又给约书亚穿上「华美的衣服」。神没有只是把污秽脱去、就让约书亚赤身站在那里;祂脱去了罪的污衣,又给他穿上了华美、洁净的义袍。这一脱、一穿之间,道尽了福音的核心:神除去我们的罪,又把祂的义,加给我们。

请特别留意:这一切,都是神主动做的,约书亚自己没有做任何事。他没有先把自己洗干净、没有先立功补过、没有先证明自己配得;他只是站在那里,污秽不堪,任凭撒但控告。是神,主动地脱去他的污衣、主动地给他穿上义袍。这正是「因信称义」的精义:我们的得称为义,从来不是靠自己把污秽洗净、靠自己挣得一件义袍;乃是神在基督里,白白地除去我们的罪,又白白地把基督的义,归给、穿在我们身上。当撒但控告我们「你这样污秽,怎配站在神面前」时,我们的答案不是「我会努力变干净」,而是「神已经脱去了我的污衣,给我穿上了基督的义袍」。

而这「华美的衣服」,新约明明地告诉我们是什么。保罗说,信徒是「披戴基督」的(加3:27);又说,神使那无罪的基督「替我们成为罪,好叫我们在他里面成为神的义」(林后5:21)。撒迦利亚异象中约书亚所穿上的那件义袍,正是基督为我们成就、又归给我们的义。所以,当你站在神面前,不要低头看自己身上还有多少污秽,就不敢近前;要抬起头,看神已经给你穿上的那件华美的义袍——基督的义。今天,你是否还在靠自己「洗净污衣」,不敢坦然近前?看撒迦利亚的异象:是神脱去你的污秽,给你穿上华美。安息在这白白称义的恩典里。

默想:当撒但控告我「你这样污秽,怎配站在神面前」时,我的答案是「我会努力变干净」,还是「神已脱去我的污衣,给我穿上基督的义袍」?我站在神面前,是低头看自己身上的污秽而不敢近前,还是抬头看神已给我穿上的华美义袍?我的称义,是靠自己洗净,还是神白白的作为?

应用:今天当你因自己的罪、自己的不洁而不敢坦然亲近神、或被控告压得抬不起头时,刻意支取撒迦利亚的异象——是神脱去了你的污衣、给你穿上了基督的义袍;凭这白白称义的恩典(而非自己的洁净),坦然来到神面前。

祷告:使我称义的主,约书亚穿着污秽的衣服、被撒但控告,你却主动脱去他的污衣,给他穿上华美的衣服。我承认,我常靠自己洗净污秽、挣得义袍,一被控告就不敢近前。谢谢你在基督里白白除去我的罪,又把基督的义归给我、穿在我身上,叫我披戴基督。求你叫我不看自己的污秽,而看你给我穿上的义袍,坦然安息在白白称义的恩典里。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
In a vision, Zechariah saw an extremely vivid, extremely profound picture. The high priest Joshua was standing before the angel of the LORD; and Satan was also standing at his side, to accuse him. Joshua was “clothed with filthy garments” — these filthy garments symbolized his and the people’s iniquity and uncleanness. Before a holy God, a high priest clothed in filthy garments should by rights be condemned, driven away. Yet what happens next is the clearest picture of “justification” in the whole Bible.

“And the angel said to those who were standing before him, ‘Remove the filthy garments from him.’ And to him he said, ‘Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments’” (Zechariah 3:4). Look at the two things God does here. First, “removing” — he actively, personally, removes the filthy garments from Joshua, representing his iniquity; second, “clothing” — he then clothes Joshua with “pure vestments.” God did not just remove the filth and leave Joshua standing there naked; he removed sin’s filthy garment, and clothed him with a pure, clean robe of righteousness. In this removing and clothing, the core of the gospel is fully laid out: God removes our sin, and adds his righteousness to us.

Notice especially: all of this was done by God, initiated by him — Joshua himself did nothing at all. He did not first wash himself clean, did not first earn merit to atone, did not first prove himself worthy; he simply stood there, utterly filthy, letting Satan accuse him. It was God who actively removed his filthy garment, and actively clothed him with a robe of righteousness. This is exactly the essence of “justification by faith”: our being counted righteous has never depended on cleansing ourselves, on earning a robe of righteousness for ourselves; it is God, in Christ, who freely removes our sin, and freely credits, clothes us with, Christ’s righteousness. When Satan accuses us, “how could someone so filthy as you be worthy to stand before God,” our answer is not “I’ll try hard to become clean,” but “God has already removed my filthy garment, and clothed me with Christ’s robe of righteousness.”

And what this “pure vestment” is, the New Testament plainly tells us. Paul says believers “have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27); and says God made the sinless Christ “to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). That robe of righteousness Joshua put on in Zechariah’s vision is exactly the righteousness Christ accomplished for us, and credited to us. So when you stand before God, don’t look down at how much filth is still on you, and dare not draw near; lift up your head, and look at that pure robe of righteousness God has already clothed you with — Christ’s righteousness. Today, are you still trying to “wash your own filthy garment,” not daring to draw near candidly? Look at Zechariah’s vision: it is God who removes your filth, and clothes you with purity. Rest in this grace of free justification.

Meditation: When Satan accuses me, “how could someone so filthy as you be worthy to stand before God,” is my answer “I’ll try hard to become clean,” or “God has already removed my filthy garment, and clothed me with Christ’s robe of righteousness”? Standing before God, do I look down at my own filth and dare not draw near, or look up at the pure robe of righteousness God has already clothed me with? Is my justification by my own cleansing, or God’s free act?

Application: Today, when you dare not draw near candidly because of your own sin, your own uncleanness, or feel crushed by accusation, unable to lift your head, deliberately draw on Zechariah’s vision — it is God who removed your filthy garment, and clothed you with Christ’s robe of righteousness; on the strength of this free justification (not your own cleanness), come before God candidly.

Prayer: Lord who justifies me, Joshua, clothed with filthy garments and accused by Satan, had you actively remove his filthy garment and clothe him with a pure robe. I confess I often try to wash my own filth clean, earn a robe of righteousness, and dare not draw near the moment I’m accused. Thank you for, in Christ, freely removing my sin, and crediting me with, clothing me with, Christ’s righteousness, letting me put on Christ. Let me not look at my own filth, but at the robe of righteousness you’ve clothed me with, resting candidly in the grace of free justification. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 铺张诸天、造人里面之灵的主——记念神的创造
entries.title_en: The Lord Who Stretches Out the Heavens and Forms the Spirit of Man — Remembering God's Creation
entries.content:
铺张诸天、造人里面之灵的主——记念神的创造

「铺张诸天、建立地基、造人里面之灵的耶和华……」(撒迦利亚书 12:1)

这一周,我们走过众先知的信息:神所要的公义怜悯、祂作患难的保障、哈巴谷在一无所有中的喜乐、神因祂百姓的歌唱。而先知一次次把我们引回同一位神——那位创造并托住万有的主。

今天安息日,默想撒迦利亚为神所作的这三重描述:祂「铺张诸天」——那浩瀚无垠的星空,是祂展开的;祂「建立地基」——这稳固的大地,是祂奠定的;而祂又「造人里面之灵」——那使你能思想、能爱、能敬拜、能与祂相交的灵魂,也是祂亲手所造。这是何等奇妙:同一位铺张浩瀚诸天的神,也俯身造了你里面那看不见的灵。祂既如此浩大,又如此贴近;祂既掌管星辰,也塑造你的灵魂。今天,在这位创造诸天、又创造你灵魂的主面前,安息、惊叹、敬拜。

"The LORD, who stretches out the heavens and lays the foundation of the earth and forms the spirit of man within him..." (Zechariah 12:1)
entries.content_en:
The Lord Who Stretches Out the Heavens and Forms the Spirit of Man — Remembering God's Creation

"Thus declares the LORD, who stretches out the heavens and founds the earth and forms the spirit of man within him..." (Zechariah 12:1)

This week, we walked through the prophets’ messages: the justice and kindness God requires, his being a stronghold in trouble, Habakkuk’s joy amid having nothing, God singing over his people. And the prophets, again and again, led us back to the same God — the Lord who created and sustains all things.

Today, on the Sabbath, meditate on this threefold description Zechariah gives of God. He "stretches out the heavens" — that vast, boundless starry sky was spread out by him; he "founds the earth" — this stable ground was laid by him; and he also "forms the spirit of man within him" — that soul of yours, able to think, to love, to worship, to commune with him, was also shaped by his own hand. How wonderful this is: the very same God who stretched out the vast heavens also stooped down to form the unseen spirit within you. He is as vast as he is near; he governs the stars, and he also shapes your soul. Today, before this Lord who created the heavens, and also created your soul, rest, marvel, and worship.

"The LORD, who stretches out the heavens and lays the foundation of the earth and forms the spirit of man within him..." (Zechariah 12:1)

entries.title: 不是倚靠势力,乃是倚靠我的灵
entries.title_en: Not by Might, Nor by Power, but by My Spirit
entries.verse: 撒迦利亚书四章六节
entries.content:
被掳归回的百姓,正在所罗巴伯的带领下重建圣殿。可面对眼前的困难——人力单薄、资源匮乏、四围拦阻,这项工程看起来实在太大、太难,几乎不可能完成。就在这灰心、觉得力不能胜的时刻,神借撒迦利亚,向所罗巴伯说了一句话——这句话,不但托住了当时的建殿工程,也成了历世历代神百姓成就一切属灵工作的秘诀。

「万军之耶和华说:不是倚靠势力,不是倚靠才能,乃是倚靠我的灵方能成事。」(撒迦利亚书4:6)请注意神所排除的两样,和祂所指向的一样。神排除的,是「势力」(军力、财力、人多势众)和「才能」(人的本事、能力、方法)——这两样,恰恰是人做事时最本能倚靠的。可神说:成就祂的工,靠的不是这些。祂所指向的,是「我的灵」——是神的圣灵自己的大能。神的工,是神用祂的灵成就的;人的势力与才能,再大,也成就不了属灵的果效。

这话,拆穿了我们做属灵之工时一个根深蒂固的错误。我们想为神成就点什么——建立一个事工、带领一个人信主、胜过一个顽固的罪、复兴一个冷淡的教会——我们本能地想的,是「我要更努力、更有能力、更有方法、更有资源」。我们把成败,押在了自己的「势力与才能」上;于是,当我们觉得自己势单力薄、才不配位时,就灰心、就退缩,以为「凭我这点本事,成不了」。可神在这里说:这工从来不是靠你的势力与才能成的;是靠我的灵。你的软弱、你的不足,从不是拦阻——因为成事的,根本不是你,是神的灵。

这真理,既叫我们谦卑,也叫我们大得安慰。谦卑的是:即使我们势力雄厚、才能出众,若没有神的灵,也成就不了任何真正属灵、存到永恒的果效——「若不是耶和华建造房屋,建造的人就枉然劳力」(诗127:1)。安慰的是:即使我们软弱、渺小、不足,只要倚靠神的灵,神的工照样能借着我们成就——因为大能在乎神的灵,不在乎我们。使徒保罗深知这秘诀,他说「我什么时候软弱,什么时候就刚强了」(林后12:10)。今天,你是否正因觉得自己「势力与才能」不足,而灰心退缩?听神的话:不是倚靠势力,不是倚靠才能,乃是倚靠我的灵。停止倚靠自己,转而倚靠那位成事的圣灵。

默想:我想为神成就属灵之工时,本能倚靠的是什么——「我要更努力、更有能力、更有方法、更有资源」这些「势力与才能」?我是否把成败押在自己身上,以致觉得势单力薄时就灰心退缩?我是否真信,成事的是「神的灵」,而非我的势力与才能?

应用:今天在一件你觉得「凭我的能力成不了」、正灰心退缩的属灵之工上(带一个人信主、胜过一个罪、一项事奉),停止倚靠自己的势力与才能;刻意求神的灵充满你、借你成事,凭信心倚靠祂而非自己去面对。

祷告:成就万事的主,你对灰心的所罗巴伯说:不是倚靠势力,不是倚靠才能,乃是倚靠我的灵方能成事。我承认,我想为你做工时,总本能地倚靠自己的努力、能力与资源,一觉得不足就灰心退缩。求你叫我看见,你的工是你的灵成就的,我的软弱从不是拦阻。求你叫我停止倚靠自己,单单倚靠你的灵,方能成事。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The returning exiles, led by Zerubbabel, were rebuilding the temple. But facing the difficulties before them — meager manpower, scarce resources, obstacles on every side — this project seemed too vast, too hard, almost impossible to complete. Right at this moment of discouragement, feeling unable to overcome, God, through Zechariah, spoke a word to Zerubbabel — a word that not only sustained the temple-building project at the time, but has become the secret to God’s people, throughout the ages, accomplishing every spiritual work.

“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). Notice the two things God excludes, and the one he points to. What God excludes is “might” (military strength, financial strength, numbers) and “power” (human ability, skill, methods) — these two are exactly what people instinctively rely on most when doing things. But God says: accomplishing his work does not depend on these. What he points to is “my Spirit” — the mighty power of God’s own Holy Spirit. God’s work is accomplished by his Spirit; human might and power, however great, can never accomplish spiritual results.

This word exposes a deeply rooted error we make when doing spiritual work. We want to accomplish something for God — establishing a ministry, leading someone to faith, overcoming a stubborn sin, reviving a cold church — and our instinct is to think “I need to try harder, be more capable, have better methods, more resources.” We stake success or failure on our own “might and power”; so, when we feel weak, ill-equipped, we grow discouraged, retreat, thinking “with what little I have, this can’t be accomplished.” But God says here: this work was never accomplished by your might and power; it is accomplished by my Spirit. Your weakness, your insufficiency, was never the obstacle — because it was never you who accomplishes things, but God’s Spirit.

This truth both humbles us and gives us tremendous comfort. The humbling: even if we’re mighty in strength, outstanding in ability, without God’s Spirit, we cannot accomplish anything truly spiritual, that endures into eternity — “unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1). The comfort: even if we’re weak, small, insufficient, as long as we rely on God’s Spirit, God’s work can still be accomplished through us — because the mighty power lies with God’s Spirit, not with us. The apostle Paul knew this secret deeply, saying “when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). Today, are you discouraged and retreating because you feel your “might and power” insufficient? Hear God’s word: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. Stop relying on yourself, and turn instead to rely on the Holy Spirit who accomplishes things.

Meditation: When I want to accomplish spiritual work for God, what do I instinctively rely on — these “might and power” of “I need to try harder, be more capable, have better methods, more resources”? Do I stake success or failure on myself, so that when I feel outnumbered and outmatched, I grow discouraged and retreat? Do I truly believe it is “God’s Spirit,” not my might and power, that accomplishes things?

Application: Today, in a spiritual work you feel “cannot be accomplished by my ability,” currently discouraging you into retreat (leading someone to faith, overcoming a sin, some service), stop relying on your own might and power; deliberately ask God’s Spirit to fill you and accomplish it through you, relying on him in faith rather than yourself to face it.

Prayer: Lord who accomplishes all things, you said to the discouraged Zerubbabel: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit shall it be accomplished. I confess that when I want to work for you, I always instinctively rely on my own effort, ability, and resources, growing discouraged and retreating the moment I feel insufficient. Let me see that your work is accomplished by your Spirit, and that my weakness is never the obstacle. Let me stop relying on myself, and rely solely on your Spirit, so that it may be accomplished. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 各人与邻舍说话诚实
entries.title_en: Speak the Truth to One Another
entries.verse: 撒迦利亚书八章十六节
entries.content:
撒迦利亚书七、八章,神应许要复兴、重建祂的百姓,使耶路撒冷重新成为「诚实的城」。而在这复兴的应许中,神具体地指明了:一个被祂复兴、真属祂的群体,当活出怎样的生命。这些吩咐,朴素得几乎不像「属灵」的大事,却恰恰是真敬虔最实在的检验。

「你们所当行的是这样:各人与邻舍说话诚实,在城门口按至理判断,使人和睦。」(撒迦利亚书8:16)请留意神所看重的,不是什么高深的宗教仪式,而是日常生活中最基本的德行:「说话诚实」——不说谎、不虚假、不两面三刀;「按至理判断」——秉公办事、不偏私、不徇情;「使人和睦」——不挑拨、不搬弄、不制造纷争,反倒作和睦的桥梁。神所要的复兴,不是停在聚会、诗歌、感觉里的「属灵」;它必然要落实为一个人怎样说话、怎样待人、怎样处事——落实为最日常、最琐碎的诚实与公义。

这拆穿了一种常见的、割裂的「属灵」。我们很容易把「属灵」与「日常生活」分成两截:在教会里,我敬虔、火热、爱主;出了教会门,回到家庭、职场、人际里,我却照样说谎、照样占便宜、照样搬弄是非、照样两面三刀。我们以为「属灵」是主日、是聚会、是感觉;却忘了神所看重的敬虔,恰恰要在「与邻舍说话诚实」这样最不起眼的日常里,活出来。一个人真实的属灵光景,不在他聚会时多火热,而在他平日里说的话诚不诚实、待人公不公义、处事和不和睦。

而真正能叫我们活出这诚实、公义、和睦的,不是靠自己咬牙做个「好人」,乃是靠福音从里到外地改变我们。基督是那位「口里也没有诡诈」(彼前2:22)的完全诚实者;祂又借着十字架,使我们与神和好,又「将劝人与他和好的职分赐给我们」(林后5:18)——祂既叫我们与神和好,也叫我们成为与人和睦的使者;祂更赐下圣灵,把祂诚实、公义、和睦的性情,一点一点地作在我们里面。所以,真敬虔从不与日常生活分家;一个被福音改变的人,他的改变,必然显在他怎样说话、怎样待人、怎样处事上。今天,省察你「出了教会门」之后的生活:你与邻舍(家人、同事、朋友)说话诚实吗?待人公义吗?使人和睦吗?求神叫你的敬虔,落实在最日常的诚实与公义里。

默想:我是否把「属灵」与「日常生活」割裂成两截——在教会里敬虔火热,出了门却照样说谎、占便宜、搬弄是非?神所看重的敬虔,恰恰要在「与邻舍说话诚实」这样最日常的事上活出来——我的真实属灵光景,在我平日说话、待人、处事上是怎样的?

应用:今天在一处你「出了教会门」的日常关系里(家庭、职场、朋友),刻意活出这三样中的一样——说一句本想含糊或说谎之处的诚实话、在一件事上秉公不徇私、或去化解一处纷争使人和睦,让你的敬虔落实在日常。

祷告:看重日常诚实的主,你所要的复兴,是各人与邻舍说话诚实、按至理判断、使人和睦。我承认,我常把属灵与日常割裂——在教会敬虔,出了门却照样说谎、占便宜、搬弄是非。谢谢基督口里没有诡诈,又使我与神和好、赐我和睦的职分。求你借你的灵,把你诚实、公义、和睦的性情作在我里面,叫我的敬虔落实在最日常的生活里。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Zechariah 7 and 8, God promises to restore and rebuild his people, making Jerusalem once again “the faithful city.” And in this promise of restoration, God specifically indicates: what kind of life should a community he has restored, truly belonging to him, live out. These instructions are so plain they hardly seem like great “spiritual” matters, yet they are exactly the most concrete test of true godliness.

“These are the things that you shall do: Speak the truth to one another; render in your gates judgments that are true and make for peace” (Zechariah 8:16). Notice that what God values is not some profound religious ritual, but the most basic virtues of daily life: “speaking the truth” — not lying, not being false, not two-faced; “rendering true judgment” — dealing fairly, without favoritism, without partiality; “making for peace” — not stirring up trouble, not gossiping, not creating strife, but instead being a bridge of peace. The restoration God wants is not something that stays at gatherings, songs, and feelings, that stops at being “spiritual”; it must be worked out in how a person speaks, how they treat others, how they conduct themselves — worked out in the most everyday, most trivial honesty and justice.

This exposes a common, fractured kind of “spirituality.” We easily split “spirituality” and “daily life” into two halves: at church, I’m godly, fervent, loving the Lord; outside church, back in family, workplace, relationships, I still lie, still take advantage, still gossip, still play both sides. We think “spirituality” is Sunday, is gathering, is feeling; we forget that the godliness God values must be lived out precisely in the most unremarkable daily matter of “speaking the truth to one’s neighbor.” A person’s true spiritual condition is not measured by how fervent they are at gatherings, but by whether their everyday speech is honest, whether they deal justly with people, whether they make for peace.

And what can truly enable us to live out this honesty, justice, and peace is not gritting our teeth to be a “good person” by ourselves, but the gospel changing us from the inside out. Christ is that perfectly honest one, “in whose mouth no deceit was found” (1 Peter 2:22); through the cross, he reconciles us to God, and “gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18) — he not only reconciled us to God, but made us messengers of peace to others; and he gives the Holy Spirit, working his character of honesty, justice, and peace into us, bit by bit. So true godliness is never divorced from daily life; a person changed by the gospel will surely show that change in how they speak, how they treat others, how they conduct themselves. Today, examine your life “after you’ve left the church door”: do you speak honestly to your neighbors (family, coworkers, friends)? Do you deal justly with people? Do you make for peace? Ask God to let your godliness be worked out in the most everyday honesty and justice.

Meditation: Do I split “spirituality” and “daily life” into two halves — godly and fervent at church, yet still lying, taking advantage, gossiping once I leave? The godliness God values must be lived out precisely in something as everyday as “speaking the truth to one’s neighbor” — what is my true spiritual condition like in how I speak, treat others, and conduct myself in daily life?

Application: Today, in a daily relationship “outside the church door” (family, workplace, friends), deliberately live out one of these three — speak an honest word where you’d normally be vague or lie, be fair without favoritism in a matter, or resolve a conflict to make for peace, letting your godliness be worked out in daily life.

Prayer: Lord who values everyday honesty, the restoration you want is that each person speak the truth to their neighbor, render true judgment, and make for peace. I confess I often split spirituality and daily life apart — godly at church, yet still lying, taking advantage, gossiping once I leave. Thank you that Christ had no deceit in his mouth, and reconciled me to you, giving me the ministry of peace. Work your character of honesty, justice, and peace into me through your Spirit, and let my godliness be worked out in the most everyday life. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 你的王谦谦和和地来
entries.title_en: Your King Comes to You, Humble
entries.verse: 撒迦利亚书九章九节
entries.content:
在撒迦利亚一连串关于弥赛亚的预言中,有一节格外明亮、也格外具体地预告了那位要来之王的形象。当时的人盼望弥赛亚,盼的是一位威武的君王——骑着战马、率领大军、以雷霆之势推翻仇敌、重建以色列的荣耀。然而,神借撒迦利亚所预告的这位王,祂来临的样式,却完全出人意料。

「锡安的民哪,应当大大喜乐;耶路撒冷的民哪,应当欢呼。看哪,你的王来到你这里!他是公义的,并且施行拯救,谦谦和和地骑着驴,就是骑着驴的驹子。」(撒迦利亚书9:9)请看这位王身上那惊人的组合。一面,祂「是公义的,并且施行拯救」——祂是真正的君王,有拯救的大能,要施行公义、成就救恩。另一面,祂却是「谦谦和和地骑着驴」——不是骑着象征武力与征服的战马,而是骑着象征谦卑与和平的驴驹。这位王的伟大,不在于祂的威武霸气,而在于祂的谦卑温和;祂的得胜,不是靠碾碎仇敌,而是靠谦卑地舍己。

五百多年后,在受难周的那个主日,这预言一字一句地应验了。主耶稣正是骑着一匹驴驹,进入耶路撒冷;门徒特意指出,「这事成就是要应验先知的话」(太21:4-5)。众人夹道欢呼「和散那」,迎接他们的王。然而,这位王进城,不是去登基作威武的君王、去推翻罗马的统治;祂是去上十字架,以最谦卑、最舍己的方式,成就那真正的拯救——不是把百姓从罗马人手中救出来,而是把我们众人从罪与死的权势中救出来。祂的王权,是借着为子民舍命而得着的;祂的荣耀,是在十字架上、以谦卑舍己的爱彰显的。

这位「谦谦和和」的王,颠覆了我们对「伟大」「得胜」「作王」的一切想象,也向我们发出邀请。世上的王,靠权势辖制人;这位王,却靠舍己的爱赢得人的心。祂不是用武力强迫你降服,祂是用祂在十字架上舍命的爱,来融化你、赢得你、作你温柔的王。而祂也呼召凡跟随祂的人,活出同样「谦谦和和」的样式——不靠强势与霸道,而靠谦卑与舍己去爱人、去得人。今天,你所迎接、所降服的这位王,是何等的一位王:祂有拯救的大能,却谦谦和和地为你骑上驴驹、走上十字架。这样一位王,值得你欢呼迎接、倾心降服。

默想:我心里所盼望、所想象的「王」「伟大」「得胜」,是威武霸气、以势力碾压,还是像基督那样「谦谦和和」、以谦卑舍己得胜?这位有拯救大能、却骑着驴驹走上十字架的王,如何颠覆我对伟大的看法?祂不用武力强迫、而用舍己之爱赢得我的心——这如何叫我降服?

应用:今天默想基督这位「谦谦和和」的王,为祂舍己的爱向祂欢呼、降服;并效法祂的样式——在一处你本可以用强势、霸道去「赢」的地方(争论、关系、权力),选择像你的王一样,以谦卑与舍己去待人、去得人的心。

祷告:谦谦和和的王,撒迦利亚预言你有拯救的大能,却骑着驴驹、谦卑地来到你的百姓中;你果然骑驴进京,走上十字架,以舍己的爱成就了真正的拯救。我承认,我心里所慕的伟大,常是威武霸气、以势力碾压。谢谢你不用武力强迫,而用十字架的爱赢得我的心。求你叫我欢呼迎接、倾心降服你这位王,也效法你谦卑舍己的样式。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
Among Zechariah’s succession of messianic prophecies, one verse foretells the image of the coming King with especial brightness and specificity. People of that time hoped for a mighty king as Messiah — riding a warhorse, leading a great army, overthrowing enemies with thunderous force, rebuilding Israel’s glory. Yet the manner in which this King, foretold by God through Zechariah, would come, was utterly unexpected.

“Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). Look at the astonishing combination in this King. On one hand, he “is righteous and having salvation” — he is a true King, with saving power, to execute justice and accomplish salvation. On the other hand, he is “humble, mounted on a donkey” — not on a warhorse symbolizing force and conquest, but on a donkey’s colt symbolizing humility and peace. This King’s greatness lies not in his might and grandeur, but in his humility and gentleness; his victory comes not through crushing enemies, but through humble self-giving.

More than five hundred years later, on that Sunday of Passion Week, this prophecy was fulfilled word for word. The Lord Jesus entered Jerusalem riding exactly a donkey’s colt; the disciples specifically pointed out, “this took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet” (Matthew 21:4-5). The crowds lined the road, shouting “Hosanna,” welcoming their king. Yet this King entering the city was not going to ascend a throne as a mighty monarch, to overthrow Roman rule; he was going to the cross, to accomplish, in the most humble, most self-giving way, true salvation — not delivering the people from Rome’s hand, but delivering all of us from the dominion of sin and death. His kingship was obtained by giving his life for his people; his glory was displayed on the cross, in humble, self-giving love.

This “humble” King overturns all our imaginings of “greatness,” “victory,” “reigning,” and issues us an invitation. Earthly kings dominate people through power; this King instead wins hearts through self-giving love. He doesn’t force you to submit by might; he melts you, wins you, becomes your gentle King through his love that gave his life on the cross. And he also calls everyone who follows him to live out this same “humble” pattern — not through force and domination, but through humility and self-giving, to love and win people. Today, what kind of King is the one you welcome and submit to: he has saving power, yet humbly rides a donkey’s colt for you, and walks the road to the cross. Such a King deserves your shout of welcome, your wholehearted submission.

Meditation: Is the “king,” “greatness,” “victory” I hope for and imagine in my heart mighty and grand, crushing by force, or, like Christ, “humble,” winning through humility and self-giving? How does this King, who has saving power yet rides a donkey’s colt to the cross, overturn my view of greatness? He doesn’t force by might, but wins my heart through self-giving love — how does this move me to submit?

Application: Today, meditate on Christ, this “humble” King, and shout and submit to him for his self-giving love; and follow his example — in a place where you could “win” through force and domination (an argument, a relationship, power), choose instead, like your King, to treat and win people with a heart of humility and self-giving.

Prayer: Humble King, Zechariah prophesied that you have saving power, yet come humbly to your people riding a donkey’s colt; you indeed rode a donkey into the city, walked the road to the cross, and accomplished true salvation with self-giving love. I confess that what I long for as greatness is often mighty and grand, crushing by force. Thank you for not forcing by might, but winning my heart with the love of the cross. Let me shout and welcome, wholeheartedly submit to you, this King, and also follow your pattern of humble self-giving. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.

entries.title: 他们要仰望我,就是他们所扎的
entries.title_en: They Will Look on Me, on Him Whom They Have Pierced
entries.verse: 撒迦利亚书十二章十节
entries.content:
撒迦利亚书,也是旧约先知书的末尾,在结束之前,射出了几道直指各各他的、最明亮的预言之光。神应许要浇灌下「那施恩叫人恳求的灵」,叫祂的百姓回转、痛悔。而在这回转的应许里,藏着一节精确得叫人战栗的预言——它跨越五百年,预告了那位弥赛亚将要受的、最深的伤。

「我必将那施恩叫人恳求的灵,浇灌大卫家和耶路撒冷的居民。他们必仰望我,就是他们所扎的;必为我悲哀,如丧独生子。」(撒迦利亚书12:10)请深思这节经文里那惊人的话。说话的,是耶和华神自己(「浇灌……我的灵」);而祂说,他们必「仰望我,就是他们所扎的」——「我」被「扎」了!那位说话的神,竟宣告祂自己要被人「扎」(刺透);而当人仰望这位被扎的主时,要为祂痛哭悲哀,如同为失去独生子而哀恸。这里已经隐隐透出那道成肉身、被钉十字架之神的奥秘:被扎的那一位,竟就是神自己。

五百年后,在各各他的十字架上,这预言应验到了字面。约翰记载,当兵丁用枪扎主耶稣的肋旁时,他特意指出:「这些事成了,为要应验经上的话……他们要仰望自己所扎的人」(约19:36-37),引用的正是撒迦利亚这节经文。那位被扎的,正是耶稣基督——是神的儿子、是道成肉身的神自己。祂被我们的罪所扎、为我们的过犯被刺透;而那使我们回转、痛悔、仰望祂的,不是我们自己的努力,乃是神所浇灌下的「那施恩叫人恳求的灵」——是圣灵光照我们,叫我们看见自己的罪何等地扎伤了那为我们舍命的主,以致我们为祂悲哀、向祂回转。

这就是整本圣经、也是这个救赎故事所指向的中心:一位被扎的救主,和一群仰望祂而得生的罪人。撒迦利亚书的结尾,更宣告那日「耶和华必作全地的王……耶和华必为独一无二的」(亚14:9)——那位曾被扎、谦卑舍己的主,终必作全地的王,祂的国度要充满全地。这正是从创世记到启示录那条主线的终点:被钉的羔羊,要坐上宝座。今天,当你「仰望那位被扎的」主时,愿神所浇灌的圣灵,叫你真看见:是我的罪扎了祂;而祂被扎,是为要赦免、拯救、赢回我。为这样的救主悲哀、感恩、俯伏、跟随——因为这位被扎的救主,正是那要作全地之王的主。

默想:我是否真「仰望那位被扎的」主,看见是我的罪扎了祂、为我的过犯刺透了祂?那使我回转、痛悔、仰望祂的,是我自己的努力,还是神所浇灌「施恩叫人恳求的灵」?这位曾被扎、却要作全地之王的救主,如何叫我俯伏、感恩、跟随?

应用:今天安静地「仰望那位被扎的」基督(默想约翰福音十九章的十字架);求神所赐的圣灵,叫你真看见自己的罪如何扎伤了那为你舍命的主,为此向祂痛悔、感恩;并以俯伏跟随,回应这位被扎、又要作全地之王的救主。

祷告:被扎、却要作全地之王的主,撒迦利亚五百年前就预言:他们必仰望我,就是他们所扎的。谢谢你,主耶稣——那位被扎的,竟是道成肉身的神自己;你为我的罪被刺透,为要赦免、赢回我。求你浇灌那施恩叫人恳求的灵,叫我真看见是我的罪扎了你,为此向你痛悔、感恩、俯伏。这位被扎的救主,你终必作全地的王;愿我一生仰望你、跟随你。奉主耶稣的名求,阿们。
entries.content_en:
The book of Zechariah, also the end of the Old Testament prophetic books, shoots out, before it closes, several rays of the brightest prophetic light pointing directly to Golgotha. God promises to pour out “the Spirit of grace and pleas for mercy,” to bring his people to turn back and grieve. And within this promise of turning back is hidden a verse of prophecy, precise enough to make one tremble — it spans five hundred years, foretelling the deepest wound that Messiah would suffer.

“And I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10). Consider deeply the astonishing statement in this verse. The one speaking is the LORD God himself (“pour out... my Spirit”); and he says they will “look on me, on him whom they have pierced” — “I” was “pierced”! The very God who is speaking actually declares that he himself will be “pierced” (thrust through); and when people look upon this pierced Lord, they will weep and mourn for him as though mourning the loss of an only child. Here already, faintly, is hinted the mystery of God incarnate, crucified: the one pierced is actually God himself.

Five hundred years later, on the cross at Golgotha, this prophecy was fulfilled to the letter. John records that when the soldiers pierced the Lord Jesus’s side with a spear, he specifically points out: “these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled... they will look on him whom they have pierced” (John 19:36-37), quoting exactly this verse in Zechariah. The one pierced is exactly Jesus Christ — the Son of God, God himself incarnate. He was pierced for our sin, thrust through for our transgressions; and what turns us to grieve, repent, and look upon him is not our own effort, but the “Spirit of grace and pleas for mercy” that God pours out — it is the Holy Spirit illuminating us, letting us see how deeply our sin wounded the Lord who gave his life for us, so that we mourn for him, and turn back to him.

This is exactly the center to which the whole Bible, and this whole story of redemption, points: a pierced Savior, and a company of sinners who look to him and are given life. The end of Zechariah further declares that on that day “the LORD will be king over all the earth... and the LORD will be one” (Zechariah 14:9) — that Lord who was once pierced, who humbly gave himself, will surely become King over all the earth, and his kingdom will fill the whole earth. This is exactly the endpoint of that thread running from Genesis to Revelation: the slain Lamb will sit upon the throne. Today, as you “look on the pierced” Lord, may the Spirit God pours out let you truly see: it was my sin that pierced him; and he was pierced in order to forgive, save, and win me back. Grieve, give thanks, fall prostrate, and follow for such a Savior — because this pierced Savior is exactly the Lord who will be King over all the earth.

Meditation: Do I truly “look on the pierced” Lord, seeing that it was my sin that pierced him, that thrust him through for my transgressions? Is what turns me to grieve, repent, and look upon him my own effort, or the “Spirit of grace and pleas for mercy” that God pours out? How does this Savior, once pierced, yet destined to be King over all the earth, move me to fall prostrate, give thanks, and follow?

Application: Today, quietly “look on the pierced” Christ (meditate on the cross in John 19); ask for the Spirit God gives, that you would truly see how your sin wounded the Lord who gave his life for you, and grieve and give thanks to him for it; and respond, with prostrate following, to this pierced Savior who will be King over all the earth.

Prayer: Pierced Lord, who will be King over all the earth, Zechariah prophesied five hundred years in advance: they will look on me, on him whom they have pierced. Thank you, Lord Jesus — the one pierced was actually God incarnate; you were thrust through for my sin, to forgive and win me back. Pour out the Spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, and let me truly see that it was my sin that pierced you, and for this grieve, give thanks, and fall prostrate before you. This pierced Savior, you will surely be King over all the earth; may I look to you and follow you all my life. In Jesus’s name I pray, Amen.
